If it is argued that there can be no cognition of absence without a locus (*dharmin*), then the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) must also be sought; for there is no cognition of absence without that either, nor is there a property (*dharma*).

If the cognition of absence could occur even without the counter-positive and the cognition thereof, why should it not likewise occur without the locus and the cognition thereof? If it could, then the cognition of absence would occur at all times. If it does not occur always, then it never occurs at all, since there is no distinction between the two cases.
If the cognition of absence were not qualified by the locus (*dharmī*) and the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*), it would not belong only to that [locus] and only to that [perceptible object];
rather, it would belong to everyone everywhere, precisely because it is unqualified. Or else, for this very reason, it would belong to no one anywhere at all.

But surely, the mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*) of everything everywhere is already accepted; how, then, can this fault be ours? Listen—the particularity (*viśeṣa*) such as mutual non-existence would not exist even if it were qualified. Therefore, it follows that whatever exists anywhere must be exactly like that [in being devoid of such particulars].
There would be something to be negated; and consequently, the erroneous notion of emptiness—that nothing exists anywhere—would follow.
If it is argued that such a negation is impossible, then the very impossibility of negation constitutes a fault; for because it is impossible, the negation itself could not occur. Therefore:

Because of the absence of a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) and other such factors, the non-existence of the Seer (*dṛk*) cannot be known. Furthermore, the non-existence of an object of knowledge (*meyasya*) whose existence is subject to doubt is itself an object of knowledge (*mānameya*). However, the Seer is not an object of knowledge and its existence is beyond doubt, precisely because it is self-luminous (*svayaṃprabha*). Therefore, there can be no non-existence of this [Seer].
It must be an object of knowledge (*meya*). Furthermore, that which is not self-luminous (*asvayaṃprabha*) cannot be established without a means of knowledge (*māna*).
And regarding self-luminosity, the fault has already been stated. Therefore, there is no absence of the seer (*dṛk*) in the seen (*dṛśya*), because of the lack of a means of knowledge.

It exists between the seer and the seen; therefore, because there is no absence of non-difference from the Seer, infinity is established in terms of space, time, and substance.
But in that case, would it not follow that there is non-difference between the seer and the seen, as well as their mutual identity?

Because they are of a mutually contradictory nature, like darkness and light, there can likewise be no cognition of their identity. Nor is there the relationship of attribute (*dharma*) and substrate (*dharmin*). The statement "it exists" implies a dual nature. Since each of those two natures must itself be either different or non-different [from the entity], there would be a dual nature for each of them as well;

thus, there is an infinite regress of natures upon natures. Likewise, if the possessor of natures is both different and non-different from its natures, then for each individual nature, two further distinct natures must be postulated. From those two...
And others [hold that] difference and non-difference are two distinct forms; thus, even for forms and their forms, there is no [end].

Because of the statement regarding being both different and non-different. In that case, how is this very state of being both different and non-different established for the two forms and the possessor of form, by virtue of which difference and non-difference belong to the forms?

The two internal [factors] are metaphorically designated as "possessing form" (*rūpavat*). First of all, the identity or difference between the two forms and that which possesses them is not direct, because such a consequence would apply elsewhere as well, and it is not desired.
Nor can identity and difference belonging to something else be metaphorically attributed there. How so? Not, first of all, those previously mentioned.

Difference and non-difference would have to be figuratively attributed to the two forms; from that figurative attribution, difference and non-difference would be established, and from their establishment, that figurative attribution would follow—thus there is the consequence of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*).
Furthermore, those two, difference and non-difference, [belong] to the two forms by means of two other forms; therefore, in the case of that figurative attribution...

Even that would not be established, because difference and non-difference cannot be established from the perspective of form alone.

And because that [distinction] is dependent upon it: even if it were established, nevertheless, the distinction and non-distinction of a form are established through its own two forms by means of those very two forms belonging to the possessor of form; not, however, by means of the possessor of form, according to the reasoning already stated. Therefore, the form—
In the position that for two material things there is difference in one form and non-difference in another,
this position is untenable because neither difference nor non-difference is established anywhere. If, however,

It might be so. If that which is the object of one cognition in a certain form is the same for another cognition in that very same form, then how could those two cognitions have multiple objects? Therefore, whether there is difference or non-difference between them, the object is one and the same. And the fault regarding these two positions has already been stated. Consequently, it is not manifold—
Form (*rūpa*) is sometimes perceived as one by some means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), or is established as such.
Therefore, if Brahman too were one, it would be rightly stated that it does not possess multiple forms.
Consequently, the claim that there is non-difference between the seer and the seen (*dṛg-dṛśya*) through the self-nature of Brahman is untenable, because the seer and the seen—
Because a single Brahman, through its two forms, is joined with multiplicity of form; likewise:

Since neither the seer nor the seen can logically possess multiple forms, it is unreasonable to claim that there is non-difference in the form of Brahman while there is difference in another form.
Furthermore, if the seer and the seen were not of the nature of Brahman, then Brahman would have to be distinct from them.
If it were distinct, defects such as birth, destruction, and non-Brahman-hood would necessarily follow, just as they do in the case of a jar or similar objects.
Moreover, [Brahman] would not be established because it would lack self-luminosity. If it were established [as distinct],...
It would be established merely as an object of perception; consequently, its difference from the class of perceptible things would be untenable.

Furthermore, if it were an object of perception, then like any other perceptible thing, neither its difference nor its non-difference from the perceiver could be established. Now, if—seeking to avoid this defect—one maintains that Brahman is indeed non-different [from the perceiver], even then, it is not [established].

It cannot be non-different from the two, because it is impossible for it to possess a dual nature. The fault mentioned applies if there is non-difference from the object seen. If, however, there is non-difference from the act of seeing, let that be so; in that case, no fault arises, provided that very [seeing] is Brahman; not otherwise, because it is logically impossible for a single entity to have multiple forms. Therefore—

There is not even a scent of non-difference between the seer (*dṛk*) and the seen (*dṛśya*). Therefore, the objection previously raised—that in the absence of difference between the seer and the seen, the threefold finitude inherent in the phenomenal world of the seen would also necessarily apply to the seer—is hereby refuted. Furthermore, how could the aforementioned defect apply to the seer if there were non-difference?

Even if there were a distinction, two forms do not exist for a single entity; therefore, it must be either the object of vision alone, or the seer alone. If it were the object of vision alone, even that would not appear. If it were the seer alone, then the object of vision would not appear at all; how then could the defects residing in the object of vision affect the seer?

Therefore, regarding the non-difference between the seer and the seen: if it were merely the seen, there would be no proof for it and it would be non-existent; thus, the defects of the seen do not apply to the seeing. If it were merely the seer, the seen would be absent, and thus the defects of the seen do not apply to the seeing. Even if the seer were different from the seen, the defects of the seen would still not apply to the seeing, as they are inherent [only] to themselves.

And because of the absence of defects, perception must be accepted by all as being indeed free from defect; for if even a defect were to exist, it would have to be perception itself, and thus it could not be a defect. Indeed, that very same thing cannot be its own defect.
I.
1] The impossibility of defining difference and so forth in any way whatsoever.

If there were otherness, there would be no relation between them; if there were both otherness and non-otherness, it is refuted by the impossibility of dual nature. Therefore, due to the absence of difference and so forth, even the slightest scent of defects such as birth and the like does not exist.
It is established that the vision does not approach [the object].

Furthermore—when these defects are examined through valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), they cannot even be conceived as existing in the object of perception (*dṛśya*); how much less could they exist in the Seer (*dṛk*) by virtue of a connection with it? For instance, the relationship of attribute and substrate (*dharmadharmibhāva*) is impossible whether there is difference or non-difference; and [the case of] both difference and non-difference is likewise untenable.

This is refuted. Therefore, since it is devoid of attributes (*adharmaka*), how could that which does not even touch qualities (*guṇa*) touch defects (*doṣa*)? Furthermore, if there were a difference in the entity itself, or if there were both difference and non-difference, then because each of those would require another difference, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Thus, [the distinction] is not established.
Someone might touch a real entity (*vastu*). However, if there is no difference [between the entity and its properties], then it is only one. And that is indeed the entity itself;

it is not merely the difference, because if the entity were absent, that [difference] would also be absent. If you say, "Let that very thing be the entity," then let it be so; nevertheless, it is still only a single entity. Furthermore, that is not perceptible, for its...
Because [the self] is dependent [on something else], non-duality cannot be established.
Therefore, it is consciousness alone, because its self-evidence establishes its oneness. Nor is oneness a property (dharma) of this [consciousness], as that would entail the aforementioned defects.
Therefore, a reality that is without differentiation and devoid of attributes is intended by the word "one.
The absence of the attribute of difference implies the negation of all other attributes, because they are dependent upon it.
For the mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*) belongs to two distinct things; therefore, in the absence of distinction, that [mutual non-existence] would not exist.
And for this reason, since the non-confusion of entities cannot be established, there would have to be only a single entity.

If one accepts the mutual absence (*itaretarābhāva*) of existents and non-existents, there is an infinite regress (*anavasthā*); if one does not accept it, the non-confusion of entities remains unestablished. Furthermore, without non-existence, the establishment of birth and so forth is impossible. Not...

If prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) were known, there would be certainty regarding the birth of something; for the mere sight of what was previously unseen does not establish its birth. Nor can the "sight of the unseen" be established unless non-perception itself is established. Therefore, in the absence of prior non-existence, there is no birth of either the visible object or its perception.
Existence. In the absence of birth, there could be no other modifications of existence either; for [all such changes] are preceded by birth. [Page 58, 24]
This is the accomplishment:
because they are not distinct from that, therefore the eternally immutable reality, which is always of a single nature, is self-evident.

Or rather, it is simply unestablished. Furthermore, because the two-fold nature [of cause and effect] is untenable: if it is unestablished, it is like a non-entity; if it is established, it is the very thing itself, and nothing else. Even if prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) were present, there is no arising of what is non-existent, just as with a rabbit's horn. Nor is there an origination that lacks an agent.

Because it is an action (*kriyā*), like the act of going (*gamana*). Nor can it be perceived as having an unestablished locus, because its locus is not seen. If it were inferable, then, like any other action, it would necessarily have an agent.
If its locus were already established, it would be fruitless; furthermore, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) regarding that which was previously non-existent.

If it is argued that there is birth, then birth itself must have a birth, because it did not exist previously. If it existed previously, then it would have existed even before that [birth], otherwise birth would possess independence. Furthermore, if there were a birth of birth, there would be an infinite regress. Therefore, what we call "birth" is nothing at all for anything.

We observe that [the faults] are logically established in consciousness. Likewise, when examined, destruction and the other [faults] also do not persist. Therefore, it has been well said: "Even in the visible object, these faults do not exist when examined;
how much less could they belong to the Seer through connection with that [object]?"

Therefore, it is established that experience is indeed infinite. If the phenomenal world (prapañca) is neither different from experience, nor non-different, nor both different and non-different, what then is its status? We shall explain that.

[Objection: Surely there is no experience without an experiencing self; therefore, how can it be infinite? [Reply: This is not a fault, because that very self is nothing other than that [experience]. How so? It is said:
If that [self] also has experience as its intrinsic nature, then there is no difference between them; otherwise, it would be non-existent.
The "Self" (ātman) is not the experiencer;
rather, it is the Self of that very [experiencer],
because of its infinity.

Alternatively—because it is infinite, that very [consciousness] is the Supreme Self, since its defining characteristic is fully present in it; and because if it were something else, that characteristic would be impossible. Therefore, due to its infinity, it is indeed that very [Self].

I. 1] The meaning of words that are not synonyms.
The Supreme Self. For this very reason, she is the embodiment of bliss (*ānanda-vigrahā*). The meaning is that bliss is her very nature; there is not even a scent of difference between the two.

If it is argued that a distinction between these two is logical—either because non-synonymous words are observed to have different meanings, or because the word "bliss" (ānanda) possesses a primary meaning—[we reply]: no, for there is a deviation [from this rule] in the case of the words "different" (bheda) and "the differentiator" (bhedī). For "the different pot" (bhinno ghaṭaḥ) and "pot" (ghaṭaḥ) are not synonyms.

This is because we also observe the expression "the cloth is divided. Nor does the word "divided" have a distinct referent, for if division itself were divided, there would be an infinite regress. For this very reason, since both difference and non-difference are non-different [from the object], the words for them—"divided" and "non-divided"—also have non-distinct referents, as in the case of the expressions "the jar is divided" and "the jar is non-divided. It is not so.

The term "non-difference" (*abheda*) is intended solely to exclude difference (*bheda*), being employed with the purpose of establishing identity of attributes; otherwise, the word "pot" alone would suffice, and the terms "difference" and "non-difference" would be unnecessary—following the maxim:
"It is better to avoid touching mud from afar than to wash it off."
According to this principle: likewise, in that very case, the two words "non-different" (abhinnau) and "pot" (ghaṭa) have a non-different meaning.

If non-difference were different from the pot, it would be a property (dharma) of it, like a cloth. If it were both different and non-different—if that non-difference were also something else—it would not be a property of the pot; and there would be an infinite regress.

Therefore, even the words "difference," "non-difference," and "pot" are non-synonymous yet have identical referents; it should be understood in this way here as well. If it is argued that, apart from the words for difference and non-difference, synonymous terms do not have identical referents, that is not so; for such identity of referent exists in the case of [words like] *prahṛṣṭa*— The final sentence fragment appears to be incomplete in the source text. If they were distinct, then excellence would be non-light; and if light is not distinct from it, then it would be non-light.

The sun is the form [of the Lord], because the sun consists solely of light. Now, one might object that heat is also a form of the sun. True; nevertheless, that is not the meaning of the word "excellence" (prakarṣa), for we also see the expression, "the moon is the most excellent light. Therefore, excellence and light do not [constitute the definition].

Because it is observed [to be so]. Furthermore, because it contradicts scripture (*āgama*). [Objection: One might raise the charge of contradiction with scripture only once the meaning of scripture has been ascertained. [Response: But the fact that the object of scripture is a non-dual reality has not yet been ascertained.

If it is argued that [the term "bliss" implies its opposite], that is not so; for [the nature of Brahman] is ascertained by the very words "endless" and so forth, and those terms do not tolerate any distinction. Furthermore, difference has been refuted by logical reasoning (*nyāya*). If it is then argued that, because it does not contradict non-difference, the meaning of the word "bliss" is suffering (*duḥkha*), that is not so.

Because the primary meaning must be accepted. Indeed, when the primary meaning is possible, a secondary meaning should not be adopted. Furthermore, the absence of suffering is established by those very words [such as "infinite"], and it does not require the word "bliss" (ānanda). If non-synonymous terms necessarily possess distinct meanings, then—

Since all the words contained in the statement of Brahman are not synonyms, Brahman would be described as having many distinctions. Now, if it should be argued that [the various terms] serve the purpose of excluding what is other—[then upon the exclusion of those others]...

Because it is a positive entity (*vastu*), it does not contradict non-difference; and since the word "bliss" (*ānanda*) also has the sense of the cessation of suffering (*duḥkha-nivṛtti*), it is not contradictory [to non-duality]. However, those words whose meaning is not cessation have distinct referents.
Therefore, even if the word "bliss" possesses its primary meaning, it is logically consistent for it to have the sense of the cessation of something else.
It does not possess the property of contradicting non-difference, like words such as "truth" (satya) and "knowledge" (jñāna). For instance, the Self—[page 61, I.
The meaning of the word is *vyānanda*.
[It is] bliss (*ānanda*), as in: "He understood that bliss is Brahman," and "From bliss..."

For from such scriptural passages as "From Him alone, indeed, these beings are born," it is understood that the words *brahman*, *ātman*, and *ānanda* have one and the same meaning. To illustrate: in the passage "From this very Self (*ātman*), ether was produced," the word *tat* (in the compound *tasmāt*) refers to *brahman*.

Having referred to the Brahman within one's own heart by the words "attains the Supreme," and having referred with the word "this" to that very same Brahman— which was characterized as "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, Infinite"— as being the object of knowledge through its nature as the inner self (pratyak) in the phrase "he who knows it hidden in the cave," [the text continues] in that very same [context].
Having employed the word "Self" (ātman) and demonstrated that this Self, which is Brahman, is the material cause of the universe,
and finally having stated by his own mouth the identity of Brahman and bliss in the words, "He understood that bliss is Brahman," [the text proceeds] with that bliss of Brahman: "From bliss alone..."
Because of the observation that "indeed, these beings are born" [from it], which shows the world's nature as its source,

and because of the perception of the identity between the previously mentioned bliss of the Brahman-Self, the oneness of Brahman, the Self, and bliss is firmly determined. In that regard, just as Brahman is distinct [from the world],...

For one who, through the delusion of "I" and "another," conceives of duality, the Śruti establishes oneness alone by eliminating the non-Brahman nature of the inner self and the non-self-nature of Brahman, [teaching] "I am Brahman."

It is taught as follows: when the difference between Brahman and the Self has been grasped by people through delusion, it is precisely that non-difference which is taught by the removal of such [delusion], and not even a scent of difference is touched upon. And this is just as [the distinction] between the space within a jar and the great space, or between the sun reflected in water and the sun in the sky, is resolved by the elimination of their perceived difference.

Non-difference alone is understood through such statements as "the space within a jar is the great space," and not difference characterized by mutual qualification and qualified status; this should be understood in the same way here as well.
Therefore, even if words such as "bliss" (ānanda) and so forth possess their primary meanings, there is no contradiction with non-difference.
The primary meaning should be accepted.
Now, an objection: the primary meaning of the word "bliss" (ānanda) is the pleasure born from the contact between the sense objects and the senses;
how could that be the very Self as described? It is not even a quality of it for you.
Attainment of the Desired Goal (iṣṭasiddhiḥ).

1] Because it is an object of cognition; and how could bliss—which is heard of as beginning with that of a sovereign of the earth and increasing by a hundredfold at each subsequent stage—be the Self? For it cannot be identical to that [Self].
If it is argued that bliss (*ānanda*) must be produced, and therefore would increase according to the excellence of its means,

and consequently the primary meaning [of "bliss"] cannot be accepted here, this is not a fault; for even though bliss is the very nature of the immutable Self (*kūṭasthātman*), it is regarded as being "produced" only through delusion, just like the experience itself.

Because this is established through logical consistency. For just as distinctions such as birth and destruction, difference, smallness and greatness, purity and impurity, and perceptibility are attributed to consciousness (*bodha*) due to a lack of discrimination regarding its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), and just as they are attributed to space (*ākāśa*), so too they are attributed to bliss (*ānanda*); thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever. To explain:

When a particular object is presented by virtuous karma (*śubhakarma*), and when a specific modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti*) arises from the contact of that sense-organ and becomes serene, the Self itself as bliss manifests— just as a face appears in a stainless mirror. That is what is called "the pleasure derived from an object" (*viṣayasukha*).

This is well-known in the world. Its manifoldness arises solely from the manifoldness of its own manifestors due to a lack of discrimination between them; it does not arise inherently, because it is of a single form. Now, since it is impossible for that which is of a single form and self-luminous not to be manifest, there can exist no other manifestor [of it].

True; nevertheless, it is as if unmanifested due to ignorance (*avidyā*). Therefore, we say that when something exists, that which makes it appear as if manifested is its manifestor. Consequently, when that [Self] is pure, the nature of bliss (*sukhātman*) shines forth; when it is impure, it does not shine forth, and it appears as if it were not bliss.

Just as the form of a face appears clearly in a pure mirror, but does not appear—or appears as if impure—in an impure one; even when the form appears, its purity does not appear, though it is non-different [from it]; and even when the differentiated [object] appears, its differentiation does not appear, though it is non-different [from it].

Thus, although bliss is non-different from the Self, it does not shine forth even when the Self shines; likewise, although it is not the non-Self, suffering appears as if it were an impurity of form. Therefore, the excellence of bliss arises solely from the excellence of the purity of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). Even though [the Self] is one, there is a progressive excellence, just as in the case of a jar—
This should be applied like the space within a gourd, the space of the sky, and the great space. And this being so,
O Śrotriya—
[page 63]
I.
1] The Self is of the nature of bliss.

Furthermore, the progressive increase of bliss by a hundredfold at each successive stage—heard in the passage beginning with "of him who is not overcome by desire"—is logically possible only on the basis of the excellence of being free from the impact of desire; it would not be so otherwise.
Therefore, the Self alone is bliss; otherwise, liberation would not be the supreme goal of human endeavor.

If it is argued that liberation is the goal of man because of the absence of suffering, then it would also follow that it is not the goal of man because of the absence of happiness. Liberation is accepted as the supreme goal of man, free from all defects;

yet, this being the case, it would not exist [as such a goal]. For if the self itself were happiness, then because it is eternally attained, [liberation would be nothing more than what is already possessed].

If it is argued that even for you there is no attainment of happiness, then, because there is no attainment of suffering, its cessation would also not occur. If it is argued that suffering is attained only through delusion and therefore its cessation is the human goal, [we reply] that happiness too is as if unattained; thus, its attainment [is likewise the goal].

The goal of man (*pumartha*) is like the recovery of gold that was forgotten but remained in one's hand. If the goal of man were merely the attainment of what has not yet been attained, then liberation (*mokṣa*) would not be a goal of man. For liberation is not something unattained that is then attained;
otherwise, it would follow that it is impermanent. Therefore, the Self alone is happiness. And because of its being dear, the Self alone [is the goal].

Happiness. For it is well known in the world that the self alone is dear; and the Śruti declares that the self alone is dear and nothing else, in such passages as, "This self is indeed dearer than a son," and so forth. Everything else is dear only because it serves the purpose of the self, but not by its own nature. But as for the self...

And the Śruti says, "Everything is dear for the sake of desire. Because everything is dear by virtue of being for the sake of the Self, the Self alone is dear; for if that [Self] were not dear, that which exists for its sake would not be dear. Nor is the Self dear as being for the sake of another, because it is not for the sake of anything else.
Because [the Self] is not for the sake of another, and because it is impossible for anything else to have the desire [for the Self] as its own object.

For a pot that exists for the sake of another is not seen to have that [other] as its own object. Even such statements as "clay is for the sake of a pot" are merely demonstrations of how the human goal [is achieved] through a means. Furthermore, even in the case of a man and a woman, it is only the body that exists for the sake of another, but not the Self.
Nor is pleasure established as something other than that [Self] for whose sake it exists;
therefore, because it has no other purpose and because it is dear, the Self alone is pleasure and nothing else.
For its dearness is logically possible only by virtue of having another [the Self] as its purpose. Therefore, the Self alone is pleasure. That for whose sake...
Of that,
The desired conclusion is established:
1] everything that is not for the sake of another is well-known as happiness; and that well-known status is not—
Since nothing exists other than the self, the self alone is happiness. Suffering, too, does not exist for the sake of another;
nevertheless, nothing is sought after or enjoined for its sake.
Weapons, the *śyena* sacrifice, and so forth, are undertaken either for the sake of the self's happiness or for the sake of avoiding suffering, and not for anything else.

It culminates in nothing but suffering. If it is argued that even the avoidance of suffering is not for the sake of anything else, we say no; for that [avoidance] is for the sake of happiness, as is observed in those afflicted by burdens and the like, who, upon the cessation of that [burden], experience the manifestation of the Self's own happiness uncolored by any particular object. Certainly; there are indeed infinite [ignorances], provided there are infinite cognitions of the mother-of-pearl. For if there were only one single ignorance of the mother-of-pearl, then it would be removed by that single cognition of the mother-of-pearl.

What is the use of other cognitions of mother-of-pearl? If those [other cognitions] do not remove ignorance, then they are useless. Or, if they are useful even though they do not remove ignorance—[as in the case of the cognition of mother-of-pearl]—then what of it?

[In that case,] those [subsequent cognitions] would likewise have been non-cognitions even previously; thus, the mother-of-pearl would always remain unknown.
Or, if the previous [cognition] was a remover [of ignorance], then the subsequent ones would be as well. [End of fragment]

From the remainder: if it is argued that the distinction is that those [subsequent cognitions] belong to one whose ignorance has already ceased, then for a person who has been born, once ignorance has ceased through the first cognition, all subsequent ones would necessarily be non-removers [of ignorance]. Or, if [it is argued that they function] in all cases...

Regarding objects— namely, those such as sound and so forth, which are distinct objects of knowledge for distinct cognitions— if ignorance must be removed simultaneously and all at once, then since an infinite number of ignorances would have to be removed by a single person, there would be multiple ignorances even with respect to a single object.

Since there is no fault whatsoever in accepting this, one must admit that all cognitions are indeed the subverters of ignorance, because they are indistinguishable in their having as their object an entity that was previously unknown. For an object is not always manifested by the very same cognition that first apprehended it; therefore—

If a distinction between cognitions is admitted, then a corresponding distinction between the ignorance to be removed by them must also be accepted; thus, since the effect of a particular ignorance—such as the appearance of silver—is not present when that ignorance is absent, there is no contradiction in its being the effect of that [specific] ignorance. [Objection: But if it does not appear because of the presence of ignorance, then upon the cognition of the mother-of-pearl...

Even when [the cognition] has arisen, it would not appear, because other instances of ignorance (ajñāna) would still exist there even in the absence of that one ignorance. Now, if the shell appears when those [other ignorances] are present despite the presence of [that specific] cognition,
and does not appear when that cognition is absent, then those [other ignorances] cannot be the cause of the non-appearance of the shell.

Because it appears even when that [knowledge] is absent; therefore, it does not appear by itself, owing to its insentience (*jaḍatva*). But when knowledge is present, it appears; in its absence, it does not appear by itself.
Therefore, knowledge alone is its illuminator; there is no such thing as "ignorance" (*ajñāna*) which could be its sublated object, nor is there that [sublating knowledge].

If it is argued that "something exists," that is not so; for in the absence of ignorance (*ajñāna*), there is an absence of the ignorant subject, which leads to the undesirable consequence of the non-existence of knowledge (*jñāna*) as well. Even though the shell (*śukti*) does not manifest by itself and thus its cognition is indeed its illuminator, nevertheless, in the absence of that cognition, [the shell...]

because it does not appear [as such], even for you, the absence of knowledge—which is what is to be removed by knowledge—is not non-existent. And if, despite the absence of knowledge being removed, [it persists]...

That [object] shines; it would have to shine even prior to the arising of knowledge. If it does not [shine then], it will not shine afterward either, because the absence of knowledge has not ceased. Now, if it should be argued that because knowledge is the cause of its shining, it shines when that [knowledge] exists, since there is no absence of a cause for its shining—[then... knowledge...

[The opponent claims: "Even when that [non-existence] has not ceased, there is no non-appearance of the entity; therefore, its [the cognition's] appearance does not cease. And [if it were] the mother-of-pearl, its manifestation would not be established because its status as a cause of cognition is unproven; thus, the cognition of it is unestablished.

If that is so, this applies equally to [the other] forms of ignorance (*ajñāna*) as well, since they too are not the cause for the non-manifestation of the mother-of-pearl.

If you say that ignorance is nothing other than the absence of knowledge, do not speak thus; for it is well known that there is a distinction between ignorance and its cessation, as expressed in such experiences as, "I did not know the mother-of-pearl, but now I know it," and "Ignorance has ceased, and I no longer know it."

If it is argued that this very ignorance is the absence of knowledge (*jñānābhāva*), that is not so; for absence is not an object of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Neither perception nor the means of valid cognition consisting of non-existence (*abhāva*) can cognize ignorance. Furthermore, because it is directly perceived (*aparokṣatvāt*).
Non-existence is not an object of knowledge (*jñeya*). Furthermore, non-existence, being a qualification of perception, is accessible through perceptual cognition.

The self (*ātman*), however, is not an object of perceptual cognition; for if it were, it would follow that it is non-self (*anātmatva*), like a jar or similar objects. Moreover, if it were an object of knowledge, it would be impossible for a single entity to simultaneously possess the status of both knower (*pramātṛ*) and object of knowledge (*prameya*). [This would require] another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*)—

And because it exists; for even in its existence, that very [Self] is the Self. Precisely for this reason, since the Self is not an object of knowledge (*aprameya*), its ignorance is not an object of knowledge even by means of the instrument of non-existence (*abhāvapramāṇa*).
Proponents of non-existence do not perceive non-existence without first cognizing the locus of existence.
[It appears] even so. If it is asked how that which is not a means of valid cognition (apramāṇa) appears, [the answer is: like silver.
For the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell does not appear by means of any valid cognition, because that would entail its being non-false.
Nevertheless, it appears. In the same way, ignorance also appears simply from experience. Thus it has been said.

This has been stated previously: if non-cognition is not the absence of a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇābhāva*), then let it be investigated what else that might be, provided there exists some other [entity] established by valid cognition (*prāmāṇika*). Nor does any other exist;
for the absence of cognition in the self is not an object of knowledge (*aprameya*), and elsewhere...

Because that [non-existence] does not exist. If it is argued that mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*) exists elsewhere as well, even that is not an object of cognition (*prameya*), because it is not an object of cognition for a cognition that is connected to its own self. Therefore, no absence of cognition whatsoever is established by valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇika*). Consequently, ignorance (*ajñāna*) itself is the absence of cognition.

If this is argued, let it be so; even then, there is no loss of the indeterminability (*anirvacanīyatva*) of ignorance (*ajñāna*), because the absence of knowledge cannot be established as non-existent since it is not accessible through the means of valid cognition that apprehend absences (*abhāvapramāṇa*). Furthermore, it is impossible to restrict the claim that every absence of knowledge is simply ignorance, for [there are] others—
Because antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) has both an object and a substratum, whereas ignorance (*ajñāna*) has the self alone as its substratum;

and because destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*) is held to be a product (*utpatti*), since there is no such cognition as "ignorance has arisen for me"; and because the cessation of ignorance is perceived, [it is not destruction].
And because there is no desire for cessation [of the series]. Now, it might be argued: "Since it possesses origination, destruction (pradhvaṃsa) is also a form of perishing;

for there is no origination of anything other than an entity (bhāva), and it is logical that an entity once originated should perish like a jar; therefore, each subsequent entity [is the destruction] of each preceding one."
Destruction is the prior non-existence of each subsequent thing; even then, [this remains the case].

9] Non-cognition is not of the nature of non-existence.

Since both absences possess the nature of being born (*janimattva*), and since ignorance (*ajñāna*) is not perceived therein, those two [absences] do not constitute ignorance. [Objection: But surely the birth of destruction is perceived in the thought, "knowledge has perished.
[Reply: Let it be so perceived; nevertheless, the birth of ignorance is not perceived, because of its prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*).
Because of [the nature of] cognition. For it is only the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of knowledge that appears, and not the non-existence of ignorance as well.

We shall later refute the position that the non-existence of knowledge is either another knowledge or a distinct entity. Therefore, ignorance is not the non-existence of knowledge. [Nor is it] destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*).

Even though it possesses an intrinsic nature (*svābhāvatva*), ignorance (*ajñāna*) is not [mere] non-existence because it is subject to origination and lacks cessation; whereas its opposite, knowledge, is so. Likewise, prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is also not ignorance, because, while being an absence of knowledge, it lacks the cognition of reality (*tattvapratīti*).
This must be so. Therefore, ignorance is not some kind of non-existence (*abhāva*).

If it is argued that no prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) other than [ignorance] is observed, and thus it is ignorance itself, do you then perceive destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*) as something distinct from it, or not? If not, then its status is exactly the same as that [of prior non-existence].

It will also belong to that [knowledge]. Surely, when one says "knowledge arose" or "knowledge perished," its destruction (pradhvaṃsa) is known. In that case, when one says "knowledge did not arise" or "knowledge will arise," its prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) is likewise indeed known. It is simply not clearly known.
If it is argued that destruction is also like this— wherein for one whose knowledge and its absence are indirect (parokṣa),
it is clear for one whose both are direct (pratyakṣa)—
then it has already been stated that for proponents of indirect knowledge, non-knowledge is not the absence of knowledge, because [non-knowledge] is immediate (aparokṣa).

If it is argued that one's own ignorance is the prior absence (*prāgabhāva*) of knowledge, because it ceases when knowledge arises, [we reply: even the prior absence of something other than that [ignorance] can logically cease upon the arising of knowledge, just as darkness ceases through the presence of a lamp. For the prior absence of a lamp is not itself darkness.
Nevertheless, even while existing, it brings that [object] to an end. But is it not the case that [this was already stated] previously regarding the lamp?
No; for—

If it is argued that darkness is simply the prior absence (*prāgabhāva*) of that [lamp], and therefore it is dispelled by it, that is not so; for even when the lamp has been produced and moves to another location, darkness is being dispelled at each respective place. Because of its momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*), the lamp, at each respective place, [dispels] its own prior—

If it is argued that [the lamp] arises by dispelling the darkness of its own existence, then for one remaining in that very place, there would be no production in subsequent moments because the darkness consisting of its own prior non-existence is absent; consequently, like a horn, the lamp would not arise even when oil, wick, and other factors are present, resulting in the cessation of its continuity. Otherwise, it would follow that darkness persists even when the wick is severed or the oil is exhausted. Therefore, darkness is not the antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of the lamp, nor is it its destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*), because moments [of darkness] are destroyed even in the absence of darkness. And how could it be the destruction of the illuminations of gems, the sun, and so forth?

Darkness would have to be either antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) or destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*). That non-existence which has as its locus the absence of light is indeed darkness.
If that non-existence were of all illuminations, it would not cease when all [illuminations] are absent;

nor would it appear when all are not remembered; nor when the substratum is not apprehended. And at the time of perceiving darkness, its substratum is neither apprehended nor remembered, as it has never been seen before. Nor...
For some, the perception of darkness appears to be preceded by the recollection of its counter-positive (the light).

Now, if darkness were merely the absence of a single light, then it would not cease even when other lights are present. Or, if each individual light were the absence of a specific corresponding darkness, then—

If, upon the presence of a single light, there were merely the cessation of its absence, then infinite darknesses would exist right there, because the lights such as lamps and the like, along with their respective absences, are infinite. Consequently, nothing at all would be illuminated, due to the abundance of obscurations. This would be the case even when a single light is present.

If it is argued that even though there is an absence of other illuminators therein—just as there is an absence of other cognitions when a single cognition exists—they do not obstruct the illumination of the object, and thus the object indeed shines forth; we say no, because it is not perceived in that way. Just as in this case, when an object is being known, [other] cognitions...
I. 9] Through knowledge, ignorance and its effects are burned away.
Just as darkness does not appear when an object is manifesting— whether there is a desire to burn it or not— so too,
darkness does not appear when an object is being illuminated by another light, even if one remembers a previous state of darkness.
Even when [objects] such as jars exist, their non-existences appear;
therefore, darkness is not the absence of light. Nevertheless, it is dispelled by that [light].
In the same way, knowledge is also capable of dispelling ignorance—even though ignorance is not an absence—by its mere presence.
Thus, it is established that nescience (ajñāna) is not the mere absence of knowledge.

And that is called "ignorance" (ajñāna) either because it is the opposite of knowledge (*jñāna*)— that is, by way of the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of knowledge— or else it is called by terms such as "māyā," being indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*) and insentient (*jaḍa*), even without such exclusion. In this context, "knowledge" (*jñāna*) refers to non-insentient consciousness (*bodha*) or its appearances.

The mental modification (*cittavṛtti*) whose object is real should be relied upon according to its application. Since the word "knowledge" (*jñāna*) is employed in both cases, one is the primary meaning and the other is the secondary (denoted) meaning. In that regard, when the cognition of mother-of-pearl arises, it removes the ignorance (*ajñāna*) concerning it; herein lies the mental modification—

Knowledge and ignorance are the causes of [the appearance of] form and so forth, and they are what is to be removed. Even in the expression "knowledge of Brahman," it is merely a modification of the intellect (*buddhi-vṛtti*) that, being illumined by the reflection of Brahman, is called "knowledge.
Similarly, "ignorance of Brahman" refers to *avidyā*, which is insentient in nature and serves as the material cause (*upādāna*) of all insentient things.

This is called "potency" (śakti). Although the knowledge of Brahman has ignorance as its body, it is accepted as being "knowledge" because its object is real and because it appears solely as Brahman; furthermore, it is held to be the sublater of that ignorance.
Its validity arises from the reality of its object, not from the intrinsic reality of the knowledge itself.

For it has been said: "Just as fire born from bamboo consumes that very bamboo along with its roots and then itself subsides—so too does the knowledge of Brahman, though born of ignorance, utterly burn away ignorance, and because it is of the same nature [as Brahman], it itself subsides. Or rather, Brahman alone, whose nature is non-inert consciousness, [is the knower].
Accompanied by the mental modification (*buddhi-vṛtti*) that appears as those [objects], one's own ignorance burns away its other effects;
having burned that modification as well, the One alone remains, just as when a king is present, all appear as his attendants.

[1.9] Just as one who, having captured a thief, strikes down all other thieves even if they are difficult to subdue, and having killed that thief, becomes secure; or as [a lamp] through the application of a wick and so forth, produces light alone— without taking up [the fuel].

Just as fire, while burning oil, ghee, and so forth, also burns the wick and other materials, so too ignorance—which is otherwise merely inert—may burn Brahman when conjoined with the modification of the intellect (*buddhi-vṛtti*). Likewise, elsewhere as well, it is consciousness (*bodha*) alone, when united with the intellect, that burns ignorance and its effects. By means of the intellect—

Because it is real (*satya*) therein, it is not combustible; therefore, it does not burn that [intellect]. Just as fire, when joined with wind, burns grass and the like but not the wind—because the latter is not combustible—so too either the intellect, illumined by consciousness (*bodha*), or consciousness residing in the intellect, burns ignorance (*ajñāna*).
The fire of knowledge burns away its own effects.

If it is objected that, just as with the ignorance regarding a mother-of-pearl shell, even when the ignorance regarding Brahman has been burnt away, it may arise again and again, leading to the consequence of non-liberation—that is not so;
for there is no possibility of the rebirth of ignorance once it has been burnt. Furthermore, ignorance is beginningless; therefore, it has no cause.
It exists; therefore, it has no birth, for nothing arises without a cause.

Thus, because ignorance—which is beginningless—is consumed by knowledge, and because nothing else is produced, liberation through knowledge is logically established. For even the ignorance regarding mother-of-pearl, once consumed, does not come into being again.
Because it would follow that [the ignorance] has not been burnt, and because it would contradict common experience (*pratyaya*). Nor does some other "unprecedented" (*apūrva*) thing arise;

rather, it is simply the beginningless ignorance that was previously not entirely burnt, because the mother-of-pearl (*śukti*) had not been fully manifested. For the mother-of-pearl does not exist at the very moment of its cognition.
Because that [ignorance] persists even at a later time, and because perception does not grasp a form connected to all times, the shell— possessing multiple forms revealed by multiple cognitions—
is not fully illuminated by each individual cognition; therefore, there is also ignorance regarding it.
It is logical that there is no cessation in its entirety. [Objection: If ignorance were to have parts, it would be an effect, like a jar;
if it did not, there would be either total cessation or total non-cessation.
[Reply: True; for this very reason, it is indefinable (anirvacanīya) by means of such categories as having parts or being partless.
I. 9] The validity of the means of knowledge with respect to Brahman.
We have said this: for instance—if ignorance were an effect, there would be an absence of bondage prior to liberation;
and for those already liberated, there would be bondage, which would entail the consequence of no liberation at all. Entirely—
If there were always cessation [of ignorance], the world would be eternally liberated; if there were no cessation, it would be eternally blind.

Therefore, [ignorance] is indeed indeterminable (*anirvācya*). Consequently, as long as any insentient object exists, its ignorance does not cease entirely. However, because Brahman lacks manifold forms, the knowledge of it [does lead to total liberation].

It indeed burns away ignorance entirely. For Brahman does not possess multiplicity of form either inherently—as a sword does—or as produced by time and so forth, according to both scripture and reasoning. Therefore, unlike the case of mother-of-pearl, no further knowledge need be sought regarding Brahman to reveal another form; it is self-evident.

And because it is luminous (*prakāśatva*), no residue of ignorance (*ajñānaśeṣa*) can be postulated. Furthermore, due to the absence of a cause for further cognition— since valid knowledge (*pramā*) and its other factors do not exist in the absence of ignorance as their cause—
and because there is no further cognition, just as in the case of mother-of-pearl (*śukti*), no residue of ignorance can be postulated.
Furthermore, if knowledge still exists, a corresponding residue of ignorance must be postulated.
If it is argued that the means of valid cognition is that which illuminates the object, whereas for another [means] there is merely the cessation of the object;
therefore, that [other means] approaches the object while it remains unilluminated— let it be so.

For even Brahman does not manifest [itself]. Therefore, that too must indeed depend upon a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). If so, then because it is insentient (*jaḍa*) like mother-of-pearl, there would be no cessation of all ignorance regarding it; but that is not the case, because it is self-luminous (*svayaṃprakāśa*). If so, then there is a contradiction.
If it is argued that what is self-luminous does not manifest, there is no contradiction. Even though consciousness is self-luminous, for some it does not exist and does not manifest;
and even those seeking the highest good (śreya) speak in that very way. Yet, it is not the case that it does not exist; nor...

And yet it does not manifest. In the very same way, Brahman also—though self-luminous and existent—does not exist and does not manifest for those who lack knowledge. Therefore, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is purposeful in that regard, just as the demonstration that consciousness (*saṃvitti*) manifests its own true nature is purposeful. [Regarding] consciousness—
If it is argued that the statement regarding the nature of taste and so forth is based on error, then even error is rooted in ignorance.
[The objection] that "it is established for those who desire it" is not valid; for them, that [object] does not manifest at all. Therefore, their statement is meaningful.
Therefore, for those who lack knowledge, there is no distinction between that which is insentient and that which is self-luminous.

For this very reason, the followers of Bārhhaspatya hold without distinction that "dharma does not exist" and "the Self does not exist. Consequently, even that which is self-luminous must indeed be illuminated by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

And since its non-manifestation is precisely ignorance, the very removal of that [ignorance] constitutes the instrument of knowledge's (pramāṇa) nature as a manifestor. Just as the removal of corporeal objects is itself the creation of space and so forth— because space is not an effect and because it was as if uncreated previously— so too [is the case with the Self].

Even light, because it was previously unilluminated and was as if non-illuminating, does not therefore become an object for that [light], even though the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) makes it known— just as a disciple, although making his teacher known,
does not make the teacher known to himself as he would a student, or as in other cases.

Furthermore, a servant does not speak to his master as he would to his own subordinate; therefore, even on this view that a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is merely an illuminator, its function of removing ignorance is established solely for the sake of its being an illuminator. But when it is indeed a remover [of ignorance], it follows by implication...
The established position is that it is "illumination"; in that case, its capacity to remove [ignorance] would be even more firmly established.
Furthermore, the authors of the Vākyas have stated: "It is established because it removes [ignorance].
Therefore, since Brahman lacks manifoldness and is self-luminous, in the knowledge of it—
It cannot be imagined that when [the knowledge of Brahman] has fully arisen, ignorance— the seed of transmigratory existence such as birth and so forth— is completely destroyed,

yet some seed of future birth and transmigratory existence remains, like the ignorance regarding mother-of-pearl which is the seed for [the perception of] silver; for such a thing is logically impossible.
Because there is a lack of valid means of cognition.

Surely, the fact that Brahman is of a single nature and self-luminous is not a reason for the impossibility of a residue of ignorance; for even prior to the arising of knowledge, that Brahman was exactly as it is. Nevertheless, that ignorance was complete [at that time]. Why, then, is there no residue of it at a later time?
It might be argued that this is because it is opposed to knowledge; but no, for even knowledge possesses a remainder.

The cessation of the ignorance regarding Brahman occurs without remainder.

If it is argued that only knowledge of an object removes ignorance—just as the knowledge of mother-of-pearl [removes the error of silver]—and not so self-luminous knowledge, we say no; for even in the case of a self-luminous result, [ignorance is removed].

Furthermore, even though that [Brahman] is self-luminous (*svayaṃprakāśa*), the delusion arises that it is born, perishes, and undergoes differentiation; for such is observed in the case of error. Nor does it possess any other form that is not self-luminous, as that would entail the loss of its self-luminosity. Therefore, even the knowledge of Brahman is accompanied by...

If it is argued that since [the knowledge] removes only the remainder of ignorance, there might again be saṃsāra, such as another birth, caused by that remainder, we say: no, because there is a lack of evidence.
For even though the knowledge of a self-luminous reality removes ignorance with a remainder, [it does not lead to further bondage].

Even so, we postulate that [residual ignorance] only as long as there exists a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the assumption of a remainder of ignorance; we do not, however, do so without such a means of valid cognition.
Therefore, even for one who directly experiences the state of being the Self that is Brahman, characterized by the aforementioned fullness—

As before, since there is no evidence for the continued existence of any residue of ignorance that could serve as a cause for another birth, his cycle of transmigration will not recur. However, prior to the aforementioned experience of Brahman as the Self, there was the cessation of ignorance within Brahman— which is self-luminous and constitutes one's own true nature.

It is accepted as occurring precisely in sequence. For this very reason, after proclaiming the nature of the Self—beginning with its existence and ending with its being the non-dual Brahman free from hunger and other such traits—the Veda provides arguments here and there to remove doubts regarding that [nature] and to eliminate contrary conceptions. Likewise:
Saying "That thou art, That thou art," he spoke nine times, dispelling each respective delusion;
and upon the cessation of all ignorance, [the text] says, "He understood it from him.
He proclaimed that hearing, reflection, and meditative concentration are the means for attaining direct vision.

He enjoins [practices] beginning with tranquility and self-control and ending with the renunciation of all actions; and he enjoins sacrifices and other rites for the purpose of realization by means of the purification of the mind (*sattva*). If the experience of the Brahman-Self could occur through mere hearing once, even without these means, [then such injunctions would be useless].

Through repeated practice, [the truth] becomes directly perceived (*aparokṣa*), because it is not seen in the case of things that are merely inferable and so forth.

Because its own establishment is dependent upon that [ignorance], the person is therefore the locus of ignorance. || 138 ||

If it were independent, then by virtue of that very independence, it would necessarily possess selfhood (*ātmatva*) just like the Self (*ātman*). Nor can there be independence for anything else, because the establishment of everything else is dependent upon the Self; for nothing else that is insentient (*jaḍa*) could be established without the non-insentient Self, since it is not established by itself. By itself—

And having smiled [at this], [we reply that] otherness and non-selfhood would not exist, just as [they do not exist] for the Self itself. If it is argued that even though that cognition is dependent upon the Self, its own nature (svarūpa) exists as something separate and independent—no; for it has already been stated that an insentient entity whose form is unknown is unestablished, whereas [the nature of] that whose form is known...

Furthermore, since there is no evidence for its being known by another [consciousness], its insentience (*jaḍatva*) is not established. Nor is it accepted that ignorance (*avidyā*) is non-insentient, because that would entail its being the Self (*ātman*). Moreover, if ignorance were independent, it could not be accessible through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because in that case, there would be no other ignorance [to perceive it], and thus no means of valid cognition could operate upon it.

Nor is it accessible through mere experience alone, because it does not have that [experience] as its substratum, just like a water-jar or other such objects. Therefore, since it is impossible for ignorance to exist independently or to have an insentient entity as its substratum—given that those who deny this are themselves denying [the very nature of ignorance]—the individual self (puruṣa) alone must be accepted as the substratum of ignorance. This is evident from such expressions as "I do not know," "I am ignorant," and "I am deluded."
And because it is well known that ignorance has the person as its locus. || 138 ||
Just as its ignorance is of such a nature, so too is its possession of that [ignorance] inherent;
for it has no capacity for knowledge, and its cessation is not like that of [ordinary] cognition. (138)
If it is argued: "If the soul's connection with ignorance were real, then transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) would be real;

if it were unreal, then the connection with ignorance would result from a further connection with another ignorance, leading thus to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*),"—this is not a fault. Just as ignorance does not [inherently] belong to the soul...

Form (rūpa) is neither different from nor non-different [from its substrate]; nor is it existent, nor non-existent, nor both existent and non-existent; rather, it is simply indefinable (anirvacanīya) by its very nature, and not due to another ignorance (avidyā). In this same way, the connection of the person (puruṣa) with ignorance should also be understood. [End of] Ignorance.
I. 140] The establishment of the self through knowledge.
206 Precisely because it is a relation; for it is not tenable that a relation with ignorance (*avidyā*) should be real.
If it were real, then because ignorance would also be real, its status as ignorance would be lost. Indeed, [ignorance] is not real—

A relationship between two things, whether real or unreal, is observed to be real. Furthermore, that which is real cannot be ignorance, because that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), because it lacks established status as such, and because it cannot be removed by knowledge (*vidyā*), just like the nature of the Self (*ātman*). Nor can there be the cessation of a real thing through any means whatsoever.
This has been stated more than once. Furthermore—when any other relation is examined, it too is found to be unreal, not only the relation between the Self and knowledge.
For instance, if the relation were non-different from the two related entities, then it would be those very entities themselves; thus, there would be no relation between them.

It would have to be so. If it were something else, then like the related entities themselves, the relation too could not be connected to those two without another relation; and if one were to postulate yet another relation, there would be an infinite regress.
Furthermore, a relation belongs to two things, not to a single one alone. And duality itself is rooted solely in ignorance. Therefore—
Knowledge alone is the connection for everything; therefore, no other connection need be sought for it.

Since there exists neither a person nor any other reality, there is no evidence for the reality of a connection with ignorance. Nor can the person himself be the connection, because of the absence of anything to which he could be connected.

Because it must be removed by knowledge (*vidyā*), because all means of valid cognition would otherwise be rendered futile, and because if it were not ignorance (*avidyā*) that is removed, there would follow the consequence of no liberation; therefore, the connection with ignorance is not real, but rather it is ignorance itself. 138.
Indeed, it has already been stated that a relation is not itself a relatum; therefore, ignorance alone cannot be its relation.
If it were so, why could the Self itself not be its relation? In that case, this [Self] would be real.

If it is argued that because the Self, whose nature is pure consciousness, is devoid of relations, and because any relation elsewhere consists essentially of ignorance (*avidyā*), therefore ignorance itself constitutes its relation—
then, in that case, ignorance does not belong to the Self, since the Self is free from attributes (*nirguṇa*). Nor does it belong to anything else.
Because it is undesirable and because it is illogical; for this very reason, it is not independent. Therefore, it is ignorance (avidyā).
210 It is difficult to establish.
The desired conclusion is established:
even the non-establishment of ignorance does not prove that [ignorance], because of that...

Whether independent or dependent, it does not cohere for you. If it is argued that ignorance is therefore resorted to on the strength of its established existence, and that it must be accepted in whatever way it can be made to cohere—that is not so; because:
The difficulty of being established is an ornament of ignorance, not a defect;
for how could that which appears in some way not be difficult to establish as ignorance? (140)

Ignorance (*avidyā*) does not simply not exist, for it is well-established. Nor is that establishment without a basis; like the establishment of knowledge (*vidyā*), it is rightly held to have a basis. If its basis were error (*bhrānti*), then ignorance is established, since it has already been stated that error cannot be established without it.
Furthermore, since knowledge (*vidyā*) is impossible in the absence of ignorance (*avidyā*), it would follow that all worldly transactions (*vyavahāra*) would cease to exist.

Therefore, ignorance does not not exist. Nor does it belong to anything other than the Self (*ātman*). But was it not stated that ignorance cannot belong to the Self either, because a relationship [between them] is impossible and thus its existence is untenable? No.

Just as in the expression "his connection," the genitive case is justified even without another relation—as in "his ignorance"—so too here. If it is argued that ignorance cannot belong to the Self in the absence of a relation, we say no; for its belonging to the Self is established just like the relation itself. If ignorance were dependent upon a relation...

It might be argued that [the relation] belongs to itself—[but] a relation does not possess its own nature through another relation, because that would lead to an infinite regress. In that case, if a relation does not belong to itself without another relation, then even ignorance (*avidyā*) would not belong to itself. Now, if a relation [does require] another relation...
Likewise, even without a self or what belongs to a self, no relation of ignorance need be sought,
because it does not depend on a relation, just like the relation itself. If a relation for that [ignorance] were to be sought—
[it would follow that] it is neither independent nor dependent.
