Even in the case of an insentient object, there is the production of ignorance.

If it were false, it would be nothing other than ignorance (avidyā), and thus there could be no connection between them; if it were real, it would be nothing other than the Self (ātman), and thus there could be no connection between them. For there is nothing real other than the Self, whether intrinsically or extrinsically.

And because that [self] is unestablished, the self cannot be the relation; for, like any other relation, it would depend on two substrata and would consequently result in being unreal. Indeed, no relation is ever seen to be real.
To say that a relation is both non-existent and real is a contradiction. Therefore, of all relations—

It is logical that ignorance belongs to the self alone as it is perceived [in its empirical state]. If ignorance were to belong to the self only insofar as it possesses a relation, then it would follow that ignorance belongs only to a self that is itself imagined. However, there can be no relation for an imagined self.
If that relation were perceivable, it would not belong to the self, just like the relation [of conjunction] with a jar or other objects.
If it were not cognizable, it could not be established. If it were self-luminous, it would be the Self itself.
Therefore, the Self is indeed devoid of all relations; otherwise, like a jar or other objects, it would be a non-Self.
Consequently, all its relations are merely imagined, like those of silver [in a shell] or like suffering and so forth; thus, they are rooted in ignorance (*avidyā*).
It is thus established that even the relationship [between the self and the body] has its very nature in ignorance (avidyā), and is not the true essence (svarūpa) of the Self.

As for what was said—that ignorance (*avidyā*) is difficult to reconcile—is that difficulty due to its being a real entity (*vastutva*) which cannot be established, or due to its being ignorance itself? If the difficulty pertains to its being a real entity, then that very difficulty is an ornament to it, not a defect. But if it pertains to its being ignorance—

And that is incorrect, because it is precisely due to the impossibility of its being a real entity (*vastutva*) that its being ignorance (*avidyātva*) is possible; furthermore, there is no lack of established proof, as in the case of a "man's horn. If its status as a real entity were possible, its being ignorance would be impossible, since ignorance is defined by its being something to be discarded through knowledge (*vidyā*).
Because it would otherwise be untenable, ignorance (avidyā) must indeed be established; therefore, it must be accepted in that very manner.
Consequently, it is proven that ignorance belongs to the Self alone and resides in the Self alone, and not in the non-Self nor in the non-Self. || 140 ||

One might object with the following nine verses that ignorance must be admitted even regarding the non-self (anātman), for the sake of removing ignorance concerning the self and for the sake of establishing the knowledge of sound and other objects which are the causes of that [self-knowledge], since otherwise such [knowledge] could not be established. The objection is stated as follows: 1. If there were no ignorance regarding the non-self, then the knowledge of sound and so forth would not exist; and if that did not exist, the knowledge of the self would not arise. Therefore, ignorance regarding the non-self must be accepted. 2. Furthermore, if one does not admit ignorance regarding the non-self, then the desire for liberation would be impossible, because the knowledge of the self cannot arise without the prior knowledge of its opposite. 3. Moreover, if one does not admit ignorance regarding the non-self, then the world’s engagement in action would be inexplicable, for activity proceeds from the notion of "I" and "mine," which presuppose the non-apprehension of the distinction between the self and the non-self. 4. Also, if one does not admit ignorance regarding the non-self, then the perception of diversity would be impossible, since the cognition of difference depends upon the failure to perceive the underlying unity of reality. 5. Furthermore, if one does not admit ignorance regarding the non-self, then the authority of the Vedas would be undermined, for the Vedic injunctions presuppose a subject who acts and attains results, which is only possible through the veil of ignorance. 6. Moreover, if one does not admit ignorance regarding the non-self, then the practice of yoga would be futile, since the dissolution of the mind's fluctuations cannot occur without first dissolving the identification with the body and the senses. 7. Also, if one does not admit ignorance regarding the non-self, then the experience of pleasure and pain would be inexplicable, for these are experienced by the self only when it is conditioned by the non-self. 8. Furthermore, if one does not admit ignorance regarding the non-self, then the process of transmigration would be impossible, as rebirth depends upon the persistence of the latent impressions of actions performed under the influence of ignorance. 9. Finally, if one does not admit ignorance regarding the non-self, then the very existence of the world would be untenable, for the world appears as a manifold only through the lens of ignorance. Thus, ignorance regarding the non-self must necessarily be accepted.
The proof of what is desired.
if ignorance regarding the non-self does not exist, what could it possibly do?
Since its own nature is unknown, that [ignorance] cannot destroy the state of being unknown.

If ignorance does not reside in the non-self, then the means of knowledge such as perception would be useless, because they would accomplish nothing. For it is not the case that [perception] destroys the "not-known-ness" of that [object], since that is its very nature; [otherwise] there would be a loss of its own nature. (141)
It does not produce cognizedness (jñātatā) for this [object], because that would contradict its own nature;
even if there were no contradiction, it would remain unknown even when that [cognizedness] is produced, just as before.

Precisely because its nature is contradictory [to knowledge], it cannot bring about its own state of being known— just as the whiteness of a coal [cannot do so] due to the contradiction with its nature. If, on the other hand, it were to produce something else called "the state of being known" without contradiction, then its own nature would remain unknwon, just like that of the coal.
If the effect is produced by another white-making [agent], then that means of knowledge is useless. || 142 ||
If cognizedness were produced by a means of knowledge, what would be the distinction between the means of knowledge and its object?
Furthermore, once something has been known by one person, it would always be known by everyone. (143)
If a modification called "cognizedness" (*jñātatā*) were produced in an insentient object by a means of knowledge (*māna*),
just as the state of being a jar (*ghaṭatā*) is produced in clay by an action (*kriyā*), then what would be the difference between action and the means of knowledge?
For an insentient object cannot attain immediacy through a modification inherent within itself, as a jar cannot bring about such immediacy for the clay.

If it is argued that [the result] is produced by the means of knowledge (*māna*), this cannot be so. For if [the result] were produced, then "knownness" (*jñātatva*) would likewise have to be produced by an action, just like a jar. Furthermore, if the means of knowledge were also a producer, it would necessarily be an action itself, just like the action of making a jar. If, on the other hand, the means of knowledge is not an action, then it must be accepted that its result is unproduced.
If an insentient object (*jaḍa*) were to become directly perceived (*aparokṣa*) by a person even through a modification inherent to itself, then—
just as its activity does not cease when its means of cognition (*māna*) perishes—
the insentient object, having been once known, would remain directly perceived even during deep sleep (*suṣupti*), because it continues to exist. And this would apply to all persons.

It might be [the case] that it belongs to no single person alone— because the particularity has entered into the very nature of the object of cognition— and because for men, [particularities exist] in every way.
Even in the case of an insentient object, there is the production of ignorance.
Because [the effect] exists; otherwise, not even a single one would exist. For it is not the case that what was produced by one [cause] belongs to others—

It would be a pot made of clay even if it were not produced by that [clay]; however, while ignorance (avidyā) persists, the cessation of that [ignorance] occurs for whomsoever and wherever it happens, and only for that person is that [object] directly perceived, not for anyone else, nor is anything else [perceived].
At the very moment of knowledge, inert ignorance ceases, just as [darkness ceases] at the very moment of the lamp.

[This is] darkness; therefore, there is no contingency of its being directly perceived during deep sleep and so forth. If it is argued that it is not logical for an insentient object to possess direct perceptibility merely through the cessation of ignorance, because it is insentient—[we reply:

no, for the direct perceptibility of an insentient object is well-established when a means of knowledge (māna) operates, and [this applies to] the means of knowledge which effects the cessation of ignorance.

Because its status as an effect is well-established, and because the operation of a means of knowledge (*māna*) upon the insentient (*jaḍa*) is well-known—since it is determined that the ignorance regarding that [insentient] is removed by the means of knowledge operating upon the insentient, its immediacy (*aparokṣya*) is established;
and it has already been stated that this [immediacy] is not produced by that [means of knowledge]. Nor is it the case that it does not exist at all.

Because it is well-known [that knowledge dispels ignorance]. Even while producing immediacy (*aparokṣya*), valid cognition (*māna*) certainly dispels ignorance regarding the insentient (*jaḍa*), for its power to dispel that [ignorance] is well-established; otherwise, it would not dispel it even in the case of the Self (*ātman*). In that case, since immediacy is established by itself (*svataḥsiddhi*), valid cognition would be useless. Furthermore, valid cognition does not [dispel ignorance] regarding the insentient.
There is not. || 143 ||
If the non-self is not cognized by perception and other means of knowledge, then those [scriptural] statements would be unestablished; and thus that self will certainly not be proven. (144)

Since there is no object [in the case] of the non-self and the immeasurable, perception and the other means of knowledge lack authority; therefore, because the Veda is not established, neither is the self established as something cognizable by it.
Since that which is born of the senses and so forth is not the self, it too is not cognized by that [self];
and because it is unestablished and unfit [to be known], the self also is not the cognition of that [object]. (145)
If it is argued that the object of perception and so forth is precisely that which is produced by the senses and so forth, or that the self is its object,
and therefore it is not without an object, nor is the self itself a non-means of valid cognition— this is not so.

Because it is non-self and because there is no difference [between them], even that which is produced by the senses and so forth is not its object of cognition. Therefore, since that [cognition] is unestablished and [the self] is unsuitable [as its object], the self also is not established by that means of valid cognition. || 145 ||
The Accomplishment of What is Desired.
If the self were an object of cognition through perception and other means, then the scripture would be purposeless;
for there would never be bondage due to ignorance, nor liberation from the knowledge of the self.
Therefore, the Self is not an object of cognition for sense-born perception and the like; nor is it a non-Self, because [it is the Self].
Thus, neither sense-born perception and the like, nor scripture, is a means of valid knowledge for establishing that which is other than the Self. (147)
If the self were indeed its own means of knowledge through the spontaneous cessation of ignorance,
then there would never be saṃsāra, nor would there ever be liberation.
The verses [numbered] 146–148 have clear meanings.
Therefore, if ignorance is called "self" for the sake of its removal through knowledge, then ignorance should be called "non-self" for the sake of establishing the knowledge of the non-self. (148)

If self-knowledge is desired for the purpose of removing ignorance regarding the self, then ignorance regarding that [self] must also be admitted for the sake of establishing the knowledge of non-self, such as sound and so forth, which is the cause of that [self-knowledge]; otherwise, it would be impossible. This is the summary of the point already stated. || 148 ||
Although I have spoken what is unsurpassed, it has not been understood by you;
therefore, I say again: it is established that ignorance is vain and is not the Self. (1.50)

I have stated more than once that even in the absence of ignorance regarding a non-self, the entire conventional usage of means of knowledge, objects of knowledge, and their results occurs solely through the ignorance of the Self, just as it does in the case of dream-objects and the like;
nevertheless, since you raise this objection out of ignorance, I shall state that same answer once again.
Listen—this much is already established: since non-sentient objects are insentient, there is no purpose for them to be veiled by ignorance;

therefore, ignorance would be useless with respect to them. Nor can the very operation of the means of valid cognition (*māna*) be the purpose, because that too lacks a further purpose. For it is not by that [operation]...

You yourself have stated that the direct realization (*aparokṣya*) is something produced (*janya*). Since that which is produced resides in the insentient (*jaḍa*), it is itself insentient; therefore, there is no distinction [between it and the world] by means of that [realization]. If it were visible, it would be insentient; if it were invisible, its production and so forth would be unestablished. Nor is the cessation of ignorance (*avidyā-nivṛtti*) the purpose [of such realization], for even upon the cessation of that [ignorance],...

155] Conclusion of the demonstration of the ignorance of the self.
Because there is no distinction in that which is insentient, [it is] ignorance.
Non-acceptance of the non-self is indeed superior, according to the maxim: "It is better to avoid touching mud from afar than to wash it off.
Nor can insentient matter possess ignorance in the same way as the self does.

It has been stated that there is no means of valid cognition [for its existence], nor is it an obscuring factor; therefore, it remains established that ignorance regarding non-selves is purposeless. || 150 ||
For this reason:
"Nor is it the case that even in the absence of ignorance (avidyā), there is a lack of established usage regarding means of knowledge (māna) and so forth;
for the usage of valid cognition (pramāṇa) also exists among them even when ignorance is present."
It would always have ignorance of the self as its sole cause, like a dream or other such states. (151)
For instance, that form which appears as silver in mother-of-pearl does not exist anywhere;
yet, although it is non-existent, it nevertheless appears through ignorance within the self. (152)

Just as things such as dreams and illusions appear with great clarity despite being utterly impossible [in reality], so too should it be accepted that every non-self appears without [the presence of] ignorance. (153)
Verses 151–153 have clear meanings.
The knower, the object of knowledge, and that ignorance—through knowledge, its destruction occurs;
this is eternally established, like a dream, even for one who does not investigate. 154.
And those established Vedic reasonings bring about the realization of one’s own Self;
nor is there any sublation of that realization, nor any defect in its cause.

But if this were so, since knowledge and ignorance do not exist in non-selves (anātman), your conventional discourse— such as "the non-dual phenomenal world produced by ignorance of the Self ceases through the knowledge of the Self, just as the serpent and other [errors] produced by ignorance of the rope cease through the knowledge of the rope"— would be entirely baseless.

Likewise, because of the absence of the knower, the knowable, and so forth; because the means of knowledge such as perception, the objects of knowledge, words, word-meanings, their relations, and cognition are not established;
and because verbal authority and the like are unestablished, [there is] the state of being beyond hearing and reflection.

The proof of what is desired.

If it is argued that this proposition— that liberation occurs through the cessation of the effects of ignorance regarding the Self upon the attainment of knowledge of the Self derived from scripture, since self-knowledge cannot arise independently of such means—

is likewise baseless, we say: no, because [the process] continues until there is awakening to the non-Self nature of sound and other objects, as well as to the ignorance of that, the knowledge of that, and the knower thereof.
For [the world] is established through ignorance alone, like a dream;
and because it is established that ignorance is removed by knowledge therein, and because the principles of verbal testimony and logic are well-known.

Because the knowledge of the Self arises from them without doubt, and because those [means] are merely imagined and thus lack any defect in their cause; for just as the true nature of a quality such as shortness or length is apprehended from that which is unreal, so too is the realization of the true Self attained from that which is unreal.

Furthermore, because there is no possibility of sublation for the knowledge of the Self— which removes all distinctions produced by the ignorance of the Self— just as the fear of a snake produced by ignorance regarding a rope is removed by the knowledge of the rope,
so too is the fear of saṃsāra produced by the ignorance of the Self removed by the knowledge of the Self.
We state quite correctly that liberation is possible and so forth; therefore, ignorance does not exist in the non-self, because all worldly transactions are established even in its absence.
Consequently, a means of knowledge directed toward an insentient object is not purposeful for dispelling ignorance, nor is it for [establishing] cognizedness (*jñātatā*).
It does not act by means of an action, because an insentient thing lacks excellence [through action], and that which is non-insentient is not something to be produced.
Nor does it remove its own state of being unknown, for that would entail the loss of its very nature. (154–155)
But with regard to the Self, it is not so. For:
Because ignorance is that which is to be removed, knowledge is purposeful with respect to the Self;
since ignorance is non-self, there is no injury to the Self when it is destroyed. (156)

Since the sole purpose of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is the cessation of ignorance regarding its own object of knowledge, and since such cessation is impossible in the case of insentient non-selves (*anātman*), while it is possible in the case of the Self— which is self-luminous and whose nature is infinite pure consciousness— it is that [Self] alone which is the fit object of the Veda.
Because its validity is possible, that alone is the meaning of the Śruti. Therefore, the non-conscious Pradhāna is not [the cause]; [it is not the Self-knowledge].
[Page 251]
156] The authority of the Vedāntas lies in non-dual Brahman. Atoms, non-existence, and the world of plurality consisting of the conscious and the unconscious as imagined by others [are not real].

Or else, Brahman is something other [than the individual self]—because in that case, the authority of scripture (*śruti*) would be impossible, as would that of perception and the other means of knowledge. Therefore, there is no suspicion of contradiction regarding the meaning of scripture, since those [other means of knowledge] do not have meanings that contradict it. Consequently, the inner self alone is the ultimate reality (*paramārthasatya*).
Since there is no other reality, it is established that this very person of the Upanishads is Brahman.

Furthermore, the statements concerning ritual action and meditation— which teach the means for attaining the desired and avoiding the undesired as conceived by one possessed of ignorance— belong only to the state of ignorance, just like perception and the other means of knowledge.

Just as in the state of dreaming, there is validity until awakening; thus, because it does not touch upon any object whose nature contradicts the reality known through the Vedānta, it is established that the Self alone is the object of correct valid cognition, and nothing else whatsoever. || 156 ||

The Second Chapter:

Because the manifestation of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell and similar instances cannot be accounted for by theories such as *anyathākhyāti* (misapprehension), etc., [the theory of *asatkhyāti* follows].

It is logical that this is merely the play (*vilāsa*) of ignorance (*avidyā*), which must be described; therefore, one has established that its cause is ignorance, accepted as *māyā*. Now, even if one accepts theories such as *anyathākhyāti* (misapprehension of something else), that [ignorance] must necessarily be accepted, just as it is when accepting *asatkhyāti* (the apprehension of the non-existent).
Demonstrating that otherwise those [theories] would not be established, he says:

"The three theories—anyathākhyāti (misapprehension), akhyāti (non-apprehension), and ātmakhyāti (self-apprehension)—these positions of satkhyāti (apprehension of the existent) are not established either without Māyā. (1)
Furthermore: "If you accept that error consists in the apprehension of something as other than what it is (anyathākhyāti), then let Māyā be accepted as its producer;
for even Māyā cannot be established without such an apprehension of one thing as another. (2)
How so?
Speak: how could that cognition of an object as otherwise be different [from error]? Is it that which presents an object otherwise, or that which itself becomes otherwise? (3)
In both cases, that [appearance] cannot be established without *māyā*. Just as the establishment of the nature of a non-existent thing,
its manifestation, and its manifestation in the form of an existent thing are impossible without *māyā*,
so too the transformation of an object and its manifestation as something else [are impossible without it].

And because it will be explained later that neither the proclamation [of one's own qualities], nor the manifestation [of them], nor the self-alteration [into another form] can be established without illusion (māyā). || 3 ||

7] It is impossible for an entity to undergo change.
In this regard:

when that "misapprehension as otherwise" (anyathākhyāti)—which is the cognition of an object as being other than what it actually is—is established, then all cognitions other than the cognition of the immutable Self are proven to be error. (4)
It is precisely my position that the cognition of the immutable Self alone is valid, while every cognition of a changing object is an error;
this is established with excellence because it is also accepted by you. || 4 ||
He states this [point]— that the cognition of a changing object is erroneous because both the change and its cognition are merely illusory (māyā):
"Furthermore, for you, the change of an object does not occur in that very same way."
If it were eternal, there would be no change because of its lack of distinction [from its prior state], due to its identity with that [prior] form; otherwise, it could not be so.
Just as it was before, so it is for your object; there is no alteration from its former state.
Otherwise, because there would be no distinction, and because it would exist eternally with a single form, there could be no alteration. || 5 ||
Even when there is the attainment of place, time, and causal conditions, [the self] remains exactly as it is;

Now, if it is held that, just as there is difference among all entities and Brahman, non-difference is also another attribute (dharmāntara) understood to exist—
just as taste exists in a colored object— then, while infinite entities exist, [the following applies]:

There is a contradiction with the scriptural text on absolute non-duality, "one only, without a second. If it is argued that there is no contradiction because the attribute of non-duality exists even when difference is present, then a jar would also be one and without a second; likewise, all entities would be so, since there is no distinction in their possessing the attribute of non-duality.

Therefore, there would be infinite non-dualities, and those would each be Brahmas; nor could there be only one Brahman, because there is no distinguishing characteristic [to differentiate them]. If it is argued that a jar and so forth do not have non-difference from everything—[we reply: no, because they are non-different from Brahman, which is non-different from everything. By the very property of non-difference, Brahman itself is also non-different. That...

And it must be one and the same for all; otherwise, non-difference would not be established even by that [non-difference]. Now, if Brahman were non-different from non-difference itself—which is distinct [from Brahman]—then let all things be so. But you do not desire that. Therefore, the Śruti teaches non-difference only by means of the complete sublation of all difference.

Otherwise, it would either be non-measurable or it would be something being measured; yet no such action appears from it. Therefore, Brahman is neither different nor non-different [from itself], due to the absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

[II.

76] Furthermore, the distinction of action is not established as something other than that [distinction of the agent], nor is it accessible through scripture in the same way as the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman. Therefore, the understanding of the distinction of action occurs solely through the distinction well-known in the world.

Nor can difference be apprehended even by means of sense-perception (*akṣaja*) and the like; for as long as difference is unestablished, the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is unestablished, and without that, non-difference cannot be understood. Even if the difference in the object of cognition (*meyabheda*) were apprehended by those [means], the difference in the cognizer (*mātṛ*), the instrument of cognition (*māna*), and so forth, would not be apprehended by them, because the cognizer and the instrument are themselves not objects of cognition (*ameyatva*). As for that [difference] as well, it is [apprehended by] the instrument...

If there were a separate object of knowledge (*meyatva*), there would be an infinite regress of means of knowledge (*māna*) and so forth; therefore, just as there is no distinction among the means of knowledge, there is likewise no distinction among the objects of knowledge.

Consequently, there is no difference between clay and the jar either. No one perceives a jar as something other than the clay—just as one does not perceive a cloth [as other than its material]—but rather [perceives it] as having the very form of clay. Therefore, there is no [difference between] clay and the jar.

The illustrative example possesses both difference and non-difference; however, it is indeed non-different. This is because of the scriptural text concerning "the beginning of speech" (*vācārambhaṇa*).

Therefore, there is neither difference nor non-difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman, nor between the world and Brahman. If that which is non-different from Brahman were nonetheless different from it, then Brahman itself would be inherently different; thus, [all distinctions would follow].

Since each [particular] is Brahman, there would have to be infinite Brahmans. Nor is it logical to say that one particular is Brahman and another is not, because there is no distinction among the particulars in their being Brahman; thus, either all are Brahman, or none at all. All particulars are subsumed within the one Brahman, not within each individual one.
If this is so—then there is nothing whatsoever distinct from Brahman, because everything is non-different from Brahman and is therefore Brahman itself.
Nor is there mutual difference among its parts; for indeed—
That very thing would then be its own part. If it were so, there would be only a single part, and thus no distinction of parts at all.
Therefore, nothing can be both different and non-different from anything else. 76.

Furthermore, you should be asked this: regarding the two—the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman—for which you maintain a state of being both different and non-different, what is their essential nature? Is it consciousness alone, or consciousness itself [as distinct from its substrate], or both, or is one of them of the nature of consciousness? Regarding the first alternative:
If Brahman is indeed pure consciousness alone, then it is already attained in its nature as the Self;
since its form is pure consciousness, how could there be any differentiation within that state of pure consciousness? (77)

If those two were of the nature of the unconscious, they could not indeed possess the nature of Brahman;
if they were of the nature of consciousness, there could be no portion of insentience, nor could there be a portion of consciousness in the born.

If those two were of the nature of non-consciousness (*acit*), then, like a jar, there would be no selfhood, status as a witness, or desire for liberation in the individual soul (*jīva*), nor would there be Brahman-hood, omniscience, or the status of being the creator of all in Brahman. If they were of the nature of consciousness (*cit*), then non-consciousness would not belong to them; nor, if they were of the nature of non-consciousness, could consciousness belong to them. For a jar [is not conscious].

The seer is seen as a portion [of the Seer]; nor is there consciousness (cit) belonging to the jar. Likewise, even though both are of the nature of non-consciousness (acid-rūpa), there is no relationship of part and whole between them. Therefore, since no other alternative is possible, both must be of the nature of consciousness (cid-rūpa); thus, there is neither difference nor non-attainment. If they were of the nature of both consciousness and non-consciousness, there would be no difference between them.

Like that of a jar and its perceiver, there is neither difference nor non-difference between the Supreme and the individual soul (*jīva*). Likewise, it is so between the world and Brahman; for if they were of the nature of consciousness (*cit*) and unconsciousness (*acit*), non-difference would be impossible. (77–78)

If it is maintained that the world is not the form of Brahman and is therefore to be known as an object, then indeed, in every case here, the object of knowledge is observed to be distinct from the knower. (78)

If the manifold of ether and so forth, as well as the individual souls (*jīvas*), were objects of knowledge for Brahman, then— due to the difference between them and Brahman and the consequent absence of non-difference— neither their identity with nor their being parts of Brahman could be established as you desire, just as in the case of a jar and its perceiver.
For a jar is neither the seer nor a part of form.

If [the world] were like the phenomenal expansion (*prapañca*), then since individual souls (*jīvas*) would likewise be parts of that [Brahman], they would not possess qualities such as ignorance, suffering, or the desire for liberation; furthermore, they would be effects, just like the phenomenal expansion. In that case—

Bondage and liberation belong to Brahman alone, or else they belong to no one at all. If these states are unknowable, they remain unestablished; furthermore, you would lose Brahman’s omniscience. And if Brahman were knowable by the individual soul (jīva), then because of [Brahman’s] ignorance, qualities such as omniscience would not be established, and thus Brahman-hood itself would not be established for the soul.

Furthermore, there would be difference from that [the knower] and its unknowability. Since both the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman are objects of knowledge, it is impossible for them to know one another—just as a pot and a cloth cannot—and it is impossible for them to know themselves. Therefore, one must admit a knower other than those two who is himself not an object of knowledge; in that case, he alone is the Self (*ātman*).

This is because of such scriptural passages as "His thought... and so forth. Because of existence. || 79 ||

If every object, such as ether and the rest, were non-different from Brahman, then because the relationship of action and agent would be impossible— since [Brahman] would both know and perform everything— it would follow that omniscience, omnipotence, and so forth,
could not exist. To this, he says:
If everything were Brahman, then that which is to be known would not remain;
for since it would be exhausted by being the object of knowledge, there would be no objectivity in its state as the knower.

Likewise, even in its state as a knower (*veditṛtva*), it would be exhausted in that very same way; therefore, there is no state of being an object of knowledge for it. Consequently, this...

If that which is known by him exists—
The state of being Brahmā has been explained. || 80 ||
If Brahman were both the knower and the object of knowledge, then there would be two Brahmans.
If that single Brahman were both, then it would be neither the object of knowledge nor the knower.
If Brahman were both the object of knowledge and the knower, there would be two Brahmans. If this [Brahman] is a single, unified entity—then it is neither the object of knowledge nor the knower. 81.

Because one would be omniscient by virtue of knowing only a single portion, even one who knows nothing at all would be omniscient.

If the world were born from Brahman as something distinct from Him, it would not be Brahman,

because it is impossible for a single entity to be both the produced and the producer; for one and the same thing cannot simultaneously or successively be both the object and the agent of an action— nor can that which is unestablished be an agent, nor can that which is already established [be so].

Because it has been stated that [Brahman] is the effect; if the world were also denotable by the word "Brahman," then there would be two Brahmans. If it is argued that this [collective] is the appropriate Brahman and not each individual part—then, since the world exists when Brahman exists, there is no birth of it; and when the world does not exist...

Because Brahman does not exist, there can be no birth of this [world] from it. If it is argued that although the full Brahman did not exist prior to the birth of the world, its birth from it is possible because of the existence of a portion (aṃśa) of it—[we reply: no, for in the absence of the whole (aṃśin), its parts cannot exist. And if the birth of the world establishes the existence of the whole Brahman, then that [existence] too—

It is precisely the state of being an effect. If it were already established beforehand, the world could not be established later, just as a part of that which is already established cannot be so established. Nor is Brahman itself a part of it; for if it were, there would be only one part, because its oneness has already been stated. Therefore, even between these two parts, there can be no relationship of cause and effect.
Because it is impossible for that [effect] to have Brahman as its cause; for if that effect were real, Brahman would cease to be Brahman.

Since Brahman is immutable and non-dual, it would lack the previously stated definition, resulting in the loss of its status as Brahman. Therefore, those who desire to maintain Brahman as it has been described must [accept that] its effect is...

Furthermore, the distinction between the world and the individual soul must be accepted as being merely constructed by ignorance (*avidyā*); otherwise, the scripture would lack authority, and bondage and liberation would be impossible. (83–84)

85] If Brahman were possessed of conceptual proliferation (saprapañca), and the embodied soul were a minute atom that is a portion of Brahman, how could he be directly Brahman? A drop of water cannot become the great ocean. ||85||

since its destruction occurs through knowledge alone, tell me then, what is the role of ritual action in that? (91)

nor is its destruction brought about by cognition alone, but rather through the separation from its limiting adjunct.

Thus, although being Brahman itself, the individual soul (jīva), through its limited mind, appears distinct from the Supreme; and being afflicted by suffering, it attains the Highest through the two paths of knowledge and action. 84.

"Surely it should be said that [the distinction] exists in the individual soul (jīva), but not in the Supreme (para). He states that very infinite regress: "When a primary mental affliction (*ādhi*) belonging to a living being who already possesses another affliction occurs, that prior affliction cannot exist without [another] affliction; thus there is no finality. (68)

Therefore, since there is an application of the Supreme alone to the entirety [of the individual] through the abandonment of parts, what difference could there be, and from what source? Thus, the individual soul (jīva) would be one with the Supreme (para).

because even when there is a distinction of presiding deities, since [the soul] is partless, it is the whole [soul] alone that is joined with those presiding deities. Furthermore, if there were a contradiction [between them], the postulation of multiple [souls] would be futile. (100)

If it is argued that even for the partless Brahman there is a distinction [of parts] due to limiting adjuncts (upādhi), like that of space, then it follows that such distinction is merely illusory. || 101 ||
For it is said:

Likewise, if there were any difference from Brahman, that would be a failure to attain Brahman due to ignorance. (102)

That which is superimposed by ignorance would not perish through action alone, but rather through knowledge;

It is said: "If the form of Brahman were the substrate (adhiṣṭhāna), then upon its destruction, the destruction of Brahman would also follow; otherwise, its destruction could not occur. (10.06)
How so?

for, due to their non-difference, the power does not perish without the destruction of the possessor of power. (107)

Even though the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) perishes when Brahman perishes, nevertheless—if another limiting adjunct exists even when one limiting adjunct has been destroyed—then the consequence would be the absence of liberation; if that [other adjunct] were absent, there would be the destruction of the world. Furthermore, in the world, when the substrate—the gem or similar object—is not perceived, no distinction based on an adjunct (aupādhika-bheda) is observed between it and its adjuncts such as lac-dye. and even if it were not of the nature of the visible, Brahman itself remains invisible. Therefore, its distinction based on an adjunct is likewise impossible.

II. 114] It is impossible for the self to undergo change into something other than itself.
Therefore, even the difference between the Supreme and the individual soul is merely due to limiting adjuncts and is nothing but ignorance;
for even a difference based on such adjuncts is false because it is a form of difference, just like the difference between [imagined] selves.
And because there is no difference in their being of the nature of Brahman, even for those who maintain that the individual soul (jīva) is subject to destruction. || 111 ||
If the limiting adjunct (upādhi) is the form of Brahman and its differentiation exists by itself, then why,
even though the individual soul (jīva) is identical with Brahman, does its differentiation not also exist by itself? 112.

If, even though the affliction (*ādhi*) is of the nature of Brahman, its difference were intrinsic rather than adventitious (*aupādhika*), then the same would apply to the individual soul (*jīva*): even though it is identical with Brahman, its difference [from Brahman] would be intrinsic. Therefore, just like the difference between individual souls, the difference between afflictions is false; or else, just like the difference between afflictions, the difference between individual souls is real.
It would not be so; duality of form cannot be established, because there is no distinction in their being the very nature of Brahman.

Therefore, he concludes: "The self is not different from itself by its own nature, nor from anything else, nor even through limiting adjuncts (upādhi).

Furthermore, the absence of the apprehender (*graha-abhāva*) cannot be accepted because it would contradict your own statement that "existence and its non-existence do not coexist," since you maintain the non-coexistence of the apprehender and the apprehended. Thinking that by stating, "And because there is no negation of non-distinction, the non-duality of the mother-of-pearl would follow as a consequence," the opponent—

And because it is accepted in worldly transactions that "this is not here" or "this is not that," it exists.
Therefore, do not reproach us alone, for you too are equal in this fault.
Do not think thus: "This [cognition] brings about the apprehension of an object of knowledge that has been offered by me;

Do not think that we are equally at fault; for by me, ignorance alone is accepted as the cause of duality, and knowledge utterly consumes it along with its body. Therefore—

This is for the sake of establishing duality, not for the sake of negating it. For as long as ignorance remains unburnt, it causes even the impossible to appear possible. Therefore, all worldly transaction—whether mundane or Vedic, including error regarding mother-of-pearl and the like, as well as within the Self, and the sublation thereof—is entirely consistent for me.
But it is established that for others there is nothing at all. || 76 ||

For them, there would be no association between teacher and disciple. One who is not deluded would not see the teacher or the disciple as deluded or suffering. Nor is there association with the unseen; nor is the teacher possessed of ignorance (*avidyā*);

[The opponent argues: "It is [only] by way of instruction from you, and not through even a trace of ignorance. And that [knowledge] would dispel the error. Error does not arise from non-apprehension due to its absence, but rather from the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of a previous error; from that impression, a subsequent error arises; from that, a distinction—

Nor does it arise from insentience (*jaḍatva*), because, like a jar, it would not be born from that [Self]. Furthermore, there is no birth for that which is non-insentient (*ajaḍa*). Nor does it arise from ignorance (*ajñāna*), because that would entail the loss of its reality (*sattva*); for silver and the like, which are born from that [ignorance], lack true existence. And if they were born from that [ignorance], they would simply be of the same nature as it.

It would [not] exist, because in the absence of an inherent nature (*prakṛti*), there is an absence of an effect. Nor does birth occur from that which is existent by way of its own self, nor from that which is non-existent by way of its own self, as in the case of a self; nor from that which is non-existent, like a hare’s horn.
Furthermore, nothing else whatsoever has been seen to become void through birth. Therefore—

The birth of that which is expressible occurs through its very own nature, just like silver and the like; therefore, everything that possesses birth is born of ignorance (*ajñāna*). Consequently, if the destruction of ignorance were also born of ignorance, it would have that [ignorance] as its essence and would exist within that very [ignorance], resulting in the non-removal of ignorance. This is not the case.

Rather, it is simply the destruction of that [ignorance], because everything must be desired by means of it; otherwise, all worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) would be annihilated. Therefore, the destruction of ignorance is neither the birth of another entity, nor is it anything else whatsoever, nor is it that very ignorance itself.

Because that would entail the loss of its very nature as destruction. Nor is it something else—if that were also of that same [nature], it would perish along with it; nor has it been stated that there is any other knower. Therefore, there is neither the reality of duality nor the existence of knowledge.

If it is held that the cessation of ignorance is not some thing other than the Self—whether it be insentient, sentient, eternal, non-eternal, non-existent, existent, or otherwise indescribable—then let the Self itself be the cessation of ignorance. If this is so, then even thus, that which I desire is established; for it is the Self alone.
If it is argued that because it always exists, there is an absence of bondage at that very time, then [it follows that] another [state must exist].

The cessation of ignorance [is established] even in the Veda; otherwise, there would be the total collapse of all conventional usage based on valid means of knowledge. Therefore...

It is not logical that the birth of anything should be the burning away of ignorance. As for what was said—that the very birth of another entity is the destruction of the prior entity—let this be so in the case of [positive] entities (*bhāva*).
However, it has been stated that ignorance is neither an entity nor a non-entity; therefore, its "burning away" is not the birth of an entity.

Nor is it well-known or logical that there is either its burning or the birth of this indefinable [ignorance]. Furthermore, it is not observed that a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) acts as the agent of something other than the removal of ignorance—just as a hammer is seen to be the agent of potsherds rather than the remover of the pot. Nor is this logical, because [the means of cognition] is not itself ignorance.

By way of a corollary: therefore, that which is indeterminable (*anirvācya*) cannot be both existent and produced by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, the non-produced nature of consciousness (*saṃvit*) has already been stated.
Consequently, the destruction of ignorance (*ajñāna*) is indeed a destruction itself, not the birth of something else.
And how could destruction possess a cause if it were the birth of another entity?

Not otherwise. If it is argued that because there is no causal operation upon non-existence, the destruction of that [non-existence] is indeed existence itself, then there is no birth of a previously non-existent distinct entity, because there is no causal operation upon what is non-existent. Nor is there [destruction] of what is existent, precisely because it already exists.

Because there is no causal function [of the cause]; otherwise, there would be no cessation of the cause. If, moreover, one thing were to arise while the causal operation pertains to something else, then even destruction would occur in that same way. How could that non-existence come into being? For that which is non-existent has no agency of becoming. If that is so, then [the effect] must be another entity.
That which is previously non-existent would [then] come into being; for even that which has already become existent is not held to undergo becoming.

If it is argued that there is no contradiction between an existent thing and a non-existent non-existence, then because there is likewise no contradiction between a previously non-existent thing and existence, non-existence itself would be existence; thus, there is no arising of the non-existent. Nor...

Because it exists as reality (*tattva*), there would be no arising of another entity. If there were a contradiction between one entity and another entity, then when that one entity exists, all other entities would not exist, because there is no distinction [between them]. Furthermore, even that [one entity] would not exist, due to the contradiction with its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

If it is argued that contradiction is with another [entity] and not with itself, then, because of being "other," there would be contradiction even with non-existence (*abhāva*), since it is other [than existence], rather than because of being an entity (*bhāvatva*).
The proof of what is desired.

If it is argued that non-existence cannot be something other [than existence] because it lacks being, then neither can existence be other than itself, for that would entail the consequence of self-difference. Therefore, if birth is accepted as real, then destruction must also be accepted as something distinct;
it cannot be the case that the very same birth is the destruction of another, because both are well-established by experience and by reasoning.

Because they are equal [in this respect]. Therefore, the destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) of an entity is not another entity; likewise for prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*). Consequently, there can be the destruction of one thing even without the birth of another. Because it is a non-entity, destruction is not something produced. If one were to admit the birth and destruction of that [destruction] as well—
"And because of the lack of stability: for an entity, cessation is indeed [the same as] non-existence.

Even without birth, its possession of a cause and its occasional occurrence would be like that of birth; for there is no such thing as the birth of birth, nor is it without a cause. Nor are birth and destruction different [from the entity itself]."
It cannot be restricted by the argument that they must exist together because it is observed so;

for there is no reason for their mutual dependence according to the reasoning already stated. Even if, in the case of produced things such as jars, destruction occurs simultaneously with another birth—that is, as that very other birth—[it does not follow that destruction and existence are inherently linked].

Even so, the destruction of that which is beginningless is likewise [impossible]. Since it is impossible for jars and other products of clay to coexist with that [destruction], their destruction would be of that nature;
and the same applies to the products of gold and the like. However, that which is beginningless, being without a cause, does not [undergo destruction].

It is logical that destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) has such a nature [of being produced]. If it is argued that only things with a beginning are seen to have destruction, and not things without a beginning—this is true; however, the destruction of an entity without a beginning is not logical, as in the case of the Self (*ātman*), nor is it observed.

It has been observed. Nevertheless, because ignorance is indeterminable (anirvācya), its destruction is accepted by all, even though it is beginningless; otherwise, the means of valid cognition would be rendered fruitless.
Therefore—
Even though the burning of leaves occurs in another birth, the burning of beginningless ignorance does not occur in another birth;
thus it is established that [ignorance] exists either by itself or together with that [burning].

The means of accomplishment (sādhaka) is to be stated:
it is the cessation of ignorance (avidyānivṛtti).
If it is argued that because all worldly transactions cease upon the arising of the knowledge of the non-dual Self, that [Self] cannot be demonstrated, even so,
having demonstrated it in the world, apply it to the Self; for even in the world, it is accepted by you.

Otherwise, that [cognition] would not be established. It is said: [The object] is known either as the object itself or as its cognition; this is the abandonment of its non-cognition. Nor is that [abandonment] unestablished, nor is it established by a means of knowledge (*māna*), because that would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Furthermore, an "object known" is not something other than an "unknown" object. Nevertheless, it is not [the case that...].
It is not known prior to the arising of the means of knowledge (*māna*), nor is it unknown after [the means of knowledge has arisen], because the means of knowledge would then be fruitless.

Furthermore, being known or unknown is not the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of the object, because that would involve logical inconsistency (*vyabhicāra*) and because the means of knowledge would be fruitless; otherwise, the state of being unknown would not be abandoned by the means of knowledge. And these...

Because of the loss of the object; for even "knownness" is unestablished by means of a pramāṇa, since it is already established, otherwise the object itself would not be established. Nor is an unestablished object the effect of a pramāṇa, nor is an established object that which is destroyed by a pramāṇa. If the pramāṇa were to produce or destroy the object, then [it would be] illumination—

Due to the absence of a means of knowledge (*hetu*), the world would be blind; for even the Self, whose nature is pure consciousness, possesses "knownness" only through a means of knowledge, and that [knownness] is indeed variable, since it did not exist prior to the arising of the means of knowledge. Therefore, it is not the essential nature [of the Self]. And this is so by the logic already stated. Likewise, "unknownness" also [does not belong to the Self], because of [the dependence on] cognition—

Because [otherwise] there would be no cessation [of error]. If being known and being unknown constitute the very nature of the object, then that object must be measured by that very means of knowledge. Furthermore, ignorance itself cannot be included within the object of measurement.

Because there is no ignorance other than that [primary ignorance]; for if such another existed, it too would likewise require another, leading to an infinite regress if one were to postulate yet another. Furthermore, if ignorance were not removed, the means of knowledge (pramāṇa) would be futile, as there would be no distinction between the state before and after its operation. Nor can that which is itself established by a means of knowledge be an object of measurement (meyatva).

Because there is no distinction [between them]; otherwise, there would be an infinite regress, since each respective means of knowledge (*māna*) would itself be an object of knowledge (*meyatva*), requiring further means of knowledge to establish its status as a means and its object.

Therefore, in such passages as "All this is what this Self is," "When the Self is known," "By which the unheard becomes heard," and "In what, O Venerable One," [it is established that everything arises] from the knowledge of the Self.
The proof of what is desired.

One should not entertain the doubt that effects (*kārya*) are also heard to be known through the knowledge of the Self (*ātmajñāna*), because it has been stated that ignorance and its effects are not objects of knowledge (*ameya*). Through the knowledge of the Self—
If everything were knowable, it would not be an effect of ignorance, just like the Self;

rather, it would be real like the Self, and would indeed be the Self itself. Otherwise, that could not be the knowledge of the Self. If even the non-Self (anātman) were knowable by it, then [that] would be the knowledge of the non-Self, not [the knowledge] of the Self.

Or why should there not be knowledge of the Self? It is more appropriate that it be knowledge of the non-Self, because of the multiplicity of non-Selves and because [the term] is designated by them, like "the village of the Brahmins. Furthermore, in this case, there is no knowledge of all through the knowledge of one; rather, there is knowledge of all only through the knowledge of all.
This position would be similar to the dualist and non-dualist positions. If it is asked, "How can everything be known through the knowledge of your single Self?", listen:
[it is said] that "when the Self is known, all this becomes known," and thus nothing remains unknown.

The meaning is that some object of knowledge remains. This is because only the Self is unknown; because only that [Self] is the object of valid cognition (*meya*); because anything else has as its very nature the ignorance regarding the Self, and thus it is impossible for it to be unknown or an object of knowledge; and because [qualities] such as being unknown do not apply to the merely conventional (*vyāvahārika*).

Furthermore, since the nature of being composed of parts (sāvayavatva) is impossible once ignorance and its effects have been consumed by the knowledge of the Self, [it cannot be the cause of bondage].
Just as in the world, when a jar or similar object is known, there may remain other unknown objects to be known, it is not so with the Self;
thus it is said: "When the Self is known, everything becomes known."

Just as when one is told, "A hundred elephants are running in this room; recognize them," the perceiver says, "I have recognized them," intending to express the absence of any object to be known that has not already been known.
For indeed, by the knowledge of one thing, there can be no knowledge of another single thing, much less so in this case.
There is knowledge of all things; yet it has been stated more than once that a single [entity] cannot possess a manifold nature.

2] The cessation of ignorance.
The meaning is that it comes into being. Just as in the world, when all that water, the lotus pond, and so forth,
as well as that army, are observed in a certain location, people say, "That location has come into existence."

Thus, here too, because ignorance and its effects cease through knowledge, and since only the Self remains, there is such a designation. Alternatively, when the Self is known, all this becomes known, for everything becomes the very substance of the Self; thus, by the knowledge of the Self, everything [is known].
The meaning is that [the self] becomes burnt. For it has been stated that the known Self is the burning away of ignorance.

Furthermore, everything born of ignorance regarding the Self has been declared in such scriptural passages as "Indra by means of his māyās" and "One should know Māyā to be Prakṛti. Therefore, in the state of one's own abiding place, there is the burning away of ignorance.

It is not said that [the Self] possesses the status of being an object of knowledge (*meyatva*), as the Self does. The passage beginning with "by which the unheard becomes heard" (*yenāśrutam*) should also be interpreted in this way. The statement "the unheard becomes heard" clarifies precisely the meaning I have already explained; for even when spoken by the Veda, the unheard does not become heard merely because of my speaking.

Excluding the specific mode [of manifestation], passages such as "All this is what this Self is" and "Brahman alone is all this" are to be explained in the same way as the statement: "That very region is the water, the army, and so forth."

Therefore, being known and being unknown are not the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of the object; consequently, they do not constitute the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and the object of knowledge (*prameya*). Nor is there even room for the suspicion that they are distinct from it, because they do not appear as such. Furthermore, it has been stated that these two are not the intrinsic nature [of the object], since the object is [known] through cognition—

Because it is impossible to establish whether an object is known or unknown either prior to or subsequent to the act of cognition. Therefore, when the object remains unapprehended, once knowledge arises in the form of that object through a means of valid cognition (*māna*), the object's fitness for practical transaction (*vyavahāra-yogyatā*) is what is called its "knownness. Nor is this [knownness] unestablished.

Otherwise, worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) would be impossible. Nor can that [negation] itself be an object of knowledge possessing an external referent, because that would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) and the non-establishment of the object. That cessation of ignorance occurs with respect to the external world. Likewise, although the Self is of the nature of immediate manifestation (*aparokṣasvabhāva*), it is obscured by beginningless, insentient, and indeterminable ignorance (*anirvācyājñāna*).

2] manifestation is the state of being unknown; and that [state] belongs to the [Brahman] born from the Vedānta, such as the "unprecedented" (apūrva) and so forth.

Because knowledge is perfected precisely through the form of the Puruṣa as presented in the *Lakṣaṇopaniṣad*, that which constitutes its direct perception (*aparokṣatā*) is its state of being known (*jñātatā*). And that [state of being known] is simply the cessation of ignorance (*avidyānivṛtti*).
Furthermore, since knowledge (*vidyā*) is beginningless, it is without a cause. Therefore, once destroyed, it cannot arise again.

Because of the absence of a cause; because that which was previously non-existent does not arise without a cause; and because this [avidyā] is itself unborn. Furthermore, that which possesses birth cannot be avidyā, since avidyā is the cause of it.
Nor is there the birth of anything else apart from it. Therefore...

Nothing other than cessation arises; because it is not an effect, this cessation is not the birth of anything, nor is it a cause, since effects alone are observed and accepted as such at the time of the great dissolution and so forth. For that which is not an effect [does not arise].

The cessation of a cause has been observed or accepted by someone in such cases; furthermore, we have stated repeatedly that ignorance is not an effect, that it possesses causality, and that its cessation occurs through knowledge—all of which must be accepted by everyone. Therefore, the cessation of ignorance [occurs] for the Self through the knowledge born of the Vedas.
The direct experience (*aparokṣānubhava*) of the Brahman-Self, which was previously indirect (*parokṣa*), is indeed not different from the Self;
nevertheless, since it does not exist prior to the arising of knowledge, there is no consequence of the defect of the perpetual non-cessation of ignorance and so forth.

In this regard, the construction of the words is as follows: whatever the nature of ignorance may be, its absence must necessarily correspond to that very nature. Since all that is insentient (*jaḍa*) has ignorance as its very body, the destruction of that [ignorance] cannot be insentient; for that which is itself cannot be its own destruction, as such a thing is not observed and lacks any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

And because it would be fruitless. Nor is the destruction of that [consciousness] the non-insentient self, for even when that [destruction] exists, the self continues to exist. Indeed, there is no coexistence of a thing and its destroyer; otherwise, since destruction would be eternal, causes would be rendered useless. For this very reason, its destruction is not real; for [it does not belong] to the self—

There is no other truth. Therefore, although it has appeared as true, since it is in fact only the Self, there is no hope for the reality of duality. Nor is the destruction of that which is unreal seen to be real, as in the case of silver and the like.
VIII. 2] The cessation of ignorance.
The mother-of-pearl is not its destruction, because it exists together with it and existed prior to it.

If the destruction of silver and so forth were a real entity, it would not arise from cognition; for an object does not come into being through cognition, but rather appears. Therefore, there can be no real [destruction] of that which is unreal.

Destruction [occurs]. Furthermore, that which is real cannot perish, just like the Self (ātman). Therefore, it is a contradiction to say that destruction is real. Consequently, the reality of the destroyer is not established by the reality of the destroyed, because only that which is unreal perishes.

Now, it may be argued: let there be no destruction of the object such as silver; rather, its cognition (*jñapti*) must exist, because it is the cause of knowledge. He says "it does not exist" and so forth with the words beginning "it is said. The meaning is that the distinction between the seer and the seen is not perceptible, because it is a distinction between the perceptible and the imperceptible, like the distinction between a blue lotus and a rabbit's horn. This is because [the distinction] depends upon a substratum (*dharmin*) and a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), meaning it depends upon the perception of the substratum and the counter-correlate. [Objection: But surely, by its very existence, it possesses the status of being a substratum or a counter-correlate.

It might be argued: "In the case of a human horn, however, existence itself does not exist; therefore, its difference [from other things] is imperceptible. Consequently, the reason 'because of being a difference between the perceptible and the imperceptible' is non-conclusive. Anticipating this objection, he says: "And it is not the unseen... If the unseen were the locus (*dharmin*), it would follow that everyone would perceive its difference [from everything]; if the unseen were the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), there would be a perception of its difference from everything.

The sense is that, by implication, it would follow that doubt and error could never arise. [Page 3] Now, one might object: "If difference is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), only the manifestation of the locus (*dharmī*) and the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is required, and not their manifestation as objects of vision (*dṛśyatā*), because there is no negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) for the case of a solitary [locus]. Therefore, [the reason you provide] is irrelevant. Thus he raises the objection with the words: "But even though it is unperceived... (*nanvadṛśyāpi*).

If even the perception of an entity's own nature (*svarūpa*) were dependent upon a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), then for the perception of that counter-correlate’s own nature, there would have to be either dependence on another counter-correlate or dependence on its own prior nature. In the first case, there is an infinite regress (*anavasthā*);
in the second, there is mutual dependence (*parasparāśrayatva*), as has already been stated. Anticipating this, one who seeks to avoid the infinite regress raises an objection:

"It is indeed seen. [The opponent argues: In every case, if there were a dependence on a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) for the perception of the essential nature (*svarūpa*), there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*);

but that is not so. Rather, the meaning is that the essential nature is perceived independently, and it is only in relation to a counter-correlate and so forth that it is seen as distinct. In that regard, is the dependence on a counter-correlate merely for the sake of perceiving the essential nature?
Or is it for the sake of another object of perception? He says "not for the sake of an object of perception" to reject the first alternative;
[he says] "not for the sake of an object of perception. The second [alternative]...

[Page 3 – “Nor does it exclude” means: Is the object of another perception merely the same nature as that previously seen, or is it something additional to itself? In the first case, there is no dependence on a counter-correlate, because [the cognition] arises from the previous causal complex alone.]

The meaning is that, in the final case, the identity of difference with its own nature is not established. Now, he restates the position regarding difference as a property (*dharma*): "Now, [if] difference is a property... In that case as well, since it would follow that a property is independent of its counter-correlate if it were non-different from the nature of the substratum (*dharmin*), he concedes by way of elimination that difference must be admitted to be distinct; and that too—

By the words "atyantabhinnatve" (in the case of absolute difference) and so forth, he indicates the impossibility of being a property (*dharma*) [if there were such a difference]. He says "kathaṃcit" (in some way) to indicate that even if there is difference, [the object] must be admitted as accessible to another cognition, just like color, taste, and so on. That being the case, if the difference does not appear in that other cognition, then only the difference itself would appear, and not as a property of the Seer (*dṛk*). Therefore, [there is] manifestation...

The sense is that because it lacks utility, [difference] is not a non-probative reason (*aprayojaka-hetu*). The word "nanu" introduces an objection regarding the admission of difference as being distinct. The meaning is: difference is not distinct from the entity, because it is not perceived separately from it, just like its own nature (*svarūpa*); furthermore, because there exists a subverting argument (*bādhaka*) against the contrary position, it is not distinct.
Thus he says, "and not [so]. The distinction between the distinct and that which is distinct is not apprehended independently;
rather, it is apprehended through the relation of qualifier and qualified, as in "this is the distinction between these two," or "the distinction is distinct."

Furthermore, since the relationship between qualifier and qualified—as seen in cases such as "the man with a staff" (*daṇḍin*)—is observed to be preceded by the apprehension of difference, another difference must first be apprehended. That [difference] would likewise require another, and thus, if the preceding cause of apprehension is unestablished, the apprehension of the qualified difference cannot be established; this is the meaning of the "collapse of the root. Therefore, difference is not distinct from the entity itself.

What is the meaning? Having raised the dilemma—whether [this difference] does not exist at all apart from the entity, or whether it is the very nature of the entity—he refutes it with the words "Is it everywhere? The meaning is: "everywhere" refers to both the seer and the seen, as well as the distinction and the possessor of the distinction. "The consequence of the aforementioned fault" means that there would be no dependence of difference upon its counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*).
The meaning is that if there were no difference from the object, it would follow that there is an absence of distinction, and thus it would be a mere thing-in-itself (*astumātra*).
He extends this same objection [to other cases] with the word "thus" (*evam*).
With the word "otherwise" (*anyathā*), he indicates the alternative.

As for what was stated during the stage of the prima facie argument— that the mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*) between consciousness (*cit*) and the object (*cetya*) is well-established— regarding that, it has been said concerning their difference:
if there is such a thing as mutual non-existence, it must be something other than difference itself.

In that case, even that [mutual absence] must be stated to be distinct from the object; otherwise, there would be no dependence upon a counter-correlate—this is the extension [of the argument]. Since no usage based on mutual absence is observed apart from usage based on difference, if mutual absence is not something other than difference, then the extension [of the argument] does not apply either.

The meaning is that [the objection] must be refuted, because it has already been refuted by the very refutation of that [position]. He states the conclusion:
"And this being so... The meaning is that [difference] is not the object of another cognition that apprehends difference as mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*).
An objection may be raised: "The nature of the Seer (dṛś) when unconditioned is self-luminous, whereas its conditioned form is luminous by another;
therefore, the establishment of difference and mutual non-existence is possible. Anticipating this, he says, "For not... (na hi).
The meaning is that the conditioned visible form is not the true nature of the Seer, because it is merely a mental construction (kalpanāmātra). Furthermore:

If the seer were to possess the nature of the seen, then its self-luminosity would necessarily be lost; for it is impossible for there to be the visibility of form without the visibility of that which possesses form. Thus he says: "by being itself the seer. Furthermore, only that whose existence is subject to deviation from manifestation can be determined to be invisible.

But since the seeing [of consciousness] is always itself seen, there is no deviation from its manifestation within its own existence; thus, he says "nor by its own seeing," meaning that another object of sight is not seen. To the question, "What is the fault if the very nature [of consciousness] were dependent on something else? [he replies:]

He says: "Because of dependence on another. The meaning is that if the manifestation of the nature [of consciousness] were dependent on another, then existence itself would depend on a cause, resulting in the collapse of the previously stated inference of its eternity. Thus, having refuted the connection between difference and non-difference by examining the nature of the Seer, he now refutes their being attributes of that [Seer] by examining the nature of difference and non-difference themselves.
Setting aside the possibility of these two being either visible or invisible, he states the defect in the first alternative with the words "If they are visible" (*dṛśyatve ceti*).

Regarding the second alternative as well, he posits the options of whether they are insentient or self-luminous, and states the defect in the first of these with the words "If they are invisible" (*adṛśyatve ceti*). He states the defect in the final case with the words "In the case of self-luminosity" (*svayaṃprabhatve*). [He explains: "In the case of self-luminosity..."

He states another defect with the words "and because it would always appear. Having concluded the refutation of the nature of the subject (*pakṣa*) as previously stated, he refers back to it with the words "nor [is it possible]" (*nāpi*), intending to set forth yet another defect. He states that other defect with the words "nor can there be for one" (*na caikasyāḥ*). The meaning is that it is well known that what possesses a single characteristic is one, while what possesses different characteristics is distinct.

Furthermore, if the single vision possesses two forms called "difference" and "non-difference," then is the vision non-different from them, or are they non-different from the vision? In the first case, the vision would not be one, because it is non-different from two [forms].
In the latter case, there would be no mutual difference between those two, because they are both non-different from the same single [vision]. Thus he says: "And not of those two..."

Furthermore, if the two forms were non-different from the vision (*dṛk*), their self-luminosity would have to be asserted. And in that case, because they would be established independently of a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), there would be a loss of their status as being the absence of difference. Therefore, he says "self-luminosity" (*svayaṃprabhatva*) [in the verse], stating that even the claim that "the two forms are the absence of difference from the vision" is not established. If they were non-different from the vision, [there could be] no difference—

[Page 4] Not understanding what was stated—that there would be no mutual difference between two entities—one raises the objection: "Then there is simply non-difference."
The meaning is that since difference and non-difference exist as the very nature (*svarūpa*) of the Seer (*dṛśi*), their mutual non-difference is indeed established.

He states the refutation of that [position] with the words, "the same would apply to the object of sight (*dṛśya*) as well. This means that difference and non-difference in the object of sight must also be non-different from each other, because they are both "difference" and "non-difference," just like difference and non-difference in the Seer. Previously, regarding the unity of difference and non-difference in the Seer—
Having accepted [the position] even regarding the visible, it was established [that there is no difference]. Now, he says that even that [visible object] does not exist;

thus, regarding non-difference therein, he extends the logic stated for the non-difference between the vision of difference and difference itself to the non-difference between the vision of difference and the visible object as well.
In this way, when difference and its absence are one, and only difference remains, such that difference is the sole visible reality—
"...of the visible."...

The meaning is that there would be no distinction between the object of perception and [its absence]. In this way, even though there is non-difference between the absence and the object of perception, the refutation should be inferred. He states another fault regarding the view that difference is merely an absence:
"What..."
