To this he says: "For this [non-existence] belongs to two things that are distinct. Now, since identity cannot possibly be attained merely through the absence of difference, why is it—?

Anticipating the objection that "mutual non-existence (itaretarābhāva) would thus be unestablished," he says, "In the absence of difference": if there were no difference, then even existence and non-existence—which lack the manifestation of non-difference in any form whatsoever—would have to be non-different; how much more so, then, for those entities that possess the manifestation of non-difference by way of such forms as reality (tattva) and substantiality (dravyatva)?
Thus he says, "In the absence of difference."

Regarding the first alternative—that [the object] is merely a difference—he states another fault with the words "And if... (*yadi ca*). Anticipating the question "What follows from that?", he says "Then of what? (*tadā kasya*) to show that even difference itself remains unestablished.
Now, concerning non-existence...

Anticipating the objection that "where there is unity, let there also be difference," he says, "And not of the one alone," meaning that at such a time, because difference would be incompatible with unity, unity itself could not be established.

[Objection: But surely the consequence of the non-existence of even one thing is a fault for you alone, the proponent of non-duality (advaitavādin), and not for us; to this he says, "the non-existence of one. Anticipating the question, "What follows from that?", he says, "then there is no one," meaning that the doctrine of emptiness (śūnyavāda) would result.

Previously, a refutation was stated by means of the alternative options of whether [the two] are visible or invisible. Now, having raised the alternatives of whether those two are of the nature of the seer (*dṛg-rūpa*) or not of the nature of the seer, he states another defect regarding the position that they are attributes (*dharma*) with the words "of those two" (*tayośca*). He states another defect if difference and non-difference were not of the nature of the seer with the words "nor indeed" (*na ca*).

Regarding the phrase "of the seer and the seen": where there is the relation of property and property-bearer (*dharmadharmibhāva*), it is observed that they are cognizable by a single cognition. That [single-cognizability], being the pervader (*vyāpaka*), when excluded, also excludes its pervaded (*vyāpya*), namely the relation of property and property-bearer; this is the meaning. Now, one might object: even though the relation of property and property-bearer is observed in cases such as sound and space despite their not being cognizable by a single cognition, it might still be so here as well.

Anticipating this objection, he says, "And not one," meaning that because there is no restrictive factor, it would follow [absurdly] in all cases. Furthermore, in the case of sound and space—which stand in the relation of signifier and signified—there is no relationship of property and property-bearer (*dharmadharmibhāva*). This is as in the case of expressions such as "fragrant sandalwood."

It should be understood that there indeed exists either the state of being the object of a single witness-consciousness, or the state of being the object of a single cognition produced by the mind when it is purified by the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the individual apprehensions [of the two]. Having thus established that difference and non-difference do not exist for the Seer with respect to the seen as their counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*), he now states [the following] from scripture to show that those two also do not exist for the seen with respect to the Seer as its counter-correlate.

By the words "evam" and so forth, [the author] states the following: The seer (*dṛk*) is the counter-correlative of the absence of difference from the seen (*dṛśya*), because it is devoid of that absence of difference [from itself].

Whatever is thus [devoid of such absence] is thus [the counter-correlative]; for example, the nature of the seen. Having stated this, he states the subverting argument (*bādhaka*) against the contrary position (*vipakṣa*) with the words "even in one [case]" (*ekasminn api*). If, in relation to the seer which is devoid of the absence of difference from the seen, those two [properties] were present in the seen...

The meaning is that if difference and non-difference were to exist [in the same thing], then there would follow the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that the perceptible object would be both different from and non-different from itself.
Anticipating the objection—"What fault is there if difference and non-difference were to have themselves as their own counter-correlates?"—he says: "Nor from itself.
It cannot be asserted that an entity exists simultaneously as different from itself, as its own non-existence, and as itself.

The meaning is that if there were the persistence of both existence and non-existence of difference, or if there were the persistence of the entity (bhāva) or the real thing (vastu), then it would follow that those two [existence and non-existence] lack power; this is because the real thing, its difference, and its non-existence are mutually contradictory. In the reading "tayorbhāvasya ca," the sense is that due to the contradiction between the entity and its correlative difference and non-existence, there is no mutual relationship between them.

Consequently, the meaning is that there is an absence of all three [the locus, the counter-correlate, and the relation] because there is no distinction [between them]. It was stated that since the Seer (dṛś) is devoid of the absence of difference, it cannot be the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) to the absence of difference residing in the seen (*dṛśya*). To this, one might object: "That is incorrect; because of its specific nature, the Seer possesses the status of a counter-correlate by its mere manifestation. Anticipating this, he says: "And not... [referring to the Seer] which is untouched by the absence of difference.

The meaning is as follows: if the status of being a counter-correlative (*pratiyogitva*) for the seer (*dṛg-rūpa*) arises merely through its own specific nature, then it would follow that even with respect to itself, there would be the status of being a counter-correlative in the cognition of the absence of difference from itself. On page 6, he states another reason for the impossibility of the absence of difference having the seer as its counter-correlative for the object of sight (*dṛśya*): "and because of the impossibility of a means of knowledge" (*mānāsaṃbhavāt*).

The meaning is that, because those two [the seer and the seen] are apprehended by a single cognition along with the object of perception (*dṛśya*), they do not possess the nature of being perceived (*dṛśyadharmatva*); just as the seeing itself, which is self-evident (*svayaṃmānā*), does not possess the nature of being perceived, so it is here. He states another refutation: "And if [the seer] were self-evident... Because those two would be self-evident, their difference would not be established, since they would stand in a relationship of identity with the seeing (*dṛk*), and [the distinction] from the perceived (*dṛśya*) as well...

The distinction between those two would not be established, because the distinction between the perceptible and the imperceptible is itself imperceptible; furthermore, the mutual distinction between them would not be established, since there is no difference in their being self-validating (*svayam-mānatva*). By the logic previously stated, [the object] together with its distinction...

The meaning is that the cognition of non-existence is intended when there is no perception of an object that has been reached—that is, perceived—in that form. To the question "What follows from this?", he says: "And not... [na ca...]. Now, in the system of the logicians (*tārkika*), the non-perception of what is fit (*yogyānupalabdhi*) is not the cause of the cognition of non-existence; rather, it is the qualification—

Anticipating the objection that such cognition arises from the very contact of the sense organ with the qualified object (*viśeṣya*), he says: "And [it is] not [the case that] it has been reached. According to the system of the Logicians (*Tārkikas*), there is a rule that whatever exists in the immediately preceding moment is the cause; and since non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) lacks the status of a cause, if its existence were ever perceived, the cognition of absence would arise only when that [non-apprehension] is already present. This is because of non-apprehension itself.
The meaning is that there is no prior factor that determines [the occurrence]. Now, even if non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) lacks the status of being a cause for the cognition of absence—
[page 425]
— Page 7] First Chapter | 361

He raises the objection that, because non-apprehension functions as an obstacle to apprehension, it is by virtue of being the absence of that [apprehension] that there is a rule regarding the prior existence of non-apprehension; this is expressed in the phrase "in the case of the apprehension of what has been reached" (*prāptānupalabdhau*). He refutes the first alternative—namely, whether non-apprehension, even as the absence of an obstacle, possesses utility toward the cognition of absence—by saying "even so" (*tathāpi*). [This refers to] non-apprehension...

The meaning is this: although non-existence (*abhāva*) is not a cause for the cognition of non-existence, it is nevertheless useful for the cognition of non-existence by virtue of being an absence of an obstacle (*pratibandhakābhāva*).

And since such [an obstacle] does not exist in the case of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), the cognition of the non-existence of that which has perception (*dṛk*) as its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) is not possible. He raises the second [alternative] with "Now" (*atha*). In the cognition of the non-existence of that for which there exists a perception distinct from itself, [non-apprehension is]—

The meaning is that even though the eye (*dṛk*) is employed for the apprehension [of objects], it has no utility in the cognition of its own absence, because the eye is not perceived by anything else.

To the objection that "in that case, even while the eye is manifest, there could be a cognition of an absence whose counter-positive is the eye," he replies with the words "even while it is manifest" (*sphurantyām api*). Furthermore, the cognition of the absence of the visible (*dṛśya*), like the cognition of the absence of the eye—

He says, "Even regarding the perceptible," [meaning] that the cognition of non-existence could occur even without non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), because there is no difference in their being cognitions of non-existence. Anticipating the objection that—since there is a distinction between the seer (*dṛk*) and the seen (*dṛśya*)—the cognition of the non-existence of the seen cannot occur without non-apprehension, just as the cognition of the non-existence of the seer does—he says, "And not... [meaning] that although there is a distinction between the seer and the seen by way of their essential nature (*svarūpa*), [there is no such distinction] regarding the cognition of non-existence.

There is no distinction in the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) by which the cognition of non-existence would not occur even in the absence of a perceptible object, nor by which it would occur even in the absence of perception. Therefore, the meaning is that the causality of non-perception for the cognition of non-existence must be accepted in all cases. One must admit that non-perception is the cause of the cognition of non-existence everywhere.

Having raised this objection, he anticipates a further qualification with the words, "But surely it is only the perception of the perceptible. Although non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is generally accepted as the cause for the cognition of absence (*abhāva*), nevertheless, because the perceptible is not perceived as something other [than its own nature], non-apprehension is essentially of the nature of absence itself.
The meaning is that a non-apprehension of something additional is not required;

for while the cognition of the absence of a visible object has that very perception as its counter-positive, the claim that "absence is known through a non-apprehension of something additional" constitutes a distinction.

In this regard, having accepted that the very absence of perception is itself the cognition of absence—just as the very perception [of an object] is itself the cognition of that object—the author raises a dilemma:
"Is it said that there is no dependence on a separate non-perception (*anupalabdhi*), or is it by accepting a distinct cognition whose object is absence?

This is what is meant by the words "Is it the perception...? Regarding the first alternative, since an absence which possesses a counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) cannot be self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*), [it would require a further means of knowledge].

Considering clearly such faults as that origination would entail the contradiction of its being non-existent at the time of its arising, he states the final [objection] with the words "If it exists," and so forth. Now, one might argue: "Since the absence of seeing is established by experience, and since no cause for that experience can be identified, let it be causeless. To this, he replies: "And it is not without a cause. Why?
[Page 426] 362 Commentary on the *iṣṭasiddhi*.

[Page 7]—Therefore he says, "due to the absence of another" (*anyābhāvāt*). The meaning is that there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even the cognition of the absence of a perceptible object would arise without a cause.
Anticipating the objection, "In that case, let some cause corresponding to this effect be postulated," he says, "and no such [cause] is obtained."
Then, suspecting that there might be knowledge of non-existence when something that has attained the conditions for perception is not perceived despite its existence, he says:
"And if it exists... He refutes another reason suggested by the word "etcetera" with: "Nor also... [This refers to] the non-perception of the seer.

The non-existence of the perception [of the jar] is not something other than the absence [of the jar]; therefore, the meaning is that the mere absence [of the jar] is not the cause for the cognition of that absence.

Having raised the objection—“Let it be that the object’s own absence is indeed the non-perception, and let that alone be the cause for the cognition of the absence of the perception”—he says: “If it were the object’s own absence. If the absence of the perception were the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), then another distinct absence must be stated as its object (*prameya*).

The meaning is that this is not possible. Having accepted the non-existence of perception as the meaning of the term "non-apprehension" (*anupalabdhi*), it was stated that there is no other object of cognition (*meyam*)—namely, another absence of perception—by means of that [first non-apprehension]. Now he says, "Nor is this [non-apprehension] established for you," because if that non-apprehension were to be known by another non-apprehension, it would lead to the consequence of an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). [This is like the case of] a non-existent thing, such as a man’s horn.

The meaning is that non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is unestablished because it is unfit to be expressed [as a reason]. Now, one might object: "In that case, just as a jar, by virtue of being an object (*karman*), is a cause of its own cognition, so too the absence of seeing itself is the cause of its own cognition; therefore, there is no need for another reason. Anticipating this, he says:

"Nor is it the case that [the absence] is the object of measurement itself" (*na ca meya eva*). Furthermore, it is undesirable for those who maintain that absence is imperceptible (*parokṣa*) that the cognition of an absence [should arise from the absence itself].

He states that [the absence] is produced by its object, saying "and because it is undesirable. Even in the view of those who deny the existence of perception (*pratyakṣābhāvavādin*), one observes that an absence whose counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is an object of knowledge serves as a cause for cognition; since such [an absence] is not itself an object of knowledge, it should be understood that the absence of its counter-correlate cannot be accepted as a cause for cognition. If that is so, then [factors such as] the recollection of the counter-correlate must be the cause.
Fearing this objection, he says, "And not here. Here, by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the apprehension of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) is intended;
for it is observed that the apprehension of the counter-positive—such as "this is not that"—is also a cause for the cognition of absence.
Now, one might object: since there is a vision of the visible, this cognition possesses parts; therein, the vision, being self-luminous, [is the counter-positive]...

The manifestation of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) shines forth everywhere as a constituent part of the manifestation of the non-existence itself; it is this manifestation of the counter-positive that is the cause in cognitions of absence, and not "visibility" (*dṛśyatva*). Therefore, he says: "even when [the object] is measured by its own nature. For the cognition of absence is indeed one and partless; it is only figuratively described as having parts because it has the counter-positive as one part and the absence as its object.
The point is this: since eternal consciousness (*saṃvit*) is the very manifestation of its counterpart, it is impossible for there to be even a portion of non-eternal knowledge of absence;

therefore, the identity of the eternal and the non-eternal is impossible. [Page 8] He states the sublation that would occur if a portion were admitted: "If [it were] a portion of all cognitions," etc. He then establishes that very sublation with the words: "If of one... and so forth. From that...
[page 427] — — Page 9]
The First Chapter.
He states that this undesirable consequence has arisen: "Thus all things, whether existent or non-existent. Just as it is seen—
Because it manifests as the cognition of the absence of intrinsic nature (*svābhāva*), the absence is qualified by the vision (*dṛk*);
thus, "the absence of vision," "the absence of a cow," "the absence of a yellow vision," or "the absence of a jar-vision"—all such presences and absences would become qualifiers of vision.
If there were no cause for the cognition of the absence of vision, then that cognition of the absence of vision [could not arise].

He offers a rebuttal, saying "let it not be," lest [the pot] be like a rabbit's horn due to being devoid of a cause; then he anticipates the objection that this contradicts experience by stating "if you say it certainly exists. He replies: "In that case, the cognition of the absence of seeing is an error, because while being occasional, it is devoid of any established cause, just like a commonly accepted error."

"Even so," he says. Now, one might object: "Is it not observed that the error of silver has as its cause the contact of the eye, which is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? Likewise, even though the cognition of the absence of sight is an error, its cause must be sought among the means of valid cognition. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And not from error... Here, *gatiḥ* means the cause of valid cognition; it need not be sought, because ignorance (*avidyā*) is the cause of the delusion.

The meaning is "because it is well-established. He states the fault in the contrary case with the words "if there were a transition" (*gatiśced*). Since there is a transition [to another object] when the cognition of the absence of a visible thing is erroneous, he concludes that the visible thing should not be postulated as a constituent part of the cognition of its own absence—on the grounds that there is no other possible recourse—with the words "therefore, even by means of self-cognition... As for what was previously argued, that "the visible thing is not an object of apprehension," that is unproven (*asiddha*).

He says "But [if you say] thus... in response. Now, one might object: "Even the definition that 'the Seer is self-luminous and devoid of the attributes of the object of knowledge,' and so forth, is itself a cognition; therefore, it is merely the manifestation of its own nature. Consequently, there is no lack of proof [for the existence of the Seer]. Anticipating this doubt, he says "And not... The meaning is that identity between the eternal and the non-eternal is impossible. [If that is so,] then even if the Seer is not an object...
Anticipating the objection that "definitions must indeed exist in order to dispel the delusion that [the self] is an object," he says, "nor is it absolutely [so].
Then, fearing that it might be an object characterized by things such as jars, he says, "nor is it an object other [than itself].
Your definition, which consists in the exclusion of other definitions, is not [itself] characterized by things such as jars.

The meaning is that it is undesirable and impossible to exclude determination (*nirūpaṇa*) regarding objects such as a jar, because that would contradict the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) whose object is that jar. [Page 9] Now, one might ask: "In that case, let them be without objects. To this he says:
"Nor can they be without objects," for that would entail the loss of their very nature as determinations. Therefore, by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*)—

"But your own definition has as its object something that is not an object [of cognition]. If that were so, my definition would likewise be such, since there is no distinction," he says with the words "For this very reason. The proponent of the previous view states the distinction regarding his own definition with the words "Now, this is not so": just as a human horn is not an object of cognition (*prameya*), even though it is non-objective (*aprameya*), the property of being an object of cognition—[is attributed to it]...
The *Iṣṭasiddhivivaraṇa*.
[Page 9] Having stated the equality [of positions] by saying that just as there would be the consequence of silence for others if negation were otherwise, so it is for me as well, the proponent now—
He states that "the two" refers to the fact that the investigation is endowed with reasoning (*yuktyupetatva*) as its specific characteristic. Now, one might object:

if the nature of seeing (*dṛgātman*) is not made an object by the cognition of investigation, then its status as a non-object (*aviṣayatva*) would not be established, because it does not manifest during the investigation into its non-objectivity. Indeed, an investigation is undertaken precisely for the sake of establishing non-objectivity.

Therefore, in order to establish its lack of being an object, one must accept that the Self, which is pure consciousness (*dṛgātman*), is the object of the knowledge of investigation (*nirūpaṇājñāna*). To this, he says: "Otherwise" (*anyathā*). Even if the Self, which is pure consciousness, is not the object of the knowledge of investigation, its status as a non-object is still established.
For instance, while the Self shines forth by virtue of its own self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*), it is the locus of the non-objectivity well-known in the world.
By the force of negative concomitance (*vyatireka-vyāpti*), a mental modification (*buddhi-vṛtti*) arises in the form of the non-objectivity of consciousness.

When the nature of the Seer (*dṛg-ātmā*) is manifested in this [modification], it becomes the cause for the empirical usage (*vyavahāra*) of that which is superimposed upon itself in the form delimited by objectivity.
Consequently, its non-objectivity is established. Therefore, no further investigation is required for the establishment of non-objectivity.

By knowledge, it is made an object (*viṣaya*). This being so, the meaning is that there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of losing its status as being defined by non-objectivity (*aviṣayatva-nirūpaṇatā*). If the substratum (*dharmin*) were the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), then, because it would be exhausted in that very way, the property (*dharma*) would not exist; to this objection, she says "let it not be" (*mā bhūt*), implying that [the property] is established. "Let it not be"—what of it? For I do not speak for the sake of establishing the substratum.
The purpose of the messenger has been set forth. [Page 10] Now, one might object: "Surely there would be a cognition of non-existence for everything everywhere;
thus, this undesirable consequence does not apply to us, because we accept such a cognition since mutual non-existence exists for everything in relation to everything.

To this he raises the objection with the word "nanu" (surely). Let it be defective; nevertheless, provided that it is not qualified by the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) and so forth, [there is no mutual non-existence].

He refutes [the objection] that there would be no specific cognition of existence by saying "śūnya" (empty). To the question, "What follows from that?", he says "ataḥ" (hence). To the question, "Even so, what is the consequence?", he says "śūnyatā" (emptiness). The meaning is that since there is no word to restrict the negative particle (*nañ*), when there is an unrestricted negation, it results in the cognition of emptiness. *Apra-* [is the beginning of the next section].

Or, there is a word-break as *meti*. In that case, the meaning is that because of the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*), emptiness (*śūnyatā*) would follow as being non-cognition (*apramā*), that is, devoid of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-śūnyā*). [Objection: One can negate only some thing in some place, but not everything everywhere, because it is impossible; with this intention, he refutes [the objection] by saying "thus... and so forth, [stating that] it is a reductio (*prasaṅga*).
[He says] "by such [statements]" and so forth. Now, one might object: "This undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) does not apply to us proponents of emptiness (śūnyavādin), because it is accepted by us.

To this he replies: "Because it is impossible. If, in the manner described, the absence of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is not tenable, then let it be unapprehendable (aprameya). To this he replies: "And it is not self-luminous (asvayaṃprabha). Now, one might object: "But what of that which is not self-manifesting?"
[Page 429] – [Page 11] The First Chapter.
because, just as an entity lacks self-luminosity, so too the absence of self-luminosity cannot possess self-luminosity; therefore, he says "self-" [to address this].

"And even in the case of manifestation" (*prabhatve ca*). Now, one might object: "Granted that there may be no mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*) between the seer and the seen because there is no evidence for the absence of the seer when the seen is present;
nevertheless, let there still be a difference (*bheda*) between them. To this, he says: "mutual non-existence" (*itaretarābhāvam*).
That which possesses both difference and non-existence is described as such. The state of being that is "the nature of non-difference" (*abhedābhāvatvam*). Therefore...

He states that such infinity is established because it is free from the absence of difference recognized by authoritative means of knowledge, saying: "Therefore, because of the absence of non-difference [between the seer and the seen]. Now, he raises an objection in order to refute what was asserted by the Buddhist proponent of the non-difference between the seer and the seen—namely, that there is finitude—and thereby to establish infinity: "But if this were so... [regarding] difference and its opposite...

The meaning is that if there were an absence of both difference and non-existence, there would be oneness and identity. [Page 11] He raises the objection, "In the refutation of difference," suggesting that contradiction with common consensus (*prasiddhi*) is not a fault; for when the consensus regarding difference is sublated by the support of powerful means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for the non-existence of difference—such as "here there is no diversity whatsoever"—then there is no contradiction with that [consensus].
It might be so. Likewise, he dismisses the objection that there is no proof for non-difference by saying, "True.

If sublation were to occur in this very manner even without a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then even the ascertainment of sublation would not exist; therefore, he says, "of each and each. Previously, it was stated while conceding that one's own [cognition] possesses the power to sublate [the other]. Now, however, even that...

He says "no" and "I too [say] no," meaning that because appearances are possible prior to the direct realization of reality (*tattva-aparokṣya*). He asks, "How so?"—questioning how the absence of evidence for non-difference is ascertained.
Are both the non-difference and its appearance empirical (*prātītika*) or logical (*naiyāyika*)? It cannot be the first, because it is not perceived.

The second [alternative] is not tenable because the seer (*dṛk*) and the seen (*dṛśya*) are as contradictory as darkness and light, and because this would contradict the well-established fact of their difference. Therefore, he refutes [the objection] with the words "What is asked here? etc., stating that one should not ask how there can be an absence of proof for non-difference; for their manifestation (*tatpratibhāsa*) is [the basis for] their non-difference.
The connection [of the argument] is as follows: it does not appear, nor is its existence possible through reasoning.

Because of the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the cognition "the cloth is perceptible," and because of the logical principle that if a visible object were established through proximity to eternal vision, it would follow that it is always established, one must state a relationship of restricted non-difference; thus, all this...
If non-difference appears from the renunciation of this self, then how can there be an absence of proof for non-difference?

Since the word "how" (katham) signifies both a question and a censure, the force of the inquiry—"What is being asked here?"—necessarily implies the further question—"What is being censured here? In that regard, he states that the censure is certainly not based on perception (pratyakṣa).
Or alternatively:
The Commentary on the *iṣṭasiddhi*. [Page 11 – Having explained the impossibility of the objection...]

Regarding the term "difference" (*bheda*): the sense is that grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is possible even through a relation of immediate perception (*āparokṣya*), just as in the expression "the light of the sun shines. Furthermore, since the establishment of specific objects of perception is possible due to the restriction [imposed] by the transformations of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which acts as the manifester, non-difference (*abheda*) is not possible even for that which is all-pervading (*vyāpin*). Thus he says.

Nor [is it from scripture], he says: "Nor is there its appearance [from scripture]," because [the scripture] merely restates what is well-known in order to establish the non-existence of any entity apart from the Self.
He states that a question is impossible, saying: "Like darkness and light. Thus, for one who maintains the refutation of duality, a question—
Having thus established the unfitness [of the opponent], he now states that those who maintain non-difference (abheda-vādins) alone must be questioned, beginning with "If.
He demonstrates the contradiction with both perception and logic through the question "How? and so forth.
[Page 12] He states "For this very reason" because, since the object is impossible, its cognition is also impossible. And for the following reason as well:

He says, "And how? to show that neither non-difference nor the knowledge thereof is possible. Having raised the dilemma—whether, in the non-difference of the seer and the seen, the seen is reduced to the mere nature of the seer, or the seer is reduced to the mere nature of the seen—he refutes it with the words beginning "If... Having stated the impossibility of non-difference, he states the impossibility of knowing it with the words "And if the seen..."

Regarding the phrase "as the nature of seeing" (*dṛgātmanā*): if the object of sight (*dṛśya*) were to be known as the nature of seeing, it would follow that it is knowable by a cognition whose object is seeing, and thus it would possess self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*). Consequently, the consequence would arise that it possesses the nature of seeing (*dṛktva*) and so forth. Conversely, if seeing (*dṛk*) were to be known as the nature of the object of sight, it would follow that it is knowable by a cognition whose object is the object of sight. From that, the consequence would arise that it possesses the nature of non-seeing (*adṛktva*) and so forth; this is the meaning.

One might object: "Just as in the case of 'the white pot,' since the pot is perceived, there must necessarily be a relationship of qualifier and qualified (viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣyabhāva), and thus the status of attribute and substrate (dharma-dharmitva) must be asserted.
And since that [relationship] does not exist if there is absolute difference, non-difference (abheda) must be asserted. Anticipating this objection, he says:
"Nor even," he says.

Why is it that the state of being a property (*dharma*) and a substratum (*dharmin*) is not possible? To this he replies, "For not... Because if the seer (*dṛk*) and the seen (*dṛśya*) were in the relation of property and substratum, they would necessarily be cognizable by a single cognition; thus, [the seer] would be entirely [cognized] as one.

The meaning is this: if the visible object were to possess visibility as its nature (dharma) or as its substratum (dharmin), then, because there is no other vision [to perceive it], it would follow that it possesses that [visibility] at that very same time; and that is improper due to contradiction. Now, one might suspect: "In that case, let the visible object have visibility as its nature or as its substratum through one part, while through another part it possesses it. Anticipating this, he says: "Nor by two parts. Furthermore:

Because the visible portion—whether as a property (*dharma*) or as a substratum (*dharmin*)—has entered into the state of being visible, it is precisely due to its visibility that the relationship of property and substratum between the seer and the seen is not established. Furthermore, it is also not established that the visible portion possesses both visibility and the nature of the seer, because that visible portion is by definition non-seer; thus he says, "And of the visible part... Moreover, regarding the property...
[Page 431]
— Page 14] The First Chapter.

Furthermore, one must consider whether the state of being a subject (*dharmitva*) is self-luminous or perceptible; regarding the first alternative, he says, "Nor even the state of being a subject or a property. The meaning is that if it were self-luminous, its status as both a property and a subject would be lost due to its non-difference from the Seer (*dṛk*).

Furthermore, it must be stated that the relationship between the attribute (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*) is a property of two perceivable things (*dṛśya*). But that is not established, because, due to its self-luminosity (*svayaṃ-prakāśatva*), a connection with a perceivable object is impossible; thus he says, "and because of the lack of connection with the perceivable" (*dṛśyāsaṃbandhāt*). Regarding the second [alternative], he says, "nor" (*na api*). If it were perceivable, its being a property of the Seer (*dṛk-dharmatva*) would not be tenable, because a perceivable thing cannot have a connection with the self-luminous Seer.

The meaning is that it is impossible for them to be bound. Furthermore, in order to refute the position of non-difference, he proposes various alternatives as far as possible, beginning with the words "Moreover, these [messengers]," and so forth. Now, one might raise the objection: "When the individual soul (*jīva*) shines, why should Brahman—which is non-different from it—not likewise shine? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "For it is not one... [Page 13]

"Of that very [Self]" means: the notion that "Brahman does not shine" is merely an illusion, because the manifestation of its own nature (svarūpa) never ceases. In reality, however, neither manifestation nor non-manifestation is possible for a single entity due to contradiction; this is the meaning. He states the intention of the third alternative—that the distinction is established through two parts called the seer (dṛk) and the seen (dṛśya)—belonging to one and the same possessor of parts (aṃśin): "of one..."

"In that case, even in this alternative, since the parts are fixed [in their respective states] and there is no part distinct from them, the appearance and non-appearance of the single [whole] alone would be established"; thus he says, "tadāpi" (even then). Now, suspecting that there might exist a whole distinct from its parts, he replies: "Even then, for a whole of a single form, there could not be both appearance and non-appearance, because of the aforementioned contradiction."

He says "not even of the whole" because [otherwise] there would be the consequence of faults. Then, having raised the objection that they might exist through two other parts in order to avoid contradiction, he says "if [it were] by means of two other parts," [implying] that the connection with the subsequent part must be preceded by the connection with the other part;
thus, since the connection with the other part would likewise require another, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). [This is stated] because of the manifestation of infinite parts.

The point is that since the manifestation and non-manifestation of the whole depend upon [the manifestation and non-manifestation of] the parts, the very root [of the argument] is destroyed. Now, one might object: "By asserting that there is no identity between what is manifested and what is not manifested, you have merely proven—on the grounds of the rule of simultaneous perception—that there is no difference between blue and its cognition;
and this is precisely our own established doctrine. To this, he says: "Now, if this were so... [nanvevamiti].

[Page 14] Now, one might object: "Just as for the cognition of the moon's plurality, the single moon alone is the objective support (*ālambana*), so too my cognition of plurality has non-difference as its objective support; therefore, there is no contradiction. Anticipating this, he says: "And not of the cognition of difference... For if that were so, it would follow that even in the case of cognitions, the manifestation of difference would have non-difference as its objective support, and thus there would be only one consciousness (*saṃvit*).
This means "it would not exist.
Now, one might object: "Let inference and the like not be the means of knowledge for non-difference; surely the word of a reliable authority (*āptavacana*) exists [as such a means].
Anticipating this, he refutes it with the words beginning with "nanu" (now, if...). Previously, regarding the mark (*liṅga*) of simultaneous perception, according to the literal sense of the text...

Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And as for the seer and the seen lacking the nature of Brahman... [Page 22]. Regarding Brahman—

Having stated the common refutation regarding its being distinct from both, he states an additional argument regarding its being distinct from the seer (*dṛk*) in the words "If it were unseen" (*adṛkta cet*). The meaning is that, like the horn of a hare, Brahman would not be established. Anticipating the objection that it might be established through a relation with the seer, he says "If it were established"; for if it were established as being related to the seer, [it would lack] distinction from the seen (*dṛśya*).

The meaning is that the nature of Brahman as the object of perception would not be established. Regarding the phrase "and if it were perceptible": if Brahman were perceptible, then—just as in the case of another perceptible object—neither its difference from nor its non-difference from consciousness (the seer) could be established. Furthermore, the failure to establish both of these in the case of other perceptible objects has already been demonstrated. If, out of a desire to avoid the faults mentioned regarding the position of difference...

If it is held that [the world] is non-different from Brahman, then is it non-different from both [the seer and the seen], or from only one? If it were non-different from both, then Brahman would possess a dual nature. If it were non-different from only one, even then, if it were non-different from the seen, the distinction and non-distinction [of the world] from the light of the seer would not be established; thus, the aforementioned defect would ensue. If, however, it were non-different from the seer, then [the following applies]:

He says "there is no fault whatsoever" with the words beginning with "atha" (now). Regarding the phrase "not otherwise": if the Seer itself were not Brahman, but rather there were also a difference in form, then there would be no absence of fault; for the fault characterized by the impossibility of a single entity having multiple forms would still exist. This is the meaning. Now, even while accepting non-difference...

...he avoids the fault [of contradiction]. How so? Even if one accepts the non-difference (*abheda*) of the seer and the seen, since their identity (*tādātmya*) has been refuted, it must be stated that either the seer or the seen would remain as a residue. In that case, if the seen remains as a residue, then the seer—

The meaning is that because there is no connection between the seer (*dṛk*) and the appearance of the visible (*dṛśya*), and because the visible is absent when only the seer remains, the defect residing in the visible cannot affect the seer. Now, he says "even if there were difference from the visible" (*dṛśyādbhede’pi*) to show that even if difference is admitted, [the defect] does not exist; the meaning is "due to the absence of contact" (*saṅgābhāvāt*). Furthermore, he says "defect also... (*doṣo’pi*) to show that for this reason as well, the seer is indeed faultless. [Page]

[Page 23–23] Having set aside the objection by accepting the existence of defects in the object of perception (*dṛśya*), he now states that even that is not the case with the words, "Furthermore, even in the object of perception" (*kiṃca dṛśye’pi*). The meaning is that, because the relationship between property and property-possessor (*dharmadharmibhāva*) is untenable through such conceptual alternatives as "itself" and so forth, the object of perception is devoid of properties; and since, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*),
contact with qualities or defects is impossible, there is no contact with distinctions, birth, and so forth.

Having indeed stated that difference, birth, and so forth are difficult to define because they are common [to all things], he says "moreover, of difference" (*kiṃca bhedasya*) to explain them individually.

Fearing that even the oneness of vision (*dṛś*) might be a property (*dharma*), and thus the non-duality [of the Seer] would not be established, he says: "Nor does this... The meaning is that [vision] cannot withstand conceptual constructions such as difference or non-difference, and because a relationship [between them] is impossible. Now, one might object: since other properties such as mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*) are possible, how can it be said to be devoid of properties? Anticipating this, he says: "The absence of the property of difference. This depends upon that...

He himself establishes this in the verse beginning with "of two distinct [things]... Anticipating the objection that there cannot be a single entity because of the existence of distinction—the non-confusion of things consisting of presence and absence—he says, "of presences and absences...
For if one were to admit the mutual presence of one thing in another, it would be difficult to establish even the principle of self-explanatory consistency (svapara-nirvāhakatva).

Another mutual non-existence (itaretarābhāva) would have to be admitted; for that too, another would be required, leading to an infinite regress. And if it is not admitted, the distinction between a real entity and a non-entity cannot be established. The meaning is: "The universe is not distinct in reality, because it is devoid of mutual non-existence, like the nature of a real entity itself. Regarding the absence of birth and so forth, he says further: "Nor [is there] non-existence..."

It refutes [the opponent's view]. The meaning is that because there is no mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*), the distinctions such as prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) are not established; consequently, birth and so forth are not established. In this regard, he first demonstrates the absence of birth in the case of the absence of prior non-existence with the words "not unknown" (*na ajñāta*). The meaning is that, due to the lack of prior non-existence, nothing whatsoever is born, just like a human horn.

Anticipating the objection that "birth is established from the perception of the unseen," he says: "For not of the unseen... The meaning is that this would lead to the absurd consequence of the birth of deities and so forth during meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and similar states. He further says: "Nor... because as long as the prior non-existence of perception is unestablished, even the perception of the unseen cannot be established. [Page 24] He explains the meaning of the term "immutable" (*kūṭastha*) by saying: "always one..."

"Form" (rūpam) means: or rather, it is immovable (kūṭastha), devoid of modification, eternal because of the absence of antecedent non-existence and so forth, uniform because of the absence of mutual non-existence, and thus non-dual—this is the meaning. Since it is immovable and eternally uniform, he says that it is therefore neither of a proven nature nor of an unproven nature, but certainly not of a nature that is both proven and unproven.

"And because of the impossibility of a dual nature. This means that, having admitted the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of the gift, one negates its birth even while that prior non-existence exists. The sense is: "The subject of dispute does not have birth, because it is non-existent, like a human horn. Furthermore, J...

and that is not possible, as he says with the words "nor" (*na ca*). [Objection: But surely there is birth for that which possesses prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*).

[The opponent claims: "It is established by perception; therefore, an inference that contradicts it is invalid. To this, [the author] says: "And it is not unestablished. Regarding the term "siddha": the meaning is that if the establishment of what is already established requires another establishment, then that prior establishment must also belong to something already established; thus, there is an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). He says "thus" (evam), meaning that the first [alternative] is not [tenable] because it contradicts its own nature, nor the second because it is fruitless.

The meaning is "he obtains. Having previously explained it as the referent of the word *tat* (That), he now explains it as the referent of the word *tvam* (Thou) with the words "or else" (*athavā*). Or rather:
Raising the objection, "How can there be infinity when the Supreme Self is that which is established by scripture? he says, "Alternatively" (*athavā*).

The meaning is that since the definition—"Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite"—is present in experience, and since infinity is impossible if it were something other than Brahman. [Page 25] The words "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) and "bliss" (*ānanda*) have distinct meanings and are not synonyms.

He raises an objection with the words "But [it is] not a synonym," because there are multiple words, such as the words "mat" and "cloth. He replies, "Or else [the word 'bliss'] would have a non-primary meaning," stating that if you have such great affection for the partless [Brahman], then you must state that the word "bliss" has the purpose of denoting the cessation of suffering.
First, he points out the inconclusiveness [of the reason] for those who maintain a difference in essential nature, regarding the phrase "the pot is different."
"It does not differ. Now, one might object: "In the theory that difference is essential nature (*svarūpa-bheda*), two distinct pots would indeed be synonyms"; anticipating this, he says:

"For it is not the case that 'different'... Even in the theory that difference is a property (*dharma-bheda*), these two words—"difference" (*bheda*) and "distinct" (*bhinna*)—[refer to the same thing].

*The Commentary on the Proof of the Desired [Conclusion]* [Page 25] Regarding the phrase "having distinct objects," he states that there is an inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) therein with the words "and they do not have distinct objects. [This is because] distinction—

He states the inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) of those who maintain difference with the words "for this very reason. The meaning is that because of the fear of an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) if difference were itself different [from the entity], there is an inconclusiveness in that—despite the empirical difference between difference and non-difference—there is in reality no otherness between them.

Now, one might object: this is not a valid example, since for the two words "knowledge" (*jñāna*) and "bliss" (*ānanda*), which denote positive entities, the word "non-difference" (*abheda*) denotes the cessation of difference...

Anticipating the objection that [the two words] have that as their meaning, he says, "And not here. The meaning is that in common usage, they are employed with the intent of referring to two properties (dharmas) in the form of positive entities. As for the phrase "otherwise": if, after denoting difference by the word "difference" and the absence of that [difference] by the word "non-difference," the intention were to establish the jar itself, then the word "jar" alone would suffice to be expressed.
The meaning is "due to parsimony" (*lāghavāt*). He states another example of the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) fallacy with the words "likewise, in that very [case]" (*tathā tatraiva*).
He explains that very point with the words "if there were non-difference" (*abhedaśced*). Regarding the term "infinite regress" (*anavasthā*):

the meaning is that if the non-difference within the phrase "different-and-non-different" (*bhinnābhinna*) is itself different-and-non-different from the locus (*dharmin*), then the non-difference in that case too would have to be different-and-non-different, leading to an infinite regress.

To avoid the aforementioned fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*), he qualifies [the term] by saying "identity-in-difference" (*bhedābheda*). To that as well, he states the fallacy of deviation with "not that. Now, it might be argued that the sentence-meaning is either excellence as a quality (*guṇa*), luminosity as a universal (*sāmānya*), or an individual (*vyakti*) qualified by both.

Anticipating the objection as to how there could be a deviation [in this case], he says, "For not... When the word *savitṛ* is asked about in its primary sense (*prātipadikārtha*), the meaning is that only that much is to be conveyed; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the answer not corresponding to the question. Thus, the meaning is that only the manifestation of light (*prakāśavyakti*) is indicated. Now, [one might object]: "But what about [the word] qualified by excellence (*prakarṣa*)..."
If it is argued that [the sun] would then be "non-excellent light," he says "nevertheless" (*tathāpi*) to address this doubt.

The meaning is: because there is a contradiction in the excellence being the locus of the quality of excellence, that specific nature by which it is the locus of the quality of excellence is itself indicated by the word "excellence" through the exclusion of non-excellence; therefore, it is not "non-excellent light."

An objection is raised: "Surely, by the word *prakarṣa* (excellence), the individual instance of a quality (*guṇavyakti*) which serves as the substratum for the property of excellence (*prakarṣatva*) is indicated; and by the word *prakāśa* (light), the individual instance of a substance (*dravyavyakti*) which manifests the universal of luminosity (*prakāśatvasāmānya*) is indicated. Therefore, because there is a difference between the two indicated portions (*lakṣyāṃśa*), the sentence cannot have an undivided meaning (*akhaṇḍārthatva*). Anticipating this, he says, "If they were distinct," and so forth. That is to say: if the two indicated objects, excellence and light, were distinct, then...

The meaning is that excellence (*prakarṣa*) would be non-luminous (*aprakāśa*) and thus could not be non-different from luminosity (*prakāśa*); and in that case, a fault will be stated. Now, one might object: "In that case, let excellence itself be nothing but luminosity. Anticipating this, he says, "If [it were] luminosity," because if it were non-different from luminosity at that time, there would be no distinction within the defined portion (*lakṣyāṃśa*). [He continues: "If it were non-luminous... (*aprakāśatve*).

He states the fault with the words "if it were non-luminous" (*aprakāśaśced iti*). For if it were non-luminous, it would lack the nature of the sun, and thus its intended meaning [would not be established].

Intending this, he offers a rebuttal with the words "True. What you say—that "heat" is the meaning of the word "intensity"—is indeed true; however, that does not hold in its primary sense (*mukhyavṛtti*), because we observe its usage in reference to the cool moon.

Nor can it be [true] even in a figurative sense (*lakṣaṇā*), for that would entail the undesirable consequence of the figurative meaning being unintended (*avivakṣitalakṣaṇā-prasaṅga*). This is because the sun, by its very nature, consists solely of light.

He concludes that there is non-segmental meaning (*akhaṇḍārthatva*) because there is a difference regarding the referential aspect (*lakṣyāṃśa*); thus he says, "Therefore, not... The words "when the sun is the object to be conveyed" are to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. The meaning is: "because of the difference in the grounds for their application" (*pravṛttinimitta*).

[Objection: "But surely," he says, "[nanu]," "just as a difference in meaning is not accepted because an inconsistency is observed, so too there is an inconsistency even when the words *prakṛṣṭa* and *prakāśa* have the same meaning. Now, one might object: "Since there exists a subverting argument (*bādhaka*) against the difference between the qualifier (*bheda*) and the qualified (*bhedī*), they must have the same referent (*abhinnārthatva*). He says, "But in this way," [pointing out] that there would be a difference in meaning. He says, "It is no problem for us," [proposing] the conclusion:

"Let them be possible. What need is there for much? Whether other examples exist or not, in any case, excellence that is not of the nature of light cannot be a qualifier of light; thus, there is indeed a deviation [from the rule] here.

He says "in every way" (sarvathā). He states that it is not merely a case of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*), but that there is also the fallacy of being "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*) because it contradicts scripture (*āgama*) which establishes its uniform nature (*ekarasa*), such as the passage "the entire mass of consciousness alone" (*prajñānaghana eva*). The meaning is that, because indicators of the intended purport—such as the uniformity of the opening and concluding sections—are observed, it is established that words such as "infinite" and "non-dual" refer to that [Brahman], and thus the reality is non-different. He raises the remaining point of objection with the word "tat" (that).
He refutes this with "tanna" (not so), on the grounds that the absence of suffering cannot serve as the meaning established by linguistic usage.
"And being free from suffering. He is not defiled by the suffering of the world, as is expressed by such words as "external" and so forth.

*Commentary on the Proof of the Desired* (iṣṭasiddhivivaraṇam) | [Page 26] The state of being suffering (*duḥkhatva*) is established. The meaning is that, because it denotes itself, it does not depend upon the word "bliss" (*ānanda*). Thus—

"By words such as 'infinite' (ananta) and so forth": even by means of words like "infinite," which exclude the limitation of objects, the state of being free from suffering is established. He says "it might be so" with the words "if [they were] non-synonymous. Furthermore, he says "and the word 'bliss' (*ānanda*)," because even if it has been stated that the word "bliss" does not contradict non-difference by having the meaning of the absence of suffering, that point is not yet established. Now, one might object: since the words "truth," "knowledge," and "infinite" have the purpose of excluding the unreal, the insentient, and the limited respectively, they do not contradict non-difference. Now, if it is argued [as follows]: "In your view, however, words such as 'bliss' (ānanda) have the purpose of excluding [what is other], and thus they indeed remain in contradiction with non-difference. for, just like words such as "truth" (satya), the word "bliss" can also be established as having the purpose of excluding what is other. Thus he says.

In this regard, the primary sense [of the word] is not intended by way of figurative implication (*vyabhiprāya*), but rather through the function of *tātparya* (purport) directed toward a reality that is positive in nature. "Thus, indeed" (tathāhi) means that this is understood through the scriptural statement of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). With the phrase "thus, indeed," he clarifies that very identity by examining what precedes and follows. If, upon examining the purport of the sentence, Brahman, the Self, and bliss are indeed one, how then is there a separate designation?

Anticipating this objection, he says: "In that regard, as follows. To show that the purport of the sentence is non-difference alone, even while restating a difference established by delusion, he provides a worldly example, saying: "And as follows.
Now, if a modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is the manifestor, why is not everything a manifestor? To this he replies: "From hearing... [Page 28]

Regarding the phrase "in that": one might object, "Bliss is not the very nature of the Self, because even when that [Self] shines, bliss does not appear, just like any other distinct entity. ...411 because it possesses excellence of birth and so forth; therefore, like [the distinction between] fair and dark complexions, it is a specific form whose intrinsic nature is purity.

[Page 291] Now, having raised the objection, "In that case, let it be mixed with human and non-human purposes," he says "niravadya" (faultless), implying that if that were so, liberation itself would not exist. Furthermore, he says this to show that the Self is not subordinate to anything else.

"And of another" means that no relationship of being a subordinate (śeṣatva) and a principal (śeṣitva) is observed between them. Regarding the phrase "nothing else": other things such as sandalwood or women are not pleasant because they exist for the sake of something else; therefore, they are not happiness. One might object that even the means of attaining a means [to happiness] is seen to be dear; therefore, it cannot be said that there is no other thing dear apart from happiness and its means. Anticipating this, he says "nothing else.
Even that [means] is dear only because it is, by way of a circuitous route, subordinate to happiness. Therefore, apart from happiness and its means, there is nothing else that is dear.

The meaning is that it does not exist. "Because the absence of material objects serves to manifest space, just as the absence of burdens and the like serves to manifest the bliss of the Self, for that very reason the older Vaiśeṣikas are mistaken"—this is what he means by "for that very reason. Summarizing the meaning, he concludes with the words "Therefore," and so forth. The phrase "because the self’s being for the sake of another is not established" means that it is not established that the self exists for the sake of others such as wives, servants, and the like. Alternatively:
The meaning is that the well-known expression "I shall abide in happiness" has as its object the Self as qualified by the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa).

[Page 31] Furthermore, he states, "But if [it were] for the self," to show that the well-known notion that pleasure is for the sake of the self is rooted in delusion.

The meaning is that because the self is the locus [of experience], pleasure is not distinct from the self. He says, "But if it should be argued," [in response] to the objection that even if primary pleasure were different from the self, its appearance as having the self as its substrate would still be possible. Once the indivisible meaning of the sentence is established through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) based on non-difference—while restating the imagined difference—the coreferentiality of words such as "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) and so forth cannot [be maintained] due to their mutually contradictory meanings.

He states, "And this being so," to show that the objection—that [Brahman] cannot arise—is refuted. He states, "Thus everywhere," to show that even though there is a difference in the expressed portions (*vācyāṃśa*), the words such as "omniscient" (*sarvajña*) and so forth must be understood as having a single flavor (*ekarasa*) as their ultimate purport through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

Now, one might object: words are conventionally established in their primary senses; therefore, how can they denote another object of knowledge (*prameya*) denoted by other words which is related to their primary sense?

And they indicate [the object] through secondary implication (*lakṣaṇā*) because [the primary meaning] is untenable. The meaning is "among the primary [meanings] as being denotable. Alternatively, there is a word-break as *amukhyeṣu* (among the non-primary). In that case, the meaning is that their primacy is in relation to the bliss of the essential nature (*svarūpa-sukha*), and not because they are undenotable.
[These are distinguished] from one another by way of excluding the false, the insentient, suffering, and the limited.
"By way of the relationship between the constrained and the constrainer" means that through the knowledge of objects existing in the relationship of qualifier and qualified,

By the qualification "remembrance of exclusion," there is the exclusion of the unreal; by the qualification "infinite," there is the exclusion of limitation. Thus, since it is impossible for anything other than that Brahman—which is of a single flavor, beyond the scope of all means of knowledge, and from which the exclusion of insentience, suffering, unreality, and limitation follows—to reach a final conclusion, even those words [denoting attributes] refer to that very Brahman as the multiform object.

The sense is this: by means of their primary referents (*mukhyārtha*), words indicate that which is related to them through the mere fact of being established (*siddhimātreṇa*) by virtue of being the locus of the name (*nāmadhiṣṭhānatayā*). Only that much is required for the status of being indicated (*lakṣyatva*); however, such qualities as being expressible by other words are not required, because—unlike the case of "fieryness" (*paiṅgalya*) in relation to fire—they are not intended to be expressed (*avivakṣitatvāt*) due to the absence of a purely negative concomitance (*kevalavyatirekābhāvena*). Let this be so; nevertheless, in the case of correct knowledge—
Anticipating the objection that, because it is produced by unimpaired instruments, its nature as a mere apprehension (*kevalagrahaṇa*) is determined, he says:

"doṣābhāve... (regarding the absence of defects). The meaning is that for the Prābhākara, the consequence would be the collapse of his own admission that [knowledge] is intrinsically immediate (*svato’parokṣatva*). On the other hand, in his own position, the inference of the pervaded from the absence of the pervader is logical; thus he says: "viparyaye... (in the case of the contrary). Furthermore:

For one who asserts that because there is no certainty regarding the object in one case, a lack of confidence (*anāśvāsa*) is inferred even in another case, we must consider the following alternatives: is this "lack of confidence" intended to mean a lack of determination (*anadhyavasāya*), or the loss of validity (*prāmāṇyahāni*), or perhaps doubt (*saṃśaya*)? Of these, first [the first alternative]:

He replies: "And there is no lack of confidence," O messenger. The meaning is that when silver or the like is being cognized in marketplaces and such places, because it contradicts the certainty that "this is indeed silver," an indeterminate state of mind such as "What is this?"—like [the doubt] "What name does this have?"—is impossible to infer. The sense is that there is no dependence on another cognition for the sake of removing doubt, but rather for the sake of ascertainment. Now, having raised the objection that the first cognition is indistinct and produced by a mere superficial impression, while ascertainment occurs later through the cognition of specific characteristics, he says: "And not [from] another.
He refutes the second alternative with: "Nor is there invalidity due to deviation."

Is it not the case that non-deviation from the object manifested is the definition of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? As it has been said: "Validity consists in arising only when the object exists. To this, he replies: "Precisely because of its existence [as the object].
A means of valid cognition is that which accomplishes valid knowledge (*pramiti*).

This is the definition. Therefore, validity arises solely from the existence of a result (*phala*), and not from the non-deviation of the object being manifested; for even the eye, though it deviates with respect to [the color] white, possesses validity. Likewise, even smoke, though it does not deviate from fire, lacks validity when it fails to make that [fire] known due to the non-awakening of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of pervasion (*vyāpti*). Furthermore, merely—

He states that "the absence of deviation [from the probans] does not constitute the cause of validity because of the absence of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)," by saying: "And even when the result is absent... Now, one might object: "But in cases such as 'Sound is eternal because it is knowable, like space,' invalidity is observed due to deviation (*vyabhicāra*). Anticipating this, he says: "And of knowability, etc. Now, if that is so, then there is indeed deviation.

In the absence of a result, there is no cause [for knowledge]. Therefore, he says "and the absence of a result" (*phalābhāvaśca*), lest it be argued that because of this indirect deviation (*vyabhicāra*), the lack of validity would follow as a consequence. To the objection—"If *prameyatva* (knowability) and so forth were indeed the [cause], how could there be an absence of a cause?"—he replies: "Because of non-deviation" (*avyabhicārāt*). Now, if it is accepted that a deviant mark is a fallacious reason (*liṅgābhāsa*), then by analogy, cognition [of such a mark] should likewise be considered fallacious.

Anticipating the objection that this [cognition] might also be an appearance (*ābhāsa*), he says: "And cognition is just like the object. Even though cognition may be erroneous, it is a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) by virtue of its existence and its capacity to make something known, just as in the case of the four [means of knowledge]. Cognition is not a means of valid knowledge solely through non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*), because cognition—characterized as the activity of the knower—is always inferable, and thus its non-deviation cannot be apprehended.
The meaning is "because of its occurrence. He refutes the third [position] with the words "nor is it ascertained," etc.

he says, "because of the existence of the silver" (*rūpyasya sattvāt*). Now, let it be granted that the mode is not insubstantial. How does this much [solve the problem]?
It is not the case that it is a manifestation of emptiness; therefore, he says, "and it has silver as its mode.

Even though the mode of silver exists [in the cognition], because silver is the absence of mother-of-pearl, the status of being a mode of silver does not exist at all in the mother-of-pearl. Therefore, just as...

He says "it is" (viti) to show that it can be stated that such appearance does not exist at all. Regarding the fact that non-existence is simply another kind of existence, he provides the authority of his own teacher’s statement, saying "for it has been said": there is no such thing as a separate non-existence, because the cognition of "non-existent" has as its object another positive entity; thus, there is no existence of a non-existence distinct from that.

The meaning is that there is a lack of valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*). [Page 47] Having thus established the proof of error within his own position regarding the theory of misapprehension (*anyathākhyāti*), he states, "In our view, sublation (*bādha*) also [occurs]," showing that sublation is likewise established in his own position.

"Whether error be self-apprehension (ātmakhyāti), non-apprehension (akhyāti), or misapprehension (anyathākhyāti), in any case it is not the apprehension of the non-existent (asatkhyāti) nor the apprehension of the indeterminable (anirvacanīyakhyāti); thus he states the summary of the prima facie view with the words 'in any case' (sarvathāpi). || 8 ||
"Indescribable as either real or unreal" means that errors, which possess objects, are ignorance itself, being indescribable as either existent or non-existent.

He states the doubt of the *vaitaṇḍika* (sceptic), who maintains that all principles are sublated, with the words "if someone. Alternatively, he states the doubt of the proponent of the theory of non-apprehension (*akhyātivādin*) with the word "if," and then refutes it.

Regarding the word "tasya" (of that): the meaning is that error and sublation must be understood as objects of common worldly consensus (*prasiddhi*). Previously, having provisionally accepted the reasoning that establishes error and sublation as being based on such consensus, it was stated that [the object] is inexpressible (*avacanīya*). The meaning is that even the sublation [of an error] cannot serve as an additional argument for [the existence of] reality, because it is a cognition and thus possesses correspondence with reality (*yathārthatva*).

Now, it may be argued: "The indeterminability (*anirvācyatva*) [of the object] is established through the otherwise inexplicability of its appearance and its sublation. In this regard, [in the case of the experience] 'this is silver'..."

[The author] says, "For this very reason," etc. Whatever knowledge is determinable is well known to have a determinable object, just as [the cognition] whose object is "existent" (*sat*).

Knowledge. And here, the pervader (*vyāpaka*), being the state of being expressible (*nirvācyārthatva*), when it is excluded, also excludes its pervaded (*vyāpya*), namely the state of knowledge being expressible; this is the meaning.
[Page 48] Regarding reality (*satyatva*), there is the state of being accessible through means of valid cognition (*mānagamyatva*).

Since being the material cause (*upādānatva*) is not the defining factor [for Brahman], he says: "and because it is accessible through valid cognition" (*mānagamyatva*). To the objection that this may be so, he replies: "And that... The meaning is that in our position, since those two [cause and effect] are established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), they are not merely accessible through valid cognition.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "not of that which has a beginning": for clay, gold, and the like, which are associated with effects, there is indeed the status of being a material cause.

It is observed that an effect does not have another effect as its constituent part (*anvaya*). Furthermore, if an effect were to take another effect as its material cause (*upādāna*), then for each of those effects, yet another material cause would have to be posited; thus, there would be no comprehension of a causal relationship free from further requirements. Therefore, he says, "and because of infinite regress" (*anavasthānāt*). In this regard, [the opponent's position] remains unestablished.

He raises an objection regarding its being a qualifier with the word "nanu" (but). Anticipating the doubt—"How can an error, which is of the nature of manifestation, be of the nature of concealment (āvaraṇa) that is ignorance (ajñāna)?"—he says "tasyāḥ" (of that). It is well known that error itself is ignorance because it is to be removed by knowledge. Thus, because it manifests things incorrectly, it conceals their true nature; therefore, it is a concealment.
The meaning is "the state of being a maker" (kartṛtva).

Since the previous delusion cannot serve as the cause [of the subsequent one] due to the intervention of deep sleep and cosmic dissolution, he says: "or of the delusions and their latent impressions. This means that the latent impression of a previous delusion is the cause of a subsequent delusion.

The meaning is that its cause is a prior error, and the cause of that [error] is the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of that prior error; thus, the meaning is that the causality belongs either to the error or to its impressions. Now, one might object: "Just as clay is seen to be present there [in the case of a jar], why is nothing seen to be present in those instances such as errors? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "But as for that which in them... But as for that...

The meaning is that the nature of false dullness (mithyājāḍya) inherent in those [objects] is seen as that ignorance which is the material cause (upādāna). He establishes its status as a material cause with the words "of that" (tasya). Now, one might object: if beginningless ignorance is the cause of error, then because it exists at all times, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of the effect existing at all times; anticipating this doubt, he says: "even though the cause exists."
"In both ways" means whether the effect is eternal or the cause is non-eternal.

The meaning is "for the purpose of a messenger."
Because they are simultaneous, there is no relationship of cause and effect between two things produced at once, like two horns on a bull.
That which exists in the immediately preceding moment is the cause; when that [cause] exists, the effect necessarily comes to be.
Thus, it is said that the effect arises immediately after the state of the cause. And so, these two do not [arise] as one—
The Buddhist objects on the grounds of time, saying "But surely...
"But surely [there is] the destruction of the seed."

Since the sprout is never seen to arise in the absence [of a seed], the absence of the seed is the cause of the sprout. Therefore, one might suspect that it is only the absence of the cause that constitutes the effect; this is raised with the word "atha" (now/if). The response is: "In that case, the seed would not be the cause," for those seeking a sprout would not collect seeds; thus, he refutes it by stating, "that is not the cause. Alternatively:

The meaning is that its effect would be devoid of a cause. Furthermore, even when the sprout exists, since the non-existence of the destruction of the seed—which is the cause of the sprout—has not ceased, the effect and the cause would coexist. In that case, the rule that "the cessation of the cause occurs at the very preceding moment" would be violated; with this intention, he says: "even when that effect exists."

Furthermore, because destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*) is eternal, it exists even when the effect has perished; yet, while that [destruction] exists, the effect is absent. Consequently, the rule that "an effect necessarily arises when its cause is present" would not hold. Thus he says, "even in the absence of the effect. In the view that non-existence (*abhāva*) is the cause, there is no such rule as "when the cause exists, the effect necessarily arises."
It has been stated. Now, he extends that same principle to the view where the cause is a becoming (*bhāva*), saying "likewise, even when it exists" (*tathā sadapi*).

The meaning is that the cause pervades both prior and subsequent times, whereas the effect does not; therefore, the cognition does not arise at all. Having thus stated the absence of restriction regarding the latter of the two previously mentioned alternatives, he now addresses the former as well.

He states that there is no necessary rule that an effect must exist whenever its cause exists, by saying "Now, if it is only at the preceding moment," and so forth. Although the refutation has already been stated, he recalls it with the words "and because it occurs when that exists" (*tadbhāvabhāvitvāt*), in order to dispel another objection. He raises this further objection with the words "But surely" (*nanu*), etc., regarding the dispute.

Intending to show that linguistic usage must proceed according to the words themselves rather than by the force of convention—since the latter lacks authority and leads to over-extension—he says: "And there is a contradiction with the established usage of word-meanings. Furthermore, he says: "And momentariness," meaning that the inference of momentariness contradicts the established fact of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*). Moreover, [the argument] has an unestablished qualifier (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇa*).

He says "the position" and so forth, beginning with "not indeed. Now, one might object: "Even if stability is well-known in common parlance, I am nevertheless making known the truth that it is momentary. Anticipating this doubt, he says "nor all," meaning that the student is not to be constrained by the rule that this causal relation belongs only to the momentary. This is because [momentariness] is established through recognition (*pratyabhijñā*).
