Like one possessing supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*). Furthermore, on the basis of the principle that "only that which is momentary can be a cause," you assert that the recognition of one's own self as a cause is an illusion. That very point is not tenable;
thus he says, "of only that which is momentary. Why is it not tenable? To this he says, "for instance" (*tathā hi*). Of the momentary...

The meaning is that since there is no distinction in the cause between its own moment and the preceding and succeeding moments, if it produces the effect at its own moment, it would also produce it during the preceding and succeeding moments. Nor is there priority and posteriority by way of space, because priority and posteriority are observed even when things occupy the same location.

Anticipating the objection, "What follows from that sequence of time? he says: "Because there is no prior or posterior [in relation to itself].

The sequence of an entity depends upon the sequence of time; in its absence, since the reasoning regarding the sequence of entities would be untenable, the entity would have to be eternally of a single form—this is the meaning. Now, even in your own view, does time not possess another time?

Anticipating the objection that "the difficulty regarding the impossibility of priority and posteriority is the same because of the absence of duration," he refutes it with the words beginning "But surely... (nanu). The meaning is: "I do not accept that time exists within another time, as that would be untenable to reason; therefore, in our position, there is no equality of the objection. "Satyokti" [means]:

One might suspect that there is a distinction because "existence" (*bhāva*) [as a positive entity] exists whereas "destruction" (*pradhvaṃsa*) is [an absence]. Anticipating this, he says "not so.

The meaning is that it would follow because another absence is not admitted for an absence that is non-distinct from its own nature. How so? how can that which lacks the very status of being a subject (dharmitva) be a subject in relation to the properties of existence? This remains so even in the absence of a specific logical reason (tarka).

Having accepted a conventional distinction, he says: "Even though there is a distinction. The meaning is that if the effect were to exist at the time of its own destruction, it would necessarily be existent. To the objection that "let it be so," he replies with the words "And therefore" (*ataśca*).
Because there would be no time unoccupied by that effect which is the product of the root cause, that effect would have no further effect of its own.
Consequently, due to the absence of causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), it would follow that it is non-existent; this is the meaning.

[Page 52] Since it is not possible for that which is the effect of a cause intended to be momentary to itself have an effect, one must therefore accept that the cause is indeed beginningless; thus he says, "Therefore, its effect... [and so forth]. Regarding this beginninglessness—
Demonstrating the fruit of this investigation, he first states, "Of one alone," relying upon the Advaita position.

Then, relying upon the positions of the Mīmāṃsakas and others, he says, "Or as many as there are," indicating that there are multiple causes such as clay, gold, thieves, and so forth. He says, "They are eternal. Furthermore, since an effect cannot be an effect if it lacks a connection to a cause, a connection with that [cause] must be asserted.

Is the relation [of the cause] to that which is unestablished or to that which is already established? He refutes the first alternative with the words "And how? He says, "But [you] say it is the cause. [and so on]. Finally, he raises an objection regarding a specific causehood even when a particular relation exists, beginning with "the preceding... [and so on].

The meaning is that an effect is not momentary because arguments such as "whatever exists is momentary, just like a lamp; and these entities exist" lack validity due to the absence of a supporting example (*dṛṣṭānta*). Therefore, he says "from this" (*ataḥ*) and so forth, [stating] that my path should be resorted to. In the phrase "effect, cause, etc.," the word "etc. includes the restriction that the agent alone is the enjoyer and the knower alone is the agent.
The meaning is based on the Vedic scripture: "You shall perish; he becomes non-existent. He concludes the great context (*mahāprakaraṇa*).

"Therefore, of the effect..."—thus, having raised the objection against the position of momentariness, he raises it against the position of permanence as well with the words "If it were permanent. Regarding the term "time" (*kāla*): the meaning is that this contradicts such experiences as "this is the morning. By saying "I speak," etc., he introduces time through the perspective of another. Now, one might object: since the usage of the present tense in "I speak" is inevitable, conventional time (*vyāvahārika-kāla*) is accepted; however, it is refuted by reasoning (*tarka*).

Anticipating this objection, he says: "And how [could one say] 'he wishes'? Now, one might object: "Just as you refute the reality of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) which is perceived as real, so too do I refute the reality of time which has been accepted.
To this, he replies with the words "the reality of that" (*tasya satyatvam*). Furthermore, he states "if time... (*kālaśced...*) to show that time is not to be refuted for this reason either.

Just as the objects delimited by that time would be unreal if the time of a dream were unreal, so too here, if the time were defective, it would follow that the things delimited by it would also be defective. Therefore, the meaning is that one who desires the reality of things delimited by time must not find fault with time. [Page 56] Now, [regarding] the present—
[The author] refutes [the opponent's view] by stating "Is it not [the case that ignorance resides] in the mother-of-pearl? and so forth.
To the question, "Why does ignorance not have the mother-of-pearl as its locus?", he says, "Because of its insentience (*jaḍatva*). That is to say, because that mother-of-pearl is insentient.

[Alternatively,] it means because that cognition is non-insentient. [Objection: If ignorance has the knower as its locus, then [one would experience it] as "I am ignorant," just as one says "I am the knower. But...

One might raise the doubt: "Could it be that 'this is silver' [is real], while 'this is not silver' is not? This objection is raised by one who considers the knowerhood (*jñātṛtva*) to belong to consciousness as delimited by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). [The response is:
for all-pervading consciousness, when delimited by mother-of-pearl and the like, there is also a connection with the mother-of-pearl of the silver produced from ignorance (*ajñāna*) residing therein.
It should be understood that because existence (*vidyamānatva*) is compatible with co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with capacity (*śakti*), no objection can arise.

One might object: "Since the material cause of the mother-of-pearl (śukti) is also ignorance (ajñāna), does this not entail the consequence that it too must be unreal? Anticipating this, [the author] replies with the words "The cause of the mother-of-pearl also... and so forth, showing that while it is established that the silver is produced by ignorance, the intention is to prove that the mother-of-pearl and other such things are likewise produced by ignorance by means of that very same example; therefore, that [unreality of the cause] is not established at present.

One might object: "Is it not the case that ignorance (*ajñāna*) is accepted as having an object because that object possesses a specific quality characterized by the obscuration of its manifestation produced by that ignorance? Since an insentient thing (*jaḍa*), being non-luminous by nature, cannot possess such a quality, the statement that it is an object contradicts your established doctrine. Thus he raises the objection with the words, "Now, ignorance... [and so on]. Prior to sublation, existence is defined by the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*).

Since capacity (*śakti*) and its absence are established as distinct states, at that time, rather than admitting that the object possesses a specific quality characterized by error produced by that [capacity], one must admit that it possesses a specific quality characterized by an obscuration (*āvaraṇa*) produced by the absence of knowledge (*ajñāna*). Therefore, this objection is merely a manifestation of ignorance regarding the principles of our established doctrine (*siddhānta-tattva*).

He refutes this, saying, "O dull-witted one, do not say so. Alternatively, he raises an objection: since it is accepted that the inert [silver] is of an illusory nature (*prātibhāsika*) by virtue of being a superimposition (*adhyāsa*), like the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, and since ignorance (*ajñāna*) is untenable in that case—just as in the case of the silver in the shell—it would contradict the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) to state that the mother-of-pearl is the object of ignorance. Thus he asks: "But is it not ignorance...?"

He refutes [the opponent's] doubt with the words "this is merely the result of your ignorance regarding our position," stating: "Even though an insentient object such as mother-of-pearl consists of repeated mental impressions (*abhyāsa*), we accept that it possesses a reality characterized by the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā-sāmarthya*) distinct from mere illusory existence; thus, because we admit a difference between mother-of-pearl and [illusory] silver, this doubt of yours is a manifestation of your failure to understand our position. Now, [the opponent asks]: "But what is this causal efficiency?"

Having raised the objection, "How is it known that there is no ignorance in the absence of a sentient being (sattva)? he says, "For not... because it has been observed to be so in the case of the silver in the mother-of-pearl shell. The meaning is: "Because it would follow that it is real," that is, because it would follow that it is unsublated while a cognizer exists. [The opponent objects: "But this reductio ad absurdum (prasaṅga) does not apply, because absolute non-existence is not accepted and its being real is desired. To this [he replies]:
He says: "And not that [is the case]. The meaning is: because there is sublation (bādhāt) while the knower exists. Regarding "the locus of knowledge" (*jñāśraya*):
ignorance, which has the knower as its very locus, extends outwards as far as the power [of the senses] according to the analogy of a long beam of light and transforms into the form of silver.
Therefore, the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the expression "I am silver" does not occur; this is the meaning.

Alternatively, the meaning is that there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the form "this is silver" because the silver—which resides within the ignorance (*ajñāna*) supported by the consciousness of the Self—possesses a connection with the illusory appearance (*ābhāsa*) of the mother-of-pearl, which serves as the delimiting adjunct (*avacchedaka*) for that same consciousness of the Self.
Regarding this, it is not the case that knowledge or ignorance of the mother-of-pearl and the silver belong to anyone. [Page 57] It is not so.
Unable to tolerate that, the Bhāṭṭa partisan who maintains the theory of misapprehension (anyathākhyāti) objects: "But have you not said...

It is not only because of internal inconsistency that the theory is untenable;
rather, he states, "Furthermore, if it were unknown," etc., [showing] that even because the impossibility of accounting for empirical usage otherwise, the cognition of silver must be accepted.
He asserts that I do not admit a valid cognitive awareness (pramāṇajñāna) having silver as its object; rather, silver—which is born of ignorance—is merely a modification (vṛtti) of ignorance.

Anticipating this objection, he says: "That is not its measure. Furthermore, if the silver were born of ignorance (*ajñāna*), it would be remote (*parokṣa*); and that is not possible, as he says: "If that were not so... Previously, remoteness was stated because of the absence of remote cognition; he now raises the doubt that this is not the case: "Now, consciousness..."
"Because of its non-apprehension, O messenger. For, according to the view that [cognition] is an action (*kriyā*), knowledge would be inferable.

Consciousness (*saṃvit*), however, is distinct from action and is of the nature of a result (*phala*); it is indeed immediate (*aparokṣa*). Therefore, the meaning is that its absence is also immediate.

Even though ignorance (*ajñāna*) is immediate by virtue of being the absence of immediate consciousness, nevertheless, its capacity to serve as the material cause (*upādāna*) for the appearance of silver— [End of excerpt]

He refutes [the opponent's position] with the words "tasyāpi" (of that too), stating that there is no effect—whether it be direct perception through form or having the nature of a positive entity—precisely because it is a non-entity (*abhāva*). Furthermore, he rejects the claim that [the world] is produced by beginningless, indefinable ignorance (*ajñāna*) with the passage beginning "ajñānaṃ ca" (and ignorance). The term "ajñāna" is a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*). According to [the grammatical rule], the negative particle *nañ* [denotes] the absence of that [thing], something other than that, or the opposite of that.

These are the meanings. In that regard, concerning non-existence (*abhāva*), according to the view of those who maintain that it is simply another kind of existence (*bhāva*), it is indeed an entity; thus, it is not indefinable (*anirvacanīya*), and because it is an effect, it is not beginningless. Now, [one might object]: if the prior non-existence and the posterior non-existence of a cognition were themselves other cognitions, then since there would be an absence of other cognitions during states such as deep sleep or fainting, [there would be no memory] of a past cognition.
Anticipating the objection that neither the destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*) nor the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of future knowledge is established, he says "otherwise" (*anyathā*).
The meaning is that the unmodified state of the self, or the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by a previous cognition, is what constitutes the absence of cognition.
Now, even if it were a distinct entity, let the absence of cognition be simply the cause of cognition; thus, by virtue of being a cause—

Anticipating the objection that "since beginninglessness is established, even ignorance will be established as beginningless," he says: "For it is not the case that [the cause] alone... Now, one might argue: "There is no consequence of the cessation of the effect when the cause exists, because the destruction (pradhvaṃsa) is admitted to have a cause. To this he replies: "Nor is it destruction... Or rather, [this refers to] antecedent non-existence (prāgabhāva).

It has been stated that destruction and non-existence (pradhvaṃsābhāva) are effects because they are inherent in the cause of cognition; this is incorrect, as one might object that those two are themselves the causes of cognition.

Anticipating this objection, he refutes their status as causes in succession, beginning with the words "For the prior non-existence is not itself the cause," and so forth. [Page 58] And [he refutes] the reality of silver and the like.

The meaning is that because it has an existent entity as its cause, there is an absence of being an effect that is indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*). Thus says the follower of the Bhaṭṭa school [page 464,
verse 430].
The *Iṣṭasiddhivivaraṇa*. He sets forth the view of the Naiyāyikas and others with the words "If someone... and so on.
[Page 58]
"Even destruction [is not non-existent]," etc.

For it is only when destruction exists that the conventional usage of "having been destroyed" occurs; the meaning is that in its absence, such usage would not occur. The fact that antecedent non-existence (prāgabhāva) is both an effect and a positive entity (bhāva) has already been stated. Therein, he first refutes its being an effect: "Antecedent... [etc.]

Regarding the phrase "and of an entity" (*bhāvasya ca*): now he refutes its status as an entity by stating "it is simply prior non-existence" (*prāgbhāva eva*), meaning that this contradicts the established linguistic usage of the term. Anticipating the objection that "to avoid those faults, let destruction itself (*pradhvaṃsa*) be prior non-existence," he replies: "In that case, its status as an entity would not be established."

[The author] says "then it would be merely destruction," and so forth. Furthermore, if the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) were simply the destruction of the lump (*piṇḍapradhvaṃsa*), then there would be no distinction between prior non-existence and the non-existence of destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*); thus he says "of these two. The implication is that this would contradict established common consensus. ... Therefore, [prior non-existence] is beginningless and endless; [this is] not desired by the Bhāṭṭas...

Since it would follow that infinite knowledge [would be required], therefore the previously raised position— that prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) must be an entity (*bhāva*) and a product (*kārya*), and that even though destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*) is a product, it is not an entity— is concluded with the words "therefore it is not an entity. He then refutes that raised position by saying, "he should be questioned."

Now, regarding its being an entity (bhāvatva): one might raise the objection that the eternality of absolute non-existence (atyantābhāva) is observed even though it is a non-entity (abhāvatva). Anticipating this, [the author says: Page 59.

Regarding that, he states "for not" (*na hi*) to show that the property of being non-produced (*akāryatva*) is a limiting condition (*upādhi*) for eternality. He establishes that even non-existence (*abhāva*) is produced by the passage beginning with "even destruction" (*pradhvaṃsa*). He further establishes this by saying "and because it has a beginning and an end" (*ādyantavattvāt*); the meaning is that, like a jar (*ghaṭa*) and other such things, it possesses both a beginning and an end.

Now, one might object that even non-existence (*abhāva*) is indeed existence (*bhāva*), and thus the statement [that they are different] is improper because its meaning is contradictory; anticipating this, he says, "and like mutual non-existence" (*itaretarābhāvavat*). Furthermore, he states, "and the cessation of the prior non-existence of knowledge," etc., to show that the Logicians' (*Tārkika*) view is inconsistent. Even if the cessation of the prior non-existence of knowledge were distinct from knowledge, it would still possess the nature of existence (*bhāvatva*).
Having raised the alternative as to whether it is "the state of being" (*bhāvatva*) or not, he states the fault in the case of non-existence (*abhāva*) with the words "If...

The meaning is that you do not accept that the cessation of non-existence is itself non-existence. To the objection that just as for you the cessation of an entity is indeed an entity, so too for me the cessation of non-existence may well be non-existence, he says: "If it were... [and so on].

[The author] says "ditu" (thus). The meaning is that because it is separated by that absence characterized as cessation (*nivṛtti-lakṣaṇābhāva*), it is not established that the possessor of cessation (*nivṛttimat*) is the prior absence of knowledge (*jñāna-prāgabhāva*). Now, he states the same [point] even regarding the position that cessation is a positive entity (*bhāvatva*): "Even if it is a positive entity, it is likewise. Even if cessation is a positive entity, because it is separated from the possessor of cessation by that positive entity...

The meaning is that it is not the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of knowledge. It should be understood that the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of [non-existence] being a positive entity (*bhāvatva*) regarding destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*) has not been raised here because it is obvious. Having restated this very position of being a positive entity, he states another refutation: "Now... (*atha*).
"The consequence of the aforementioned fault" refers to the infinite regress of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and the non-cessation of cessation (*nivṛtti*).
The meaning is that the state you have described would result in applying [this fault] to you yourself.
[Page 60] Now, one might object:
In that case, since the destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*) of the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of knowledge is not admitted, he says: "And there is no destruction of that.

The meaning is that if the prior non-existence of knowledge were not removed, the birth of knowledge would not occur. Or rather, [he says this] so that there may not even be the destruction of knowledge—which is the very destruction of the prior non-existence of knowledge—lest such a thing happen; thus he says: "of that."

And so on. Since it is accepted that knowledge possesses the nature of a prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) with respect to its subsequent effect, if that [prior non-existence] were destroyed, the subsequent effect would not occur; thus, there would be an infinite regress of knowledge—this is the meaning. For the refutation regarding "destroyed" and "not destroyed" applies equally to the opponent as well; [for instance], the destruction of a positive entity (*bhāva*) is eternal, whereas the destruction of a non-entity (*abhāva*) is non-eternal. This is because... [the text continues].

The conceptualization that antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is beginningless while the antecedent non-existence of that non-existence has a beginning, and so forth, involves an excessive burden of complexity (*kalpanā-gaurava*).

Therefore, he concludes with the words "tasmāt" (therefore), stating that one must accept that both the destruction of knowledge and its antecedent non-existence possess the nature of being an entity (*bhāvatva*) and being an effect (*kāryatva*).
He further states, "yadi" (if), indicating that even if the position of the logicians (*tārkika*) were accepted, the establishment of the "indefinable" (*anirvācya*) would not follow.

Regarding the word "nāma": it should be understood that the statement that destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*) is "not an effect" is intended to show that it lacks the nature of being an effect—defined by its inherence in a substrate—which it does not possess because it is non-existent prior [to its occurrence]; it is not, however, intended to mean that it is beginningless (*anādi*), like antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*). Now, having raised the objection concerning another meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*), he states the impossibility of establishing [destruction] as indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*) with the words beginning with "firstly" (*prathama*): for that which is other than cognition...

The object of knowledge, the knower, and so forth—all these are determined exactly as they are perceived, whether as existing or as non-existing. Therefore, ignorance is not something indefinable, nor does it have any characteristic other than that of cognition; this is the meaning. Now, he raises the position that the negative particle (*nañ*) has a contradictory sense, beginning with "Or rather, it exists. [Objection: But if it exists, how can it be said "it does not exist"?

Or, if it is not so perceived, then because of the very absence of such a perception, it would be indefinable; anticipating the objection that it would therefore be a void or ignorance, he says, "and yet it appears. Anticipating the further objection as to why this appearance might not be like an appearance imagined by a mere wishful thought, he replies that it is not so, because it appears in a form capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā-samartha*).

Intending this, he says "all. He refutes it with "that is incorrect. Even though there is no establishment [of the object] through valid cognition, recollection, or restatement—since these lack validity—the appearance would still occur just as it does for the self; therefore, he says "insentient" (*jaḍa*). In the view that negation is a positive entity (*bhāvāntarābhāvapakṣe*), [it is established] by the means of valid cognition consisting of the perception of existence (*asti-pramāṇa*); in the view of the Logicians (*tārkika*) that negation is a non-entity, [it is established] by the means of valid cognition consisting of the perception of non-existence (*nāsti-pramāṇa*).

[Page 60] He concludes that it is not indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*) because its insentient nature is also apprehended by the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) consisting in the judgment "it does not exist," stating: "Therefore, as I have said. This is because the experience "I am ignorant" is universal.

The *māyā* (or *hava*) is indeed impossible [to define as either existent or non-existent]. Since it is the adversary of knowledge and cannot be apprehended by the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as being either existent or non-existent, its nature is precisely "indefinability" (*anirvacanīyatva*), which consists in its being distinct from both the real and the unreal. Intending this, he says: "To this it is replied. Furthermore, regarding the defect characterized by contradiction—that that which is not a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*) and is insentient (*jaḍa*) should yet be manifest—he says: "This is not a defect."

Anticipating the objection that ignorance (*avidyā*)—because it is inexpressible—is likewise accessible only through delusion (*bhrānti*), just like the appearance of silver and so forth, the author states "its effect" (*tatkārya*).

The meaning is that there is a deficiency in the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*), because even the appearance of silver is not admitted to be accessible through delusion, since it is accessible solely through experience (*anubhava*).
[Objection: But do you not know eternal experience, given that all cognitions are accepted as being non-eternal? [Reply: Even that...

Anticipating the objection that [the self] must necessarily be one or the other of those [categories], he says, "And of experience... Now, an objection is raised: "Indeed, it is observed that only an experience produced by the eyes and other sense organs, which delineates an object, is seen to be a means of proof. But for you, eternal experience is not produced in that way; therefore, like space, it is not a means of proof. Anticipating this, he says, "Even so... Even though it is eternal—

Nevertheless, the establishment of the insentient (*jaḍa*) occurs precisely through the relation characterized by the repeated practice of its identity [with consciousness]. For it is the relation with manifestation (*prakāśa-saṃsarga*) that is the determinant for the establishment of the insentient, and not "being produced" (*janyatā*), because there is an absence of pure negative concomitance (*kevala-vyatireka*); this is the meaning. He states the fault if the relation with manifestation were not the determinant with the words "otherwise" (*anyathā*). Now, [one might object]: if [the insentient] is established through its relation with eternal experience (*nityānubhava*), [then what of it?]
Anticipating the objection that everything would be established at all times and that the eyes and other organs would be useless, he says: "But of form and so forth...

The meaning is this: because the connection with the experience of form and so forth depends upon the modifications (*vṛtti*) of the internal organ produced by the eyes and other organs, there is no futility of the eyes and so forth; and since these modifications are occasional, there is no consequence of [the objects] being established at all times. [Page 61]
[The opponent objects: "But surely, since the experience favored by you is immutable (*kūṭastha*), it does not illuminate [objects]; thus, the designation of it as an agent is untenable.
Furthermore, because it is unattached (*asaṅga*), its contact with an object is also impossible. To this he replies: "Just as though it were eternal...

He establishes that it is not accessible through the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) with the words: "For even a means of valid cognition... It is also not something to be removed by the means of valid cognition.

The meaning is this: because it would lead to the fallacy of infinite regress, a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is not itself cognizable by another means of valid cognition; how much less so can that which is to be removed—such as ignorance—be cognized by another means of valid cognition, whether it be of the same class as that which removes it or otherwise? Even if it were cognizable by a means of valid cognition, one must choose between it being cognizable by inference or cognizable by perception; regarding the first alternative, he says: "By a means of valid cognition... (*pramāṇataḥ*).

Regarding the phrase "dabhāvau": furthermore, for the Bhāṭṭa, what is called a "result" (phala) is manifestation delimited by an object. However, in the case of memory and so forth, because there is no rule of necessity regarding their being true to the object, there is no result. If it does exist, then due to the rule of necessity regarding being true to the object, there is validity (*prāmāṇya*).
[Page 467]

This leads to an undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*). Therefore, he says "smṛtibhrāntau" [in the verse], meaning that it cannot be an object of inference. He refutes the second alternative with "na ca jñānam" [knowledge is not...]. If that were so, then that action (or quality) would have to make itself its own object;
therefore, he says "nāpyātmānam" [nor itself]. Knowledge does not make itself its own object, nor its own substratum, nor its own attributes.

One might object that [the argument] "it acts because it possesses the quality of being an action, like that which is commonly accepted" is sublated by the impossibility of establishing its status as an object; this is raised with the words beginning "clay, etc. and ending with "if they are made into objects. He refutes this with the word "tadvat" (like that). Now, one might argue that pleasure and so forth, as well as their absences, possess the status of being objects of a cognition that has a common locus.

Fearing that this might also apply to knowledge (*jñāna*), he concludes the previously stated point—that ignorance (*ajñāna*) is known through internal perception (*sākṣivedyatva*)—by stating "therefore" (*tasmāt*) and so forth. The meaning is: pleasure and the like do not have as their object a locus identical to their own, because they are immediate (*aparokṣatva*), just like knowledge. [This is established] by positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).
It should be understood that there is "otherwise-established" (*anyathāsiddhi*) because [the self] is the cause of its own production, not the cause of its cognition.
[Page 62] Now, let it be that [the self] is self-cognizable; what follows from that? To this he says: "Therefore, [there is no over-extension] regarding existence and non-existence.

Here, he raises the objection of an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) with the word "Now" (*nanu*). He replies that there is no such over-extension because the self is cognizable through the means of valid cognition concerning existence (*bhāvapramāṇa*).
He refutes this, saying "no. [The opponent objects: "Is it not the case that whatever produces an excellence (*atiśaya*) in something is its object?

Since the Self is self-established (*svatasiddha*), how can scripture—which does not produce an excellence therein—have it as its domain? He raises this doubt with the words "because it is non-inert" (*so 'jaḍatvāt*). Although [the Self] is self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*) and thus possesses no excellence produced by the illumination generated by scripture...

It is true that there is no objectivity [in Brahman]; nevertheless, precisely because it is self-luminous and thus not an object for anything else, it is accessible solely through scripture (*āgama*). And since scripture possesses the excellence of being the cause for the exclusion of what is unmanifested despite having been practiced, it has that [Brahman] as its object—intending this, he offers the rebuttal with the word "true. This is an incidental rebuttal of an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

He concludes with the words "Therefore," and so forth. Having raised the objection as to how the knowledge of Brahman can have reality as its object, he states, "And because it has reality as its object," noting that there is no disagreement regarding the reality of Brahman.

He concludes the present topic with the words, "Thus, this would lead to an over-extension. Previously, it was established that [the world] is indeterminable because it cannot be apprehended by the means of valid cognition for either existence or non-existence.

This secret has been stated by way of a bold assertion (*prauḍhivāda*); now he says "na ca vayam" (and we do not [hold that...]). Alternatively, having raised the objection that there might be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of the cessation of ignorance in the fifth mode, he says "na ca. Now, even if it is something to be removed by knowledge, how can it have the meaning of the word "indefinable" (*anirvacanīya*)? To this he says "tadekam" (that one). It is not one—
It is not a single [cognition], because once that has ceased, it would follow that there could be no further error. Nor is it multiple, for [there is no] means of valid cognition [to establish that].

Because it cannot be grasped at its extremity; because it is not a real entity (*vastu*), as that would entail contradiction; nor is it a non-entity (*avastu*), because it possesses causality; it is not different from the Self, because it is not perceived independently; nor is it non-different, because it is insentient (*jaḍatva*); it is not with parts (*sāvayava*), because that would entail the consequence of being an effect; nor is it without parts (*niravayava*), because that would entail the consequence of total cessation. Having thus determined this, it is inexpressible.

The meaning is that [the object] is the referent of a word that is itself indescribable (*anirvācya*). It should be understood that the first *ca* (and) serves to indicate the conjunction of the various modes, such as "one with it," along with its existence and non-existence; whereas the second *ca* indicates the conjunction of the establishment of its being a word-referent along with the logical proof of the nature of the indescribable. Alternatively, let there be knowledge—

Anticipating the objection—namely, that while the ignorance regarding mother-of-pearl and the like is indeterminable because it is to be dispelled by valid cognition (*mātrāpanodyatvāt*), how can *māyā* and the rest be indeterminable?—he says: "That is one," and so forth.
This is because *māyā* and the rest possess the same properties as ignorance, such as unity and so on.
The meaning is that because it is impossible to speak [of it] after having determined [it], its unfitness for definition is understood.
Now, one might ask:

"In that case, for what purpose was it stated that it is inaccessible to the means of knowledge regarding existence and non-existence? To this, he says: "Existence and non-existence... [and so on]. Now, [one might object]: "But [what of] non-duality (advaita)..."

To refute the objection of sublation by non-perception from the perspective of another, he offers a dilemma: "Is it destruction? (*kiṃ pradhvaṃsam iti*). This is the meaning. The proponent of the final view (*siddhāntin*) says: "Even destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*)," and so on. The second is rejected with the words "and of another. The meaning is that because ignorance has no beginning, the production of another ignorance is impossible. There is also an illustrative example [to this effect].

He says "deficient in the probandum" (*sādhyavikala*), for even the cognition of "white" [is not so]. Regarding the phrase "the state of being burnt," he says "because of contradiction with experience" (*prāptivirodhāt*).

The meaning is: because of the contradiction with the experience of being burnt. Now, if that which is burnt does not come into being again, nor is something new produced, how then is there the repeated conventional usage of "ignorance"? To this, he says:
"But what [is the case]?"—this is the objection. Now, one might object: "Whatever form exists in the shell, all of that is perceived as being manifested by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*);

so how can it be said that it is not manifested in its entirety? Anticipating this doubt, [the author replies: because direct perception, which grasps a form qualified by the characteristic of the present time, does not possess the capacity to grasp multiple forms qualified by many future temporal characteristics.
He says "by Śukra" to indicate that, due to [the aforementioned] connection, there is no manifestation in its entirety; [he states this] regarding the non-cessation in its entirety on page 476,
line 442.

He raises an undesirable consequence—namely, that Brahman would be non-luminous—on the grounds that it is superimposed upon Brahman, saying: "But if [Brahman] were ignorance... It is true that defects exist regarding both having parts and being partless;
for this very reason, we have stated that it cannot be defined by means of having parts and so forth.

He answers with "We [say] thus," meaning "It is true for this very reason. It has been stated that if [the Self] were possessed of parts, it would be an effect. Anticipating the objection—"Even if that were the case, what fault would result?"—he says, "For thus...
Since persons would be liberated prior to the arising of ignorance, there would be an absence of bondage; and once ignorance has arisen, for those who are [already] liberated...

The meaning is that there would be the undesirable consequence of no liberation from bondage. It has already been stated that under the view of partlessness (*niraṃśatva*), there must be either total cessation or no cessation at all.

He states the resulting conclusion with the words "kṛtsna" (total): the meaning is that since ignorance would be removed in its entirety by any single cognition whatsoever, we would be liberated at all times. Furthermore, because Brahman is self-luminous (*svayaṃprakāśatva*):

He says "and because of its self-luminosity" (svayaṃprakāśatvāt) to show that there is no other form [of Brahman] that is not manifest. Because Brahman is self-luminous, it has been stated that there is simply no unmanifest form at all. In this regard, one might raise the undesirable objection that "there would be no knowledge of Brahman at all," on the grounds that knowledge is merely a manifester [of an object]. [The response is: Even with respect to Brahman, knowledge is a manifester because of the superimposition of non-manifestness upon it.
Anticipating that [the opponent] will say "it will be so," he provides the rebuttal: "Let it be so.
Not understanding the intention behind the statement "so be it," [the opponent] raises the objection that Brahman would likewise be insentient and composed of parts:
"In that case, like the power (śakti). He refutes this: "That is not so. [The opponent] then raises the objection: "In that case, there is a contradiction."

Intending to show that there is no contradiction because that which is non-luminous is merely imagined, he states the illustrative example: "even though it is self-luminous. Since they speak in such a way for the purpose of deluding others, he says: "even those seeking the highest good. Anticipating the objection that if they say so, let it be exactly as they say, he replies: "and yet it is not so. ... Now, [an objection]:

He raises the objection that the statement regarding the non-existence and so forth of consciousness is meaningless, on the grounds that since consciousness is self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*), there is no such thing as its non-manifestation; therefore, their claim that "it does not exist" or "it does not manifest" lacks substance. For when an object is manifested exactly as it is, error is impossible; thus, it is precisely the effect of error that postulates non-manifestation. Furthermore, the superimposition of non-manifestation—whether upon itself or another—[is untenable].
He provides the rebuttal that there is no infinite regress because it serves as the sustainer, stating "even the error...

[Page 72]. Although there is a difference in that the non-manifestation of the self-luminous is merely conceptual while that of the insentient is inherent, nevertheless he says "therefore" to show that there is no distinction regarding mere non-manifestation. There is no [distinction] regarding mere non-manifestation.

Regarding the term "distinction" (*viśeṣa*): for this very reason, since there is no distinction [between them], the Cārvākas employ the conventional expression "it does not exist" with respect to both the insentient (*jaḍa*) and the sentient (*ajaḍa*). Thus he says, "for this very reason. Now, one might object: even by means of the removal of ignorance, a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is indeed informative (*bodhaka*).
[Page 477] – Page 75] The First Chapter.

Anticipating the objection that it must be stated everywhere in the same form simply by making it an object [of cognition] in order to establish uniformity, he says: "For this very reason, it is not that.
Due to the diversity of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of things, as evidenced by the examples already mentioned and those yet to be mentioned, there is no uniformity at all times.

This is the meaning. Having established that even by adopting the Bhaṭṭa view—that a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is merely illuminative—there is no contradiction with one’s own position, he states his own view in the words "But when... It is established that the scripture consisting of such texts as "That thou art" possesses validity because it removes ignorance along with its effects by producing a cognition in which Brahman appears; it does not [possess validity] by generating consciousness (*saṃvit*).

This is the meaning of what was stated by Brahmanandi. Having concluded the incidental discussion, he concludes the resolution of the previously mentioned contingency of non-liberation with the words beginning "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). Stating that the two aforementioned reasons are not decisive, he again raises the doubt regarding the continued existence of a residue of ignorance with the passage beginning "But [if it is argued] that there is uniformity... and ending with "...if it is said that there would be transmigratory existence" (*saṃsāraḥ syāt* iti cet).

The proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntin*) raises an objection: "Previously, because there was no opposing factor, ignorance was complete; now, due to the arising of its opposite, not even a remnant of it remains. The opponent (*pūrvavādī*) refutes this, stating: "Knowledge does not [contradict] the remainder of ignorance," for knowledge is not in opposition to the residue of ignorance. [The *siddhāntin* replies: "Brahman-knowledge is that which removes ignorance along with its remnants."

The formal argument is: "Because it is a cognition, like the cognition of mother-of-pearl. [Page 73] Here, one raises the objection that "insentient cognition" (*jaḍajñānatva*) is a limiting condition (*upādhi*), stating "it is not so. He refutes this by stating "even in the case of self-luminous [cognition]," because [the proposed upādhi] does not pervade the probandum (*sādhyavyāpaka*). Since error is rooted in ignorance (*ajñāna*), even the fruit-cognition which is self-luminous is accompanied by...

It must be stated that [the knowledge in question] is what removes the remaining ignorance. The meaning is that there is no pervasion (vyāpti) such that whatever removes ignorance with a remainder is necessarily inert knowledge (jaḍajñāna). Now, one might object: "Since the fruit (phala) has parts, it is logical that one aspect of it remains unmanifest; however, for self-luminous knowledge (svaprakāśajñāna), which is partless, there will be the removal of all ignorance. Anticipating this doubt, he says:

"And not even for that [knowledge]"— here, having raised the alternative as to whether a remainder of ignorance is being established subsequent to the complete knowledge of Brahman or subsequent to the initial (āpātataḥ) knowledge, he refutes the first case with the words "that is not so, because of the absence of proof," etc., stating that it would be sublated by non-perception (*anupalabdhi*). Regarding the second case, he states that it is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatva*).
Regarding the word "yathā" (as):

[Page 74] He raises an objection with the words "nanu yadyapi" (now, even if... and so forth, suggesting that since the persistence of ignorance is understood through the impossibility of establishing liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*), there is no sublation by logical inconsistency. Now, let it be granted that the maintenance of the body exists; that...

One should arrange only for food, drink, and so forth, and not for anything remaining from ignorance; regarding this, he says: "And of that, its root is ignorance. Now, one might object: "But since liberation while living (jīvanmukti) does not exist at all, there can be no arising of presumptive testimony (arthāpatti) based upon it. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "If indeed... [Page 75]. Furthermore, one might argue: "Because ritual actions intended for the sake of knowledge are powerful, they possess the capacity to burn away that [knowledge]."
The *Iṣṭasiddhivivaraṇa*.
[Page 75] Anticipating an objection, he says "because," etc. Just as the sun, although capable of dispelling all darkness...

Just as a lamp, due to its obstruction by a covering, does not dispel the slight darkness remaining within it, so too knowledge (vidyā), due to its obstruction by the fruits of karma already set in motion, does not sublate the residual trace of ignorance (avidyā-leśa). However, at the time of that [residual trace’s] destruction, that very same knowledge, existing in the form of a continuous stream (saṃtati), sublates even the residual trace of ignorance; thus he says: "until the exhaustion of the enjoyment of what has been commenced" (ā-prārabdha-bhoga-kṣayāt). Now, [an objection]: [The text continues: "But surely..."
Anticipating the objection that if there is enjoyment (*bhoga*), it necessarily obstructs knowledge (*vidyā*) because it is opposed to it, he says: "In that regard, as...

The point is that since enjoyment is merely a manifestation (*pratibhāsa-mātra*), it does not oppose knowledge. Anticipating the further objection—"If there is enjoyment even for one who possesses knowledge, what is the difference between him and an ignorant person?"—he says: "The body... [and] preceded by egoism (*ahaṃkāra*).
The meaning is that non-existence is a specific state (*viśeṣa*). Now, one might object: "Knowledge does not arise while a body has been commenced for the sake of experience;
therefore, there is no coexistence of knowledge and experience. Anticipating this doubt, the author refutes it with the words beginning "Now, if it be said," and so forth.

Previously, it was stated that because it would entail the fault of excessive conceptual complexity (*kalpanā-gaurava*), it is untenable for knowledge to be produced within a body that has already begun its own course.

Now, even having granted the objection, he states the fault with the words, "even when begun by oneself. It has been said that even if the body is begun by oneself through actions for the sake of knowledge (*vidyā*), knowledge would not arise at another time because there is no difference in the lack of composure of the mind (*cittāsvāsthya*). He challenges that point with the words, "the body for the sake of knowledge" [Page 76], [referring to] the departure from the body (*utkramaṇa*) and so forth.

The basis [of this objection] is mental unease, and that is not possible in the absence of death; having thus conceded this much—that liberation while living (jīvanmukti) must necessarily be asserted—he says, "even so" (evamapi).
But [one might ask]: in the absence of a teacher, from where [could it come]?

Fearing the objection that actions might be fruitless—since it is possible for them to yield results even without a teacher, as is the case with actions such as those leading to heaven—he says: "Not indeed merely [the actions] themselves. This means independent of a teacher. Having thus refuted the non-arising [of knowledge] due to the impossibility of the meaning [otherwise], he raises another possibility regarding the attainment [of results] through the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) alone: "From the latent impression itself... [and so on]. Regarding the latent impression...

He refutes that [objection] by stating, "That is not so, because of the absence of ignorance," since the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) possessing those [attributes] has ignorance as its material cause (upādāna), and thus cannot exist in the absence of that material cause. He dismantles the illustrative example with the word "fear" (bhaya):
the meaning is that since fear, trembling, and so forth have the body as their material cause, they can continue to exist even when the efficient cause (nimitta) has ceased.

Having accepted that the state of being an effect arises from mere mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) in the case of the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*), he states the disparity in the case of the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*) with the words "Let it be so," and so forth. Now, one might object: since a rope consists of parts, a remnant of ignorance is possible; however, because the Self is partless, there can be no trace of ignorance. Anticipating this doubt, he says, "Even though it has a remnant. Furthermore, one might ask: even when knowledge has arisen, how can a trace of ignorance remain?
Anticipating the objection, "If it exists, why should it not also be the initiator of another birth?", he says, "And it is not merely this much," speaking with bold assertion.

One might object: "Since the Purāṇas record that even those who possess knowledge, such as Apāntaratamas and others, manifest in the form of Vyāsa and so forth, it follows that even a knower may experience the fruits of karma in another body. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And not [in] a body whose momentum has begun" (*na cārabdhaśarīra*).

This is because it would contradict such scriptural passages as "Then I shall attain [Brahman]" (*atha sampatsye*), which indicate that even for Apāntaratamas and others, there is no further engagement with a body once knowledge has arisen.
The experience of another body consists of the bondage of karma remaining after [the exhaustion of] past karma; however, this occurs solely by the force of *prārabdha* (commenced) karma.

[Page 77] Now, an objection: according to the scriptural text, "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself," it is impossible for one who has become Brahman through knowledge to have the experience of *prārabdha* karma, because of the prohibition of experience for Brahman in the text, "The other looks on, not eating."

Anticipating this doubt, he says: "But when the enjoyment of the commenced [karma] has begun. The obstruction caused by karma whose fruit has already begun to manifest is established both by the authoritative means of knowledge regarding liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*) and by the experience of those who know Brahman; thus, it is stated that the commencement of the enjoyment of *ārabdha* [karma] is the cause [of the body's persistence].

The designation "the state of Brahman" (*brahmabhāva*) is intended to exclude the delusion of being Brahman itself, and not to signify the actual attainment of the archetypal form (*bimba*), as indicated by the scriptural passage, "Then he will become [Brahman]" (*atha saṃpatsye*). Now, one might object: if the attainment of the state of the archetypal form does not occur immediately upon the arising of knowledge, then liberation would not result from knowledge alone, but rather from the destruction of the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). And so it is said:
Fearing that the Vedic scripture stating, "The wise man becomes immortal here," might be contradicted, he says, "Therefore, upon the arising of knowledge...

To the question "Why?", he replies, "Because of the entire cycle of transmigratory existence. The designation of one as "liberated" even while living is intended to signify the cessation of the causes for future bondage. For this very reason, the expression "living and yet liberated" is not contradictory.

There are two points. Just as the seed of a *kauṭadaṣṭa* banyan tree, even though its power to produce future sprouts and so forth has been obstructed, still maintains the designation of being a "seed," so too it is not contradictory for the ignorance that constitutes the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the individual soul (*jīva*)—though burnt in the form of initiating a future body and so on—to persist in the form of accomplishing present effects. Thus [it is said].

"The proponent withdraws [the objection], even from the wise," [he says]. Since liberation is established, there is no sublation by the undesirable consequence of non-liberation; thus he concludes with "therefore, of the knowledge of the mother-of-pearl.
Thus, in this position that indeterminable ignorance (*anirvacanīyam ajñānam*) is the cause of error, there is no undesirable consequence whatsoever.

Having thus established [the argument], he concludes the rebuttal of the objection regarding the non-establishment of the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) with the words "of the cognition of mother-of-pearl" (*śuktijñānasya*). Since the water of indeterminable ignorance (*anirvacanīyājñāna*) has been established through both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), he states that the challenge raised by the *vaitaṇḍika*—namely, that neither error (*bhrānti*) nor sublation (*bādha*) exists—is thereby refuted: "Therefore, so-called error and sublation... (*ato bhrāntibādhau nāma*).
Someone raises again, with the intention of saying more, the objection of the caviller (*vaitaṇḍika*) even though it has already been refuted, beginning with the words "someone" and so forth.
If error and sublation must be accepted because the establishment of conventional practices such as refutation is otherwise untenable, then the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) must also [be accepted].

He states that this must be accepted by the very same logic with the words "But if that were so," and so forth.

To the objection that the accomplishment of life and other functions is achieved through imagined food and the like, he says, "Or [through] the unseen" (*adṛṣṭa*). Furthermore, he says, "Nor for him... because one must accept the manifold of words, logical marks, and so on, either for the purpose of refuting the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) or for the purpose of establishing non-duality (*advaita*). Now...

Since the Vedas and other means of knowledge are instruments by their very nature, and truthfulness is not a necessary factor for being an instrument, one might suspect: "I shall rely upon the phenomenal world (prapañca) in its form as the Vedas and so forth, and then refute it in its form as reality. Anticipating this, he refutes it with parity through the passage beginning with "atha tam" (Now, him...). [Objection: But for one who asserts that "whatever is perceived is real," both error and sublation must exist.

If it is argued that since the status of being erroneous and sublatable is established in relation to knowledge, those two [erroneousness and sublatibility] are themselves real and thus not to be refuted—then we respond: in that case, since the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) would also lack reality, it would follow that it is non-existent like a rabbit's horn and therefore incapable of serving as a means [to liberation]; thus, its reality must be admitted. And if that is so, it cannot be refuted. Anticipating this, he says: "If those two... [and so on].

By the words beginning with "śritau" [the author] addresses the following objection: "But since the attributes (dharmas), such as birth and so forth—even those that are non-conditional (anau-pādhika)—are not definable through categories such as difference from their substrate (dharmin) known as the phenomenal world (prapañca), they are false; and because they are false, the phenomenal world which serves as their substrate must also be false.
Having raised this doubt, he then considers that even for error (bhrānti) and sublation (bādha), there is a dependence upon distinctions, birth, defects, the eyes, and so forth.
He refutes this by stating "Now, as for the arising of difference," and so forth, on the grounds that since those two are unestablished, they themselves are unestablished.

Having raised the objection, "Even if these two are thus untenable, they must nevertheless be accepted because they are well-known," he refutes it by stating "Nevertheless, both of them," and so forth, showing that the same applies elsewhere as well. Thus...
Having stated that the same logic applies [to both], he states the distinction: "But in the absence of those two, it is even more so. This concludes the refutation of the opponent's view.

He offers a rebuttal with the words beginning "For what purpose... [Page 80], showing that since it is impossible for one to act toward the negation of something if one considers it to be non-delusory, even the *vaitaṇḍika* (caviller) must necessarily accept both delusion and its sublation. Anticipating the objection, "Why should I be avoided even more than a madman?", he says, "For not his... [referring to the view that] "it exists" or "it does not exist."

Or else, there is delusion on the part of one who is insane. But for you, since neither delusion nor sublation exist, it follows that at the very time of certainty, there is a cognition that "delusion and sublation exist," whereby there arises the ascertainment of its being a delusion and its being sublatable.

Thus, there is the additional [fault] of possessing two contradictory properties and the non-cognition of contradiction; therefore, the meaning is that for this reason as well, you are to be rejected.

The phrase "there is also disagreement" means that there is disagreement regarding the specific nature of the substratum—such as whether it is existent, non-existent, or inexpressible; or whether it is manifold, unitary, a perception, or a memory—as well as regarding the existence or non-existence of the superimposed object in the location before one;
however, there is no disagreement regarding the actual existence of error and its sublation. This is because [the substratum] serves as the locus for such disagreement.

The first chapter.
He states the fault [arising] from the non-acceptance of error and sublation with the words "of those two. Even though they must necessarily be admitted—
Anticipating the objection, "In that case, in which position are error and sublation possible?", he says: "And this being so, even though...

[The phrase] "like real silver, a sky-flower, etc. provides the second negative example (*vyatireka-dṛṣṭānta*). Now, one might argue: "The indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*) cannot be sublated because it is distinct from the non-existent (*asat*), like real silver; nor can it be manifested [if it were non-existent], because it is distinct from the existent (*sat*), like a man's horn."

Anticipating this objection, he says: "And precisely by means of manifestation and sublation. The meaning is that since error and its sublation are impossible under any other alternative, the indeterminability [of the world] is understood through the impossibility of otherwise accounting for their establishment; thus, the inference [of the opponent] is sublated by *arthāpatti* (presumption). Furthermore, as stated by Vaitaḍika: "Just like error and its sublation, the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) must also be accepted as being truly real."

Otherwise, such worldly activities as living would be untenable; to this he replies with the words "of the phenomenal world as well. The meaning is that even though the indeterminability (anirvacanīyatva) of the world is established through scripture and reasoning, all worldly transactions are possible for the ignorant solely by virtue of its empirical reality (vyāvahārikasattva);
thus, there is "establishment otherwise" (anyathāpyupapattiḥ). [Page 81] As for the phrase "but for those who know":

The sense is that sublation occurring through imperceptible means does not necessarily result in non-existence. Regarding the argument that was stated—that if everything were indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*), then the sublated object would not possess sublateness as the sublator does, nor would the sublator possess sublativeness as the sublated object does, and thus the relationship between the sublated and the sublator could not be established—in response to that, he says: "And of error and sublation... [bhrāntibādhayośca].
The sublated nature and the indeterminability (*anirvacanīyatva*) of the cognition of silver depend upon the establishment of the sublativeness of the cognition of mother-of-pearl.
Subsequently, by that very same example, the indeterminability of the cognition of mother-of-pearl is established.
Therefore, the meaning is that indeterminability—which depends on the establishment of the relationship between the sublated and the sublator—is not itself the sublator of that [cognition].

Previously, having accepted the indeterminability (*anirvacanīyatā*) of the subverting cognition of mother-of-pearl and so forth, the possibility of the relationship between the sublated and the subverter was stated. Now, however, at the stage of establishing the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*), even the subverting cognition of mother-of-pearl and so forth lacks indeterminability, because that indeterminability occurs only subsequent to the establishment of the illustrative example. Thus, [the subverter] is not indeterminable.

To this he says, "And not by that. The meaning is that since, at present, only the error regarding silver is sublated, it is that [error] alone which is indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*). Now, just as the earthen nature of a tree and so forth, though existing, is not clearly manifested as it is in the case of a jar and so forth, so too the indeterminability of the cognition of mother-of-pearl and the like, though existing, [is not manifested].
Lest it be suspected that [the ultimate] is merely unmanifested and not non-existent at all, he says, "If even for that...

He recalls the very solution already stated with the words, "of the sublater (bādhaka)... When the status of being a sublater is established, and when [the object] is being examined by way of establishing its own position (sapakṣasiddhi), the indeterminability (anirvacanīyatā) that results does not belong to that [sublater].

[Page 81] The meaning is that it does not destroy (*hinasti*). Now, one might object: "Even when examined, since there is no illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) for the sublation (*bādhakatva*) of that which is itself indeterminable (*nirvacanīya*), there is no relief here"—thus he raises the doubt with the words "nanu satyasya" (But surely, of the real...). True.

Although there is no illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*), there is no rule that [a thing] must be accepted only as established by an example; for even the power of mantras and the like, which is not established by examples, is admitted. Furthermore, no evidence has been shown for the claim that what is unreal is incapable of sublation (*abādhakatva*). Moreover, even if it is not seen elsewhere, here itself—in the cognition of this power—there is the sublation of the inexpressible (*anirvācya*).

He dismisses [the objection] with "Let what has been done be seen," [meaning] "It is true. [The opponent objects: "Because no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is observed, the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*.

[The proponent replies: "There is indeed inference (*anumāna*)," [saying] "Is it not because of its being indefinable (*anirvacanīyatva*)? He dismisses this with "That is not so," [arguing] that it is not thus because inference is untenable. When the expectation arises as to why inference is untenable, [he explains] regarding the knowledge of power (*śakti-jñāna*)—

The construction [of the argument] is as follows: since there can be no logical reason (*hetu*) or illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) for something being a means of cognition (*bodhaka*), one might ask why that is so. This is because the establishment of the indeterminability (*anirvacanīyatva*) of the cognition of silver, and likewise the establishment of the indeterminability of the cognition of nacre, depends upon the establishment of the status of the cognition of nacre as both a means of cognition and a sublater (*bādhaka*). Now, as for this indeterminability...

If it is argued that sublation (*bādha*) is established by this much alone in the case of the theory of indeterminability (*anirvacanīyatva*), then the existence of the silver in another place and so forth would also depend upon sublation; likewise, its absolute non-existence (*tucchatva*) would also depend upon it. Therefore, fearing that sublation might be established even in the two views of absolute non-existence, he says: "And such being the case, there is no reality," [and] "indeterminability."

Just as its falsity is not caused by sublation—since the reality of the Self, which is itself unsublatable, is observed—it is, on the contrary, caused precisely by its unsublatability; so too, insubstantiality (*tucchatva*) is not caused by sublation, because that which is insubstantial cannot be sublated due to its being indefinable. Therefore, sublation belongs only to the indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*).

This is the meaning. Having thus established the unreality of the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*), he raises an objection in order to apply it to the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*): "Now, even if... and so forth. The argument is as follows: the subverting cognition of the Śruti and so on is real because it is a means of knowledge (*bodhaka*), like the cognition of a jar and the like. Anticipating the objection that the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*) in that case, he says: "For not... [Page 82].

He raises the objection that the example is devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*) with the words "even in the case of the cognition of a jar, etc. He refutes this with "that is not so," meaning that the cognition of a jar, etc., is real because it makes an object known, just like the cognition arising from Vedic revelation (*śrauta-jñāna*); therefore, there is no deficiency in the property to be proven. For that purpose—that is, for the sake of the Vedic cognition—the objects are words, word-meanings, and so forth; [the cognition] has as its domain the words, their meanings, and the relationship between them.

Regarding the object: by the phrase "from perception and so forth," it is shown that because perception and the rest are the basis upon which [scripture] depends, they possess greater force and are not to be sublated by scripture. Now, one might object: since even something unreal, such as a letter-sound (*varṇa*) or a dream-vision (*svapna*), can establish a real object, could the unreal also [be authoritative]?

Scriptural knowledge (*śrauta-jñāna*) indeed accomplishes the goal of truth; therefore, fearing that there might be a deficiency [in practice], he says "even though" (*yadyapi*).

Anticipating the objection, "What is the result of the truth of knowledge?", he says: "Because it is the object of knowledge. The meaning is: the world under dispute is real, because it is the object of knowledge, like the Self (*ātman*). Anticipating the objection that the inference for the reality of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is sublated by such scriptural texts as "One only, without a second," he states that in the face of a conflict with the inference for reality, the scripture [establishes] the oneness of the general category of existence (*sattāsāmānyaikatva*), and so forth.

He says "from scripture" (śruteḥ) because the meaning that conforms to the literal form (rūpācarita) is what should be accepted. He refutes this by saying "that is not so" (tan na), on the grounds that it is inconsistent to claim that when there is a contradiction with an inference establishing reality, another meaning must be accepted from the scripture; for non-sublation of the object is indeed a necessary condition for an inference. Therefore, since the inference is fallacious when it contradicts a scripture whose primary purport (tatparatva) [is established], whereas the scripture possesses both the capacity and the intention [to convey that meaning]...

The sense is that since both [cognitions] are independent in their apprehension, and because we observe that even a cognition which is the basis for another— such as the knowledge "this is silver"— is sublated by a subsequent cognition dependent upon it, such as "this is not silver," it would be in vain to abandon the meaning of the Śruti.
He states "also by means of inference" (*anumānato’pi*) to show that there is indeed an inference that supports the scripture.
Anticipating the objection as to what is established by the falsity of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), he says "therefore, of the cognition of jars and so forth.
He states "and all indeed... to show that the claim made—that what is unreal is never seen to be a communicator [of truth]—is unproven.

Since knowledge, even though unreal in its own nature, is capable of making things known, sublation by a sublating cognition is possible; thus he concludes with the words "therefore, of all this. Since it has been established that [the nature of reality] consists of knowledge, the cessation of ignorance is itself the cessation of error; thus, he restates the position favored by the proponent with the words, "the cessation of ignorance alone. Thinking that the question "What is this cessation of ignorance? need not be asked because it is already established, he asks, "What is that? And this objection is not tenable.

Thus he says, "That [cessation] must also be accepted by you. Since the cessation of ignorance is not admitted to be liberation, why should it be desired by me? To this he replies, "For one who does not desire that... [and so on]. Regarding the phrase "even to live": if there were no cessation of the cognition regarding rice, there would be no certainty that "this is rice," and consequently, no taking up of it.
The meaning is that there is no possibility of consumption. Regarding the phrase "to dispute":

the meaning is that if the ignorance of another is not removed by your statement, then your statement is useless. This is said in order to determine for which [position] that [statement] would be appropriate.

The meaning is: in order to determine whether cessation is tenable in the view of indeterminable ignorance (*anirvacanīyājñāna*), in the view of ignorance as the absence of knowledge (*jñānābhāvājñāna*), or even then, in the view of negation as a distinct entity (*bhāvāntarābhāva*) or in the view of mere negation (*kevalābhāva*). Tell me that: what is it?

[Page 83] Is it existent, or non-existent, or both existent and non-existent, or something to be removed by mere cognition? Regarding these, he refutes the first alternative:

Regarding the passage beginning with "If that [Self] exists," etc.: for the proponents of non-duality (advaitavādins), the consequence follows that the state of being accompanied by something else (*sadvitīyatva*) is produced by ignorance (*ajñāna*). Regarding the phrase "if it were the Self itself": having raised the doubt that [the Self] would exist eternally because it is not dependent on anything else, he says, "and because it would be causeless. Then, to the objection that it might therefore have a cause, he says, "even if it had a cause," regarding the Self—

The meaning is that, because it would have a cause by virtue of being merely that [beginningless entity], it would follow that the Self is not the substratum of beginningless ignorance. If there is a persistence in maintaining that it is its substratum, he says: "or else it would be beginningless. He says "having an impermanent substratum" (anityāśrayam) to show that [the opposite] would be the case. Having restated the second [position], he refutes it with the words "or non-existence" (athābhāva), etc. If the cessation of ignorance were merely the Self by way of having the characteristic of non-existence, then, like the Self, it would exist eternally. If it were a property (dharma) of the Self, then, if that property were distinct from its substrate (dharmin), there would be the consequence of duality (sadvitīyatva).

The meaning is that the fault already mentioned—namely, that [ignorance] would possess the nature of both existence and non-existence, and that it would exist eternally because it is non-different [from the Self]—would apply.

He addresses the third alternative with the words "likewise, if it were both existent and non-existent. The meaning is that if that [ignorance], which consists of both existence and non-existence, were different from the Self, the Self would have a second entity; if it were not different, ignorance could not exist [as a distinct entity]. Furthermore, it cannot consist of both existence and non-existence due to contradiction.

He states that the object itself does not exist with the words "nor is that [the case]. He refutes the fourth position—that it is indeterminable—with the words "nor even [is it indeterminable]. The meaning is that this would lead to the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of the impossibility of knowledge. With the words beginning with "furthermore" (kiṃca), he states another refutation regarding the positions of existence and so forth. Now, since ignorance is indeterminable, its cessation must be either existent, non-existent, or both existent and non-existent.
Or, if that [third category] is not possible, then let there be another mode distinct from the triad;

to this he says, "nor any other. He states another fault regarding its being indeterminable (anirvācya) with the words, "nor is it that very same thing," meaning that this would contradict the well-established distinction between cessation and that which ceases. Now, just as for our opponents, existence...

Furthermore, he states that "it would also have ignorance as its cause," because, while being occasional, it would be indeterminable, and thus it would necessarily have ignorance as its material cause (*upādāna*).

The meaning is that because it cannot be apprehended by the two means of knowledge (perception and inference), there would follow the consequence that even the means of knowledge itself would lack the conventional status of existence.

Now, an objection is raised: if ignorance were a non-entity (abhāva), its being the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) of cessation would be untenable, since a non-entity cannot possess a counter-positive belonging to the category of non-existence.
To this, he says: "And of that... Furthermore, regarding what was stated concerning its not being accessible through the means of knowledge for either an entity or a non-entity—

Regarding that, he states [the reason] for the indeterminability of both knowledge and ignorance with the words "jñānājñānayośca" (of knowledge and ignorance). To the question, "Let there be this lack of logical consistency;

Having accepted that ignorance is the absence of knowledge (*jñānābhāva*), it was stated that its cessation is simply the arising of knowledge. Anticipating the objection that a jar, being a distinct entity, might likewise be the cessation of ignorance, he states that since the prior ignorance characterized by the absence of knowledge ceases when knowledge arises, the cessation is simply the subsequent state of knowledge within the very self that was the locus of that ignorance.

He offers a rebuttal by adopting a fifth category— distinct from the manifest, the unmanifest, and the indefinable— stating, "This fault does not arise," and so forth. The meaning is that the entire mass of faults, which has the impossibility of the cessation of ignorance as its sole cause, does not exist when another category is possible.

[Page 86] Now, one might object: "The cessation of that which is indefinable is never observed to be itself indefinable. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Even the indefinable... The meaning is: "because of the impossibility of its manifestation. Now, one might object: "If a corresponding cessation must be stated, then let the cessation of such an indeterminable ignorance (*anirvācya-ajñāna*) be precisely that [indeterminable ignorance] itself.

Anticipating this doubt, he refutes it with the words, "then that very thing would be its own," and so forth. Furthermore, if that which is to be removed is not itself its own cessation, then [one might suggest] something of the same genus as it—

Anticipating the objection that "let there simply be cessation," he says: "Therefore, it is not anything else. Just as the cessation of darkness caused by the light of a lamp is not another form of darkness, so too the cessation of ignorance caused by the light of knowledge is not an ignorance of the same genus as that which is to be removed; this is the meaning. And in this context, the indeterminability (*anirvācyatva*) of the cessation of ignorance is of exactly that same nature.

The indeterminability (*anirvacanīyatva*) of ignorance—which consists in its being removable by knowledge—is what is being refuted here; however, this does not mean that it is entirely incapable of being defined in terms of its real nature. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the collapse of the inference for falsity (*mithyātva*). Furthermore, indeterminability is accepted [by us] in the eighth chapter [of the *Brahmasūtra*]. Therefore, [the text says]: "In this [world], there is no diversity whatsoever."

The secret point is this: since scripture, by means of negation, leads one to understand that anything other than the Self lacks reality, cessation [of bondage] is of a fifth kind and is therefore false (*mithyā*). Furthermore, it should be observed that there is no rule that what is false must necessarily be either ignorance (*avidyā*) or its effect, because this would be contradicted in cases such as the connection with ignorance or the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman. This is because [cessation] has knowledge as its cause.
