Now, one might argue that even a lump of clay, which is of a single nature, undergoes a transformation into the form of a jar, and subsequently further transformations such as a water-pot (*karaka*) and so forth.

Anticipating the objection that intermediate stages are observed [in the process], he states "of clay and so forth" to show that there is no uniformity of the cause due to the varying degrees of the entry of air and water therein. Now, one might argue: just as gold alone, which persists through various states such as bracelets, crowns, and earrings, is the partless material cause and does not cease when the effects cease, so too—
One might object that even the self does not depart when the transformation ceases; therefore, the argument "because it is absent in the absence of that" is unestablished.

In all three remaining positions as well, he recalls the previously mentioned defect with the words, "If they are not distinct.
He states that qualities such as cognition, which arise from the conjunction of the mind (*manas*), are difficult to define, using the phrase, "of the self and the mind.
If some specific excellence (*atiśaya*) conducive to the effect is postulated there, he replies with the words, "if there were a specific difference."

The meaning is that [if it were so], there would follow the undesirable consequence of [the self] being subject to excellence (*sātiśayatva*), impermanence (*anityatva*), and so forth. He raises the objection, "Even though there is no distinction among selves," suggesting that the occasional nature of the conjunction resulting from the movement of the mind is what regulates [the experience]. [This is because], since all selves are equally present in various places and there is no distinction in the action of the mind, that [conjunction]— [...is not restricted to a specific self].

He raises a doubt regarding the specific nature of mental action with the words "that which is caused by the unseen" (*yad-adṛṣṭa*). [This refers to] the mind of whichever individual soul has the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) as its cause—

The meaning is that conjunction with karma occurs through that very [specific] self, not merely by proximity to all [selves]. He refutes [the objection] with the words "adṛṣṭam api" (even the unseen merit/demerit), stating: "Even the unseen merit is restricted; it is not yet established that the mind's action is the cause of that conjunction, because the unseen merit is born from it. This is because, once the uniqueness of the unseen merit is established, [the conjunction] would have as its cause the action of the mind prompted by that [unseen merit].

The uniqueness of the conjunction [of the mind] would be established, and upon its establishment, the uniqueness of the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) would follow; thus, there is mutual dependence (*parasparāśrayatva*).

Furthermore, the postulation of beginninglessness is merely a succession of the blind. Therefore, he concludes that because the unseen force and so forth are common to all persons, there would be a conjunction of the mind with all [souls] at all times, stating: "And therefore, of the selves... and so on. Moreover—
He states with the words "of the self," etc., that [the cessation of knowledge] is not established by valid means of cognition (*prāmāṇika*).
The syntactical connection is as follows: when it is accepted that knowledge and so forth are qualities of that [self], and that the absences of knowledge and so forth are qualifiers of that [self].

[Page 92] Having raised the objection, "From what [source] does this restriction arise—that the fifth mode alone is what you have stated?"—[he replies: because the object to be negated is indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*)...

He says "you [say] so" because [it would follow that Brahman] is not an object of knowledge (*aprameyatvāt*). Now, one might raise the objection: "In that case, since the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is an object of knowledge, ignorance and its cessation will be established as having that [organ] as their locus, based on valid means of knowledge. Anticipating this, he says "but for whom... He explains precisely what is to be proven with the words "for him indeed... by way of refuting the notion of the cessation of ignorance.

He also refutes the cessation of *saṃsāra* with the words, "And because of the cessation of *saṃsāra*... As for the phrase "But if it exists": if the cessation of *saṃsāra* were non-existent, then, like the Self (*ātman*), it would exist eternally; consequently, the teachings of the scriptures and the instructions of the teacher would be rendered useless—this is the meaning. [Regarding] ignorance, which is called sleep, the internal organ...
The Sāṅkhyas maintain that [the effect] is an effect by virtue of being a modification (*vṛtti*). For that [effect], there must be either difference from or non-difference with its own cause.

He says "moreover" (*kiñca*) to reject the first alternative: the meaning is that because it would lack existence in the form of the cause, one would fall into the doctrine of the non-existent effect (*asatkāryavāda*). As for the second [alternative], is the effect non-different from the cause, or is the cause non-different from the effect?

Having raised this doubt, he replies with the first [verse]: "But while the cause remains undivided. The sense is that, in such a case, there would be no production of further effects. Anticipating the objection that even a ceased cause might arise again, he says: "And not again... [Page 93] Now, as for the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which is the cause of ignorance...

Anticipating the objection that the primary cause (*pradhāna*) exists as the cause, he says: "If it exists. Anticipating the further objection that because the root cause is beginningless, its destruction is not logical, he says: "Not so, without the production of a cause. Alternatively, just as the production of an effect occurs without the production of a [new] cause, so too the destruction of an effect occurs without the destruction of [its] cause; therefore, he says: [the following].
[Page 492] And here begins the *Eṣṭasiddhivivaraṇa*.

[Page 93] "Likewise, it is not the cause" means that if there were no distinction [between cause and effect], the cause would either lack beginning or be unproduced; consequently, either everything would arise from everything, or nothing at all would arise. Furthermore, if there were no distinction, there would be no production of anything whatsoever, because the cause—

He says, "And there is no arising of the cause," because its arising is impossible. The meaning is that when there is no arising of that [cause], i.e., when there is no arising of the cause of the cause. Furthermore, he states that total non-distinction would also follow, saying, "of the effects from the cause. He refutes the second alternative with the words, "otherwise, [there would be] the same for the cause as well."
Anticipating the objection that "let there be difference even in a form non-different from the effect; what is the fault?", he says: "And not of one... (na caikasya).
This refers to what was stated [previously]: that at the stage prior to the cessation of cognition, the silver is not born of ignorance (*ajñāna*).

Regarding this, he says "and of silver, etc. Alternatively, even though the cessation of ignorance occurs in the manner already described, the cessation of effects such as silver possesses substantial reality; therefore, he says "and of silver, etc. [Page 94] "Caused by knowledge":
the meaning is that because it is caused by knowledge, the cessation of silver and so forth is indeed the cessation of ignorance itself.

To the question, "Why is it that [knowledge] has the nature of the cessation of ignorance because it is the cause of knowledge? he says: "For knowledge is indeed the cessation of ignorance. Otherwise, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*); the meaning is that it would follow that even a jar or similar objects must be ceased.
To the question, "Why is this not possible? he says: "Regarding the object (*artha*). Its essential nature (*svarūpa*) consists solely in the making known of the object.

The meaning is that, because there is no operation other than that [of making known], it is impossible for this [cognition] to be subverting (*bādhaka*). Anticipating the objection that "a cognition is subverting precisely by making the object known as it truly is, not by removing it," he says: "And it is not merely making known. Anticipating the objection that "since a cognition arises in the form of merely making the object known, there is no operation distinct from its birth; if such an operation were to exist..."

Anticipating the objection that "since [knowledge] consists merely in the cognition of the object, it is impossible for it to remove ignorance because this contradicts the word 'merely' (*mātra*) in the phrase *arthabodhanamātrātmakatvāt*," he says: "But it is the remover... Since knowledge that has not yet removed its own prior absence cannot logically be the cause of that removal, [knowledge acts] by the mere acquisition of its own existence, through a specific nature or an intermediate operation (*avāntaravyāpāra*).
Knowledge functions as the remover [of ignorance], but not through any other primary operation of the intellect, nor through the operation consisting of the cognition of an object.

And since this is well-known in the world, no further means of proof need be sought here. Furthermore, it is established by the analogy of light and darkness that knowledge possesses the power to destroy its own opposite; thus, the meaning is that ignorance must be removable by knowledge. Let it be so.

Anticipating the objection, "What follows from this regarding silver and the like?", he says, "Silver and so forth also," in order to establish that they consist of ignorance (*ajñāna*). To support the view that sublation consists in cessation, he considers the alternative: if sublation is simply the act of making known (*bodhana*), does that sublation of the object of negation arise from the cognition of that very object, or rather from a cognition whose object is something else? Having thus raised the dilemma:

He refutes this sequentially with the words "If it were merely cognition," and so forth. Now, even on the view that sublation (*bādhana*) is simply cessation, the cognition of silver would still possess the quality of making its own object known, while the cognitions of jars and other things would possess the quality of being sublaters.

He raises the objection that the consequence applies equally to both cases by stating, "This is the same. Therein, he first refutes the consequence that the cognition of silver would sublate its own object. He says, "That is not so": because the cognition of silver does not arise with a previously established silver as its object, it cannot be a cognizer of that [silver]. Precisely because it lacks the status of being a cognizer...

The meaning is that there is no possibility of [the definition] being over-extensive (*bādhakatva-prasaṅga*), because there is an absence of the cessation of that which is invariably concomitant with it. He refutes the over-extension of the status of "sublater" (*bādhakatva*) to cognitions such as those of a jar by stating, "both of those. It is not merely the sublation of ignorance alone that is called a "sublater," but rather the sublation of ignorance as it has evolved into the form of cause and effect; therefore, there is no over-extension—this is the meaning. For example:

"Food indeed is non-food. Just as one who eats earth that has been transformed into the form of food is called an "eater of food" (annāda) and not merely an "eater of earth," so too, [the knowledge of Brahman] is a sublater (bādhaka) only by removing ignorance that has been transformed into the form of an effect, and not by merely removing ignorance in its abstract state. Some maintain that the cognition "this is not silver" is the sublater; to them, he says:

"Only from the sublater" (bādhakāt) means that the reflective cognition (*parāmarśajñāna*) regarding the absence of silver established by direct perception is a specific kind of memory, and not a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends an unknown absence of silver. He states "but in the absence of the reflective cognition" (*parāmarśakābhāve tu*) to show that it is not only non-sublating because it is not a valid means of knowledge, but also because it is not invariably concomitant. When, immediately after the cognition of the mother-of-pearl, the object—

If, due to the mind being occupied with something else, the awakening of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) for the non-existence of silver does not occur, then—in the absence of that awakened impression as a cause for reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*)—reflective awareness itself will certainly not arise. Therefore, the meaning is that because it is not universally concomitant (*ananugata*), it cannot serve as a sublater (*bādhaka*). Now, if you [the opponent] consider the sublater to be qualified...

[Page 95] He raises the objection: "But surely it can be said of me as well that the same consequence applies," thus anticipating the argument with "nanvevam" (but surely thus). Anticipating the doubt—"How can there be sublation (*bādhakatva*) without either the power of turning back or the removal [of an object] by means of 'this is not'?"—he says "or preceded by that. "Nothing else whatsoever" refers to that which was previously [discussed regarding] the theory of erroneous cognition (*anyathākhyāti*).

The meaning is that the cognition of positive entities such as a pot and the like, and the cognition of mutual absence between two such things, possess only the capacity to inform (bodhakatva) and not the capacity to sublate (bādhakatva). It has been stated that correct knowledge preceded by error is a sublater;

however, one might think: "This would only be so if something capable of being sublated could be identified. [Thus, one asks: Is it the silver that is the object of sublation, or its relation [to the substrate]?

Having raised the alternative—"or of anything else whatsoever"—he refutes the first option with the words "of what... and so forth. The meaning is that, in that case, there would be no sublated status for the silver, because it is not sublated by virtue of its existence.

[The opponent] objects: "Is it not true that what exists cannot be sublated? Since silver also does not exist in the mother-of-pearl, it will therefore be sublatable. [The author] replies: "It is true that it does not exist [there]. [The opponent] objects: "If it does not exist at all, then it must be sublatable; in that case, the doctrine of existence (*sadvāda*) is abandoned. Anticipating this, [the author] says: "But by its own nature... [The opponent asks: "In that case, where else does it exist?"

Having raised the dilemma as to whether the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is known here [in the negation], he states the fault in the first case with the words "then, by its own self" (*tarhi svātmanā*). Having restated the second alternative, he refutes it with the words "of that which is known here itself in the form of power" (*atraiva śaktyātmanā khyātasya*), and so forth. Previously, having conceded the negation, it was stated that the existence of the object to be negated would not be established.

He says that even a negation is not possible [in this case], stating: "If it is manifested in the form of mother-of-pearl (*śukti-ātmanā*). Now, one might object: "Even you accept that silver is sublated (*bādhyatva*) in the mother-of-pearl; what then? Why do you refute its sublation for me? Anticipating this, he replies: because you do not admit the kind of "removability" (*nivartyatva*) that we intend. This is the state of being negatable (*niṣedhyatva*).

For you accept that [the world] is sublated, yet there is no negation of it; therefore, its state of being sublatable is what is being refuted—thus he says, "For there is a negation... Alternatively, one might ask: "Let there be an impossibility of negation; what follows from that?
To this he replies, "For there is a negation... It has already been stated that there is no negation of this [world]; he now elaborates upon that by means of a pervasion (*vyāpti*).

By the passage beginning with "For that which has such-and-such a form," etc., [the author] states the subverting argument (*bādhaka*) regarding the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) in order to dispel the suspicion of deviation (*vyabhicāra*), saying: "In whatever place...
[He then says: "Because both are attained through cognition, there is no contradiction."

Anticipating this doubt, he says: "But in the absence of contradiction... [Page 97] He asks, "And how [is it that] the cognition of silver... in order to refute that invalidity which is asserted by the proponents of *anyathākhyāti* (the theory of misapprehension) on the grounds of its being a cognition of something otherwise.

It has been stated that because the sublated [object] is unestablished, the sublator is also unestablished. Regarding this, he raises an objection based on common consensus, beginning with "nanu" (but surely).
The meaning of "kiṃkṛtaḥ" is "by what cause," that is, by what efficient cause produced. Although [the distinction between] the sublated and the sublator—
Although such common usage exists, when investigating the cause [of sublation], one must consider the alternatives:

is the cause of being sublated the fact of conveying a different meaning, or the fact of having a contradictory meaning, or the fact of occurring earlier, or the fact of having a negative nature, or is it all of these combined? [The author] states that it is not the first, saying: "Nevertheless, it is not because of conveying a different meaning. As for the second—
He refutes this by stating, "because of the contradiction in meaning," and so forth. Now, one might object:

even if the prior [cognition] does not arise because it contradicts the subsequent one, there is nevertheless a factual contradiction between the two, since they have existence and non-existence as their respective objects. Thus, the prior cognition must be sublated. Anticipating this, he replies that, in that case, the subsequent cognition would also be subject to sublation.
He offers a rebuttal with the words "nevertheless, as for the meaning," etc., because there is no difference in the fact that the meaning is contradicted;
this refers to the subsequent [section].

"If the former [cognition] were not subject to sublation, then the latter would also not be subject to sublation, as there would be no distinction between them"—thus he says, "If not, then not even one.

He clarifies this very point by raising an objection with the words beginning "of that which is sublated," etc.: [the opponent suggests] that, having proposed a third alternative, the cognition "this is not silver" occurring after the cognition of silver would then have to be the sublater.

[The author] refutes [the objection] with the words beginning "it first removes that which is to be sublated" (*harati pūrvaṃ bādhyam*). Now, one might object: "But even that [sublating cognition] is itself sublated by the subsequent cognition 'this is not silver,' and therefore it is not a sublating [cognition]. Anticipating this doubt, [the author] replies with the following [verse], showing that despite this, it remains a sublating cognition because the definition of a sublating cognition is still present.

By the words "tyādinā" (and so forth), he shows that it is not only the previous cognitions such as "this is not silver" that are sublated by the cognition of silver; rather, even subsequent ones are [so sublated], because at a later time there can still arise the cognition "this is silver.
Thus he says, "evamuttareṣāmapi" (likewise for the subsequent ones). He states the conclusion with the words "evaṃ ca sati" (and this being so): that only the knowledge of Brahman is non-sublatable.

The meaning is that the cognition of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) would itself be subject to sublation. Having restated the fourth [position], he refutes it with the words "of the cognition of silver" and so forth, showing that even though it consists of negation, its status as a sublater is due to its contradictory nature, and this [contradictory nature] exists in the cognition of silver as well. Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that being of a contradictory nature, while possessing the character of negation, constitutes sublativeness?"

Anticipating the objection that [the cognition] might be the instigator [of doubt], he says, "This is not the person": "In that case, because it is mediated, because of immobility, and because it is a fallacious mark (*liṅgābhāsa*), this cognition—'this is not the person' or 'he does not live'—must indeed be subverting (*bādhaka*), since its object contradicts a prior cognition and it is of the nature of a negation. Let there be a sublation of the cognition that "he lives."

Then, to the question "What follows from this?", he says: "Therefore" (*ataśca*). He raises an objection, saying "But [in the case] of the person" (*nanu puṃsaḥ*), on the grounds that because of the difference in time, the qualification "having contradictory meanings" does not exist in the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*). And [he says] "when those cognitions have ceased."

There is a consequence resulting from transformation. [Page 99] When a person’s life has ceased and the conditions for that life have ceased, since there is no perception of life—which is otherwise perceptible—there arises the knowledge of the absence of life; this occurs in the case of the example. If it is argued that there is no contradiction between life and death because they occur at different times, then [the same would apply to] silver—

"The cognition of existence (*bhāva-jñāna*) is also produced by non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), because it is a cognition of absence (*abhāva-jñāna*), like the admitted cognition of absence. Therefore, he provides the rebuttal that "the definition is non-pervasive (*avyāpaka*) because there is no contradiction due to the difference in time," with the words "so too here" (*evam atrāpi*). The phrase "and when that cognition is absent" (*taj-jñāne ca asati*) is to be supplied. He states the fault in the case of contradiction with the words "otherwise" (*anyathā*), [referring to] the silver (*rūpye*).
If the cognition of non-existence that arises when the cognition of that [prior existence] is absent were to contradict the prior existence, then— in the case of the example as well—
life would not have existed even previously, because it would be contradicted by the cognition of the absence of life; and this would apply to other perishable things as well.
iṣṭasiddhivivaraṇam | [Page 99–]

The meaning is that there would be no prior existence. Having first conceded the contradiction, it was stated that [the reason] "because of having contradictory meanings" and so forth is non-conclusive (*aprayojaka*). Now, he says "what [contradiction]" (*kaśca*) because even the contradiction itself cannot be defined.
There is no contradiction between the two cognitions—"this is silver" and "this is not silver"—because each does not sublate its own respective object.

Such is the meaning. Now, one might object: since there is no contradiction among positive attributes (bhāvarūpa-dharma) in a single locus, there would likewise be no contradiction among the cognitions of those attributes.

Anticipating the objection that "since there is a contradiction between the existence and non-existence of silver in the very same object standing before one, there must indeed be a contradiction between the two cognitions," the author raises the challenge: "But even for a single [object], there are many... [regarding the existence of silver].

Regarding these two entities, does perception exist with respect to this "this-aspect" (idamaṃśa) or not? If it exists, then since both [entities] are perceived even within a single [cognition], there is no contradiction between the cognitions of those two. If it does not exist, then because the cognitions of those two simply do not exist, there is no contradiction. He refutes [the objection] with the words "that is not so" (tanna). He clarifies this very point with the words "if those two... (tau cet). Thus, regarding entities—

Having established the non-contradiction between the cognitions of existence and non-existence—whether [the objects] are perceived or unperceived—one raises a further objection to demonstrate the non-contradiction of the objects themselves: "But surely, [an object] seen in one place is not seen elsewhere... This is because there would be no limit [to such shifting]. Therefore, existence and non-existence are determined in accordance with the two cognitions that follow [the nature of] perception.

He provides the rebuttal that "this fault does not apply" by stating that these two must be accepted as being of the nature of form (*rūpya*). Furthermore, regarding the claim that multiple positive entities (*bhāvarūpa*) can exist, he states that this too is merely conventional (*prātibhāsika*) and not logical (*yauktika*), saying "even by means of positive entities. To the question "Why is this not logical?
he replies with "one," because a single entity cannot possess multiple forms. [Page 100] Because one thing cannot have many forms—

"Because it is the cause of existence by way of its own nature as a single form. He states the reason for the excellence expressed by the word "more than possible" (*saṃbhavatitarām*) with the words "by having two forms" (*dvairūpya*). Since difference is impossible within the state of being (*bhāvatva*), multiplicity is not tenable even for the forms therein. But here, because there is a distinction between existence and non-existence, there is even the possibility of a difference in forms; thus, the dual-naturedness of a single entity is all the more evident.

The meaning is that it is possible. Elsewhere, non-contradiction was asserted by accepting the observation of the coexistence of existence and non-existence; now, however, in the doctrine of difference-and-non-difference (*bhedābheda*), he says "moreover" (*kiñca*) and so forth, stating that in the case of a jar and the like, whether it is different from the clay or not, both the existence and non-existence of a single difference are observed simultaneously. But [one might object]: for the proponent of difference-and-non-difference—

He raises an objection, saying "by which form," [suggesting] that even in a single entity, the coexistence of existence and non-existence is not desired. He responds, saying "even so," [arguing] that since the distinction or non-distinction of a single substratum occurs by way of two forms, the illustrative example (dṛṣṭānta) is established. [The opponent objects: "But surely that substratum itself is not of a single form, because of its other form..."

Anticipating the objection that this is because of their real existence (*sadbhāva*), he says: "by means of other forms" (*rūpāntara*). Even by means of other forms, there is neither difference nor non-difference.

463. Even in that case, it would belong to a single [entity] alone; furthermore, if there were the existence of another form, then for that single [entity], there would be the state of being both different and non-different from it. That...

The meaning is that there would be an infinite regress, as one form would require yet another form for its negation. If the reading is *ekam rūpam* (one form), the meaning is clear. Now, an objection is raised:

"But difference and non-difference are not the affirmation and negation of an entity; rather, both are indeed positive attributes (*bhāvadharma*). Therefore, it is never observed that existence and non-existence coexist. To this, he replies with the words "nanv abhinnam" (but is it not non-different).

Even though the substratum possesses the properties of difference and non-difference, since it is impossible for difference and non-difference to possess further properties of difference [between themselves], one must state whether they are distinct or not in their own right (*svarūpeṇa*). Thereby, my statement—that existence and non-existence would occur in a single locus—would be established; thus, he rejects the alternative position by saying, "those two, difference and non-difference."

[Objection: But surely, even in the case of the two properties of difference and non-difference, those properties themselves are neither existence nor non-existence; rather, they are simply further properties (*dharmāntara*). [Response: To avoid the aforementioned fault, he anticipates the doctrine of non-absolutism (*anekāntavāda*) with the words "not different" (*na bhinnau*). [Objection: But surely, since difference and non-difference are devoid of non-difference from the locus (*dharmin*), they are distinct from it.

To address how they might be distinct from one another or from something else, he says, "and not mutually" (*na ca mithaḥ*). By defining the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*), he refutes the doctrine of non-absolutism (*anekāntavāda*) through the word "distinction" (*prabheda*) containing that negative. Having stated that it would be illogical to claim that there is no mutual distinction between difference and non-difference within the positions of "otherness" (*tadanya*) or "contrariety" (*tadviruddha*), [he proceeds] regarding the position of their absence (*tadabhāva*).
He says, "If there were no difference," providing this as an illustration for me. To the question, "What is the consequence of that?
he says, "And such being the case. Here, by the words *sva* and *svayam*, the thing which is the subject (*dharmin*) is denoted.

He applies this to the subject at hand with the words "of everything. The meaning is: if those two—the knowledge of silver and the knowledge of its absence—do not exist in that cognition (the cognition of the shell), then why do you not accept them according to the nature of the cognition?

[Page 101] For one who does not admit both existence and non-existence as residing in a single locus, there would be the abandonment of the doctrine of difference-and-non-difference (*bhedābheda-vāda*).

He states the fault with the words "atha rūpyeti" (Now, [if you say] "it is silver," etc.). The meaning is that for you, who do not accept existence and non-existence in one and the same place, that apprehension of difference and non-difference is unestablished. He raises an objection, fearing that even if one does not admit existence and non-existence in a single thing, the position of difference and non-difference would still be undermined, by saying "na tyajāmi" (I do not abandon it). He does not [abandon] that adherence to the doctrine of difference and non-difference.

The meaning is: "I renounce [non-duality] because it possesses two properties in the form of positive entities (bhāva), and I do not accept those two, namely existence and non-existence. The reason for this is stated as "na hi" (for not). Furthermore, he states "nāpi" (nor also) to show that the objection raised—namely, the suspicion that the negative particle (*na*) in the term "non-difference" (*abheda*) has a contradictory meaning—is likewise futile. Now, one might object: even if one accepts that non-difference is other than difference, its status as a non-entity (*abhāvatva*) does not follow.

Fearing that it might be argued that [the negation] would be prohibited because even non-existence (abhāva) is distinct and different [from existence], he says: "It is indeed existent" (sanneva). This refers to its nature as a positive entity (bhāvarūpa).

[Page 101]—The meaning is "only. Now, it may be argued that non-difference does not consist merely in being other than difference; rather, it also possesses non-otherness (*ananyatva*).

Furthermore, having raised the objection that—since difference and non-difference cannot possess the nature of being both different and non-different due to the impossibility of any further attributes—it must be stated that their nature as existence and non-existence consists in their very own form (*svarūpa*), and thus the [opponent's] position is established; [the author] replies that even this is inconsistent by saying, "nor is it other than or non-other [than itself].

Because it apprehends a form of silver that does not exist, the cognition would result in being devoid of an object (*arthaśūnyatva*); and that is undesirable, because the doctrine of baselessness (*nirālambanavāda*) has been refuted—this is the meaning. If it is argued that [the cognition] is sweet, he replies with the words "and being employed. He demonstrates the very absence of being endowed with reason through the passage beginning with "it is known—[the object].
Anticipating the objection, "But surely even though silver is absent in mother-of-pearl, the cognition of silver is perceptual; how then can it be denied?", he says, "even perception..."

In the view that even perception is a cognition (jñāna), the meaning is "well" (su). However, for you, the Bhāṭṭa, for whom cognition is to be inferred from its effect (phala-liṅga-anumeya), this is even more impossible to assert; thus he says: "But [if it were] inferable."
For the Bhāṭṭa, the inferential mark (*liṅga*) for inferring cognition— which consists in the activity of the cognizer— is the manifestation (*prākaṭya*) that resides in the object.
For manifestation is indeed dependent upon the object.
The meaning is that since there is no object, there is an absence of the result delimited by it; therefore, because inference is impossible, a cognition devoid of an object cannot be inferred.

Now, if one argues that even in the absence of an object, such a consciousness is observed in cases like inference and so forth, and thus the result does not inhere in the object but rather in the self—

Anticipating the objection that [the silver] might be real, he says, "consciousness also [exists]. He explains this with the words beginning "If it is argued that 'this is not silver,'" and so forth. ...

[Page 106] Thus, having first established the falsity of the silver through an examination of the initial cognition, he raises an objection by means of the power of the second cognition, ending with the words "If it is argued that 'this is not silver,'" and so forth. the meaning is "even in the absence of the silver's having the nature of mother-of-pearl. If that is so, then by way of conforming to the two cognitions, that silver must be both existent and non-existent—

he says, "Of both cognitions as well. The meaning is that because they are cognitions, it is impossible for them to be devoid of an object; therefore, there is no other alternative. Now, [the opponent asks]: "But..."

Anticipating the objection that even if there is a sublation (*bādha*) of its identity, there can be no figurative application of falsity (*mithyātva*) and so forth because of the existence of the shell (*śukti*), he says: "And existence is desired. Then, having raised another distinction, he refutes it by stating that after sublation, the perception of the silver-aspect is equally present through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) in its own delimiting locus, just as it is for the "this" aspect of the shell; thus he says: "Even by the direct perception of the shell..."
By the words "tyādinā" and so forth: the intention is that it is another silver seen in another place;

otherwise, "of that" [would mean] it would be a silver that is not sublated. The meaning is: since it exists as having the nature of silver because it was seen as such in another place, its identity with silver (*rūpyatādātmya*) would not be sublated by the cognition "this is not silver."

"Silver, too, is likewise" means that it is seen as pure. Previously, having admitted that identity (*tādātmya*) is sublated, it was stated that the well-known status of silver as being sublatable and so forth is difficult to establish. Now, he says "nor is there an identity between the two," and so on, to show that even that does not exist. He refutes the aforementioned fault...
The proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvavādī) establishes that identity alone is what is sublated by the words beginning with "nanu aikyam" [Page 108].

Regarding the phrase "otherwise": if the cognition of difference arising in an object already pervaded by the cognition of identity were its opposite and its sublater, then [the subsequent cognition] "this is silver" arising at a later time in that very same place...
The meaning is that knowledge would be the sublater. He says "nanu" (but surely) to show that this is a fallacious *prasaṅga* (reductio ad absurdum), as it lacks a locus (*āśraya*).

"Even for you" [is the phrase].

because there is an absence of the cognition "I am perceiving the identity of the mother-of-pearl and the silver," there is no ascertainment of a previously established difference.

"Otherwise" (*anyathā*): having thus refuted the second alternative through a twofold analysis, he restates and refutes the first [alternative] with the words "then, when difference is known. This is the meaning. He refutes the first [position] with the words "yadi" (if). Anticipating the objection that "because it is a cognition of non-existence (*abhāva-jñāna*), it cannot negate the former," he says "bhāvārthatve ca" (and if it has the nature of a positive entity). Anticipating this, [he replies] because it is a cognition of non-existence...
He states that it is not a sublater, like the cognition of the absence of what is currently perceived, by saying "and because it has a different object.

He raises a doubt regarding the disparity between the example and the subject of the argument with the word "nanu" (but surely), based on the space and time that delimit the object of the cognition of existence.

The meaning is this: because that [perception] makes known the non-existence [of an object] in another place and time, it is not a sublater; however, because this [inference] makes known [the non-existence] in that very same place and time, it is contradictory and thus a sublater. Even though there is such a difference, the author addresses the point of similarity regarding the intended aspect and provides a rebuttal with the words "nevertheless" (*tathāpi*), stating that just like that [perception], in the case of non-perception of what is accessible, there is non-existence—

The meaning is "as if it were cognition. He further analyzes this with the words "and also" (*api ca*). The meaning is that it is devoid of the state of being a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*). Now, one might object: [this refers to] the specific cognition that "one thing is the absence of another.

"This applies to the two silver-parts as well. He states another fault regarding the negation [of the silver] with the words "yadi nāma" (even if...).

The meaning is that since only the qualified entity (viśiṣṭa) possesses the status of being a whole (aṃśin), by the negation of that [whole], there would necessarily follow the negation of its parts, namely power (śakti) and silver (rūpya).

Regarding the phrase "of power (śakti) and silver": if that which is called the "whole" (aṃśī) were essentially a collection of two parts, then its negation would entail the negation of those two parts as well. But it is not so; rather, it is something entirely distinct, produced from power and silver through their mutual relation. And that [distinction] is established by the negation of their mutual identity in the form "this is not silver."

The object to be negated is like a cloth [negated] by the disjunction of the conjunction of its threads; therefore, the absence of negation in the form "this is not" is not a fault—this is the meaning. "It is only the state of being a substratum (*dharmitva*) and not the state of being a counter-correlative (*pratiyogitva*); for while another entity possesses the state of being a counter-correlative, even in that other entity it is only the state of being a counter-correlative and not the state of being a substratum, since that which is distinct from it has the state of being a substratum for something else. Anticipating the attachment of the proponents of duality (*dvaitavādins*), he specifically states the impossibility of the cognition of difference regarding the subject at hand: "In perception...

"In that case, if... Whether a property belongs to a single entity or to multiple entities is irrelevant if the substratum (*dharmin*) itself is imperceptible.

The meaning is that there is no difference [between them] by virtue of their true nature (*dharmatā*), as this is directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*). Anticipating the objection that a difference might be inferred because they are denotable by multiple non-synonymous words—just like "blue" and "yellow"—or that it must be postulated because such denotability would otherwise be untenable, he replies:

"Nor even... [is the case]. Having further accepted the cognition of difference and so forth, he states its non-sublativeness with the words "And how," etc.

Does the cognition of difference and so forth destroy the error directly, or by the cessation of its cause, or by making known the absence of its object? First, it cannot be the first two positions, because for you, the error and its cause—such as the Self and so forth—[are eternal].

The meaning is that because cognition is a positive entity (*vastu*), it is impossible for it to remove a positive entity. Now, although the cognition of difference (*bhedajñāna*)—since it arises merely by making known its own object of measurement (*prameya*)—does not possess the capacity to remove error, nevertheless, because the cognition of absence (*abhāvajñāna*) consists in the negation of what was previously apprehended, it stands in opposition to error; thus, it may indeed function as a remover. It is [the cognition of] the opposite.

Anticipating the objection that in the world one also observes the cessation of an object even during a conjunction [of causes], he says: "If [it were] from the cognition of difference (*bhedajñāna*).

The meaning is that since both [cognitions] are equal in their opposition by way of the object of knowledge (*prameya*) and in their capacity to make known their own objects of knowledge, there is no distinction between them regarding the cognition of non-existence (*abhāvajñāna*). Now, even for a cognition that makes an object known, there is no—

If it is claimed that the king's [knowledge] has the property of removing ignorance, then one should not say that identity and its knowledge are themselves merely the ignorance of mutual non-existence; thus he says, "nor is it ignorance. The meaning is that the status of being the ignorance of mutual non-existence regarding identity and its knowledge is neither established nor desired by you. Not only is the non-acceptance of their being ignorance [the case],...

He states "and the object" (*vastu ca*) to show that there is also the acceptance of a contrary reality. Having restated the third alternative, he refutes it with the words "the absence of identity" (*aikyasyābhāvam iti*). It is maintained that only the absence of something established by valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇika*) is itself graspable by a means of knowledge.
Therefore, the meaning is that even the identity between the shell and the silver might be some kind of real entity (*vastu*). Furthermore, as for the absence of identity...

He says "Who? to show that it cannot be determined by inference. The meaning is: how can this be stated by you? Furthermore, no other absence related to a non-existent entity is observed on the ground of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Now, let it be that there is no object— [page 507]

for that which has the nature of non-existence, is its form identity, or is the very essence of identity merely non-existence?
Regarding the question "What is the object that is conceptualized?", he refutes the first position with the words "Not, first of all...

Your established doctrine (*rāddhānta*) is indeed that the nature of non-existence (*abhāva*) is another positive entity (*bhāvāntara*), and not the very positive entity that serves as its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*). Therefore, the meaning is that for the non-existence of unity, unity itself cannot be the nature. [He now addresses] the second...
"It does not even cast away identity" means that identity is not the nature (*rūpa*) of the manifestation;

the sense is that [the manifestation] is the object of a positive cognition in the form "this is silver," and is not the object of a negative cognition. He says "if" to show that by making known the absence of identity, it is not possible for the cognition of absence to sublate the cognition of identity.

"And it is indeed identity" means that if identity has the nature of non-existence (*abhāva-svarūpa*), or if non-existence has the nature of identity, then even the cognition of non-existence takes as its object precisely the cognition of identity, because identity is of the nature of non-existence; therefore, by that [cognition of non-existence] as well, the cognition of identity becomes stable and is not sublated—this is the meaning. "That very thing" means identity itself, just as it was previously known.

The meaning is: "exactly as it was known. He raises the objection that there might be sublation (*bādhakatva*) on the grounds that previously [the identity] was understood through the method of affirmation (*vidhimukhena*) as "it exists," by stating "otherwise than that" (*tadanyathā*). Therein, having raised the dilemma—whether non-existence is to be understood as another aspect (*rūpāntara*) of that very identity, just like its existence, or as something distinct from identity—he refutes it with the words "what of that itself? (*kiṃ tasyaiva*). [This concerns] the definition of identity...

The meaning is that when there is no material form (*rūpin*), it is impossible to cause the cognition of that form or anything delimited by it as something other [than itself]; therefore, there is no impairment whatsoever to the nature of identity and existence. Regarding the case where another thing is cognized, he says "and of that" (*tasya ca*):
since by means of the cognition of absence (*abhāva*) only something other than identity is to be cognized, it is established that identity is not the object of the cognition of absence.

Therefore, the meaning is that there must indeed be the existence of identity. Now, one might object: "The identity between this [object] and the form of silver is already established in places such as a marketplace;
it is merely the relation of capacity (*śakti*) with respect to that which is denied. To this, he raises the doubt with the words "even if it exists" (*sattve 'pi*).
He refutes this with the words "that too" (*so 'pi*). That relation also is known as being present before one.

Or rather, [it is not so]. If it were not [known], there would be no sublation—just as in the case of "blue is not yellow"—because it would be a negation of something unperceived; if it were known, it would simply exist. This is the meaning. He concludes the present topic in brief with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). He states that just as the cognition of non-existence is not useful for the cessation of error, so too the cognition of difference is not useful.
"So be it.
Confirming the stated point through the words of an authoritative source, he summarizes it with the phrase "it has been said.
It is impossible to determine whether sublation consists in identity with that [sublated object], or some other form of relation.
because—

He concludes with "therefore" (*tasmāt*). He extends the defect stated regarding the theory of misapprehension (*anyathākhyāti*) to the theory of self-apprehension (*ātmakhyāti*) by saying "likewise" (*tathā*). The meaning is that even for the proponent of self-apprehension, there would be no erroneous cognition at all, or else every cognition would be erroneous. Thus: does the form (*rūpa*) or aspect (*ākāra*) of a given cognition (*buddhi*) become established by that very same cognition, or by another cognition? It is not the first case, because of the contradiction of a single entity being both object and agent; having stated this, he says "of the cognition" (*buddheśca*) to show that it is not the second case either. He states the reason for its not being an object of another cognition as "because of equality" (*samatvāt*). ...

Regarding your acceptance of self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*), he says "itself" (*svayam*). The meaning is that because another cognition and itself are not objects [of cognition], the cognition's having the form of silver is not established. Now, one might object: "Self-luminosity does not consist in being luminous independently of oneself and others, but rather in being cognizable by itself; therefore, the establishment of the form of silver [is possible]. Anticipating this, even then—

That cognition which produces the form of silver—does it know "this is silver" at the very moment of its own arising, or at a later time? Regarding the first alternative, he says: "If that very cognition [is the knower]. For one proceeds toward the object present before one having known "this is silver," and not from the knowledge that it merely appears as if external; such is the meaning.

He refutes the second [position] with the words, "Nor does it go elsewhere. Having accepted that self-cognizability is characterized by self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*), the refutation was stated; he now says that even this is seized by the impossibility (*asaṃbhava*) with the words, "Nor does it [cognize] itself.
Because a cognitive act (*vṛtti*) in which a thing mounts upon its own shoulder is impossible, it cannot be said that "it grasps itself as if it were external."

The meaning is that because there is no delineation of its own dissolution, it does not possess self-awareness (*svasaṃvedyatva*). Alternatively, he states the flaw in the position of self-awareness: "Nor does it [perceive] itself," for if this [consciousness] were to grasp itself, it would have to grasp even the form of silver as being external, just like the form of consciousness;
thus, the flaw in self-awareness is stated. If self-awareness is not tenable, then what is the recourse?
Nor should it be argued that [the cognition] is cognizable by another due to the absence of an intermediate state; thus he says, "nor is there another than that.
Alternatively, having raised the objection that the externality might be grasped by another cognition, he says, "nor is there another than that.

The meaning is that, according to your own view, since [the object] would be distinct from the cognition because it is its object, you would fall into the fallacy of contradicting your own tenets (apasiddhānta). "Another—"
He states another reason for its being an object: "and because of momentariness, etc.

[Page 114] Now, if that is so, then just as silver born of the ignorance (avidyā) of the Self is to be manifested by the Self itself according to you, so too should silver born of the ignorance of the intellect (buddhi) be manifested by the intellect itself.

Even so, it cannot be accepted as being indefinable (anirvācya), because that would result in the adoption of our own position. Therefore, if those two [existence and non-existence] are to be maintained, it must be stated that it is capable of withstanding definition (nirūpaṇasahatva).

Consequently, there must be either difference or non-difference [of that object] from the cognition. If there were non-difference, it would lack the status of being an object, just like the nature of the cognition itself.

Or rather, that [error] is not established; thus, the non-establishment of error has been stated. To this, one might object that error is established through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedyatva*), beginning with the words "Now, of the cognition... For the Buddhist, the nature of cognition is indeed self-aware. Now, if both the appearance as silver and its externality—which are currently occurring—are also self-aware, is it the very same form as the cognition, or is there something else as well?

He provides a rebuttal with the words "What is that? and so forth, stating that in the first case, every cognition would be false, and thus there would be no sublater (*bādhaka*); whereas in the last case, the cognition is indeed not false, and thus there would be nothing to be sublated (*bādhyābhāva*). Furthermore, he states with the words "Even if it were of a false nature" and so forth that the position of self-cognizability (*svasaṃvedyatva*) is untenable for another reason as well. To the question "Why?", he says:

"Likewise, because of its manifestation" means that it appears precisely in a non-false manner as "this is silver. Now, one might argue that its falsity would follow from the manifestation of a sublation; to this he says, "for not by itself," meaning that since no valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) apprehending otherwise-ness operates regarding what is self-cognized, there can be no manifestation of being sublated.

Nor is it that [the cognition] itself [is the object]. He says that there is no fault of contradicting the experience of sentient beings because of the statement "due to error. thus [it is argued]. The meaning is that there is a circularity (*itaretarāśraya*): the establishment of "misapprehension" (*anyathākhyāti*) depends upon the establishment of "error" (*bhrama*), and the establishment of "error" depends upon the establishment of "misapprehension. Anticipating the objection that "there is no proof of error because of [the resulting] similarity," he says: "But in my view... Since false silver, like real silver, lacks the status of being an object of the cognition that constitutes the operation of valid knowledge (*pramā*), it is logical that its cessation—through the removal of ignorance by means of knowledge—is its sublation (*bādhyatva*), as it is essentially of the nature of ignorance. And the removal of ignorance through knowledge is well-established.
The sense is that since [the cognition] is established by its own means alone, one should not raise objections such as mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*).

Having thus established that where perception (*pratyakṣa*) acts as a sublater (*bādhaka*), "sublation" consists in the cessation of ignorance along with its manifestations (*savilāsājñānanivṛtti*), he extends this principle to inference and other means of knowledge by stating: "Therefore, regarding the sublation by perception..."
The meaning is that they are of this very nature—that is, they consist solely in the cessation of ignorance along with its latent tendencies (*savilāsājñāna*), and not in the removal of objects.
"Otherwise" means: in the case of the removal of objects, whether [the means of knowledge] such as inference and the rest have the same object or different objects.

The meaning is that, because it would be impossible for [perception] to be sublated, the very establishment of sublation could not occur. Now, one might object: "In cases where there is an immediate (aparokṣa) error, is it that inference and the other means of knowledge do not function at all, or are they useless even when they do function?
Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And inference and the others... Although inference and the others operate only upon objects that are mediate (parokṣa)...

Although [objects] such as the moon are frequently perceived through inference and other means, the word "also" (*api*) indicates that the Self (*ātman*) and bliss (*ānanda*) function as eternally immediate (*nityāparokṣa*), because they are of the nature of light, identical with its manifestation, and self-luminous (*svayaṃprakāśa*). Therefore, even in the case of something like the oneness of the moon—which is remote (*parokṣa*)—or in the case of the mere luminosity of the Self and bliss which is immediate, there is no non-functioning of inference and the like, since they operate upon what is immediately present. This is the meaning.

If it is argued that [the scripture] is therefore redundant, he says: "Therefore, by them... The meaning is that there is no redundancy, because [the scripture] serves to reveal that the appearance contrary to reality consists of an indefinable ignorance (*anirvācyājñāna*). Now, one might object: "The moon seen today is not accompanied by a second [moon], because it is a moon, like the moon of a past day"—thus, through inference or the word of a reliable person (*āpta*), the non-existence of a double moon and so forth is established.
Anticipating the objection, "Why does one not know [the object], and why is it established that the indefinable [error] consists precisely of the nature of ignorance (*ajñāna*)?", he says:

"Because of sublation by perception" (*pratyakṣabādha*). Wherever there has been sublation by perception, there the nature of ignorance is understood to belong to the appearance of the contrary; therefore, here too, it is established as consisting precisely of the nature of ignorance. However, it is not the non-existence of the double moon and so forth [that is established].

The meaning is that when an object is pervaded by the cognition of its existence, the cognition of its non-existence is impossible for the reasons stated. Now, one might object: "Why not simply accept that the duality of the moon—the object of the error—is to be abandoned by means of the cognition of the natural non-existence of that duality? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And in the case of sublation by perception," [meaning] cessation occurs only through the cessation of ignorance.

The purport [of the statement] is that the perceived [duality] is indeterminable (anirvacanīya), by means of making known the absence of an intrinsic duality of the moon and so forth.

Therefore, the meaning is that there is a determination of indeterminability from the purport of the negative word (*nañ*). Having stated the purport of a negation sentence in common worldly usage, he extends it to the Veda as well with the words "not here, not manifold" (*neha nānā*). [This refers to] the absence of an intrinsic plurality in Brahman.

The meaning is that the intent [of the scripture] is directed toward the diversity of practices and falsity through awakening. With the words "therefore" (*tasmāt*) and so forth, he concludes the application of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*) by restating the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*). Now, one might object: "Verbal knowledge of the *agnihotra* and other rites is observed to be entirely mediate (*parokṣa*); how then can verbal knowledge of Brahman be said to be immediate (*aparokṣa*)? "Also, [the word] *mapi* [means this]: knowledge that manifests immediacy (*aparokṣya*) is immediate; there is no other kind of knowledge whatsoever that can be called immediate.
