Alternatively, it is not the manifestation of the non-existent (*asat*) or the manifestation of the indefinable (*anirvacanīya*) that is being negated; rather, it is the manifestation of the insubstantial (*tuccha*), because that lacks any essential nature (*nissvarūpatva*).
Therefore, he says "tuccha. || 28 ||

One might raise an objection: "But surely, in order to establish the indeterminability (*anirvacanīyatva*) of silver, you too have stated that there is an appearance (*ākhyāna*) of the non-existent (*tuccha*). In that case, an account of its manifestation (*khyāti*) must be provided; and if so, there can be no denial of manifestation. Thus, the very same fault you pointed out will apply to us as well. This counter-argument is raised with the word "nanu" (but surely).
[Page 530] 466 Commentary on the *iṣṭasiddhi* (iṣṭasiddhivivaraṇam).
Is it not so, according to the Gṛhya...]
How so? In that regard, first, the proponent of *anyathākhyāti* (the theory of misapprehension) states its impossibility: "It is said:

not at all... Just as there is a delusion regarding the relation between silver and mother-of-pearl, so too there is a delusion regarding the relation between the non-existent (*tuccha*) and the existent;
thus, just as the cognition of silver has mother-of-pearl as its object, the delusion of the cognition of the non-existent has the non-non-existent as its object.

Alternatively, those who maintain the theory of misapprehension (*anyathākhyāti*) must state that just as there is the error of perceiving silver in the perception of a mother-of-pearl shell, so too there is the error of perceiving the non-existent (*tuccha*) in the perception of the non-existent. However, that is not possible;

the meaning is that, unlike the cases of silver and its perception, the non-existent and its perception are not admitted by [the opponent] anywhere else. To the question, "What is the fault if they were admitted? [it is replied:]...

Regarding the phrase "and even if [the object] were established": since even a void (*tuccha*)—just like silver—is necessarily established by valid cognition elsewhere, it is impossible to deny that "a void does not exist anywhere. This is the meaning. Now, he states that such a rebuttal is impossible even for the proponent of non-apprehension (*akhyātivādin*): "Likewise, even by the proponent of non-apprehension... and so forth.

I do not maintain that error consists in the non-discrimination between what is being perceived and what is being remembered, such that there would be an illusory manifestation (*tucchakhyāti*) or the like, whereby the non-existent (*tuccha*) and so forth would have existence elsewhere, as in the case of silver; rather, it is the false attribution of manifestation to that which is unmanifested for the ignorant. Thus he objects with the words "in the case of manifestation" (*prakhyātau*). Here, he refutes [the objection] by means of an alternative analysis (*vikalpya*): "Is it [unmanifested] for all? and so on.

[The author] explains: "In the manifestation of all objects" means [in the case of] the manifestation of every object. Furthermore, he refutes [the opponent's position] by means of a dilemma—asking what the nature of that conceit (*abhimāna*) is which occurs when there is the conceit "this is unreal" despite the non-manifestation of the real object: is it of the nature of non-manifestation (*akhyāti*), or is it of the nature of manifestation (*khyāti*)? He states: "Some say... [meaning] that the error is the manifestation of the non-existent (*asatkhyāti*). This refers to an error consisting in the manifestation of the non-existent.

This is the meaning. Regarding the phrase "the fault has been stated": if there were non-apprehension (*akhyāti*) of everything, then the misconception of the unreal would occur only in states such as deep sleep; if there were non-apprehension of anything whatsoever, then [the misconception] would always exist—this is the meaning. He states another fault regarding the theory that the error consisting of the apprehension of the unreal (*asatkhyāti*) is actually non-apprehension (*akhyāti*), with the words: "In the case of non-apprehension, there is no non-apprehension. [Page 1421]

When it is argued that since the error called *asatkhyāti* (the apprehension of the non-existent) is already established by the term *akhyāti* (non-apprehension) alone, the repetition "non-apprehension of non-apprehension" (*akhyātākhyāti*) is useless, the author raises an objection to show its purpose, stating "not in vain. The meaning is this: by the first word *akhyāti*, the non-perception of the real object is intended; by the second, the failure to grasp the distinction between non-perception and perception is intended.

"In that case, just like the manifestation of silver, the manifestation of non-existence (*abhāva*) must also be accepted in some instances; otherwise, it would be impossible to distinguish between them. Thus he answers with the word "non-existent" (*asad*). He restates the second alternative with the words "now, manifestation" (*atha khyātiḥ*). In that case, since there is a rule that a manifestation must have an objective support (*ālambana*), is it non-manifestation (*akhyāti*) that is the objective support, or—

Having raised the alternative that it is a "true manifestation" (*satkhyāti*), he refutes the first [option] with the words "of that," etc. [Page 531]—[Page 143]: "of that error, the non-manifestation... (*tasya bhramasyākhyāti-*).
First Chapter:
If [the object] is the object [of cognition], is it the manifestation of all objects or the manifestation of only a few objects? The same fault has already been stated.
This is the meaning of the messenger's purpose. Regarding the second [point], he says: "It is indeed the cognition of the non-existent" (*asatkhyāti*).

The meaning is that if the cognition of the non-existent (*asatkhyāti*) alone were the objective support (*ālambana*), then, because the "this-portion" (*idamaṃśa*) of the power would be indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*), it would follow that the cognition of the non-existent is what is intended.
He states another fault regarding the cognition having the cognition of the non-existent as its objective support: "and the state of being non-delusive" (*abhrāmatvam*).

Furthermore, there would be non-delusiveness for a cognition that has the apprehension of a non-existent object (*asatkhyāti*) as its objective support; for the meaning is that when there is the cognition of a jar, the cognition "this is the cognition of a jar" does not constitute a delusive cognition. In this regard, the non-delusiveness of the apprehension of a non-existent...

He anticipates an objection with the words, "Now, [the opponent] says it is non-apprehension (akhyāti). The meaning is that, due to the influence of defects, they consider non-apprehension itself to be the apprehension of the non-existent (asatkhyāti), rather than there being a distinct category called "apprehension of the non-existent" as a real entity. He refutes this with the words, "[It is] otherwise-apprehension (anyathākhyāti).
That [non-apprehension], because it is perceived in the form of the apprehension of the non-existent, would indeed be otherwise-apprehension. That...
The meaning is that it would also be desired by you. The word *mā* connects with both sides, like a lamp placed in the middle.

Alternatively, the meaning is: "And let it not be seen," that is, non-existence (*asat-khyāti*) would be undesirable. Having thus refuted the meaning of the term "error as non-apprehension" (*akhyāti*)—namely, the error of apprehending the non-existent—he now asks: is even the non-apprehension that constitutes the substratum itself something that is apprehended?
Having raised the dilemma of whether existence (*bhāva*) is something real or merely an appearance (*khyāti*), he refutes the first alternative by stating, "Even non-appearance" (*akhyātirapi*).

The meaning is that the non-existence of the unreal and its appearance must be accepted for the sake of the manifestation of the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*). He refutes the second alternative by stating, "If it is only an appearance. Now, even the Vijñānavādin [must admit] that the void (*tuccha*) appears—

He states that [the view] beginning with "that" (tyādi) cannot be accepted as an error, saying "likewise, in the case of *ātmakhyāti*. The meaning is that if one accepts that [the object] has the form of cognition (*buddhyākāratva*), then a negation such as "it does not exist anywhere" would be untenable.

Furthermore, if non-existence (*abhāva*) is not admitted, the conventional usage of "there is no non-duality" (*nāsty advaitam*) and so forth would be impossible; likewise, if the "indefinable" (*anirvacanīya*) is not admitted...

He says, "And how [could there be] non-existence? because for the Vijñānavādin, conventional expressions such as "the emptiness of the world is not tenable" would not be established. Now, even you, who accept the error of things like "nothingness," must admit the establishment of "nothingness" and so forth in some instances; otherwise, there would follow the consequence that there is an absence of prior experience and mental impressions—which are the causes of such an error—and an absence of scriptural authority. Therefore:

He says, "But in my view... The refinement (*saṃskāra*) of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) alone is not the cause of error, because error is observed even from the refinement of error itself. Therefore, since that which is not established by any means of valid cognition appears in delusion solely through the power of ignorance (*avidyā*), it should not be accepted as being established elsewhere; this is the meaning.
Previously, it was stated that what is non-existent or inexpressible cannot be negated by means of such terms as "existent" and so forth.
[Page 532]
Commentary on the *iṣṭasiddhi* | [Page 143]

This has been established. Now, [the author] says, "Your mutual positions," because if the *pradhāna* and so forth were merely objects of delusion, it would follow that they must exist elsewhere; thus, even a negation such as "there is no primacy" or "there is no causal application" (*niyoga*) would not be established. This is the meaning.

[Objection: Is it not the case that, having restated an alternative position—which is established by your own statement as being produced by ignorance (avidyā) and realized by the witness-consciousness (sākṣin)—[the following is said]?

Anticipating the objection that "just as you refute [the opponent's position] through reasoning, we too may refute the positions of others by restating what is established for them based on our own admitted error," [the author replies: "In that case, you too must admit *avidyā*, for it generates another alternative category— one which is fit for cognition as being distinct from the non-existent (*asat*), yet fit for refutation as being distinct from the existent (*sat*)."

It might be so; otherwise, however, since the error characterized as *akhyāti* (non-apprehension) and so forth—which you favor—is established by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it would be impossible to refute it.

Thus he says, "unexamined," and so on. To the question, "Why is the refutation of that which is established by valid cognition not possible? he says, "by logic" (*nyāya*). The term "what is desired by others" (*pareṣṭam*) is to be connected both with what precedes and what follows.

Regarding the phrase "desired by others" (*pareṣṭam*), he states that its meaning refers to the difference of the self as established by the delusion of the Vaiśeṣikas and others, and momentariness as established by the delusion of the Saugatas; thus he says: "Or else, the difference of the self desired by others... (vv. 31–32).

Since ignorance cannot be denied by disputants—either because worldly error would otherwise be untenable or because the establishment of alternative positions would be impossible—the example is proven; thus he says, "Therefore" (śrataḥ). || 33 ||

Having thus established through inference, by means of an illustrative example, that the world of manifestation (*prapañca*) possesses falsity characterized by being composed of illusion (*māyāmaya*), he states [the same] from scripture as well: "Illusion and ignorance" (*māyāvidyā*). Now, one might ask: "Granted that it has illusion as its material cause (*prakṛti*), how does that entail falsity? To this he replies: "Because they are composed of illusion" (*yataḥ māyāmayāḥ*). In the world, [those things produced by] an illusionist...

The meaning is that since the term *māyā* is etymologically derived from instances such as the display of elephants, horses, chariots, and so forth, as well as from illusory errors like silver in a mother-of-pearl shell—all of which are false—it is logical that even in the Veda it should be understood in that same sense; thus, being of the nature of *māyā* is itself the definition of falsity (*mithyātva*).
This [verse] speaks of its skill in manifesting various diverse appearances within an entity that is of a single, uniform nature.
Regarding "māyā":

although it exists together with the Self, he describes its fitness for cessation by means of its unmanifest nature as "avidyā. He describes its fitness for abiding in the non-dual reality without distinction between locus and object as "tamas."
The messenger says: "It is not merely the cause of movement and so forth like well-known darkness, but rather the cause of everything.
Thus he says, "the cause. Because it is the ground of dissolution, it is indeed the material cause (*upādāna*) and not merely an instrumental cause (*nimitta*); thus he says, "dissolution."
[Page 533] – Page 145] The First Chapter.

Regarding the word "six": since both the Self (*ātman*) and ignorance (*avidyā*) would then be material causes (*upādāna*), the state of non-duality (*advitīyatva*) would be destroyed; therefore, he says "power" (*śakti*). The meaning is that because it has the Self as its substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*), it does not exist separately from it. [It is] its own substrate—

He states that "sleep" (*supti*) is the state of not obscuring the Self’s own self-luminous nature; he states that "great sleep" (*mahāsupti*) is the state of obscuring the manifestation in the form of bliss; and he states that "deep sleep" (*nidrā*) is the cause for the delusion of multiple conscious beings within the one Self. Without the knowledge produced by the scriptures, [this is not realized].

He says "the Imperishable" (akṣara) to indicate cessation. He says "space" (ākāśa) to indicate that, because it possesses the nature of the Self, it is devoid of space and time. To the question, "What is the result for you if the manifest world of the visible is of the nature of *māyā-prakṛti*?
he replies with the word "therefore" (tasmāt). Since the manifold of agency and so forth is merely *māyā*, it is subject to cessation; therefore, [the result for the Self is...]
The meaning is that the fruit consists of a twofold nature. || 34 ||

Having explained the meaning of the word *māyā* by relying on the Vedic lexicon (*nighaṇṭu*), [the author] states the object to be excluded by saying, "Now, as for the word *māyā*... He applies the verse as a refutation, beginning with, "That is not so, because of its effect...

Having raised the doubt, "How is this understood?", he addresses the non-duality and the perception thereof within the Self, which is Brahman, when the limiting adjuncts have been sublated, according to Scripture.

He states "because it is being negated" with the words beginning "for by that," etc. [The meaning is: "in the very substrate that has been apprehended, namely, in the Self which is Brahman. [Page 145] Now, let it be granted that duality and the perception thereof are indeterminable; but how is it so for Māyā? To this he says: "its cause also," etc. Previously, regarding the word *māyā*—

It has been stated that even though the word *prajñā* is listed among the names [of Brahman], because it would contradict its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word for the material cause (*prakṛti*), one must abandon the sense of "wisdom" and accept that it refers to *māyā*— which is established in the world as being indefinable (*anirvācya*) and conforming to its effects. Now, even assuming that it denotes wisdom, does it refer to the consciousness of Brahman?

Having raised the alternative—whether "prajñā" (wisdom) is the defining characteristic [of the Self] or whether it is characterized by the intellect—the author first refutes the former, stating: "Even if it were wisdom. Why?
To this he says: "Of the others," and so forth.
Mind, the Great One, intellect, Brahmā, the ancient wisdom, renown, the Lord, illusion, discernment, as well as thought and memory— these are attained.

The meaning is that, in this context, words such as *manas* and so forth, which are recited alongside *prajñā*, do not have that [specific] meaning. He states, "But the second [alternative] is accepted," saying "from scripture" (*śruta*). By the etymology "that by which an object is measured (*mīyate*)," the word *māyā* may be a name for *prajñā* characterized as the intellect (*buddhi*); this is the meaning. || 35 ||
[Page 534] 500. Commentary on the *iṣṭasiddhi*.

[Page 145] — By the statement "There is no diversity here" (*neha nānāsti*), it is said that there is no diversity in the causal Brahman, as in the case of atoms, but it is not meant that the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) does not exist. To this, he says: "And nothing else" (*nānyat ca*). In the cause...

The effect is negated; therefore, apart from that [Brahman], the existence of an effect—whose being and manifestation are dependent upon a cause—is not possible. Thus, the meaning is that the phenomenal world of effects (*kāryaprapañca*) does not exist at all. Now, since the word *iva* (as if) has the sense of comparison, the diversity of the phenomenal world of effects and the perception thereof might serve as the ground for comparison with the diversity residing in Brahman and the perception thereof.

To the objection that [the world] exists, he says, "as it were manifold" (*nāneva*). To avoid redundancy with the preceding verse, he raises an objection based on the view of Bhāskara, which would undermine the meaning of the previous verse: "But is it not the case that... Since perception and other means of knowledge possess only empirical validity (*vyāvahārika-prāmāṇya*), he says, "on account of the scriptural teaching of creation" (*sṛṣṭi-śruteḥ*). [The opponent objects: "But one sees it as if manifold..."

Since it might be argued that the manifold of effects (*kāryaprapañca*) is negated by this sentence, he says: "as it were" (*nānā-iva*). He explains that even by this sentence, only the perception of multiplicity in Brahman is negated, and not the perception of the manifold of effects;
for the meaning of the sentence is: "he does not see multiplicity in Brahman as if it were the manifold of effects. This is the sense.

Now, one might object: "The word 'nānā' (various) denotes only the manifoldness of effects (*kāryaprapañca*) and not diversity itself; therefore, this sentence merely negates the phenomenal world of effects. Anticipating this doubt, he says, "And how [could it be so]?"—meaning that even if that were the case, since the manifold world of effects is employed as a point of comparison (*upamāna*), there can be no negation of its perception.

Regarding this, having raised the alternative— whether the word *nānā* is conventionally established as denoting "manifoldness" (*nānātva*) or as denoting the objects characterized by that manifoldness— the author first refutes the former, stating "not, firstly," because it is observed [to be used] with words such as *eka* ("one") and so forth. This is the meaning.

He states the fault in the opposing view with the words "if he should say... He says that the second [view], however, is favorable to our own position with the words "...therefore not here. Because the word *nānā* denotes variously existing things (*nānābhūtavastu*), the effect is something that exists as various.
It is established that plurality is negated in Brahman. And thus, it could not exist anywhere;
for if its existence and manifestation—which are dependent upon a cause—are negated therein, its existence elsewhere cannot be established. This is the meaning.
Furthermore, as for the claim that plurality, which exists elsewhere, is merely negated in Brahman—

Having raised the dilemma as to whether that [difference] is something produced (*kārya*) or unproduced (*akārya*), he says "even difference" (*nānātvam api*) regarding the first case, meaning that its existence elsewhere [than in Brahman] is not established. Regarding the second case, however, he says "if it were unproduced" (*akāryaṃ cet*), meaning it would not be fit for negation.
To the objection that it might then be something distinct from both, he says "and not" (*na ca*). [This refers to] in the system of Bhāskara, [the view] of Brahman—
The state of being "second" means being empty of that which is distinct from it along with its effects; for otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of its loss.
[page 535] [page 148]
First Chapter. 501.
The meaning is as follows: having thus established that manifoldness (*nānātva*) is difficult to define, [he proceeds] with regard to the phenomenal world of effects (*kāryaprapañca*) as well...

He states that [the relation] is difficult to define through the conceptual alternatives of difference or non-difference by saying, "of the cause and the effect. The meaning is this: just as there would be a difference in the effect, there would likewise be a difference in the cause; consequently, it is incorrect to say that the difference of the cause is negated by scripture. For if there were a difference between cause and effect, then just as the effect [is distinct] from the cause, the cause would also [be distinct] from the effect.

[The opponent] might say: "It would grant [that]. And consequently, by the principle that "division exists only as far as there is modification, as in the world," it would follow that even Brahman is an effect; thus [the author] says, "If there were difference, [it would apply] to the cause as well. He states another fault in the position of difference with the words, "And if there were difference. He states the fault in the position of both difference and non-difference with the words, "And if it were both different and non-different."

Brahman would become non-Brahman in nature; that is to say, the Brahman-hood of Brahman would be lost because of its non-difference from the effect. Regarding this, he states the defect concerning the aspect of the effect being of the nature of Brahman with the words "tadāpi" (even then). If the effect were of the nature of Brahman, then like the cause, which is Brahman, there would be no mutual distinction among effects; yet if such distinction did exist, it would follow for Brahman as well.
The meaning is "it might be so. Now he states the defect regarding the aspect of not having Brahman as its self: "And if it were non-Brahman" (abrahmatve ca).
He states another defect regarding the aspect of having Brahman as its self: "And of that which has the form of Brahman" (brahmarūpasya ca).
By connecting the latter half [of the verse], he states the meaning of the scripture: "Precisely for this reason" (śruta eva), [referring to] that which serves as the object of comparison.

The meaning is that it is simply because of the non-existence of various distinct objects anywhere at all. He states "through ignorance" (ajñāna) to show that the appearance here is not like the illusory nature of perceiving fire and so forth in a young boy or similar cases, which is considered a mere semblance when compared to the primary reality. || 36 ||

He states that the falsity of the dualistic phenomenal world is stated even more forcefully through another scriptural passage containing positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), beginning with the words "where indeed... (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1). ... || 37 ||

Anticipating the objection that the reality of the dualistic phenomenal world (prapañca) consisting of the knower and so forth must be asserted because otherwise the knowledge of Brahman—which sublates that phenomenal world—could not be established, he says: "Of the seen and the seer. Even though the knower and so forth are false, since the Vedic knowledge is pervaded by the vision of the ultimate Self, the knowledge of Brahman which takes that [Self] as its form is possible; otherwise—

The meaning is that [the world] arises as such. Alternatively, having raised the objection that the reality of the dualistic phenomenal world must be asserted so that the power of vision (*dṛkśakti*) of the Self may have purpose, he says "of the seen and the seer" (*dṛśyadṛśyoḥ*), meaning that the power of vision has purpose in relation to its own self.
The meaning is that the vision of the Self has the Self as its object. Or, just as there is a relationship between the seen and the seeing of it... [the text continues].
Since there would likewise be an absence of the recollection of that [recollection], he says: "of the seen and the seer.
[Page 148] Because this meaning—that the self alone, which is the immutable vision, is the ultimate reality, whereas duality is non-existent—is supported by numerous arguments—[page 536]
502 Commentary on the *iṣṭasiddhi* | [Page 148–]

He says "and by reasonings" (yuktibhiḥ) to show that there is no suspicion of the non-sublation of duality. Anticipating the objection that "even if this is consistent with scripture and reasoning, this meaning is not established because it contradicts perception and other means of knowledge," he says "it has been shown and will be shown," which carries over from the previous context. || 38 ||
Likewise, regarding "perception and so forth":
he states "by knowledge alone" because the falsity of bondage is also understood from the fact that the scriptural teaching of liberation through knowledge would otherwise be untenable.

[Page 149] He establishes that bondage and silver are not removable by means other than knowledge in the verse beginning with "muktiśaktau. The mention of "bondage" is illustrative; the meaning is that this applies to the destruction of silver as well.
To the objection, "Let there simply be the destruction of silver through its causal power (śakti); what is the harm?", he replies with "rūpye mṛd-iva."

And thus, the silver would possess reality like a clay lump that has been destroyed; and if the silver were real, then the cognition of silver would not be an error—just as the cognition of a clay lump is not—and the cognition of mother-of-pearl would not have the power to sublate it, just as the cognition of a jar does not sublate the cognition of a clay lump. This is also an elliptical indication (upalakṣaṇa) for this bondage. || 40 ||
Previously, it was stated by accepting that liberation and the capacity for action exist through the activity of bondage and form;
now, he says "of you" (*bhavataḥ*) to show that otherwise, transformation itself is not possible.
The meaning is: neither for one who exists (*bhavataḥ*) nor for one who does not exist (*abhavataḥ*) could there be transformation or destruction. [Page 150]
"And silver is likewise" means that it is born of ignorance and is removable by knowledge alone. || 41 ||

The objection is raised: "But [if] indefinability [is established] through the impossibility of otherwise accounting for appearance and sublation regarding the example, that is actually accounted for in quite another way by relying on the view of Bhāskara. Anticipating the objection that "in that case, appearance and sublation would imply that the silver consists of both existence and non-existence," he says: "But then..."
First, establishing existence by means of its being manifest, he sets aside the theory of "misapprehension of the non-existent" (*anyathākhyāti*) with the words "because it is not non-existent.

[Objection: In that case, sublation (*bādha*) would not be established, as in the case of real silver; or if it were established, it would apply even to real silver. To this, he says: "Sublation also... Since it is impossible for manifestation and sublation to have different objects, they must both have either the existent or the non-existent as their object.

When it must be stated, it is more logical to assert existence (*sattva*) alone, in accordance with the primary rule of reasoning. Furthermore, if there were any sublation (*bādha*), it would have to pertain only to that which exists; the point is that there is no non-sublation of what exists everywhere. He explains the portion beginning with "If it is not non-existent, how can it be existent? with the words "Moreover" (*kiñca*). For example, as in the case of "This person is not a non-Brahmin"—
[Page 537] – [Page 152] The First Chapter.
The meaning is this: if it were not non-existent in this way, it would have to be existent. Therefore, "from the existent itself in some manner.
The intention is that although it is sublated in its own essential form (*svarūpa*), it is sublated in its associated form (*saṃsṛṣṭarūpa*). || 42 ||

Since manifestation and sublation are not possible for that which is other than the existent, he concludes with the words "not therefore" (*nātaḥ*). Even if there were no scriptural statement regarding the reality of the effect, its reality would nonetheless be established through reasoning;
thus he says, "and of the cause. Furthermore, even in the absence of scripture and reasoning, it is established by means of perception (*pratītyā*).

To the objection that [the world] must be established [as real], he says: "The cognition of that [is the proof]. Now, one might object: "But it has been stated that the cognition 'it does not exist' has for its object the *nirvācya* (the indefinable), which is distinct from the *tuccha* (the absolutely non-existent). Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Even 'it does not exist'...
The meaning is that even non-existence (*abhāva*), being a modification (*vikāra*) of Brahman like space (*ākāśa*) and so forth, possesses reality alone. He concludes with: "Therefore..."

It should be understood that because "manifestation" (*jani*) and "cognition" (*khyāti*) are impossible, the mere impossibility of the cognition of a void is the reason for the absence of non-existence in the case of the phenomenal world (*kāryaprapañca*), just as it is the reason for the absence of non-existence in the case of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell (*śuktirūpya*). || 43 ||
Intending to show that there is no other possible explanation because other alternatives are impossible, he first refutes the position that [the world] is non-existent, stating:

"It is said: not of the non-existent. Since non-existent things such as a hare's horn are never observed to have manifestation or birth, whereas the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is both manifested and born, it cannot be non-existent; the meaning is that since the silver is manifested, it is not non-existent. Now, [he addresses the next point...]

He states the reason for the impossibility of both [properties] residing in one [entity] with the words "for instance" (*tathā hi*), and so forth. With the intention of pointing out a fault in the example "sound like sound," he raises the objection: "But sound...
He refutes this with "nevertheless" (*tathāpi*). Those for whom sound is the denotable object—those sounds and so forth—are also "sounds" by virtue of the universal *śabdatva* (soundness).

Even while expressing another meaning, by virtue of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*), they indicate the individual instance (*vyakti*) through indication (*lakṣaṇā*), and thereby indicate their own self as well through indication, but not through the primary function (*mukhyā vṛtti*). For that alone constitutes the state of being a signifier (*vācakatva*). Therefore—

The meaning is that since even words such as "sound" lack the capacity to denote themselves, the example is devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*). For those words—such as "pot"—whose denotable objects are characterized as pots and the like, they are not perceived as being self-denotative; rather, they are perceived only as denoting objects distinct from themselves. He says, "It would be sublated," and then, "But [the object] is denoted by the word. To the question, "What follows from that? he replies, "Therefore, there is no non-duality of sound.

Since objects such as jars are non-different from the words "jar" and so forth because they are illusory manifestations (*vivarta*) of those words, and since those words themselves are non-different from the words that denote them because they too are illusory manifestations of those [denoting] words, the non-duality of sound (*śabdādvaita*) which you intend to establish [is undermined].

The meaning is that this would not be established because of the difference between the word and its object. Furthermore, he states "even if there were non-difference between the two," and so forth, to show that the reason is *aprayojaka* (inconclusive), as it is refuted by a counter-argument (*pratikūlatarka*) characterized by the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of universal blindness in the world. He refutes this with "then," meaning: if that is so, your own position—that the object, by abandoning its own nature, would undergo the state of having the nature of the word that denotes it—would be abandoned. For example, as the word "self" [denotes] its own object...

The meaning is that, in that case, words such as "jar" and so forth would also be non-different from their own objects, and thus the doctrine of the non-duality of words (*śabdādvaita*) would not be established. The meaning is that if that which is the object of the cognition of existence were itself the object of the cognition of non-existence, then there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even in other cases such as the word "jar," there would be the status of being the object of both the cognitions of existence and non-existence.

Because of the etymological derivation that "vivarta" (illusory manifestation) means "functioning through a reversal of reality," one might ask: how can there be non-difference between those two and Śabdabrahman? To this he says, "In that very [text]," etc.

This refers to a sentence that brings about the realization of the oneness of the Self (*ātmyaikya*).

The word "nāma" means that the Śruti is intent upon the injunction for the meditation on the syllable *oṃ* by way of viewing it as the higher and lower Brahman.

Now, one might object: why is the purport of the Śruti not assumed to be the teaching that the syllable *oṃ* is Brahman itself? Anticipating this doubt, he says "uktābhyaḥ" (from what has been stated).

This refers to the reasons already mentioned: because it is denotable (*vācyatva*), because it is perceivable by the senses (*indriyagrāhyatva*), and because it is cognizable by the intellect (*buddhivedyatva*).

This is the meaning. He clarifies the reason already stated for Brahman being beyond verbal expression with the words, "And because Brahman is not of the nature of sound. By the phrase "that by which speech is uttered," the emergence of the entire aggregate of sounds is declared; thus, its lack of verbal nature is stated.

It should be understood that its lack of being denoted by words has already been stated. "Because the Self is not Brahman. Why is that [Self] not Brahman? To this he says: "The Self..."

[The opponent] objects: "But since it is admitted that the 'I-maker' (*ahaṃkartṛ*), who is known as 'I', is non-self, its being non-Brahman is precisely what is desired"—thus the proponent of the established conclusion (*siddhāntin*) raises a doubt. [The opponent] replies: "That very [I-maker] is denoted by words expressive of the Self, such as 'I myself' (*aham svayam*); it is not so for anyone else. Therefore, it is not non-Self. He thus refutes [the objection].
"It is not that of that very [sound]. If so, then in my position as well, the phoneme (varṇa) denoted by the word "sound" does not possess the nature of Brahman.

However, he refutes [the objection] by stating "so too is the word," meaning that it belongs only to the *sphoṭa*, which is the intended object (*lakṣya*). [The opponent objects: "But [if so], it would follow that Brahman alone is [the word]," for the meaning is that [the word] is indeed that which is called *sphoṭa*. And as for the claim that [Brahman] is well-known to be unknowable, that too has already had its answer stated.
This is the syntactical connection. Regarding the phrase "because it has that as its object":

the meaning is that since the Self is not an object of perception and the other means of knowledge, its being Brahman is not contradicted by perception and the rest. An objection is raised: since we observe that the Self, as qualified by pleasure and so forth—as in "I am happy" or "I am miserable"—is indeed an object of perception and the rest, its status as a non-object is unestablished.

Therefore, since there is also a contradiction [here], he says "pleasure, pain, etc. Because the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*), which is experienced as being qualified by pleasure, pain, and so forth, is the witness (*sākṣin*), its identity with Brahman is not what is being taught; rather, it is that of the witness itself. And because that [witness] is not an object of any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there is not even a scent of contradiction—this is the meaning. Now, [an objection]: [The text continues: "But..."

Even the witness-consciousness (sākṣin) has its nature as Brahman understood solely through words. Thus, since it is denotable by words, one might object that it would also become an object of other means of knowledge (pramāṇa); therefore, [the author] says, "And that is the Self. Now, an objection may be raised: "In that case, since the word 'I' (aham) does not function with respect to the conscious Self (cidātman), it is improper to convey the realization 'I am Brahman' through such a word"; anticipating this, [the author speaks of] the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra)—

[Page 175] — Intending that the word "I" (ahaṃ), when applied to the qualified [self], indicates by secondary figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) the Witness (sākṣin) who conforms to that [Self], because the grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) with the word "Brahman" would otherwise be untenable; thus, there is the application [of the word "I"] to the Self as qualified by the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra).

He shows this with the words "In that [case] also. Since the conscious self (cidātman) possesses neither the state of being an object of knowledge nor externality, it does not contradict its being Brahman; thus he says, "Therefore, not of the self. Having thus established the Brahmanhood of the self, he now establishes the selfhood of Brahman as well, with the words, "Nor of the non-self."

Alternatively, having established the Brahmanhood of the Self by examining the nature of the referent of the term "thou" (*tvaṃpadārtha*), he now states that the Self's Brahmanhood is also established by examining the referent of the term "Brahman," with the words: "And not of the non-Self. The meaning is that it is not logical for something other than the Self—such as a pot—to possess Brahmanhood, just as [it is not logical for a pot to be] Brahman. This is because of the scriptural declaration of omniscience.

Anticipating the objection that its consciousness might be accepted as being due to force (*balāt*), he says "even though it is conscious" (*cetanatve 'pi*) to show that because it possesses characteristics distinct from those [of the Self],
it is not different from the Self. Anticipating the further objection that even if it is conscious,
it might still be different from the Self, he states that in that case, it would not be the referent of the term "Brahman," since the word "Brahman" naturally [denotes the Self].

He says "even in the case of difference" (*bhedepi*) because it is impossible for that which is being perceived—which is devoid of the threefold limitation—to exist when there is a limitation of the object. He concludes his own position with "therefore" (*tasmāt*). The meaning is that since the Brahman-Self, by virtue of its being consciousness, cannot consist of the *sphoṭa* which is the indicated sense of the word "word," it is not the indicated sense of the word "word. || 75 ||

He states another defect in the opposing position with the words "Moreover" (*api ca*). Since the nature of being the inner self (*pratyaktva*) is understood through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the nature of the indicated object (*lakṣya*) as the inner self is understood even by a word denoting an external object (*parārtha*); therefore, he says, "it does not make known.

Anticipating the objection that there is no non-introspective cognition [of the moon] because it is an object of perception (*lakṣya*), but rather that the moon was already previously apprehended, he says, "For not even a Śākya... [etc.], meaning that even one who has been devoid of the apprehension of the moon since birth does not apprehend its introspective nature from that statement. He concludes this incidental discussion with the words, "Therefore, the Self... [etc.].

The meaning is as follows: because those very [entities] are Brahman, and since the effects of Brahman are the effects of the Self (*ātman*), when all effects have dissolved, it is possible to say that the Self is non-dual (*advaya*); however, this cannot be said of the Word (*śabda*), because the Word lacks the nature of Brahman, and thus its transformation (*vivarta*) cannot be a transformation of the Word. In the phrase "or the non-duality of the jar," the word "or" (*vā*) has the sense of "just as" (*iva*). Thus—

He states that the established conclusion—that the relationship between the signified and the signifier would not exist if they were non-different in the manner described—has been proven by the words "Thus" (śrataḥ). || 76 ||

Having asserted that if the non-existent were denotable by a word, its difference from the word and its existence would have to be admitted, [the author] first elaborates upon its difference; now, he elaborates upon its existence when the non-existent is the denoted object.

With the words beginning with "ityādinā," he introduces the verse by stating the meaning: "He says this. Even though there is the word "non-existent" (*asat*), it cannot be the designator of a non-existent thing; the meaning is that in the case of a non-existent thing, there is no possibility for a ground for the application of a word (*pravṛttinimitta*).
He states the fault in the non-existent being expressible by a word with the words: "Therefore, [it would follow that] it is non-existent" (*tato'saditi*). || 33 ||

He states another argument for the fact that what is void is inexpressible by words, beginning with "itaśca" (for this reason as well). Having raised the doubt as to how the void could be unknowable, he says "buddhiḥ" (the intellect), explaining that because it is devoid of any essential nature (*nissvarūpa*), it cannot serve as the locus for the fruit produced by cognition, since it does not impart a form to the intellect. ... || 78 ||

[Page 177] Having thus elaborated upon the fact that the void possesses a nature of its own (*sātmakatva*) by means of the otherwise inexplicable establishment of the term "non-existent" (*asadādiśabda*) as having an objective referent (*sālambanatva*), [the author now proceeds] by means of the otherwise inexplicable establishment of the cognition of the non-existent as having an objective referent.

He elaborates upon its being endowed with a self (*sātmakatva*) by means of the passage beginning with "if it were known as empty," and so forth. The meaning is: let its "otherness" (*anyatva*)—that is, its distinction from the non-existent (*asat*) as conceived by the proponents of the Void (*tuccha*)—also be accepted for it. In that regard, he first states the fault in accepting non-otherness (*ananyatva*) according to the view of the Vijñānavādins, saying "of the intellect" (*buddheśca*). Having raised the doubt as to why this is so:

He says "of the void" (*śūnyasya*) because it is observed that only that which possesses a self-nature (*sātmaka*), appearing as the differentiator of cognition, can be an object of knowledge (*jñeya*); for that which is devoid of its own nature cannot possibly be an object of knowledge. The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is that if the void were a mere nothingness (*tucchatva*), it would be non-cognizable.
He explains the second half [of the verse] with "If it were not other... (*ananyaccet*). || 78 ||
Furthermore, he states that it is not possible for the intellect (*buddhi*) to be an object of cognition (*bodhya*), saying: "Moreover, if [it were] by the intellect...

The meaning is: if the subsequent cognition were to arise by apprehending the preceding cognition due to the absence of an external object. || 82 ||

"Do not say so; do not urge this, for apart from the ineffable Māyā, there is no establishment of the non-existent.

"From itself" means that it is intrinsic, like the heat of fire and so forth. "From another" means having arrived from another location and so forth. In connection with what follows, the term *rūpya* [in the compound] is a *bahuvrīhi*, meaning "that which has silver (*rūpya*) as its form (*rūpa*), namely this void (*śūnya*).

To the question "Whence is this so?", he says: "Because of the reality of the object" (*vastutattva*). The meaning is that the reality (*tattva*) of the object—which is empty—is its nature as silver, and because it makes [that nature] known exactly as it is. "Upon the disappearance of the silver, of those two... (vv. 88–89).

Regarding the acceptance of the appearance of silver located in another place within the void, he states another fault with the words "silver situated elsewhere" (*rūpyamanyastham*). By the word "or" (*vā*), another alternative is implied: "or without having come. The meaning is: "if it appears either by having come or without having come. for one does not observe them appearing as identical in the form "the empty is silver. || 81 ||

Furthermore, as for that silver which appears having come into the void—is it due to the very nature (*svabhāva*) of the void, or is it due to the influence of causes such as desire (*kāma*) or impurity (*mala*)? Regarding these, he addresses the first alternative with the words "śūnyagau" (in the void). Just as in the case of a shell, there is the possibility of a rule wherein an error arises from perceiving the general aspect (*sāmānyāṃśa*), and subsequently a sublation (*bādha*) occurs from perceiving the specific aspect (*viśeṣāṃśa*). However, this is not possible here.

Likewise, it is impossible for that which is empty [of intrinsic nature], because there is no distinction in it even over the course of time. And thus, if error and sublation were to exist therein, they would have to exist at all times; if, however, they do not exist due to contradiction, then the meaning is that they would never exist at any time. "At that time" refers to [the time of] error and sublation.

The meaning is that it refers to the time of its own existence. He states the reason for the absence of any distinction as "because of its insubstantiality" (*tucchatvāt*). Regarding the second [position], he says: "Precisely for this reason, not even from a cause. The meaning is: precisely because of the absence of any distinction in the void (*śūnya*), there is also an absence of connection with a cause;
therefore, a fixed rule regarding error and sublation (*bhrānti-bādha*) caused by that [connection] is not possible. Previously...

This was stated by accepting the existence of other locations and so forth in relation to space (*śūnya*). Now, since space is unlimited (*anavacchinna*), there is no possibility of stating that the silver has gone to another location in relation to it, because other locations and so forth do not exist in relation to it; thus he says "time and so forth" (*kālādi*). Furthermore, regarding the phrase "and sublation," [it means] it would either always exist or never at all.
The word "diti" is understood to follow [from the previous rule]. || 82 ||

[Page 182] He states the fault in its maturation with the words "syāccet" (if it were so).
"Thus" means that there would be a total destruction all at once. Anticipating the question "What follows from that?", he says: "always, all at once, of the whole."
He says that there would either be constant birth or the destruction of what was done once; thus he explains "once and always" (*sakṛtsadā*) as "always" (*sadā*).

Having accepted a sequence between the destruction of the prior [state] and birth, it was stated that there would be either the simultaneity of the entire birth or the simultaneity of the entire destruction. Now, he says "or they may exist together" to show that even for birth and destruction, a sequence is not possible.
To the question "Why do those two occur together?", he says "Because of necessity," referring to the causes of birth and destruction.

The meaning is that even if [the two] are empty, they must exist only successively because there would otherwise be no cause for them. Anticipating the objection that their existence is impossible due to contradiction, he says "mutually" (*mithaḥ*), implying that those two [origination and destruction] themselves are not established.
The syntactical connection is: "Origination and destruction could never exist. This means that there can be no birth of what is non-existent.
...it manifests as a dual nature. That which is empty and whose nature is called "birth" is non-existent; the meaning is that it has the form of non-existence (*abhāva*).

[Page 183] For this reason as well, it is incorrect to say that the void (*śūnya*) arises as something stable, characterized by persistence, and devoid of modification; thus he says, "indeed, without modification. The meaning is that if one does not accept the attainment of the form of silver through the activity of transformation (*pariṇāma*) on the part of the void, then silver could not be the effect of the void. Now, [the opponent might argue] regarding the silver of the void...

Anticipating the objection that its being an effect is undesirable because it is admitted to be an effect of the transformation of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), [the author] says "If it were so" (*syāccet*), meaning that the postulation of the Void as a cause would then be useless.
To the question "Why is it useless?", he replies "Because of its non-establishment" (*tadasiddheḥ*). This is because the Void lacks the nature of being a cause of silver; otherwise—
The meaning is that [the inference] is untenable because the conceptualizing factor characterized by the effect is unestablished. || 88 ||

It has been stated that just as the existence of a jar ceases with the destruction of its state as a lump of clay, so too, if the existence of silver were to cease with the destruction of its state as emptiness, then a second effect such as a snake could not arise from that emptiness. Anticipating an objection regarding a distinction in this case, he refutes it.

"Is it not lost?"—the connection [of the verse] is as follows: just as milk exists in the state of curd, so too the void (śūnya), though lost in the state of silver, arises again like darkness upon the extinction of a lamp and becomes the fruit. From what is that void born? Is it from the silver or from its destruction?
Having thus raised the alternatives, he refutes the first by stating: "Because it is its own effect, it does not arise from the silver. (88)

Regarding the statement "from silver, the birth of emptiness," he states another fault with the words "if [it] is born from silver. The meaning is that, just as a pot made of clay has the nature of clay, so too emptiness born from silver would have the nature of silver. Furthermore, having raised the dilemma—whether the birth of emptiness is from silver that has not perished or from silver that has perished—he addresses the first alternative with the word "silver" (*rūpye*).
"‘Lost’—he explains the second half [of the verse] with the words ‘just as when clay is lost. Why is it not logical?

To this he says: ‘If silver exists. The meaning is that if silver exists, being established as the cause, then universal emptiness (*sarvaśūnyatva*) would not be possible. Or else: if that silver were the existent cause, then..."
By that example, the meaning is that every cause whatsoever is indeed existent; therefore, emptiness is not possible for any cause. || 100 ||

He states the second [alternative] with the words "even when the silver has not perished. Regarding the second position among the two previously mentioned alternatives—namely, whether the birth of the non-empty [silver] occurs from that which has not perished due to the destruction of the silver, or rather from that which has perished—he refutes the first by saying "not even from its destruction, provided it has not perished. If the destruction of the silver were itself non-empty, then for that [destruction]...

The meaning is that if the destroyed object were the cause of the void, then consequently, the void of everything would not be established. He refutes the second [position] with the words "even in the destruction of destruction. As before, just as there is no birth of a void from silver upon the destruction of silver, so too, even in the destruction of destruction, there would be no birth of a void from that destruction. He explains the third quarter [of the verse] starting with "rūpyanāśā-".
By the verse beginning with "dityādi," he explains the fourth quarter [of the verse] with the words "nāśasyāpi" (even of destruction). || 101 ||

When the birth of the void has been thus conceptualized and refuted, the proponent of the void (śūnyavādī) says: "That very [birth] is the destruction of the void. That which is for you the birth from the destruction of silver is, for me, the birth of the void. Therefore, the meaning is that the birth of the void from silver is possible. Furthermore, because even the birth from the destruction of silver is for us indeterminable (anirvācya), it does not exist in reality.
He refutes [the opponent's position] with the words "when the silver exists," meaning that as long as the silver persists, its destruction is contradictory;
for if there were no contradiction, it would follow that its destruction would occur at all times. If that is so, [then it occurs] only when [the silver] does not exist...

To the objection that "let there be its destruction while it is silver," he says: "because it is non-existent in the silver. Since non-existence itself constitutes destruction, once non-existence is established, further destruction would be redundant and would lead to an infinite regress; thus, the meaning is that when the silver is non-existent, the possibility of its destruction does not arise. || 102 ||

[Page 185] By the same reasoning through which the arising of silver from what is non-empty was refuted, he extends that reasoning to the arising of silver from what is empty, saying "thus of the empty. The meaning is: just as the arising of silver from silver would not occur upon the destruction of silver, so too, upon the destruction of the empty, the arising of silver from the empty would not occur. If that is so—
Anticipating the objection that "the birth of silver may occur from the destruction of emptiness, or the birth of silver may be the very destruction of emptiness," he says: "While emptiness exists.

The meaning is that just as the destruction of silver is not tenable whether silver exists or does not exist, so too the destruction of emptiness is not tenable whether emptiness exists or does not exist. || 103 ||

He summarizes the extensive subject matter in brief with the words "not from the non-existent" (*nāto 'sataḥ*). This means: "not from that which was previously non-existent as an effect. Regarding the statement "neither from a non-existent cause," he first explains the nature of the produced (*janya*) entity with the words beginning "therefore, by what has been said," and so forth. [The phrase] "nor from a non-existent cause" refers to whether [the cause] is existent or non-existent.

The word "because" (*kāraṇāt*) is to be supplied [to complete the sentence]. Now, one might object: "If the birth of an effect that is non-existent is asserted to be in the form of existence, then let its birth be in the form of non-existence itself. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Nor in the form of non-existence. It is contradictory for an existent effect to be born in the form of non-existence; furthermore, since the state of being non-existent is already established for that which is non-existent, it cannot be produced.

Birth occurs only as that very essence; therefore, the meaning is that there can be no birth from any cause whatsoever even for a non-existent thing in its own non-existent form. As for the question of how destruction and sublation could then occur, it was stated therein that because birth and manifestation are impossible, destruction and sublation are likewise impossible. In that regard, since the produced cannot exist, there is no destruction—

He first explains origination with the words "to nāśa" (up to the word "destruction"). He states the meaning of the word "ataḥ" (hence) as "jātābhāve" (in the case of the non-existence of what has arisen).
He connects the second half of the verse with the passage beginning "ato'sato'khyāteḥ" (hence, because there is no manifestation of the non-existent), and so forth. || 104 ||

Regarding what was stated—that if liberation were non-existence (śūnyabhāva), then non-return would be possible—the author replies with the words "in the case of the attainment of emptiness" (śūnyāpattau). The meaning is that since even liberation in the form of emptiness is something produced, there can be no non-return under that view either. Furthermore, he states that in the position where liberation is characterized by the attainment of emptiness, the scriptural teaching on non-return would be purposeless.

Regarding the phrase "and in liberation" (*mokṣe ca*): the word division is *vṛtti-saṃbhavaḥ*. The meaning is that in that liberation where even the mental state (*vṛtti*) called "the state of being ourselves," characterized by the void-like self, does not occur, there can be no suspicion of non-return (*anāvṛtti*). Alternatively, the word division is *anāvṛtti-saṃbhavaḥ*; in that case, it is like one who has gone to another place by way of the path of light (*arcirādi*).

The meaning is that, since one who has become void in his own country cannot possibly return, there can be no apprehension of returning. Now, it might be argued:
"It is not the attainment of oneness with the Void that is to be accomplished—which would imply impermanence—but rather [that state] is itself unachievable; nevertheless, in your position..."

He raises the objection with the words "of the void alone" (*śūnyasyaiva*), suggesting that there might be a requirement for means (*sādhana*) in order to dispel the delusion of not attaining that [state], and that upon its cessation, the designation "liberation" (*muktatva*) would apply. He explains the second half of the verse according to the word-division "the possibility of a mental modification" (*vṛtti-sambhava*), saying "if [it were] as you desire," and so on. [The reason given is] "because there is no mental modification (*vṛtti*) of the void," meaning of that which has become the void.

The meaning is that there is an absence of the function (vṛtti) called "becoming that" (tadbhāva) in the self (ātman). Following the alternative analysis of the compound as *avṛtti-sambhava*, he explains it as "from one place to another. The meaning is that if the possibility of movement were present, there might be a suspicion of [its] non-existence; since that [movement] is absent, the prohibition would be redundant. || 105 ||
Furthermore, the very state of emptiness is not even possible; far less can it be liberation. With this intention, he asks: "Whence is the state of emptiness? (106)
Regarding that scripture cited as an authority for the state of emptiness (*śūnyabhāva*) concerning liberation,
he states its intended meaning as follows: "the destruction of specific cognition" (*viśeṣajñānanāśa*).

Now, one might object: "Let it be granted that there is no cessation of ignorance in the form of a void; nevertheless, let the cessation of the specific cognitions that cause the cessation of the limiting adjuncts such as the body—along with ignorance itself—be a void-like state, just as elsewhere than in liberation, the cessation of specific cognition is indeed a void-like state. Anticipating this objection, [the author] provides a counter-example based on the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*).

"Annihilation does not [mean] emptiness. Why is it that even in the state of conventional usage, the destruction of specific cognitions does not have emptiness as its nature? To this he says: "Because of existence" (*bhāvāt*). This means that even after the time of destruction, cognitions exist in the form of their cause. Existence in the form of the cause is precisely what is meant.

He confirms [the argument] by means of a refutation regarding the opposite case (*vipakṣa*), stating "because of its empty nature. Furthermore, the word "again" (*punaḥ*) is also an elliptical indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the word "previously" (*prāk*).
Now, one might object: "If the effect exists by virtue of its identity with the cause, it must also exist by virtue of its identity as an effect;
since the two are identical, what then becomes of the conventional distinction between 'effect' and 'cause'?
Anticipating this objection from those who maintain their difference, he states the resolution: "That very [cause] is the effect."

[Page 188] Now, it may be argued that even if there is identity of essential nature (*svarūpa*), there is no absolute non-difference between cause and effect due to the difference in their qualified forms (*viśiṣṭarūpa*). To this, he says: "And the unmanifest itself is the manifest. This is because manifestation would otherwise be impossible.

By way of non-occurrence (*anupapatti*), it is understood that even that which is unmanifest is indeed manifest; therefore, the meaning is that even a specific difference [between them] is not established by valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇika*). Alternatively, having raised the objection that there is indeed a difference between cause and effect because they are the substrata of contradictory properties characterized as manifestation and non-manifestation, he states that there is no contradiction even in a single entity due to the difference in time.
And it is indeed unmanifest.
For this reason as well, he says "moreover" (kiñca) to show that there is no difference between the two [states] characterized by manifestation and non-manifestation. || 111 ||

Now, does some specific quality arise at the time of manifestation due to the cause of manifestation in that which has non-manifestation as its nature, or not? If it does not, then what is the "manifestedness" of that which was previously unmanifested? None whatsoever.

If it arises because of that very state, then [the question remains] regarding the entity whose nature is manifestation—now possessed of a specific quality—as opposed to that whose nature was non-manifestation.
He raises the objection that there would necessarily be a difference [between the cause and effect] due to their non-manifestation with the words "nanvavyakte" (But [if it were] unmanifest...).

The sense is that, since the manifestation of its own specific quality must otherwise be purposeful, one must accept that the qualified [effect], though previously non-existent, is born [into being]. || 112 ||
He refutes [the objection] with "Not so," stating that even in the case of difference (*bheda*), the lack of meaningfulness regarding manifestation (*abhivyakti*) is equally applicable.

One might object: "Since that which is manifested is identical to that which was unmanifested, let there be no non-existence prior [to manifestation]; rather, let it be that the manifested thing and the specific quality produced by it arise while being previously non-existent. Anticipating this, he refutes the non-existence of both of these with two verses, beginning with "Not of the unmanifested" (*nāvyaktasya*). He explains the second verse with the words "For not of two unestablished things" (*na hyasiddhayoḥ*). Of this...
The commentary on "of the non-existent" [states]: "not belonging to another. The meaning is that it would not be the property (*dharma*) of anything.
"Just as for another" means that there is no relationship of property and property-possessor (*dharmadharmatā*) between two distinct substrata (*dharmin*). || 114 || 115 ||

He says, "And why is there a messenger? to show that not only does reason exist, but there are also Śruti and Smṛti texts regarding the absence of birth for one who is non-existent and the absence of emptiness for one who exists.

Thinking that by the very scripture which precludes the non-existent from attaining reality, the possibility of the existent falling into emptiness is also implicitly precluded, he says: "And the existent does not become empty. The meaning is that destruction consists in the attainment of the state of being the cause [of its own effect]. ... || 116 ||

Thus, having refuted the doctrine of emptiness (*śūnyavāda*) by relying on the doctrine of existence (*sadvāda*), and intending to establish the doctrine of the inexpressible (*anirvacanīyavāda*), he challenges the doctrine of existence with the word "nanu" (is it not so?). [He argues that] at the time when the state of a thing is unmanifest, there is a non-existence of manifestation; therefore, there is identity between the two.

If one accepts that [the unmanifest] exists, then there would always be manifestation alone; thus, the meaning is that there would never be non-manifestation at any time. To the objection that "let there be non-manifestation even at the time of manifestation," he says:
"of manifestation and non-manifestation. Because manifestation exists simultaneously with non-manifestation, it cannot be the remover of that [non-manifestation].

The meaning is that [the effect] would exist even while unmanifest due to its continued existence [in the cause]. Now, one might object: "Manifestation coexisting with non-manifestation is itself unmanifest; even if that [unmanifest manifestation] does not remove it [the non-manifestation], nevertheless, that [manifestation] when it becomes manifest will remove it, because they exist together. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "In that case, the consequence would be that the effect is non-existent [prior to its production]."
Regarding the phrase "there, unmanifest": having raised the doubt that even that manifestation might be unmanifest therein, he says "of manifestation.
"If it were so" means: if it were the case that there were non-manifestation even at the time of manifestation. "Due to the absence of its cause" means:
due to the absence of a cause for its cessation. || 117 || 118 ||

[Page 191] In that case, by process of elimination, origination and manifestation must belong to that which is indeed indeterminable (anirvacanīya).

He refutes [the objection] with the words "it is true. He states, "manifestation and non-manifestation," because even manifestation and non-manifestation, being subject to birth and appearance, are indeed indeterminable (anirvācya). Anticipating the objection that it is improper to say that only the indeterminable has appearance and birth—since the existent Self (ātman) is also seen to have appearance—he replies with "and appearance."

Since it is accepted that all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) is inexpressible (*anirvācya*), he states "or all" to indicate whether what is intended is a non-consciousness (*asaṃvit*)—that is, insentience (*jaḍa*)—or a manifestation (*ākhyāti*). [The phrase] "of that whose nature is unmanifested" means "of that whose nature is consciousness. Now, one might ask: how can things like jars, which are not subject to sublation, be inexpressible, just as a false manifestation (*khyāti*) is? To this he says "of all. But here, what is meant by "manifestation"?

Whether it be the appearance of silver and so forth, or the appearance of mere insentience (*jaḍamātra*), how could that be possible for that which is indeterminable (*anirvācya*)? To this he says: "And of that whose nature is unmanifested" (*akhyātasvabhāvasya ca*). Since, just as whiteness cannot belong to blackness, it is impossible for insentience—which is by nature non-conscious—to have the quality of being manifested; therefore, the meaning is that it is only the indeterminable insentience that appears. Now, [if you object] regarding the unmanifested—
Anticipating the objection that "let the insentient nature itself be manifested through the knowledge residing in the knower," [the author] raises the dilemma:

is it said that manifestation occurs because the manifestation of that [nature] has been effected by it, or is it said that manifestation occurs from mere knowledge even though nothing is effected? Having thus formulated the alternatives, he addresses the first with the words "of that which is unmanifested" (*akhyātasya*).

The meaning is that if the relation between the unmanifested (akhyāta) and manifestation (khyāti) is not established, then that [relation] must necessarily be established for that which is itself indeterminable (anirvācya). Regarding the second [alternative], he says: "If it is not produced.
If manifestness (khyātatā) is not produced in the insentient (jaḍa) by the knowledge residing in the knower (pramātṛ), then [the claim that] "the insentient manifests" would belong to the insentient.
The *Iṣṭasiddhivivaraṇa* | [Page 191] It was stated that the linguistic usage of manifestation through co-referential manifestation would be without a basis (*nirālambana*). Regarding that:

He states the reason for this with the words "of that, by itself," etc. Since even manifestation (*khyāti*), like birth (*janman*), cannot be determined as belonging either to the existent or the non-existent because it occurs only occasionally, he says "therefore" (*ataḥ*), meaning that it must belong only to that which is indeterminable (*anirvācya*). Having raised the objection that the indeterminability of birth is the cause for the indeterminability of that which possesses it, [the author] proceeds.

Then, since even the manifestation characterized by the appearance of identity for that which is insentient is of a contradictory nature of unity, it too is indeterminable—just like the identity of a rope and a snake—the author says "and itself" (*svayaṃ ca*). Because it is certain that whatever possesses manifestation and birth is indeterminable, and because both manifestation and non-manifestation possess manifestation and birth, they are likewise indeterminable; thus he says "therefore... (*ataḥ*).

Regarding the term "manifestation" (*vyakti*): since, by the reasoning already stated, there is only the manifestation of that which is of the nature of non-apprehension (*akhyāti*) and is itself inexpressible (*anirvācya*), and that manifestation is likewise inexpressible, it is therefore illogical for even a non-existent thing to have a real manifestation; thus he says, "for this reason also.

Here, the proponent of the doctrine of emptiness (*śūnyavādin*) raises an objection by means of a counter-argument regarding *māyā*, beginning with "But surely... (*nanu*). [This concerns] the identity of the insentient (*jaḍa*) with its own manifestation (*sphuraṇa*).

The meaning is as follows: just as [the nature of] insentience would be lost [if it were identical with consciousness], so too, if Māyā were identical with the manifestation [of consciousness], its status as Māyā would be lost; therefore, since such identity of manifestation is impossible, the appearance [of Māyā] cannot occur. He refutes [the objection] by saying, "True, for this very reason," because the identity of the manifestation of Māyā is merely an appearance, and it is not proper to employ the counter-example of unreal Māyā against that which is ultimately void.
The meaning is that even renown (*khyāti*) is merely an appearance (*ābhāsa*). He states the fault [that would arise] if it were not an appearance with the words "otherwise" (*anyathā*);
the meaning is that even that [renown] would be *māyā*. || 118 ||

[Page 192] Previously, it was stated that the insentient (jaḍa) possesses the nature of indeterminable illusion (anirvācyamāyātva), because its manifestation as something prior would otherwise be inexplicable. Now, he states "And that" (sā ca) to show that its status as illusion is also established by the fact that being expressible by words is only possible in the case of illusion itself, since that too would otherwise be inexplicable. ... || 120 ||

[Objection: "In that case, just as with the self (*ātman*), let it be that even for the void (*śūnya*), all worldly transactions such as birth and so forth have their locus solely through ignorance (*avidyā*).
To this, he says: "Not even through ignorance. (121)

[Page 193] Now, one might raise the objection: "Could it not be that the cessation of ignorance occurs spontaneously by itself, or through knowledge (vidyā) that has a different locus or object? Anticipating this, he says: "He whose ignorance... [This implies that] [the cessation occurs] only when the locus and object of the two are identical.

The meaning is that the relationship between knowledge (*vidyā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*) as that which is removed and that which removes is well-established. Furthermore, he states "even of the existent" (*sato 'pi*) to show that for the non-existent (*asat*), there can be neither the status of being the locus nor the object of knowledge. "Not without that knowledge" means not without knowledge whose locus and object are the non-existent. "By another knowledge" means by a knowledge whose locus and object are some other entity different from the non-existent. || 122 ||
