In the context of refuting [the view that] knowledge is void, he refutes the ignorance (avidyā) that has an insentient locus, as maintained by the Sāṅkhyas.

Regarding the phrase "of which there is ignorance": "due to the absence of knowledge" means that because it lacks the status of being a substratum for knowledge, it cannot be the substratum for the ignorance that is to be removed by that knowledge. To the question, "Even if it were an object of knowledge, why could it not be the substratum for knowledge?", he says:
"For [it is impossible] for one and the same [thing to be both]. (123)

Furthermore, gain and loss, liberation and bondage— characterized respectively as the error that is the effect of ignorance and its cessation— are not possible for an insentient entity (*jaḍa*). Therefore, he states that for this reason as well, it is impossible for an insentient entity to be the locus of the ignorance that serves as the material cause of error.

Regarding the phrase "the ignorant": the meaning is that the insentient (jaḍa) is not the locus of knowledge, because it does not participate in the goal of human life (puruṣārtha), like a void. He states the subverting argument for the contrary position: "If [it were] ignorance belonging to the insentient. To the question "Why?", he says: "Of that," meaning:
because that insentient thing lacks the capacity to be the locus of knowledge, which is the opposite of ignorance. || 124 ||
Furthermore, because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that can apprehend ignorance, the establishment of ignorance in an insentient (*jaḍa*) entity is impossible;

thus he says, "I am ignorant. It is not the Seer (*dṛk*); it is the non-Seer (*adṛk*), for that which is not the Seer is the object of sight (*dṛśya*). How could even the experience of ignorance—namely, "I am ignorant"—occur in an insentient object? Not in any way whatsoever. Therefore, regarding that [insentient object]:

The meaning is that it does not have ignorance as its substrate. And the first *ca* (and) has the sense of including what has not been mentioned; the meaning is that not only is ignorance impossible in an insentient thing (*jaḍa*), but there is also no means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) to apprehend it. Now, since ignorance has an insentient thing as its substrate, even if it is not cognizable through the experience that constitutes its own substrate, might it still be cognizable through another means of knowledge?
Anticipating this objection, he says: "It is not an object of valid cognition" (*aprameya*). To the question, "Why is it not an object of valid cognition?

he replies: "Because it is already established" (*prasiddheḥ*). Since that ignorance—which is qualified by the insentient—is already established prior to the operation of any means of knowledge directed toward the insentient, how could it be established by a measure (*māna*), i.e., a valid cognition? Not at all; for [a cognition] cannot apprehend a qualified object (*viśeṣya*) when its qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) has not been apprehended.

Because of the maxim that "the cognition [resides] in the qualificand," it follows that ignorance is not an object of knowledge (*meya*); this is the meaning. The proponent asks for the reason why ignorance is established even prior to the operation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), asking: "By what?
Intending to show that since you too must admit its establishment even before the operation of the means of valid cognition, you should not ask me for a reason, the proponent replies:

He asks her whether he asked without knowing; for a question is inappropriate once something is already known. Skipping the second [alternative] and taking the first, he refutes it with the words "I ask without knowing," and so forth. That "ignorance" means ignorance qualified by reasoning (*yukti*). "Prior to that knowledge" means prior to the knowledge of reasoning. [The reason is] unestablished (*asiddha*).
"Regarding 'if' (*cet*): if, prior to the knowledge qualified by reasoning, that ignorance qualified by it has not been apprehended, then [the term] 'ignorance'...
The meaning is that there would be no certainty regarding the existence of ignorance (*ajñāna*), nor would there be the designation by that term. If that is so, then the reasoning—

Anticipating the objection that "the establishment of the non-cognition of that [object] may occur even prior to the cognition of the object and its means of knowledge," he says: "If it were already established.

To the question "What follows from that? he says: "For this very reason. The meaning is: the non-cognition of the object under dispute is established even prior to the operation of the respective means of knowledge regarding that object, because it is a non-cognition, just like the non-cognition of a logical reason (*yukti*). And in the case of the contrary position (*vipakṣa*)...

He states that the consequence of infinite regress (*anavasthā-prasaṅga*) is the subverting argument, beginning with the words "for this reason" (*ita eva*). Since a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is that which makes known an object not previously known, if ignorance (*ajñāna*) itself were to be accessible through a means of valid cognition, then prior to the comprehension of that [ignorance], another instance of ignorance regarding its object would have to be admitted;

and since that too must be accessible through a means of valid cognition, yet another instance of ignorance regarding its object would have to be admitted prior to the comprehension of that—thus there is an infinite regress.

The meaning is that since the non-establishment of each preceding ignorance based on its respective locus results in the non-establishment of each subsequent ignorance, ignorance is not established anywhere at all. "That ignorance, that ignorance" means: there is an ignorance whose object is something unknown through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and there is another ignorance whose object is that [first] ignorance, and yet another ignorance whose object is that [second] ignorance, and so forth. Of each and every object of knowledge, by means of a *pramāṇa*...

The meaning is: "of the stream of ignorance that is to be traversed. "Having first known [each] object of knowledge" means that as ignorance arrives one after another, having first known the preceding ignorance, the subsequent ignorance is to be known thereafter. Furthermore, he says that in his own position there is no fault characterized by the non-establishment of the unknown object, because he accepts that the unknown entity is established by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*).

Regarding the phrase "the experience of the eternal self": since the witnessing consciousness (*sākṣicaitanya*) lacks the status of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there is no possibility of another ignorance (*ajñāna*) to be removed; thus, he says "another ignorance" to show that there is no infinite regress (*anavasthā*). He raises the objection regarding contradiction with inference—namely, that ignorance is established by a means of knowledge, like a pot—as expressed in "Now it might be said. [The term] "ignorance of everything" refers to ignorance regarding all objects.

The meaning is "ignorance. As for the inference that [ignorance] is ignorance, it is established as a *siddhasādhana* (proving what is already proven), because its existence in its own nature (*svarūpeṇa*) is admitted even prior to the knowledge produced by the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇajñāna*).
Thus he says, "It is established by its own nature" (*svarūpataḥ siddham*). The point is that there is no infinite regress (*anavasthā*), because it establishes both itself and others.

He states that the example is also deficient in the probandum (*sādhyavikala*), saying "your ignorance of reasoning as well. The meaning is: "Having known by means of valid cognition"—that is, having known that specific ignorance by means of the very valid cognition whose object is reasoning. He first offers a rebuttal by conceding the validity of the ignorance of reasoning, saying "even so. [This refers to] the ignorance specifically qualified by reasoning.

Since the qualification itself is established as authoritative, the authority of the reasoning (*yukti*) that serves as its qualification must also be established, according to the maxim that "there is no cognition of a qualified object without the apprehension of its qualification. Consequently, because my thesis— that ignorance is established through perception even without [separate] means of valid cognition— is supported by this reasoning, my proposition remains free from any flaw.

The meaning is that it is established. [Page 195] Now, it might be argued that ignorance is characterized by reasoning alone, and not otherwise.

Anticipating the objection that the state of being qualified by that [ignorance] might be apprehended through a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) that grasps ignorance even via reasoning (yukti), he says, "Even of that which is established by valid cognition," meaning that even in that case, the validity of my reasoning must be admitted at some point; otherwise, it would be impossible for that ignorance to be established by valid cognition. Established either as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) or as a mere indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), such reasoning is not a valid reason (*samyagyukti*), but rather a fallacy of reason (*yuktyābhāsa*). Previously, regarding the fallacy of reason... [the text continues with the discussion of its lack of] authority.

Having accepted that this ignorance has existence and is established by valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇika*), it was stated that because it is an ignorance regarding fallacious reasoning (*yuktyābhāsa*), it is not an ignorance regarding reasoning itself. Now, since fallacious reasoning—like the appearance of silver—is established as an error, it lacks validity (*aprāmāṇikatva*); for this very reason, its existence is not something to be negated by valid means of knowledge, nor is there any ignorance whose object is that [fallacious reasoning].
He says that it cannot be established by fallacious reasoning (*yuktyābhāsa*). And as for that which is established through error (*bhrāntisiddha*):

because that which is established through error lacks the nature of being unknown (*ajñātatva*), and because it is itself of the nature of ignorance (*ajñānātmaka*), if one were to further admit another ignorance within that which is already of the nature of ignorance, it would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Therefore, neither ignorance nor the knowledge that removes it is possible therein.
The meaning is that there would be nothing more than a mere appearance. He states the conclusion: "Because of the reasoning from the Madhu[-vidyā] passage.
If reasoning possesses authority, then precisely because it is the object of correct reasoning, the lack of authority residing in ignorance is established;
if it lacks authority, then since that ignorance itself does not exist, its lack of authority is all the more firmly established.

This is the meaning. "And of that" means "and of the ignorance of reasoning. Now, one might object: even if ignorance is not accessible through the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), since an insentient object is the domain of such means, the very cognition that apprehends that object would also perceive its being the locus of ignorance.
To this he says: "Therefore, of ignorance... Now, [one might ask] how it is different from external darkness? Internal...

One might argue that some means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) must be accepted as the establisher of this darkness called ignorance; therefore, let it be understood that ignorance has an insentient substrate. Anticipating this objection, [the author] states "ignorance" (*ajñāna*), meaning that even if one accepts a means of valid cognition that apprehends ignorance alone, it is impossible to apprehend the fact that ignorance has an insentient substrate from that very apprehension.

"Even the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)," [he says]. Now, one might object: "Is there not some other insentient entity (*jaḍa*) that is indeed apprehended by the means of valid cognition regarding ignorance? The intended meaning is that if it were apprehended by the means of cognition that grasps ignorance, then that [entity] itself would necessarily be of the nature of ignorance.

Because, by virtue of being undivided, there is no illuminator distinct from itself; and because, being insentient (*jaḍa*), it lacks self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*). Therefore, it is not [the Self].

The meaning is that [the Self] would be established. Now, one might object: "Even for you, since the Self is distinct from the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and other such factors, it follows that it must have a beginning;

To this, he says: "But of the non-inert (*ajaḍa*)," and so on. Now, as for ignorance...

Since its beginninglessness is unestablished due to its being *tāmasa* (of the nature of darkness), he says, "And ignorance (*ajñānam*)... [He explains] "otherwise": the meaning is that if it were beginningless, it would not be ignorance at all, just like a jar or other such objects. By the word "ignorance," which denotes being removable by the arising of a contradictory state, its existence throughout all time prior to that arising is established as its very nature of being ignorance.

This is what is meant by [the statement] "it has been said. The meaning is that this would not be possible if [ignorance] had a beginning. Furthermore, he states that ignorance is beginningless with the words "of those previously liberated" (*prāṅmuktānām*). The meaning is that if ignorance—the cause of bondage—did not exist prior to the arising of ignorance, then there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the possibility of ignorance arising again in liberated souls (*jīvas*), which would result in the impossibility of liberation (*anirmokṣa*).

It is stated in the Siddhāntaloka that because the Self is immeasurable, the ignorance (ajñāna) resting upon it is likewise immeasurable. Taking that as his basis, the opponent objects: "But surely ignorance belongs to the Self alone. [Page 196] He first refutes this by accepting for the sake of argument that ignorance has a non-sentient (jaḍa) substratum, saying: "That is not so. Even if the non-sentient were established by valid means of knowledge (prāmāṇika), regarding the ignorance...

The meaning is that because it is sublated by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and because it cannot be apprehended by that which sublates it or by what is of the same class as that which sublates it, nescience (*ajñāna*)—even if it were to have an insentient (*jaḍa*) locus—is not supported by valid authority. He says "And not... [Page 1971] to show that it is impossible for nescience to have an insentient locus in the first place;
how then could its status as being supported by valid authority exist through such a locus?

One might object: "Just as 'knownness' (jñātatva) does not arise from a means of valid cognition (māna), so too 'unknownness' (ajñātatva) is not produced by a pramāṇa; rather, unknownness, being already established, is simply known through the impossibility of the operation of a pramāṇa upon an insentient object. Anticipating this objection, he says, "nanu māna... [Is it not the case that... from a pramāṇa?].

Fearing the question, "What is gained from this?", he states, "śrato nājñātārtha... [Therefore, there is no [need for] an unknown object...], meaning that the previously mentioned defect does not apply.

The meaning is that the fault previously stated—that for an unknown object, there would be the consequence of it being perceived as inert (jaḍa)—would not apply. Furthermore, he says "nor from the means of knowledge" (nāpi mānāt) to show that the fault which was raised—that through the means of knowledge (māna), only "unknownness" (ajñātatva) would be established and not "knownness" (jñātatva)—would also not apply. [This is because] the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) must be antecedent and not otherwise established (ananyathāsiddha).
The meaning is that it is the cause merely by virtue of being known. For this very reason, since a single means of knowledge cannot be established as having both purposes, [it serves] both purposes—

He states that even the negation of [the object] being unknown is a negation of what has not been established, saying: "And not of the state of being unknown. The logical connection (*anvaya*) is that it is not possible to know "that [object] is unknown" by means of a means of knowledge (*māna*). Why is it not possible to know this?

To this he says: "because the state of being unknown is not established prior [to the operation of the means of knowledge]. Since the operation of a means of knowledge directed toward an insentient object (*jaḍa*) occurs only after the insentient object's state of being unknown has been perceived, and since it is impossible to know that "the insentient object is known through the means of knowledge itself and not by itself," [the claim is untenable].

This is the meaning. Why is it impossible to know? To this he says: "Because of its being of that nature. The meaning is that it is possible to ascertain that an insentient object has the nature of being known. Why is it possible to ascertain that it is of that nature? To this he says: "Of that very thing, in that very way. Just as in the case of a jar perceived as having a white nature, [it is never perceived otherwise].

Likewise, the insentient object, being perceived in the form of the cognition "it is known," never possesses an unknown nature; therefore, its status as having that very nature is certain—this is the meaning. Now, one might object: "In that case, let the well-known state of the insentient being unknown exist at a time subsequent to the operation of a means of knowledge. To this he says: "Even when [the means] has operated. Even when...
The logical connection (*anvaya*) is that it is not possible to know "this is unknown" by means of a means of knowledge (*māna*). Why is it not possible? To this he says:

"because of its [the means of knowledge's] operation" (*tatpravṛtteḥ*). The meaning is: because of the absence of "knownness," which is the result that determines the operation of the means of knowledge.
Let the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of the means of knowledge be the cause for determining its operation; for those things that possess prior non-existence, [their subsequent...]

Having raised the objection that [the means of knowledge] must exist at a specific time because its activity is observed, and that it possesses prior non-existence due to its momentariness, he says "the means of knowledge also" to show that this is not so, because there is no cognition of prior non-existence. Now, having raised the objection that the non-existence of the means of knowledge should likewise be cognized just like the non-existence of the object of knowledge, he says "for this very reason," because there is no distinction between an entity and its non-existence.

Anticipating the objection that, just as in the case of cognition, there is a perception of difference and so forth because non-existence (*abhāva*) also exists, [the author] states "of existence also" (*bhāvasyāpi*), meaning that since existence too would entail self-luminosity (*svayaṃprakāśatva*) if it were known, difference and so forth are not established. To the question "What follows from that?", he says "therefore, of everything indeed" (*tasmāt sarvasyaiva*). [Objection: In that case, then, would it not be the case that only that which is self-luminous is unknown?

To the objection that [ignorance] might arise from a means of knowledge (*māna*), he says: "And there is no such thing as its being unknown [by that means]. The meaning is this: it is impossible for innate ignorance to be produced by a means of knowledge, because that would contradict its very nature as self-luminous (*svayaṃjyotis*). Furthermore, regarding its self-luminosity, [there is the question of] its state of being unknown prior to the operation of a means of knowledge.
He says that even the limit of "non-existence" (abhāva) is not tenable, because the means of knowledge (*māna*), which consists in the manifestation of its own nature, is always established.

"Refuted" means that even though the objection has already been dismissed, it is restated with the intention of pointing out another defect, namely: "as for what you have said.

This refers to the meaning of this insentient object (*jaḍārtha*). First of all, since the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that makes the object known is exhausted merely by grasping the object, another means of knowledge must be stated to establish its state of being unknown (*ajñātatva*). Furthermore, does that [other means of knowledge] also have the object as its domain?

Alternatively, he formulates the alternative that [the word] has "unknowability" as its object, using the phrase "of the object" (*arthasya*). First, having restated the second alternative, he refutes it with the words "if it has another object" (*anyaviṣayaṃ cet*). The meaning is that if there is an absence of the object being the word's referent, it is impossible to convey a connection to that [object]; therefore, it would not cause one to understand unknowability as being connected to the object. Having restated the first alternative, he refutes it with the words "if it has that very thing as its object" (*tadviṣayameva cet*).

The meaning is: "by means of another means of valid cognition (*mānāntara*) that is intended to be a cognizer of the state of being unknown, but which is other than [the cognition] that has the object as its domain.

He states the fault in the opposing case (*vipakṣa*) with the words beginning "atha na tena" and so forth. To the question, "Why would the state of being known not also occur for the object by means of another means of valid cognition that has the object as its domain? he replies with the words "tadviṣayatve" and so forth; [the reason is] because there is no distinction in their having the object as their domain.

To the objection that this [reason] is unestablished (*asiddha*), he says: "And not by means of that which does not have it as its object. The sense is that [otherwise] there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Previously, having raised the dilemma as to whether the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that establishes the unknownness of an object has that object as its domain or not, it was stated that in either case, its capacity to establish unknownness is impossible. Now, regarding its capacity to establish that...
Having accepted that which is to be made known (*jñāpya*), he refutes it by means of an alternative analysis (*vikalpa*) starting with the words "Now, if something... and so forth.
The meaning is that even the object would have to be already known; and if that were the case, its state of being unknown (*ajñātatva*) could not be established.

[The phrase] "the state of being unknown related to that [object] would not be made known" means that if the object itself is unknown, then the state of being unknown related to it [the object] is likewise [unknown].

The meaning is that it would be impossible to know [the unknown], because the cognition of a relation depends upon the cognition of the related terms. To the objection, "In that case, let there be no communication of the state of being unknown," he replies: "Even the state of being unknown... Therefore, he says, "Hence, the state of being unknown... meaning that even if you persist in your insistence, no means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) can establish mere unknowability for you. He accepts [this].

He states that even the operation of a means of knowledge (*māna*) is fruitless for you by saying "because," and so forth. The meaning is: if, because of that [operation], the object does not attain the state of being known—since it is contradictory for that which is unknown (like the whiteness of Kṛṣṇa) to be unknown—then the object does not attain the state of being known through the means of knowledge. This is because the means of knowledge does not produce any excellence (*atiśaya*) residing in the object, nor does it remove its state of being unknown.
He raises the objection that there is no futility because [the word] conveys meaning in a specific form, beginning with "Now, if it be argued" (*atha manuṣa iti*).

[Page 199] He states "If this were so," meaning that if it does not produce an excellence in the means of knowledge (*māna*), then not only would the state of being unknown (*ajñātatva*) fail to be established, but even mere insentient matter (*jaḍamātra*) would not be established. This applies elsewhere as well, regarding the exclusion of the state of being unknown...

If the very nature and function of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is that it does not produce any excellence (*atiśaya*) even when produced from an insentient cause, then it would be nothing more than an insentient thing.

The meaning is that [the cognition] would not be established precisely because there is no distinction [between the object and its cognition]. Now, even in your own view, since the means of knowledge (*māna*) is not a causal agent (*akāraka*) with respect to its own object—

He raises the objection that [the means of knowledge] is equally non-probative because it lacks the capacity to produce an excellence characterized by "cognizedness" (*jñātatā*), stating: "But surely it is not a means of knowledge. He refutes this, saying: "True; for this very reason. Because of the qualification that the means of knowledge is futile with respect to the insentient (*jaḍa*), its efficacy with respect to the non-insentient (*ajaḍa*) is intended. He challenges this point, saying: "But surely even in the case of the non-insentient... [if it does not produce an excellence...]

He provides the resolution that it is indeed fruitful because it removes ignorance, stating "tatreti" (in that regard). Now, one might object: since the Self is already established by its own manifestation, there is no need for the removal of ignorance; therefore, a means of knowledge that removes ignorance cannot be a prover of the Self and must be useless.
To this, he says: "even though [the Self] is established by itself. One might further object: if it is like a prover, then it is only a secondary prover.

The status of being a means (*sādhakatva*) has been stated. But why is the primary status of being a means not accepted? To this he says: "Regarding the status of being a means... Since in that which is self-luminous (*svayaṃprakāśa*), the production of an excellence characterized by manifestation is impossible, the status of being a means is described as secondary (*amukhya*) by way of removing that which conceals [the object]. This same [principle] applies to the means of knowledge (*māna*) even in the case of an insentient object (*jaḍa*).

To the question, "How could there not be success [in this]? he says, "But of the insentient (jaḍasya tu). Even regarding the insentient, having accepted ignorance and its cessation as a bold assertion (*prauḍhivāda*), he says, "Even when it has ceased. The meaning is that there would be no linguistic usage of "manifestation" in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the insentient, such as "the insentient manifests. Now, [if one objects]: "Of the means of knowledge (*māna*), white and so forth..."

"Even if it does not produce a specific characteristic (*lakṣaṇa-viśeṣa*), it will certainly produce the specific characteristic known as 'cognizedness' (*jñātatā-lakṣaṇa-viśeṣa*). And thus, such linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) would be established. Thus he raises the objection with the words "Now, if it be argued... [Page 200]. He refutes this, saying "Then," meaning: "In that case, what I stated—that there would be no establishment of an unperceived insentient object through a means of knowledge (*māna*)—is proven."

The word "up to" (*yāvat*) indicates that, having thus established the lack of validity for the insentient (*jaḍa*), he extends this [argument] to ignorance (*ajñāna*) as well by saying "by this too. Now, one might object: "Just as a means of knowledge (*māna*) regarding an insentient object is accessible through a [further] means of knowledge, since ignorance also has an insentient object, it too should be accessible through a means of knowledge. To this, he says: "of the means of knowledge also," meaning that even for the means of knowledge regarding the insentient, it is likewise [the case].

The meaning is that because there is no distinction in their insentience (*jaḍatva*), the possibility of being known by a means of valid cognition (*māna*) has been refuted. He states the conclusion regarding the absence of a means of valid cognition for both that ignorance and the means of cognition themselves with respect to the insentient: "Therefore, the insentient [is not known]," etc. He concludes the refutation of the opponent's view with "Therefore, [it is] through ignorance," etc.; the meaning is "in the absence of ignorance regarding the Self. Regarding the phrase "of that, therein": "of that" refers to the insentient.
In this context, the meaning is that ignorance is impossible with respect to an insentient object, because ignorance cannot have an insentient locus nor can it have an insentient object.

He concludes his own position with the words "therefore, from the perspective of ultimate reality. Now, one might object: in the verse of the final conclusion (*siddhānta-śloka*), it was shown that silver and the like are born from ignorance regarding mother-of-pearl and so forth, for the purpose of establishing them as examples; however, here it is said that there is indeed ignorance regarding the insentient mother-of-pearl and such.

[Page 200] It is said that "it does not exist. Anticipating the objection that this results in a contradiction between what precedes and what follows, as well as a lack of an illustrative example (*dṛṣṭāntābhāva*), he says:
"of this very matter. The ignorance regarding mother-of-pearl and so forth, established by worldly experience, was mentioned previously; however, here it is...

The status of being authoritative is negated; therefore, the meaning is that there is no contradiction between what precedes and what follows. It has been stated that one should not suspect that the example for the falsity of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is unestablished, because in the absence of the ignorance regarding mother-of-pearl, silver cannot be its product.
He states the reason for this as "well-known in the world" (*lokaprasiddha*). This is by one who asserts the unreality of all duality.

The meaning is that since only that which is established through worldly experience is accepted as an illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*), one should not suspect the absence of an illustration on the grounds of its lack of authoritative validity (*aprāmāṇikatva*). || 125 ||

Having refuted ignorance (*avidyā*) in the case of both the void (*śūnya*) and the insentient (*jaḍa*) individually, he states a common refutation for both with the word "void" (*śūnya*). Anticipating the objection that "error is the result," he considers the alternatives: is the error the result as residing in its own locus, or does it reside in the observer? He rejects the first alternative with the words "from the erring one" (*bhramataḥ*): those two, the void and the insentient, [cannot be so].
The meaning is "of that which wanders. He refutes the second [position] with the words "of the visible" (*dṛśyasya*).

[Page 201] To avoid the over-extension (atiprasaṅga) mentioned previously, he anticipates a restrictive rule (*niyama*) with the words "by the power of the observer's ignorance" (*draṣṭravidyāvaśena*). The meaning is that when a particular observer possesses ignorance, then at that very time, for that observer alone, there would be an error (*bhrama*) regarding the object of perception (*dṛśya*) through that very ignorance; it would not occur for others, nor would this [error] belong to anyone else—thus the restriction is established. If that is so, then as for the error...

He refutes [the objection] with the words "it is useless for others," stating that since it is through the ignorance of the seer (*draṣṭṛ*) alone that positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) are expressed, it follows that the material cause (*upādāna*) is that very ignorance; thus, the postulation of ignorance residing in the object (*dṛśya*) is redundant. Anticipating the objection that the postulation of ignorance is not redundant because silver and so forth cannot be established in the absence of ignorance in the object, he refutes it with the words "not without that. Furthermore:

He says "it would be useless" (*vyarthā*) with the words "and if it were born from that" (*tajjatve ca*). The meaning is that if error had ignorance (*avidyā*)—as the visible world—as its material cause (*upādāna*), then, due to the rule that an effect is dependent upon its material cause, there could be neither a connection [of the error] with the knowledge (*vidyā*) residing in that [Self], nor its cessation by that knowledge. He explains the third quarter [of the verse] with the words "even though" (*yadyapi*), etc.; for that which is not born from ignorance regarding a thing [such as a shell] cannot be removed by knowledge of that [thing].

This [object] does not exist, just like a rope-snake, water in a mirage, and so forth. Therefore, the meaning is that since the perception of mother-of-pearl as silver and the like cannot otherwise be accounted for, the ignorance of the object must be asserted. Rejecting *arthāpatti* (presumption) on the grounds that it can be explained otherwise, he explains the fourth quarter [of the verse] with "That is not so. || 120 ||

“Because of the absence of mother-of-pearl” means that the cognition of silver as mother-of-pearl in a dream does not arise from the non-cognition of mother-of-pearl, because mother-of-pearl is absent there. For this reason as well, the object of error is produced by the ignorance of an insentient entity.

"Nor is that so," he says. The meaning is that since agency and other such qualities can arise for the *jīva*—which is the essence of consciousness reflected in beginningless ignorance—through the modifications of its own limiting adjunct, the *ahaṃkāra*, not even a single fault applies. || 70 ||

[Page 239] Now, having granted that the object of cognition, such as the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra) and so forth, undergoes a change of state such as agency, he negates the self by means of the words "for this reason also" (itaśca) and so on. || 71 || 72 ||

It has been stated that the property of "alteration" (*anyathābhāva*) is not a characteristic of the Self (*ātman*). In that regard, having raised the objection concerning its self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*), he says "Now, of the Self," and so forth. Anticipating the objection that the fact that alteration is not established as having properties such as impermanence (*anityatva*) is contradicted by experience, he says: "Because [if it were] impermanent, it would be an object of perception" (*anityatve dṛśyatvāt*). Why?

He states that the self does not possess the quality of change because it is eternal, like [the state of] destruction; thus he says, "nor does it have impermanent qualities. One should not say that impermanence must be attributed to the self in order to establish its capacity for change;
therefore, he says, "and the self is eternal. || 73 ||

Having set aside the idea of the Self undergoing a change of state, he refutes the attainment of another nature by stating, "the state of being another entity. [Page 240] Furthermore, he states the reasoning: "even for one who possesses transformation and a second thing. (Verse 74)
"Otherwise" means that if the self-nature (*ātmabhāva*) were not always established, then even the means such as karma and so forth [would be ineffective].
[Page 591]— Page 242.
The meaning is that it would not exist due to the absence of a proving agent.
Chapter Two.
For, in reality, that which is limited cannot possess the nature of the Self.

It follows from this very point that the position held by the Vaiśeṣikas and others—that the Self is distinct from God—is refuted; thus he says, "For this very reason, the Self also [is not different]. He applies the subsequent portion of the text, "Then, how could there be anything else?", as the answer to the question regarding its being the Self. He then addresses the previously mentioned contradiction through the perspective of the opponent.

He clarifies this with the words "nanv anya eva" and so forth; then, having raised an objection regarding the contradiction once more, he provides the resolution with "nanv anya śrama" and so forth. On page 241, he summarizes what has been stated in conclusion with the words "śrata ātmāntarābhāvāt" and so forth. || 75 ||

It has been stated that there is no other form of the Self to be accomplished through knowledge and action. To this, an objection is raised regarding contradiction with scripture by the word "nanu" (but surely). Anticipating the argument that even scripture does not declare the becoming of one thing into another—and therefore there is no contradiction—he says, "na ca brahmaṇa eva" (nor indeed of Brahman itself). [He explains] "otherwise": if the state of being Brahman were to result from knowledge, then...

The meaning is that, previously, the non-establishment of Brahman would have occurred. As for what was stated—that it is not logical for anything other than the Self to possess the nature of the Self, just as in the case of a jar—that contradicts the scriptural texts regarding Brahman’s status as the knower; thus he says, "And not of the insentient. Having explained the distinction between sentience through the relationship of the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman, and having described the attainment of a different state of being, he now establishes the difference of the Self in each body.

By the words "and in the case of the wicked," etc., [the author] states that the distinction between individual selves (*jīva-bheda*) is established not only because the classification of the wise and the foolish would otherwise be untenable, but also because, if there were no difference between selves, the attainment of the knowledge of the Self (*ātmavidyā-lābha*) would be impossible; thus he says, "and for the learned one from the teacher. Furthermore, he says that the distinction between individual selves is also established by the unaccountability of the injunction "one's own Veda is to be studied" (*svādhyāyo 'dhyetavyaḥ*); thus he says, "study..."

"Also of the Mapī [Hiraṇyagarbha]"— anticipating the objection that there is no rule that study must come from another source because Hiraṇyagarbha’s Veda manifested spontaneously, he says, "so also of Hiraṇyagarbha. Having raised the view of the proponent (the Siddhāntin),
he introduces the fourth quarter of the verse, *bhinna-abhinnaṃ ca tat tataḥ*, with the words, "But this being so, one..."

[Page 242] He connects the second half of the verse with the words "Because of the non-difference from Brahman" and so forth. Having stated the consistency of all worldly transactions within his own position, he states their impossibility in the alternative position with the words "In the case of absolute non-difference. For if there were absolute non-difference, the relationship between the object of knowledge and the knower would be impossible; and if there were absolute difference...

The meaning is that liberation in the form of Brahmanhood is impossible. Furthermore, he states that those arguments favored by the proponents of Māyā (Māyāvādins) are merely fallacious reasonings (*tarkābhāsa*) with the words "of the goal and the attainer" (*prāpyaprāptrośca*). He states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) exactly as previously refuted, beginning with "it is said" (*atrocyate*), and so forth. Thus, the state of being both different and non-different (*bhedābheda*) between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman is not something accessible through scripture.

Having thus established that even for earth and so forth, as well as for Brahman, the state of being both different and non-different is not the meaning of the scripture, he says "In the same way,
of the world and Brahman," and so on. Furthermore, if the difference previously apprehended—
If one were to understand difference by relying on scripture, then Brahman would become both different and non-different; however, that is not the case.
Rather, by negating all difference through the statement "there is no diversity whatsoever here," scripture teaches non-difference.
Thus he says, "And it is not one. He then raises an objection regarding its status as perfect knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) on the grounds that it teaches the attribute of non-difference.

Regarding the phrase "of all entities": through the repetition of words such as "one" and so forth, it is understood that the intention of the scripture lies in absolute non-difference. He states "then, in the infinite [entities]" to show that there would be a contradiction with that [scriptural teaching]. Anticipating the objection that there might be no contradiction through another mode [of interpretation], he refutes it with the passage beginning "even if there were difference. [The point is that] while Brahman possesses non-difference from everything, this is not the case for a jar or other such objects.
He raises a specific objection regarding the case of a jar and so forth. He states that this cannot be asserted by one who maintains both difference and non-difference:
namely, that a jar and such are non-different from that [universal] by virtue of a certain non-difference, but not by virtue of any other.
If it is argued that there is no such equality, let all phenomena be so.

The non-difference from Brahman [is established]; otherwise, it would not be a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) with respect to reality, because it lacks the capacity to bring about true cognition. Or rather, it may be a means of knowledge regarding the act of perception, as in the case of the statement "Brahman is indeed Name."
This is the meaning. One should not say that this [text] is merely an injunction for the act of seeing;

to this he says, "And not," meaning that because there is an apprehension of a single essential nature through the reference to a conceptualized difference—just as in the case of "This is that Devadatta"—it cannot be so.
[Page 244] Now, one might object: in the Karma-kāṇḍa, the distinction between rituals is established by means of proofs such as the use of different words (*śabdāntara*) and so forth.

And since action is the work of Brahman, one might suspect that Brahman itself is differentiated by that form; anticipating this objection, he says, "and also of action. The meaning is that if it were already established, it would be a mere restatement (anuvādaka), and if it were not established, it would be impossible because there would be no production [of such a distinction]. He further states that even in the world, the establishment of difference is not based on valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇika*).

"Even by means of speech and so forth": he says this because the distinction between the knower and the rest is not established by valid cognition (*prāmāṇika*), since they themselves lack such status.
"Even when the difference in the object of knowledge is understood through that [distinction]"—he says this to show that for other reasons as well, reality is neither different nor non-different.

With the words beginning with "If it were non-different," he addresses the consequence of an infinite regress of Brahman. He resolves the objection regarding the infinite number of distinctions with the words "All distinctions..."

Regarding the claim that individual souls (*jīvas*) are parts (*aṃśas*) of Brahman, distinct in each body, he says: "And not [of] those parts. The meaning is that because of the scriptural text, "All this indeed is Brahman," everything is denotable by the term "Brahman"; and since Brahman is one, no internal division is possible. (76)
He introduces the verse by raising an alternative: "But if this... [page 593] ...because it is characterized by a single defining mark;
thus ends the second chapter.

He says that [if this were so], it would be exactly our own position that there is no ontological difference between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman; for how [could there be a difference] if both are pure consciousness (cinmātratve)?

He explains this with the words "bhideti" (it splits). On page 245, he states the defect in the second alternative with the words "brahmātmatve na hi" (for it is not so in the case of Brahman being the Self).

He uproots the third alternative with the words "cidātmatve jaḍāṃśatvaṃ na syāt" (if the Self were of the nature of consciousness, there could be no insentient part). He rejects the fourth alternative from the outside itself with the words "tathaikasyācidrūpatve 'pi" (likewise, even if one [part] were of an insentient nature). It is not only that the relation of part and whole [is untenable].

He states that even non-difference is not possible within the context of the fourth kalpa of manifestation, because of the nature of being both conscious and unconscious: "cidacidrūpatve" (in the state of having the form of consciousness and unconsciousness).

Furthermore, the proponent of the doctrine that Brahman is the world-process (prapañca-brahmavādī) must be asked: Is the world cognizable by Brahman, or is it uncognizable? Regarding the first case, he says: "The world is not the form of Brahman. Regarding the second case, he says: "If it were uncognizable, those [worldly things] would be unestablished. Furthermore, is Brahman also cognizable by the individual souls (jīvas), or uncognizable? Regarding the first case, he says: "And of Brahman..."

Regarding the phrase "jīvavedyatve" (if it were cognizable by the individual soul): he states another defect in the case where it is an object of cognition, saying "of both the individual soul and Brahman.
[Page 246] Having raised the objection, "But even in the view that Brahman is not an object of cognition, how can the knowledge of Brahman be possible?", he says:
His knowledge. || 78 ||

Having stated the possibility of omniscience and so forth for the one who maintains that space is real, [the author] states the impossibility of that for those who maintain the existence of manifoldness (*saprapañca*) with the words "If all, such as space, etc. The proponent of a Brahman characterized by manifoldness (*saprapañca-brahmavādī*) should be questioned: "If everything is Brahman, then what..."

Is it only the object of knowledge (*vedyam*), or only the knower (*veditr*), or are both mutually distinct, or are both together Brahman? Regarding the first case, he states the refutation: "The knower does not remain. Regarding the second, he states the fault:
"In being the knower, there is no state of being the object of knowledge. He extends this very point to the absence of omniscience as well: "Likewise, not for him..."
"Even omnipresence," so it is said.
And [the author] states that the messenger does not possess the status of being the creator of all things with the words, "nor of one who is unestablished."
He refutes the fourth alternative with the words "If Brahman... [He refutes the fourth alternative?
Since the nature of Brahman as a single unity is distinct from both [the knower and the known], Brahman would be distinct from the object of knowledge and the knower.
This is the meaning. || 81 ||

Having raised the objection that there exists a relationship between the object of knowledge and the knower due to a distinction of parts, he refutes it with the words "tadekāṃśasya" (of one part of that).

[Page 247] It was stated that even by accepting a distinction of parts, omniscience is not established; he now says that even this [distinction] does not exist, with the words "tadaṃśayorapi" (even of those two parts). || 82 ||
[Page 594] 560 Commentary on the *iṣṭasiddhi*.

[Page 247] Thus far, the elaboration regarding the refutation of omniscience has been presented; now, the elaboration regarding the refutation of the creatorship of all is set forth with the words "If Brahman... and so on. One who asserts that Brahman is accompanied by the phenomenal world (prapañca) must be asked: Is the phenomenal world [identical to] Brahman?

Does "possessing manifoldness" (*saprapañcam*) mean that it exists together with its effects? Or is the manifoldness itself an independent category, such that both the effect and the cause constitute the referent of the term "Brahman"? Or is Brahman the combination of both? A refutation has been stated for each of these three positions in the verse. Taking the position of their combination as a basis, he raises an objection with the words "prior to the creation of the world" (*jagajjanaiḥ prāk*), referring to the relationship between the whole and its parts.

He states that "in the absence of the whole" it is inconsistent to claim that "its part exists," because a part is never observed apart from the whole. Regarding this, he asks whether the establishment of the part occurs at the time of the world’s birth or even prior to it; he points out the defect in both positions with the words beginning "if [it exists] at the birth of the world. Furthermore, he states another defect regarding the [Brahman’s] being the ultimate creator of all.

By the words "the reality of its effect" and so forth, it is stated that the distinction between individual souls (*jīva-bheda*) is imagined by ignorance (*avidyā*), with the intention of referring to reflections within the various portions of *māyā* that constitute ignorance; however, this is not intended to mean that their essential nature (*svarūpa*) is imagined like that of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), because such a view will be refuted in the sixth [chapter]. || 83 || 84 ||

It has been stated that not only is the non-dualistic scripture (advaita-śruti) invalid in the view that Brahman possesses the world of plurality (saprapañca-brahmavāda), but even the established order of liberation (mokṣa-vyavasthā) is impossible. In this regard, he first states the impossibility of liberation in the verse beginning with "If [Brahman] were with plurality" (saprapañcaṃ yadi). || 85 ||
Fearing that there might be the attainment of identity rather than a conjunction characterized by contact, he says: "But of that which exists separately.
The meaning is that since the conjunction between a part and the whole is eternally established, it cannot be something to be accomplished.

Furthermore, does the individual soul (jīva) become Brahman by abandoning its status as a part, or while that status remains? He states that it is impossible in either case, saying: "having abandoned the status of being a part of Brahman. If its status as a part remains, how can there be Brahman-hood? Not from any source; the meaning is that because a part is limited (paricchinna), [it cannot become Brahman]. || 89 ||

Anticipating the objection that the part of the partless Brahman is not inherent but rather adventitious due to limiting adjuncts (*aupādhika*), he refutes it with the passage beginning "of the individual soul" (*jīvasya*). Since that which is adventitious— like the blackness of a reflection— is false (*mithyātva*) and its destruction is logically possible through knowledge alone, the acceptance of a combination of ritual action (*karma-samuccaya*) is redundant.
This is the meaning. || 80 || 81 ||
If, even while accepting that [the self's attributes] are adventitious (*aupādhika*), one does not conclude their falsity (*mithyātva*), then the effort of the Naiyāyikas is indeed in vain.
The second chapter.
He states that [the opponent's] abandonment of the distinction between souls as intended is [impossible], with the words: "And even if [the difference] were due to limiting adjuncts... (82).
0.00 561 [Page 249] If, out of fear of the aforementioned faults, one were to establish the existence of the individual soul (*jīva*) as qualified by each preceding further attribute—

Regarding this, he says: "If it were established beforehand. Since there would be an infinite regress if that which is already qualified by one adjunct were to be joined with another adjunct, it must be stated that the connection with adjuncts belongs to the Supreme Being alone.

Furthermore, because He is partless, that connection with adjuncts pertains to Him in His entirety; just as the universal "cowness" (*gotva*) is manifested in its entirety within individual cows such as the spotted one (*khaṇḍa*).

This being the case, of what could a distinction be known from what, by means of valid cognition? Of nothing, and from nothing at all, because there is no distinction in their own nature. ... || 97-98 ||

To the objection that "there exists a distinction among individuals due to the difference of adjuncts (*adhibheda*), such as the distinctions characterized by being human, divine, animal, and so forth," he says:

"If it be argued that there is a distinction of souls based on the difference of adjuncts. Just as the distinctions in the reflections—such as roundness or darkness found in a gem, a sword, or a mirror—are merely properties of the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) and do not reside in the face itself, so it is with respect to the individual souls (*jīva*).
He says "no" to the claim that the distinction characterized by sentience and so forth belongs only to the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) and not to the individual soul (*jīva*).

He introduces the verse as a reason with the words "since" (*yataḥ*). Even if you accept the plurality of limiting adjuncts as authoritative, because consciousness is partless, one must assert that its connection with all the adjuncts occurs in its entirety—as in the case of a reflection.

The meaning is that there is no contradiction by way of this door [of the limiting adjunct]. If it is argued that when the entirety [of the Self] is delimited by one limiting adjunct, a second delimitation is contradictory, then, O proponent of delimitation, your postulation of multiple limiting adjuncts is in vain.
Let it be exactly as I maintain: the distinction between individual souls (jīva-bheda) based on indeterminable ignorance (avidyā) is what is established by valid means of knowledge.
The meaning is that the postulation of a distinction based on limiting conditions (upādhi) is, however, futile. || 100 ||
Having raised the objection that there is no contradiction in multiple delimitations by the force of an example, he refutes it with the words "even of one" (ekasyāpi).

As for what was stated—that scripture itself proclaims through knowledge and action that one conscious being exists as another conscious being—that too is refuted by this [explanation], as he says: "of the difference which is conditioned by limiting adjuncts" (śraupādhikasya bhedasya). || 102–103 ||
[Page 250] He restates what was said regarding the reality of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) in order to refute it, beginning with the words "But surely the adjunct... (verses 104–105).
Is the limiting adjunct (upādhi) a form of Brahman or not?
Regarding the first [position], it is said: "It is stated."
[Page 596] 562 Commentary on the *iṣṭasiddhi*.

[Page 250] By the words "otherwise" (*anyathā*), the meaning is as follows: if there were no destruction of Brahman, there would likewise be no destruction of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), because the latter is of the same nature as the former. || 106 ||
The very power of transformation (*pariṇāma-śakti*) of Brahman, when unfolded in the form of an effect, is called the "effect.

The dissolution of the effect means its remaining in the form of mere potentiality (*śakti-mātra*). When it is asked how, therefore, there could be the destruction of Brahman, the proponent replies: "Because of the residue of potentiality" (*śakti-śeṣāt*). [This occurs] because during the dissolution (*pralaya*), [Brahman] exists in the form of potentiality.

The meaning is that, just as for those who remain [in bondage] there is a re-emergence at the time of creation, so too, because the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) that was dissolved during liberation re-emerges at the time of creation, there would be no final liberation. To the objection, "In that case, let the power (*śakti*) also be destroyed," he replies with the words "because of non-difference" (*abhedāt*). This is because the power is identical in essence (*tādātmya*) with the possessor of the power, which is Brahman.
The meaning is that without destruction, power does not perish. || 107 ||

The nature of Brahman, when possessed of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), does not become [identical with] Brahman; otherwise, even upon the destruction of Brahman, there would be destruction [of the soul]. To this, he says:

"Even though... (*yadyapi*). However, the connection of the word "nevertheless" (*tathāpi*) is not with the phrase "liberation would not follow" (*anirmokṣaḥ prasajyeta*) in the world [or in a certain portion of the text]; rather, it is that if, upon the destruction of one limiting adjunct, another limiting adjunct were also not to exist, then [the consequence would be] liberation for all at once.
The meaning is that there would be the destruction of the world. || 108 ||
...and he states with the words beginning "na ca" that the attributes of difference based on limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) are difficult to establish in Brahman;
for wherever there is visibility due to a limiting adjunct, there visibility of the thing as qualified by that adjunct is observed. That [visibility], being excluded...

The meaning is that [the text] excludes any distinction in Brahman that is based on limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). Since a distinction based on limiting adjuncts cannot be ultimately real, the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*) serves as the conclusion. Now, [the author] states the falsity of the distinction consisting of limiting adjuncts: "Even the distinction of adjuncts, because it is a distinction... [109–111].

He states the defect in the opposing view [that Brahman has form] in the words: "The limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is the form of Brahman. He says, "Nor [is it the case] due to a difference in adjuncts," to show that it should not be argued that even the distinction [between Brahman and the world] is necessarily dependent upon a further difference in adjuncts. (112–114)

Having concluded the incidental discussion, he states "tadeva śukteḥ" (that very [nature] of the mother-of-pearl), meaning that he now explains with the remainder of the chapter—using the guise of an illustration—the very nature of the mother-of-pearl as silver, which was previously recalled.
Having stated the purport of the remainder of the chapter, he states the purport of the immediately following verse: "pūrvaṃ vastunaḥ... (previously, of the object...).
Thus [ends the verse]. 115.
It was stated after accepting [the theory of] origination that if silver were a transformation (*pariṇāma*) of mother-of-pearl, there would be no sublation (*bādha*), just as there is none for a jar.
[Page 597]— [Page 253]
The Second Chapter.
Now, [the author] states that even birth is not possible due to the absence of a cause: "If the pure [nature] were born in the form of silver... and so forth.

Even if no external cause—corresponding to the activity of a potter or the like—is perceived, one might suspect that there could nonetheless be an internal cause called "cognition"; [anticipating this, the author] says: "And not born from the object of cognition," etc. (verse 116).
Having raised the objection that there might be another cause for the production of the mother-of-pearl in the form of silver, he refutes it with the verse beginning "śuktikā" (117).
Having accepted that even the cognition based on mother-of-pearl is indeed an error, he now states the objection with the words "If...
and "by those who are non-deluded. Let it be seen by those very ones who are non-deluded; he states the reason for this with the word "by delusion."
"Tviti" means that because the error is exhausted when the production of that [silver]—namely, the production of the nature of silver in the white shell—occurs. || 118 ||

Furthermore, since the disappearance of the effect cannot occur merely through the disappearance of its cause, he says, "In the production of silver," [implying that] even when the error arising from a defect has vanished, the silver might still persist. He concludes the meaning of the chapter with, "Therefore, it is only illusion (māyā). If the manifestation of silver were to occur while the power [of the substrate] remains as it truly is, then...

Its status as an error would be lost, just like the manifestation of a jar when clay has been transformed into the form of a jar. Therefore, the meaning is that by one who asserts that the manifestation of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell is an "apprehension otherwise" (anyathākhyāti), its very nature as being composed of illusion (māyāmaya) must be accepted.
Thus ends the second chapter of the *Iṣṭasiddhivivaraṇa*.
[Page 598] Now begins the third chapter.
[Page 254] Among the collection of alternatives introduced at the beginning of the second chapter, this concerns the second alternative.

The third chapter is commenced in order to refute [the opponent's position]. Since the refutation of the erroneous conception of cognition (*buddhi*) is preceded by the refutation of the erroneous conception of the object, there is a relationship characterized as that of cause and effect. [Regarding the phrase "yānyathā": therein, the first half of the verse is a restatement (*anuvāda*), while the second half is the formal proposition of the fault (*doṣapratijñā*). He recalls the reason with the words "na hi" (for not). || 1 ||
Since cognition is inherently formless (*nirākāra*), its representation otherwise must be said to be due solely to the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the object.
And it has already been stated that this is impossible if there is no "being otherwise" (*anyathābhāva*) in the object itself. To this, he raises an objection with the word "atha" (now).

"...as 'another place' and so forth. In common worldly experience, it is well known that something which is apprehended in its general form but not apprehended in its specific details serves as the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*). Since objects located in another place and so forth are not apprehended in any way whatsoever, [the superimposition] does not occur there.
The meaning is that [an error] is possible for one whose cognition is otherwise. He states the subverting argument for the contrary case (vipakṣa) with the words "even in deep sleep" (suṣupte’pi).
The meaning is: even if there is no apprehension whatsoever, if error were to exist, then it would also exist in deep sleep due to the defect of sleep. || 4 ||

He asks for the reason why other places and so forth are not perceived, saying, "From what? He replies, "Because of unfitness," explaining that it is because that which belongs to another time lacks the possession of form and other qualities at present, and that which belongs to another place lacks sensory contact; thus, even in the delusion of waking life, there is no perception of objects situated in other places and so on. However, in a dream, even the senses [are involved].
It has been withdrawn; therefore, the meaning is that the perception of an object there is even more impossible. || 5 ||

He completes what is required for the latter part of the verse with the words "even in the absence of [external] objects" (*sacādyabhāve’pi*). If it is argued that there is a perception of dream-objects even in the absence of external things due to a defect (*doṣa*), the proponent asks: "How can there be a defect? The meaning is that if [the cognition] were to reveal a real entity, it could not be a defect at all. If it is argued that its status as a defect arises from being the cause of error, he replies regarding that [error]: "In perception... (*dṛṣṭau*).

"Whence the delusion? means that the perception of a real object is not a delusion. Having provisionally accepted the perception of something existing due to a defect (*doṣa*), its status as a delusion was stated. He says "of that which has perished in delusion" to show that even such [perception] does not exist; the meaning is that since there is the manifestation of a son or the like who has actually perished due to defects such as grief, a delusion is not the manifestation of something currently existing. || 6 ||
The Third Chapter. [Page 256] [Page 599]
The proponent of the previous position says, "It existed previously," implying that existence at a later time must also be understood in that case. || 7 ||
Anticipating the question, "What is the result of this? he says: "That [Self] is known. (8)

Regarding the two established conclusions (*siddhāntau*), he states that "this is not sound" (*naitat sāram*) because the manifestation of an object belonging to another time in a direct error is impossible.
If, in order to avoid the charge of being without a basis (*nirālambanatva*), an object existing at the time of the cognition is postulated, he replies:
"If there is an object, it is not an error. "In that case" (*tathā*) means: as when there is an absence of an object at the time of the cognition.

Furthermore, if [the object] exists, there is no manifestation of the existent (satkhyāti), nor is there error; likewise, memory, doubt, and so forth would also not possess the nature of manifesting the existent.
"Otherwise" means that if it were a manifestation of the existent, it would lose its status as memory and so on, just like valid cognition (pramāṇa). || 8 ||

It was previously stated that "this [object] did not exist before; let it now be the object of the mental modification (*vṛtti*) regarding dancing. In that regard, having raised the doubt that its status as an object of the mental modification cannot occur because of its current non-existence, he says: "not now. Just as a jar, although currently non-existent, is designated by you as "knowable" due to its prior existence, so too [is this case], even though it is currently non-existent.
The sky will become a dance-pavilion by virtue of his former merit; such is the meaning. || 12 || ... || 13 ||

He says, "If [the object] were the agent of the act for the cognition," because a messenger who does not exist cannot function as an agent. Even if a son or other such object has perished, if one considers it to be the agent of the act for the cognition, then why does it not also perform purposeful action (arthakriyā), such as generating faith?
The meaning is that there is no reason for a definitive distinction. Let it be, then, that it performs purposeful action as well.

Anticipating the objection, "What then of the causal agent?", he says "of the two" (*dvayoḥ*). The meaning is that if the causal agent were to exist even after having perished with respect to both cognition and purposeful action, there would be no distinction between it and one that has not perished. [Page 256] In order to avoid the aforementioned fault, he raises an objection with "But surely" (*nanu*) to deny that past and other objects possess the status of being causal agents for cognition. ... || 14 ||

He completes what is required for the following verse with the words "even if destroyed" (*naṣṭam api*). If even that which is destroyed appears, let it be seen as having been produced, distinguished by its future particularity; and in that form, let it perform causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).

The meaning is that in that case, there would be no effort toward an object that is yet to come into being. By another method, he states the difference between error (*bhrānti*) and inference (*anumāna*) and so forth: "Nor [is it possible] in the case of inference and the like. In inference and such, it is not possible to postulate that the object is the generator of the cognition, because [the cognition] is established through other means alone. In error, however, since no other cause is possible, [it must be the object].
Activity is the cause. The meaning is that in the absence of an object, there would be no error therein...
[regarding] the eye and so forth—
[Page 600] 566 Commentary on the *iṣṭasiddhi*.

[Page 256—The resident [view] means that because it is the cause of immediate knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*), it depends upon a present object. Raising the question, "What is the result? he says, "As from what is heard, as from what is produced by the senses. This refers to what was stated in the passage beginning with, "If the producer of the cognition were destroyed," and so forth.]
"Otherwise" means that defects would follow in the case of a subverting cognition (*bādhakajñāna*).
The meaning is: "when there is an absence of mental activity. ... || 15 ||

It has already been stated that if even an object such as a past entity were to produce its own cognition, then the aforementioned fault would indeed occur. He introduces a verse as the reason for this with the words "yataḥ" (since). Validity would necessarily be [dependent on something else]; here he states the reason: "for that [cognition] does not exist without the object of knowledge. For (*hi*) because, without the object of knowledge—that is, apart from the object—there is no such means of knowledge (*māna*).

If the object of cognition (*meyam*) were the producer [of the validity], then validity would not arise, because in the absence of a cause there is an absence of the effect. Thus, the meaning is: to what would validity belong? If, for the sake of establishing validity, the object of cognition is also a producer, then whose existence would it be? The meaning is that it would simply be a present perception (*pratyakṣatā*). "If it exists" refers to its present form.
The meaning is that, just as [the object] is the object of cognition for my present consciousness. || 16 ||

because if an object were the producer of knowledge, it would necessarily be perception; therefore, he says "in the case of inference and so forth from an object" (*śrato'numānādiṣvarthasya*) to show that inference and the like are not produced by the object. ... [Regarding] the prior inference of the elements and so forth, the knowledge—

Having accepted that even in the absence of an object at the time [of perception], error possesses an objective support (*sālambanatva*), its distinction from that [valid cognition] was stated. Now, he says "And how... and so forth, to show that even for inference regarding past things and the like, the possession of an objective support is difficult to establish. The meaning is that because past things and the like do not exist at the time of the cognition—just like a man's horn—a cognition [of them] is not possible. For this reason as well, it is not [the case].

He states that "knowledge of the elements and so forth is possible" with the words "and not knowledge. Anticipating the objection regarding its distinction from the void (*śūnya*), he refutes it with the passage beginning "but not... [Page 258]. Regarding the phrase "otherwise": the meaning is that if it possessed a distinction from a human horn, it would necessarily be existent, and thus its status as an element and so forth would be lost. [This concerns] the co-location of the cognition and the object of cognition.
Thinking that there is no rule of simultaneity just as there is no rule of necessity, he raises an objection with the words, "Now it might be said.

Regarding the statement that [an object] is unknowable because of its non-existence, he replies: "Nor is it otherwise. Even for an object that exists at its own time, its non-existence at another time is not the cause of its unknowability; for instance, in the case of lightning, due to its momentariness, immediately after the moment of contact with the sense organ—

The meaning is that even though [the object] does not exist at that moment, its being an object of knowledge (*jñeyatva*) is observed. However, the two proponents of the established doctrine (*siddhāntin*) state that since it is difficult to define another time as a delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*), it is likewise difficult to define the knowability of that which is delimited by such a time; this they express with the words "What is that other time?
and so forth. Furthermore, he states that the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is dissimilar with the words "In another place," etc., because of the error pertaining to its own time.
