Chapter Twenty-Six.

The verses, which were previously interpreted as being intended to show that in the absence of an object there would be a lack of a supporting basis (*nirālambanatva*), may also be interpreted as being intended to refute the inference [of the existence] of the elements (*bhūta*) and so forth; thus he says, "In this case, however... (*asmiṃstu*).

He states that validity is indeed incapable of withstanding inquiry according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) by saying "it is exactly thus. He declares that the cognition of elements such as the *bhūtas* is included within insentient cognition by saying "for not... (verse 17).

[Page 259] Regarding the claim that "even a non-existent thing is seen due to a defect," he states "and due to a defect" (*doṣācca*) to show that this has been refuted by the logic already stated. He concludes the point—namely, how a defect could lead to perception and where the error lies—by stating:
"Even a defect is indeed a quality" (*doṣo 'pi guṇa eva*). || 18 ||
And as for what was stated—that it constitutes a fault merely because of a different understanding—he refutes that by raising the objection beginning with "nanu" (but surely), etc. (verse 19).
The refutation of the views regarding the beginning and the end will occur later in the remainder of this chapter. First, he states the fault in the middle alternative:
"If there were no sublation of the error regarding the silver... (vv. 20–21).

It was previously stated that even if one were to admit the perception of an object located in another place due to a defect, there could be no sublation because of the absence of the perception of the true nature of the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*). Now, he says "the appearance of what is not connected" (*ayuktabhāne*) to show that, due to the defect, the very perception of an object in another place is not possible. The meaning of the phrase "due to the absence of operation" (*avyāpārāt*) is "because of independence from the operation of the sense organs."
To avoid the consequence of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), he states "it might be thought" (*syān matam*) to explain the meaning of "there is an error when grasping a similar object.
He states "even then it is not due to grasping" (*tadāpi na grahāt*) to explain the meaning of "that [error] is not there because of grasping.
[The phrase] "grasped by correct cognition" (*samyagjñānena gṛhītaḥ*)...
If that object were the objective support (*ālambana*) due to its appearing through error, then even a jar or similar object would be so;

thus he says, "otherwise" (*anyathā*). He raises the objection regarding the equality of defects with "But those [objects] too," and he answers by partial acceptance with "True. For us, the objective support of the delusion is the indeterminable (*anirvācya*) product of ignorance (*avidyā*), but not this "this-portion" (*idam-aṃśa*).

The meaning is that for you, only this "this-portion" (idamaṃśa) is the objective support; therefore, we two do not share the same fault. Furthermore, he states that error has the "this-portion" as its objective support with the words, "And not of the substrate... [Page 260]. He says, "And when unperceived... to show that it is within one's own experience; for the silver is nothing but the experience itself, delimited by the "this-portion."
The meaning is that it is the substratum of error.
Having accepted that the cognition of whiteness and so forth is a cognition of a particular, he raises the objection regarding its non-contradiction by error, stating "whiteness and so forth.
He states the fault externally with the words "True, and yet... [The particular] is indeed blackness and so forth.
[Page 602]
Commentary on the *iṣṭasiddhi* | [Page 260]

...because it serves as a differentiator. Furthermore, he states "even the word 'power'" (*śaktirityapi*) because there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) if the apprehension of a universal-cum-particular were not opposed to error. And [he says] "nor is it without particulars" (*na ca nirviśeṣam*).

For the Vaiśeṣikas postulate two kinds of particularities (*viśeṣa*): first, the "particular universal" (*sāmānya-viśeṣa*), such as *śaktitva* (potency-ness) and so forth; because it is the cause of a cognition that conforms across its own individual instances and the cause of a cognition that excludes [them] from other instances, it is both a universal and a particular. [The second kind pertains to] eternal substances cognizable through the perception of yogis, which are absolutely similar to one another.

The ultimate particulars (*antyaviśeṣas*) are the differentiators. If it is argued that because they are eternally inferable, their non-perception would lead to the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) that [the world] would be as if non-existent, this objection is raised from the perspective of the Mīmāṃsakas, on the grounds that there is no proof for the existence of ultimate particulars, and thus the non-perception of a particular is merely due to its being unperceivable. To this, he provides a rebuttal by means of an alternative analysis (*vikalpa*).
"What is its fitness? and so forth [is the question]. || 25 ||
"For non-apprehension is not accepted as being due to a defect" means that prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) is beginningless. || 26 ||
Then, raising the objection as to how there can be non-illumination for Brahman, whose very nature is illumination, he says: "without Māyā.
For the non-illumination of Brahman, whose nature is illumination, is not produced by anything else; rather—
The meaning is that it is merely an illusion of self-luminosity. || 27 ||
He raises a doubt regarding the intention behind the statement that the defect resides in the organ (*agraha*), saying "a part of the visual faculty" [Page 262].

Anticipating the objection that even in the absence of a relation such as conjunction, there is a relation consisting in having a single person as their locus, he says "having a single locus. And [he says] "not," because the organ has the self as its locus, whereas the defect has the eyeball and so forth as its locus.
The meaning is that it also possesses the nature of having a substratum (*sāśrayatva*). "As in the time of non-apprehension" (*akhyātikāle*) means "as in deep sleep and so forth.
If you say, "The apprehension (*graha*) is possessed of an object," then one should not say, "Let it be exactly so"; thus he says:
And not so. || 28 ||

Having raised the objection that "non-apprehension" is what is meant by "anger," he provides the resolution with the verse beginning "vyaktyoraikyadhiyaḥ" (due to the cognition of identity between the two individuals). || 28 ||

Regarding the position that [the universal] is manifested by the individual, one must consider the alternative: is there no single cognition of two individuals manifesting the same universal, or is it that there is none between two individuals manifesting different universals? Having raised this doubt, he answers the first case with the words: "depending on one... (30).
[Page 263] Sometimes, when two things such as a broken horn and a hornless one are in close proximity, even without the perception of the [individual parts], [the cognition of "cow" arises].
[Page 603]— Page 264]
The twenty-fifth chapter.
It has been stated that "the one-pointed mind remains [in its own nature]"; regarding that...

Anticipating the objection that [the suffix] refers to the genus (*jāti*), he refutes it with the words "only in the genus" (*jātāveva*). Since the nominal stem *go-* denotes the genus, if the dual suffix were applied to the genus alone, then the misconception that "gāvau" (two cows) exists would be false, because duality does not belong to the genus. And yet, the nominal stem *go-* [is indeed used in the dual].
The dual number arises from the word *padika*. Therefore, the meaning is that the word "cow" does not terminate in the genus (*jāti*) alone.
Anticipating the objection that the non-difference between two individuals based on a single genus is unestablished, he says: "Nor is there only difference between the genus and the individual. (31)

[The author] raises an objection regarding the disparity between the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*) with the words "by way of the universal" (*jātyātmanā*). The identity of the "lumpy" and the "hornless" [cows] is by way of the universal, not directly as in the case of the universal itself; however, the direct identity of the shell and the silver cannot exist without non-apprehension (*agraha*).

The meaning is "it fits. It has been stated that there is no identity between the universal (*jāti*) and so forth and the individual (*vyakti*), just as there is none between the two [the universal and the individual]. Having raised the doubt as to how, in that case, there could be direct oneness for the universal and so forth, he says: "For not of one...
and "Even though... etc.

By one who asserts the identity of Khaṇḍa and Muṇḍa through the nature of their genus (*jāti*), it is implied that absolute identity does not exist, just as it does not exist for the genus and so forth. That is incorrect; the meaning is that even the genus and so forth lack such [absolute] identity. ... || 32 ||

Thus, it has been stated that the non-apprehension [of difference] is useless; for just as there is a cognition of identity even while the difference between the cow and the individual is manifest, so too there will be a cognition of non-difference between the power (*śakti*) and the silver-form even without the apprehension [of difference]. Furthermore, he states another reason for the uselessness of non-apprehension with the words "between the universal and its other": those two whose distinct forms are being perceived.

The meaning is as follows: just as there is an error even without the apprehension of the two parts—the general and the particular—which are being produced and deformed, so too [an error] would occur even without the apprehension of the mother-of-pearl, because there is no difference in their status as substances that are objects of perception.
[Page 264] He says "nanu" (but surely) by relying on experience. || 33 ||

Now, one might object: "In the cognition 'this is silver,' it is only the universal *rajata-jāti* (silverness) that appears, not the identity (*tādātmya*) with individual instances belonging to a different class.
Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And not there... [The cognition] of the direct perception of a universal is dependent upon the individual instance.

The meaning is: "because of the perception of [the two]. Regarding the phrase "as long as" (yāvacca): the meaning is that it has been stated that difference appears due to the employment of two non-synonymous words. || 34 ||

It has been stated that just as there arises a single cognition of two individuals due to their exclusion from two other classes even without grasping the individuals themselves, so too it will be for the two individuals of shell and silver. To this, he raises an objection regarding the disparity between the two cases with the words "vyāpyavyāpaka" (the pervaded and the pervader).

Here, "shell-ness" is the pervaded (*vyāpya*) and "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) is the pervader (*vyāpaka*). The cognition of identity in that case is based precisely on that [common property]. As for shell and silver—
[Page 604] 570 Commentary on the *iṣṭasiddhi*.

[Page 264] The meaning is that without the apprehension of the non-existence of that [silver], there could be no cognition of identity. The proponent says, "The mother-of-pearl," and so forth. Even in the case of the two entities, mother-of-pearl and silver, which are in close proximity, [the cognition occurs] without [relying on] the nature of the pervaded and the pervader as universals; rather, it is a substance—

The meaning is as follows: "But surely, the cognition 'this is silver' will arise just as the cognition 'this is one' is well-established; therefore, the relationship of pervader and pervaded (*vyāpyavyāpakabhāva*) is not a necessary factor."...

[Page 265] To the inquiry, "How is it that you abandon the subject at hand (*prakṛta*) and speak of something else? he first states the subject at hand with the words "he did not say. Now, he states the other's objection regarding speaking of something else with the words "But you...
That genus of "mother-of-pearl-ness" which does not exist in the silver, for that very reason does not appear there as silver—

The construction of the sentence is as follows: you state that "silver" does not appear as an individual capacity (*śakti*), yet now you do not state that there is no identity between two individuals belonging to different classes (*jāti*). What is meant is this:
when I have stated that there is a cognition of identity between two individuals of different classes, it is not for you to merely negate that [cognition].

It must be stated that there is an absence of the cognition "silver" where there is silver. Now, one might object: "In a formal debate (*vādakathā*), as long as the disputant has not become mute, he has not been defeated; therefore, the refutation of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) must indeed be carried out.
Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And how? ... || 36–38 ||

He restates and refutes the objection raised regarding the difference [between the two cases], namely that the cognition of identity between the two previous cow-individuals is not possible without the mediation of a universal (*jāti*), by stating "without the universal as a medium. In the case of a real shell and a false silver, sometimes there arises the single cognition "this is shell," and sometimes the cognition "these two. This single cognition does not [arise] for those two...

It exists by way of its universal (jāti), nor does it arise from the non-apprehension [of particulars], because it arises precisely from the apprehension of the aggregate (puñja). The point is that the cognition of an aggregate does not occur when there is no apprehension of the distinct individuals. He states another example with the words "of two existents" (sattvayoḥ):
a unity is perceived between two existents, namely a substance and a quality; and existence (sattā) is not there as a primary means or door [to that perception]. || 38 ||

[Page 266] It is not stated in the verse that "there is no genus or individuality for those two. Anticipating the objection, "How then has something additional been said?", he says: "by the word 'the state of genus and individuality'.
He states the connection [with his own position] with the words: "But in our view... (v. 40).

[The author] states "moreover" (*kiṃca*) to present another refutation against the position that there is no cognition of the identity between two individuals without the mediation of a produced universal (*upajāti*).
He states the meaning of "not from anything else" as "the non-difference of the genus."
[This is explained] by the verse beginning with "Even if there is otherness," etc. (41).
...he explains the second half [of the verse].
[page 605]
— Page 270] The Third Chapter | 571

[Page 267] If it is argued that the cognition of non-difference between two distinct things occurs even without non-apprehension (*agraha*), then there would be the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Therefore, he says "being perceived" (*mauyamāna*) to state that the utility of non-apprehension must be explained in order to avoid that [fault]; for the over-extension is not being leveled against you by me, but rather arises from a consideration of your own position.

To the objection that this would lead to an undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*), he says, "Certainly. If it is argued that practical usage (*vyavahāra*) exists precisely because [the distinction] is perceived, then in that case, do not imagine—do not postulate—the state of being both different and non-different in all instances; for it has been stated that there is an absence of practical usage corresponding to such [a nature]. Anticipating the objection that even for you there is no practical usage corresponding to the reality (*vastu*), he says: "For me..."
Thus [it is said]. || 42 || 43 ||

He raises the objection that non-apprehension (*agraha*) is useful for error because it possesses positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), using the phrase "the form of silver" (*rūpyākṛti*).

It is true that the utility of non-apprehension for error is established through positive and negative concomitance; however, he says "it is true" (*satyam*) to show that this is consistent with our own position. [Page 268]

Having raised the objection that there is a distinction [between the cognition of a jar and the cognition of its absence] because of the non-apprehension of the jar and so forth, he refutes it with the words "non-apprehension, because there is no difference," and so on.

The causality of the sense-organ (*graha*) for error, which was previously refuted in brief, is now undertaken to be explained in detail with the words "the causality of the sense-organ for error," and so forth. (48)

And since the messenger has been apprehended, there is no "apprehension-as-other" (anyathākhyāti); thus he says, "it appears as having the nature of silver. There is no such thing as its appearing otherwise—precisely because it has appeared.
Certainly not; for that which appears cannot be otherwise.

The meaning is that it is in accordance with those who follow consciousness. If this silver-aspect does not manifest by its own nature, then an "otherwise-appearance" (anyathākhyāti) is all the more impossible, precisely because it would have to be already manifest; such is the meaning. || 51 ||

Again, having raised the objection regarding *anyathākhyāti* (the theory of misapprehension) based on subsequent experience, he refutes it with the words beginning "If it appears as having the form of silver," and so forth. By the phrase "by the previous quarter [of the verse] alone," the meaning is: by the statement "in no way is this not that. In that regard, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvavādī*) raises the doubt concerning the identity intended by him between those two.
"In the case of mutual difference, it appears as 'not this'"; because of non-difference, it was stated that there is an identity between the "this" and the "silver" portions.
To the objection that in that case the non-difference of the two portions is not possible, he says: "Not, first of all... [by the proponent of the whole].
Because the whole (avayavin) possesses a nature distinct from each of its individual parts, there arises the cognition "this is silver" and "this is silver.
[Page 606]
572 Commentary on the *iṣṭasiddhi* | [Page 270]
It has been stated that [the whole] would be a distinct entity (*dharma*). If, out of fear of this fault, one does not accept a part (*aṃśa*) with a different characteristic form, then he says:

"a part that is not of that form. For the cognition of a distinct form is the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding the composite whole (*avayavin*); in its absence, the meaning is that there is simply no part existing apart from the aggregate (*samudāya*), which is otherwise indefinable.
Anticipating the objection, "Why is it not accepted that [the object] possesses form?", he says: "Of the one... [referring to] the one [entity] consisting of multiple parts.
Furthermore, in order to demonstrate the uselessness of apprehending the mother-of-pearl substrate (*śukti*), he restates the opponent's argument with the words "the form of silver" (*rūpyākṛti*).

Just as when a portion of ground is not apprehended, the absence of a jar therein cannot be known, so too, when that mother-of-pearl which is the locus of the absence of silver is not apprehended, it cannot be known that "silver does not exist there"— this is what was stated.

He states the opposite of that: "But in the case of a perception (graha), both of those [apply]. [Page 271] It has been stated that in the case of a perception, both the non-existence and the appearance of the form of silver are appropriate, because there is no distinction between the distinct power (śakti) and the silver.
To the inquiry "How so?", he first states the non-existence resulting from their difference with the words beginning "the form of silver."
And he states that the manifestation is conditioned by non-difference [of the power] in the words: "And because of the non-difference of the power" (verse 53).

Although the non-existence and the appearance of the form of silver in mother-of-pearl are not established by the power of error, one might suspect that they will nevertheless be established by the power of sublation; anticipating this, he says: "The appearance of the form of silver in mother-of-pearl," and so forth. ... || 54 ||
Now, he begins with the words "Who... (kaśca) and so forth, in order to demonstrate the lack of utility even by means of an investigation into the nature of the non-grasper. || 55 ||

Now, "athānyadhīḥ" is a restatement of the second alternative. The refutation therein is as follows: if there were a cognition of something else, it would be an error; for even in the case of grasping a power (*śakti*), you maintain that non-apprehension (*agraha*) is the cause of error, and that [non-apprehension] consists in the apprehension of something else. He states another refutation: "but there is no error when there is no apprehension of something else."

[Page 272] He says "nanu" (surely), meaning: if, while there is apprehension of something else, non-apprehension were observed even when [the object] is not apprehended, then that absence [of the object] would be my fault; however, it is not so observed. By the word "non-perception" (*adṛṣṭi*), is the absence of visual cognition intended, or rather the absence of cognition in general? As for the first [alternative]:
He replies, "That is not so. Having restated the second [position], he refutes it with the words beginning "tatrendriyāntara... (In that case, by means of another sense organ...). 56.

Now, having raised the objection that the non-apprehension of power is simply impossible when there is apprehension of something else, he refutes it with the verse beginning "The apprehension of power is the non-apprehension of something else," etc. (vv. 57–58).
Furthermore, having restated the opponent's argument, he refutes that specific point— that the non-apprehension of the mother-of-pearl is untenable when there is apprehension of something else—
on page 607 [page 275].
The third chapter:

[It begins] with "the apprehension of capacity (*śaktigraha*), the non-apprehension of another," and so forth. If there were a non-apprehension related to that [capacity] distinct from the two apprehensions—
In that case, there would be no apprehension [of either], and it would be eternal, because it would be empty of an intrinsic nature distinct from itself, like the self (ātman).

If, however, there were apprehension of both, why would there not be non-apprehension of both together? The meaning is that the two apprehensions themselves constitute apprehension only through mutual dependence. || 58 ||
For this reason as well, the position that the apprehension of one thing is itself the non-apprehension of another does not hold; thus he says, "Furthermore" (kiñca). || 60 ||

What is the meaning of the statement that there is no non-apprehension (*agraha*) apart from apprehension (*graha*)? Does it mean that the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and other forms of non-existence of apprehension do not exist, or that they are indefinable (*anirvācya*)? Regarding the first alternative, he says: "If non-apprehension were non-existent...

If apprehension exists as a real entity (*vastu*), then it must be said to exist at all times; otherwise, if it were merely occasional, then non-apprehension would have to be accepted as something distinct.
It should be as follows: since that [grasping] is not desired by you, therefore that grasping would have to be eternal in all things—this is the meaning.
With this very intention, he says "in the case of mother-of-pearl and so forth," stating that I have established the coexistence with grasping and other such factors.
He refutes the second alternative with "or else. Even in the absence of being a remover [of ignorance], in its capacity as an illuminator—

He does not raise the objection regarding the purposefulness [of the sense organs], but rather refutes it with the words "perception is for the sake of illuminating the object," and so forth. || 61 ||

What is this so-called "seizing of what is heard"? Is it the absence of grasping, or is it another cognition? Having thus formulated the alternatives, the refutation of the position that it is another cognition has been elaborated. Now, with the words beginning with "tat" [Page 274], he begins to elaborate the refutation of the position that it is the absence of grasping. || 62 || || 63 ||

"...even in the case of difference. This means that even if prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and so forth were distinct entities from the apprehension (*graha*), as long as that [non-existence] exists while that apprehension exists, prior non-existence and destructive non-existence (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*) simply do not exist— that is, they are impossible— because mere difference [is insufficient].

The meaning is that coexistence depends on the absence of contradiction because it is contingent upon being the cause [of one another]. Intending to show that if coexistence were established, then contradiction would be established, but in fact you are unable to define coexistence itself, the proponent of the final view (siddhāntin) says:
"Of those two, there is no... (64–65).

[Page 275] Previously, it was stated that contradiction is unestablished; now, even if that were admitted, he states that coexistence is unestablished with the words "if not at one time. For, in the second case, there is existence. The meaning is that since both difference and contradiction have a dual substratum, when the substratum is absent, that which depends upon it cannot exist. || 66 ||
Furthermore, he states that it cannot be said that apprehension does not occur at the time prior to non-existence (prāgabhāva):
The *Iṣṭasiddhivivaraṇa*.

[Page 275] Regarding the phrase "if, when its prior non-existence exists," he first states the refutation from the perspective of common worldly experience (*lokāihir eva*): "the cessation of that..."

[The opponent says: "Its cessation, too, is either opposed to antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) or not. In the first case, it would not occur as long as the antecedent non-existence exists, just like the [object] itself. [The author replies: If one objects that "cessation does not occur because time is occupied by an antecedent non-existence that is beginningless," then [the author], anticipating the doubt that "once the antecedent non-existence has ceased, its cessation [of cessation] would follow," says: "nivṛtyanta... [etc.]

The meaning is that if the cessation of each preceding [moment] is not established, the cessation of each subsequent one cannot be established. He refutes the second [alternative] with the words "if they were non-contradictory" (*avirodhinī ced*). The meaning is that apprehension (*graha*) would not occur because its contradictory, the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), is present. Having accepted the absence of the defects mentioned in the two alternatives, [he states that] its cessation is distinct from apprehension.

He states the meaning of the portion of the verse beginning with "yadi nāma" as follows: the objection was stated that if the cessation of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) were something that is opposed to prior non-existence, it could not occur; in response, the admission is made that it can indeed occur even if it is opposed. On the alternative view—that there is no opposition—the prior non-existence would also [persist] along with the cessation.

Thus the fault has been stated: "It would follow [that there is no prior non-existence]. Even if that is accepted, since its cessation occurs when it exists, if that prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) were not to exist, then its cessation would have to be described as something distinct from the apprehension (*graha*) and as occurring prior to it; consequently, that very cessation would be the prior non-existence of the apprehension itself, because the apprehension would be absent when the cessation exists.
The meaning is that [the effect] exists when there is existence. Anticipating the objection, "Why does this not also apply to the grasping (*graha*)?", he says, "But not of the grasping.
The meaning is that birth is admitted to occur in the moment immediately following cessation.
Then, anticipating the objection, "In that case, let cessation itself be the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*)," he says, "Another prior non-existence must also be stated. When [it exists]...

The meaning is that since the existence of a "grasper" (graha) is impossible upon cessation, if one were to posit another prior absence for the cessation of that cessation, there would be an infinite regress (anavasthā). If, in order to avoid this infinite regress, one does not even accept a prior absence for the grasper, then he says: "When... (yadā). || 67 || || 68 ||

[Page 276] Now, he elaborates upon omnipresence (*vibhutva*) by means of an objection, beginning with the words "nanu kūṭasthe 'pi" (But even in the case of the immutable...). By the statement that there is no apprehension of capacity (*śakti*) in things such as a jar, you do not deny apprehension itself—since you are a proponent of the theory that non-existence is merely another state of being—but rather you assert that something else exists. Therefore, [the following applies]...
The meaning is that all-pervasiveness (vibhutva) is established because there is no evidence for its being cut off [or limited]. || 68 ||

Thus, having first elaborated upon the immutability and omnipresence of the Grasper (*graha*), he now elaborates upon the non-duality of the object (*vastu*) by means of the passage beginning with "And in the apprehension of power" (*śaktigrahe ca*), and so forth. ... || 70 ||
[Page 609] —
Page 278] Chapter Twenty-Six.
575 [Page 277] Having raised an objection against the non-duality of the mother-of-pearl shell itself, he provides a resolution with the words "nanu śaktigrahavat" and so forth.
Anticipating the contradiction between agency and objecthood in a single entity, he says "nanu. The proponent of the established view (siddhāntin) replies:
"By this [verse], 'O Mountain'... || 71 ||

Having stated the general refutation regarding the existence of the absence of apprehension (*grahābhāva*), he now states the refutation by means of an analysis of its specific nature as an entity (*bhāva*), beginning with the words "Furthermore" (*dūtaśca*). First, he states the general refutation for all four positions with the word "in every way" (*sarvathā*). This is because there is no proof for the distinctness of those [factors]—the apprehended object and so forth—from the act of apprehension (*graha*), or from one another; thus, there is no evidence for a difference in their ontological status (*bhāvabheda*).

The meaning is that the absence of apprehension cannot be cognized as something other than the existence [of apprehension]. If you ask, "How is there an absence of means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) regarding the difference between existents?
you are asking while having forgotten [the answer]. Listen: first, we state that there is an absence of means of valid cognition for the difference in apprehension itself.
Is the difference in apprehension intrinsic (*svataḥ*), or is it due to a difference in the object (*artha*), or rather due to a difference in the cognition (*jñāta*)? It is not [any of these].

To this he replies with the words "firstly, not non-different. For the manifestation of a single form is the proof for the unity of an object, while the manifestation of different forms is the proof for its diversity. Since no distinction is manifested in the very nature of the apprehension, diversity is not possible;

otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of even the nature itself being divided. Therefore, in the absence of any basis in valid cognition (prāmāṇikatva), [diversity cannot be established].

The meaning is that for whom a difference appears, it is due solely to the power of inexpressible ignorance (*anirvācyājñāna*). He addresses the second [position] with "of both," and he refutes the third with "therefore, nor even... The phrase "therefore" means because there is no proof for a difference in the nature of the apprehension (*graha*). He states this very point in the *Vivaraṇa*: "when there is the apprehension of one... of one.

If, when there is the apprehension of a person's capacity, there were no apprehension of this [other], then there would be a difference consisting in the non-apprehension of a distinction by the knower.
And for you, since the negation of apprehension is not admitted, the distinctness of apprehension is not established; such is the meaning.

[Page 278] Now, if it is argued that there is a difference in apprehension for each individual because they serve as the means for establishing distinct linguistic usage, he replies: "And if there is no non-apprehension... etc.

The knower is independent with respect to the act of knowing; however, that would not be possible if knowledge were eternal. Therefore, since the status of being a knower cannot otherwise be established, one must admit a distinction between acts of apprehension; thus he says, "because the apprehension is non-eternal. For us, the conventional usage of the distinction between the knower and the known is possible even through a distinction created by indeterminable ignorance (*anirvācyājñāna*).
The meaning is: "Let this fault belong to you alone, since you do not accept indeterminable ignorance (anirvācyājñāna). || 72 || 73 ||

Having stated the lack of evidence for the distinction between the grasper (*grāhaka*), he states the lack of evidence for the distinction between the grasped (*grāhya*) and so forth with the words "Furthermore" (*kiṃca*).

The meaning is that because there is no deviation from the cognition of a single [object], it is possible to ascertain that everything has the nature of that [single object]. [This is] like fire and heat...
It was stated [by the opponent] that "they are perceived together" according to the Buddhist view; now, he states the distinction from that [view]:
Śrāvaṇatvasya...

*The Commentary on the Proof of the Desired* (iṣṭasiddhivivaraṇam) | [Page 278]—“But it is not so,” he says. Even when a fire is seen from a great distance, because its heat is not perceived, there might somehow be a cognition of difference there; but that is not the case here.
The meaning is that it is because there is an invariable rule regarding such a manifestation. He concludes: "Therefore, there is no other apprehension.
The word *graha* (apprehension) found in the verse is intended to indicate by implication the objects of apprehension (*grāhya*) and so forth as well. || 74 ||

Thus, having first refuted the non-existence of the apprehended object (*grāhya*) and so forth in a general manner, he now states a further refutation for each individually, beginning with "And not the apprehended object" (*na ca grāhya*). If, in the existence of that [object], there is no apprehension— due to the contradiction of their coexistence— then one must not say that the apprehended object is the absence of apprehension, because those two cannot exist together.

The meaning is "because of existence. He states the fault in the opposing view (*vipakṣa*) with the words "it does not praise silver" (*na rūpye stauti*). In the position that there is no grasping of the object to be grasped (*grāhya*), even if silver exists or if mother-of-pearl (*śukti*) exists, those two [the cognition and the object] would not exist; or, if those two graspings were accepted, then silver and the shell-silver (*śaktirūpya*) would not exist. Thus, since co-existence is impossible, there can be no relationship between the grasped and the grasper (*grāhyagrāhakabhāva*).

The meaning is that it would not be so. This very point is shown in the *Vivaraṇa*: "Otherwise, those two would not be established. For if the silver were non-existent as something illusory, and the mother-of-pearl were non-existent in its ultimate reality, then both [the cognition and the object] would be impossible due to the absence of an objective support (*ālambana*). Some say, "And of those two," because the object of apprehension (*grāhya*) is the absence of apprehension.

He extends the principle demonstrated regarding the case of *saṃbhava* to other instances as well, stating "of the *grāhaka* etc. The meaning is that for the *grāhaka* and so forth, the state of being non-existent (*abhāvatva*) is not possible, because they are co-existent with the *grāhya*. || 75 ||

By another method, through the statement that difference is not established by valid means of knowledge (*aprāmāṇika*), he negates the status of "being another entity" for the absence of apprehension by means of the phrase "it is not an apprehension," and so forth. [Page 279] Mutual...

Does the cognition of existence establish difference when difference is unestablished, or when it is already established? Regarding the first case, he states that there is an impossibility of establishing difference with the words "tatrāsiddhe" (in that case, when [difference] is unestablished), etc. Regarding the second case, he says "na ca siddhe" (nor when it is established).
Anticipating the objection that this explanation contradicts the words of the verse, "nānyā gaurbhedikā tayoh" (the cow is not other than those two as a differentiator), he says:

"By the word 'cow'": it has been stated that there is no other means of valid cognition for difference. To this, he raises an objection: "But [it is] desired," and he refutes it: "Not even of that. The meaning is that even in the case of a prior cognition of difference, whether the difference between the locus (*dharmin*) and the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is established or unestablished, that [prior cognition] cannot be the prover of difference, because it would be either redundant or impossible. || 76 ||

He extends the stated reasoning to other cases as well with the words "In this way, in all [cases]. The meaning is that whether difference is established by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) or not, mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) cannot be established by that means; therefore, there would be only one entity (*bhāva*), and no other entity whose nature as a non-apprehension you maintain. || 77 || || 78 ||

"Non-apprehension is either different from apprehension, or it is simply the absence of apprehension, or it is apprehension itself"—thus it has been analyzed in three ways.
Having refuted the first [position] at length, he refutes the remaining two positions with the words:
"only a difference in name. Even when one denies that what is called "non-existence" is a real entity, it is merely a matter of names.

There would be a contradiction of the very definition [of the terms]. The sense is that it would follow that the words "grasping" (graha) and "non-grasping" (agraha), which are well-known to be non-synonymous, would instead become synonyms. || 78 ||
Anticipating the objection that there might be another way [to explain] non-apprehension, he refutes it with the words "If the self were unchanging," and so forth.

[Page 280] Thus, having first stated the uselessness of non-apprehension because it is difficult to define for those who maintain the theory of misapprehension (anyathākhyāti), he demonstrates the uselessness of the apprehension of a similar object with the verse beginning "sadṛśārthagraha" and so forth. || 82 ||

When it was asked, "Tell me, what are the two ways in which there is the apprehension of a similar object and the production of error," the proponent, observing the silence of the opponent, himself formulated the alternatives and said: "Is it in the cognition of silver, or in its being otherwise? (83)

It has been stated that where the perception of one thing arises from the perception of another, that [perception] is dependent upon the apprehension of a relation; therefore, a relation must be asserted for the sake of pervasion (*vyāpti*). To this, an objection is raised: "This is not a case of pervasion," suggesting that the apprehension of pervasion occurs even without the apprehension of similarity. As a rebuttal, he applies the verse with the words "No" (*na*). 84.
For the determination of the causal relationship is indeed established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).
It has been stated that because such concomitance is absent in the case of similarity (*sādṛśya*), it cannot be a cause. He explains this with the example: "The conch is yellow."

In the case of owls, there exists a superimposition of darkness upon the sun, yet there is no similarity whatsoever. The universal delusion that "the sky is black" or "the firmament is dark" involves no similarity consisting of a commonality of qualities or parts, because both the sky and blackness are partless. This is also the case in the instance of "two moons."

There is a similarity between duality and the moon; likewise, how [could there be] a cognition of svarita-ness in that manner? The meaning is: "from nothing at all. Now, if it is argued that even there, a similarity consisting in the non-perception of difference exists within a single entity, he replies:
"In every case, there is some degree of similarity. This applies even to such instances as "the cow is a fragment" or "the jar is white."
The consequence is that [the cognition] would be erroneous; the meaning is that the defect of similarity, characterized by the non-apprehension of difference, is present. One might argue:
"Let there be no error born of similarity where similarity does not exist, but it will occur in cases such as the silver in a shell.
Iṣṭasiddhivivaraṇa | [Page 281–]

Anticipating this objection, he says: "Because it arises from similarity to what is heard. The meaning is that since an error can occur even through another defect, one cannot postulate similarity as the cause, because it is an external factor (*bahir-aṅga*), like the heat of a gem.
Anticipating the objection that the apprehension of the mere object might then be the cause of error, he says: "If [it were] from the apprehension of the mere object... (vv. 85–86).

Furthermore, regarding the status of the apprehension of similarity and the apprehension of the mere object as causes of error: is this [cause] past or present? It is not the first; thus he says: "In one who is deluded, or whose eyes are closed. He restates the second alternative: "If the impurity consists of the erroneous apprehension and the [mere] apprehension. In that case, do these two have the same object or different objects? It is not the first.

Thus he says, "not one or the other" (*naikacet*). Regarding the alternative, however, he states more extensively that it is "neither the left nor the other. Elsewhere, the phrase "if there is grasping" (*ced-graha*) is a restatement of the second alternative; regarding that, he states the refutation: "What would happen to this [cognition] from grasping in such a way?
On page 282, he explains the meaning of the statement "if even a portion of grasping exists in the error" with the words "fearing the aforementioned defects" (*uktadoṣabhautya*).

He states the meaning of the question, "Why is another part not an apprehension (*graha*)? as follows: "Why should the error (*bhrama*) not be an apprehension, since there is no difference in its being a part of a single cognition? Anticipating the objection, "In that case, how is the distinction between error and apprehension made in the world?", he says: "But the apprehension is that which is connected with the sense organ. This is just as, for example, although a bull is a cow, one says, "This is a cow," while "That is a bull."
The distinction in conventional usage arises from internal differences; likewise, even though perception is erroneous, it is considered valid because it originates from a defect [of the senses].
This is the meaning. || 87 || 88 ||
Furthermore,

he states "and the portion consisting of error" because even by the fact that the well-known status of error as a cognition would otherwise be inexplicable, the apprehension of the aspect [of the object] must be accepted by everyone. This is because it arises from the identity with the apprehension of the general aspect of the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*).

The proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntin*), considering that the conventional designation "planet" (*graha*) applies to the delusion (*bhrama*) and not because it possesses a portion of a planet, refutes its status as a partial portion by stating: "It is said... Here, the word *sva* refers to the delusion. *Svārtha* means the object of the self (the delusion).
That which is suitable for this [delusion] is *tattvārthayogyākṣam*. He who has a planetary portion (*grahāṃśa*) produced through connection with that is [the subject].

Thus it has been stated: "O portion of such a planet, salutations! [The meaning is that] due to the absence of eyes (akṣa), it would not exist in the void (kha). When there is wandering in the mere planet without distinction, and when the two are seen, at some point there might be the wandering of delusion. || 8 ||
Anticipating the objection that the cessation of all sensory activity is not established even in a dream, he refutes this with the passage beginning "even in a dream" [Page 283].

Having first rejected the mind's status as a cause for non-perceptual (parokṣa) apprehension by assuming its status as a cause for perceptual (aparokṣa) apprehension, he now states that even its status as a cause for non-perceptual apprehension alone is not observed in the waking state.
"And yet there is no grasping of something imperceptible. He states the distinction from the waking state with the words "even though not seen here.
Nevertheless, he says "that too" to show that the nature of error as a partial apprehension is still not established. || 80 ||
[Page 613] —
Chapter 284:
The Twenty-Eighth Chapter on the Āyuṣman.
It is heard that even in a dream, there occurs an error regarding the perception of pleasure and so forth, which are not merely objects of the mind.

Anticipating the objection that a dream might be merely a delusion, he says "by the mind alone" (*manomātreṇa*). If it is not accepted that there can be a delusion of taste—such as hearing that milk is bitter—then that which is not suitable for the mind, such as color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth, should not be said to be experienced by the mind in a dream; otherwise, it would follow that one could have a delusion of taste arising from the ear. This is the meaning.

Previously, having accepted that pleasure and so forth are grasped by the mind (*manas*), it was stated that there might be an error of taking pleasure for pain or pain for pleasure, but not an error regarding blue, yellow, and so on. Now, he says that even the grasping of pleasure and so forth by the mind does not exist, because it is admitted that they are known by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*): "In a dream, for someone, [it occurs] by the mind alone."

He says, "Even in a dream," because even the apprehension of a non-present object would result in the undesirable consequence of being sublated. Sublation consists either in the knowledge of the true nature of the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna-yāthātmya-jñāna*) or in the knowledge of mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva-jñāna*). Regarding the first [alternative], it has been stated that it is difficult to establish whether the single cognition that grasps multiple substrata is itself one or many. As for the second—
He says that even this is not possible: "Nor at one time" (nāpyekadā). || 82 ||

Anticipating the objection that even obstructive cognition arises solely from the defect of sleep, he refutes it with the words "If it were so" (*syāccet*). He concludes the intermediate point of inquiry with the words "Therefore, of the defect of sleep. The meaning is that when there is an absence of defects, the cause of cognition exists; however, when a defect is present, there is no valid cognition. This refers to what was previously under discussion.

He concludes with the words "so too in other cases. If there were doubt regarding silver in another location and so forth, then sublation would not occur whether a defect exists or does not exist; this is the point under discussion. Thus it is established that a defect lacks the capacity to apprehend what is not present; such is the meaning. || 83 || ... || 84 ||

Regarding the phrase "if it were silver": since it has been established that the cognition of the substrate (adhiṣṭhāna-jñāna) possesses sublativeness, that [cognition] which is silver would be a sublater [of the erroneous cognition], provided it were not so experienced; this is the meaning. || 85 ||

Thus, having first set aside the middle alternative among the three alternatives by declaring it to be difficult to explain, [the author] refutes the first alternative by stating "then, in that case" (*tarhi tarhi*) and so forth. The meaning is that in the case of an error where silver is perceived in mother-of-pearl, such a perception is not possible;

The explanation of the phrase "at another time" (*kālāntare*) is "either before or after. The meaning is that when indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpaka-pratyakṣa*), which consists in the apprehension of pure existence (*sanmātra*), arises, there is no manifestation of spatial or other limitations; therefore, a difference in the nature of the object is not established.

The meaning is that since a delimited valid cognition is impossible, there can be no valid cognition of absence whatsoever, because its object—an absence delimited by a locus and a counter-positive—is impossible. || 18 ||

[Page 302] Thus far, it has been stated that non-existence (*abhāva*) is devoid of epistemic authority because it is illusory (*māyāmaya*). Now, he states another defect for the Prābhākara, who does not accept even non-existence as being of the nature of illusion, beginning with the words "meyābhāve" (in the absence of the object of cognition). When an object is intended to be grasped—that is, desired to be apprehended—and the causes for its apprehension are present, [the following occurs regarding] illusions...

If it is argued that the conventional usage of non-existence occurs even without an actual non-entity because there is no arising of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) [for it], the refutation of that is as follows: "because the conventional usage of the existent and the non-existent would always occur. This means that at the time of perceiving a jar or the like, there would necessarily be the conventional usage of the non-existence of that jar and so forth, since there is no separate cognition of an absence to be required. This refers to the conventional usage of the non-existent.

Having explained [the previous point] by means of word-analysis (*padaccheda*), he further explains that the conventional usage of "existent" (*sad-vyavahāra*) should also always be [understood as such], stating: "and the conventional usage of 'being' (*bhāva-vyavahāra*). If it is argued that the conventional usage of "being" is postulated for the sake of avoiding [the extreme of] mere consciousness (*vijñāna-mātra*), he replies: "if it has an object" (*sārthaśced iti*). The conventional usage of "non-being" (*abhāva-vyavahāra*) is a usage that possesses its own corresponding objective support (*ālambana*).

The meaning is that it is like the conventional usage of "non-existence" [derived] from you. Furthermore, he states "nor... because non-existence must be accepted as an object of cognition (*prameya*).
He explains the portion beginning with "nanu... and so forth, preceded by the word "śāpūrvaka," showing that even the desire to grasp (*jighṛkṣā*) is fruitless in the case of non-apprehension.
He further states "nor... to show that the desire to grasp is useless when there is no apprehension. [If it were otherwise,] its being a particular would entail its being an existence (*bhāvatva*).
The meaning is "by way of a logical consequence" (*prasaṅgāt*). It was stated that there is no manifestation of non-apprehension (*agraha*) because it is related to a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*);

he explains this with the words "for not... (*na hi*). Anticipating the objection that while non-apprehension does not indeed manifest, there is nevertheless the conventional usage of "non-apprehension" when apprehension does not arise, he says: "If that [non-apprehension] does not manifest... (*sa cenna bhāti*). What is denoted by the word "non-arising" (*anudaya*) is the absence of apprehension (*grahābhāva*).

It was stated that if it does not appear, then how have you understood that there is the conventional usage of "absence" when there is no apprehension? Anticipating the objection that "in that case, let there be the appearance of the absence of apprehension," he says: "If the absence of apprehension... If even the absence of apprehension—which is impossible for that which is self-luminous—appears, then the absence of the object of apprehension (*grāhya*) appears all the more so. As for the apprehension...

The meaning is that it is precisely the positive entity (*bhāva*) that serves as the cause for the cognition of the absence of the object of apprehension (*grāhyābhāva*). With the words "Alternatively" (*athavā*), he introduces the verse by another method; having set aside the cause for the cognition of absence as accepted by the Logicians (*Tārkika*), he restates and then refutes the view of the Bhāṭṭas and others with the passage beginning "the object being absent" (*arthamukte*).

[Page 303] Furthermore, does the non-apprehension (*agraha*), when unknown, serve as the cause for the cognition of "not being so" (*atadvat*), or does it do so when known, like a logical mark (*liṅga*)? It is not the first case; thus he says:

He raises a second objection with the words "tahīti" (then). [The opponent asks: "But surely it has been observed that what is known functions as a cause, like the sense organs and so forth, by virtue of its invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) and other factors; however, by what power does non-apprehension (*agraha*) function as a cause? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"By way of invariable concomitance (*nāntarīyakatvena*)" means by the force of logical impossibility (*anupapatti*). He explains this very point:

[the objection] being raised—"If the difference between objects is established through perception, why should non-existence not be a property (*dharma*) due to its non-apprehension?"—he replies, "And there is no specific object. The meaning is that for that which apprehends only a positive entity (*bhāva*), there is no operation in the apprehension of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*).
He goes...
"And of the means of knowledge" (*mānasya ca*). The meaning is that the means of knowledge must be either insentient (*jaḍa*) or sentient (*ajaḍa*).

In the first case, there would be universal blindness; in the second, it would result in the loss of non-duality (*advaita*). Furthermore, the means of knowledge is not an object of measurement (*aprameya*).

"Whether the entity (bhāva) is self-luminous or not self-luminous," [the author] replies regarding the first case with the words "And of that... [meaning] "due to the absence of a counter-correlative" (vyatirekābhāvāt). The meaning is this: it is impossible to understand that an absence does not exist when there is no apprehension (agraha), because if the apprehension itself is not cognized, it is likewise impossible to cognize the absence delimited by it.
Having refuted the causality of non-apprehension by relying on the causality of the desire to grasp (*jighṛkṣā*) and so forth,
he states "if" (*yadi*) to show that even that [desire] does not exist. This is because two cognitions of existence and non-existence, which are contradictory effects, cannot have a single cause.

The meaning is that because there is no basis for postulating the causality of an object—such as an inferable entity—that is yet to come into being. Having accepted the second alternative, he states the fault with the words "yadi nāma" (even if...).
Anticipating the objection that "if the causal relationship itself cannot be apprehended without some prior cognition at some time, then let there be such a cognition," he says:
And not so. || 21 ||
It was stated according to his own view that the non-existence of the mind, which is established by the witness-consciousness (sākṣin), is also established by the witness-consciousness;
now, having raised the objection from the perspective of the Bhāṭṭas, he says "by the absence of the fruit," and so forth. || 22 ||

Having raised an objection to the statement that "the non-existence of the object of cognition (*meyābhāva*) is not established because there is no arising of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding illusion," he provides a rebuttal beginning with the words "The means of cognition is action" (*mānaṃ kriyā*). On the ground, the absence of a jar is perceived due to the non-arising of the means of valid cognition for the absence of the jar; likewise, one might suspect, why should there not be an absence of the establishing proof (*sādhaka*)? Anticipating this doubt, he says: [Page 305] On the ground, the absence of a jar is seen because of the non-arising of the means of valid cognition for the absence of the jar. Likewise, one might suspect, why should there not be an absence of the establishing proof? Anticipating this doubt, he says:

"Even the absence of an object," etc. For this reason as well, he states that the non-existence of a means of knowledge (*māna*) is not established by the absence of a result (*phala*): [page 625] [page 307] *mānā-*...

Regarding the phrase "if [it is argued] precisely because the knowledge of existence does not arise," he explains the portion of the verse beginning with "the intellect is never [so]."
For when he says "hau," || 23 ||
It was previously stated that you do not say, "Having perceived the absence of a fruit, I know there is an absence of a means.
Now, even if that were asserted, the desired conclusion would still not be established; thus he says: "If the means is measured by the absence of the fruit," etc. (24).

It was asked, "What is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for that absence of fruit? [The opponent] raises the objection that this is inconsistent, beginning with the words "bhāvo yasyeti" ("of which there is existence"). Whatever is fit for a linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*) prompted by something is well known to be an object of knowledge (*prameya*) by that thing. Since the existence and non-existence of consciousness are fit for linguistic conventions prompted by the very nature of consciousness, the nature of consciousness itself is the means of valid cognition (*māna*) for those two.
This is the meaning. || 25 ||

[Page 306] "Even that non-existence (abhāva) always implies existence (bhāva). He joins the second half of the verse again with the words "tathāpi" and so forth, by breaking the compound as "abhāvāt" (from non-existence). Furthermore, he says "yadi ca" (and if), meaning that it is not possible for non-existence to be established by the very same means by which existence is established. [Non-existence is] other than existence...
"Why is it that non-existence does not exist? To this he replies: "Therefore, why is it not the case that there is no existence other than that [non-existence]?

Having raised the doubt that this might be so because there is no distinction or difference between existence and non-existence, he says: "Even though there is non-difference between existence and non-existence.
The meaning is that non-existence is dependent upon existence. Since everything would consequently result in being existence...
Thus is the conclusion. || 26 || || 27 || || 28 ||

[Page 307] In response to the inquiry, "How is there non-establishment in all three ways?", he first states the impossibility of the two positions [of cause and effect], beginning with: "If it is established by itself in the absence of the fruit. He says "then" (*tadā*); the meaning is that because the fruit is absent at the time of its non-existence, and because that which is non-existent cannot be a producer. He says "nor" (*na ca*); [it is not established] while it persists...
The meaning is that it is incorrect to say that there is a proof for the non-existence of the state of being a fruit (phalatva). || 29 ||
He states the impossibility of excessive practice [of the means] with the words "nor even another" (nānyo vāpi). || 30 ||

It was stated that the valid cognition (*pramā*) by which a person knows the result must itself be denoted as the valid cognition. In that regard, having raised the objection that [the result] might be known merely through the nature of the self (*ātman*), he refutes this with the words "if it were known by that" (*vetti tacced iti*). This is because even by means of the object of knowledge (*vedya*),...
Anticipating the objection that "let it be so that the object of measurement is seen by means of a lamp," he says, "just as by a lamp.

The meaning is that even a lamp performs merely the removal of darkness; it is never observed that an insentient thing (jaḍa) can initiate the conventional usage of "immediacy" (aparokṣya) with respect to anything. || 31 ||

[Page 308] He states another defect regarding the result being an object of cognition with the words "Furthermore" (kiṃca). || 32 ||

Thus, having first established that because the result (*phala*) is not an object of cognition, its non-existence (*abhāva*) is likewise not an object of cognition, he states another reason for the impossibility of non-existence with the words "pradhvaṃsa" (destruction). This means: by the very same arguments stated starting from the passage "non-existence is another positive entity" (*bhāvāntaramabhāvaśca*).

[Objection: But surely, according to the view of one who maintains that non-existence is simply another positive entity, the nature of both the result and its non-existence is the Self (*ātman*) itself, and the Self is also the substratum (*guṇin*) of the result.
It will come to be. Therefore, raising the doubt as to how it is possible for that which is of the nature of non-existence to be perceived, he says "na hi" (for not).

The meaning is that there is a demonstration of pervasion (*vyāpti*): whatever is visible and impermanent does not constitute the essential nature (*svarūpa*) and so forth of the seer, just like a jar and other such objects. ... || 33 ||

For this reason as well, he states that consciousness (*saṃvit*) is not a quality of the self (*ātman*) and so forth, saying "guṇaguṇyaikayā" (by a single cognition of the quality and the qualified). The meaning is: when there exists that single cognition (*tāvad-dhīḥ*) by which those two—the quality and the qualified—are apprehended. If the illumination of objects were accepted as being a quality of the non-self (*anātmaguṇatva*), it would result in the fallacy of falling into the doctrine of the Lokāyata (Materialists).

Regarding this, he says: "If it were a quality of the jar. He states another defect if it were a quality of the jar, saying: "If consciousness were a quality of the jar. Anticipating the objection that consciousness differs from color and other qualities because it is non-inert (ajaḍa), he says: "And not so. || 34 ||
Fearing that consciousness might be subject to modification in order to avoid the defects of being an insentient quality (*jaḍaguṇatva*), he refutes this by stating "for consciousness is...
(1.3.4). Thus, since the status of consciousness as either a quality or a modification has been examined and its non-existence is impossible, its eternity [is established].

Having thus established [the permanence of consciousness], he now begins to demonstrate that consciousness is indeed immutable (*kūṭastha*) because destruction— whether from itself or from another— is impossible, starting with the words "not of that which has arisen," and so forth. Since objects such as a jar, once they have acquired their own nature,
are seen to undergo destruction caused by external factors, it would be illogical for consciousness— which has likewise acquired its own nature— to undergo causeless destruction.

Anticipating the objection that "in that case, let there be the destruction of only that which lacks an intrinsic nature," he says: "And [an entity] not having attained its own nature... Furthermore, by one who asserts a causeless destruction while maintaining the doctrine of momentariness, destruction would have to be accepted as the very nature [of the entity].
And in that case, because it would be pervaded by destruction, there could be no arising; thus he says: "And for that which has destruction as its nature... Destruction—

He says, "of that which is unborn," because birth must be explained precisely through the impossibility [of its existence]. Well then, is this birth imagined by you something belonging to the non-existent or to the existent? He says, "of the non-existent," for it is neither way. By stating that the destruction of the non-existent is not possible, he rejects the destruction of the existent; yet that [destruction] is not tenable.
Thus he asks, "And how? If destruction were simply the abandonment of the nature of existence, even that would not be possible for that which exists.

The meaning is "due to the contradiction of its nature. Anticipating the objection that "in that case, it would be abandoned by being non-existent," he says: "By not abandoning [it], there is no non-existence."

The meaning is that there is a fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*): non-existence occurs through the abandonment of the nature of existence, and the abandonment of the nature of existence is performed by means of non-existence.
Furthermore, he says "nor" (*na ca*) to show that the abandonment of the nature of existence cannot be accomplished by non-existence.
Thus, it has been stated that a momentary entity does not exist because the birth and destruction of existence and non-existence cannot be established. Now, another reason [is given]:

Furthermore, regarding the impossibility of momentariness, he says "of birth and destruction. Is the cause an external operation, or is it internal cognition, or another consciousness? He refutes the first [option] by saying "nor like a jar.
He refutes the second alternative with "nor also... (verse 36).
He replies to the third [objection] with the words: "Not [to one] unborn," etc. (37).
The destruction of a prior action is well-known to occur upon the arising of a subsequent action; thus he says: "They produce another consciousness.

If consciousness were a single primordial nature (*prakṛti*), then there would be a contradiction in their coexistence; thus, upon the arising of a subsequent [consciousness], the preceding one would perish. Yet it has been stated that this is not the case. To address the inquiry as to how this is so, he offers the following alternative: "Or in all things," etc. This is because [consciousness] arises with respect to each object as its producer.
Nature is established as one; and it either pertains to the immeasurable or pertains to the measurable—such is the division of the words. || 40 ||
Having restated the first [position], he refutes it with the words "in all things," etc. (vv. 41–42).
Having refuted the first alternative along with its elaborations, he refutes the second by stating,

"If it were one with respect to each object": if [the cognition] were one with respect to an object— whether that object possesses as many qualities, as many powers, or as many parts as it may have— then...

The meaning is that consciousness (*saṃvit*) is the primordial nature (*prakṛti*); at that time, through the perception of a jar, its power would become directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*), because the primordial nature—which pervades the entire jar—has become the result. He rejects the third position with the words "the measure for each" (*pratyekamāna*).
If there were a single primordial nature of consciousness corresponding to whatever object falls within the range of a single means of knowledge (*māna*), then, by the perception of form...
The meaning is that there would be reliance on the eyes, because the knowledge produced by the five sense organs is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). || 43 ||

He refutes the fourth [position] with the words "pratyekendriya" (each individual sense organ). If the nature of the consciousness that illuminates the entire range of each single sense organ were one, then there would be the simultaneous perception of all forms.

The meaning is that because all form is visual, it is the result of consciousness whose nature is to manifest all forms. He uproots the fifth alternative with the word "pratyeka" (each): the object of a single mental modification (*buddhivṛtti*) is [perceived] by each individual consciousness.
Iṣṭasiddhivivaraṇam | [Page 311] If that were its nature, then there would be no destruction of the consciousness that has already arisen, because of the arising of a subsequent consciousness.
For you accept the destruction of the preceding [moment], yet two cognitions are not observed as objects of a single mental state; such is the meaning.

He states a common defect regarding all four positions in the verse beginning with "pūrveṣu" (in the former cases). The meaning is that the cognition of one person regarding a certain object would not belong to another person, because it is contradictory for multiple transformations to occur simultaneously from a single primordial nature (*prakṛti*). Having raised the doubt as to why the fifth alternative was disregarded, he states the specific reason.
"Together with one" (sahaikasya). || 84 ||

He refutes the sixth alternative, [the claim] that "the proposition is contradicted. The meaning is: "one should remember what was stated beginning with 'if there were a unity in all things,' etc. He states another common fault with the words "in every way" (sarvathā). At this very point, he states another refutation with the words "not of men" (na puṃsām), and further states another fault here externally.
"Not yet," and so forth... || 48 ||

It has been stated that if consciousness were inherent in the self (*ātman*), there would be no such thing as the non-perception of external objects. This very point is explained by the two verses beginning with "If that same... and so forth. It cannot be said that consciousness illuminates only that which does not produce it, for otherwise it would follow that even the eyes and other sense organs would be self-luminous. If this were the case—

Out of fear of [the aforementioned] defects, it is maintained that consciousness alone is the material cause of the manifestation of an object; to this, he replies: "If consciousness were the material cause...
Zero...
One.

[Page 313] Previously, it was stated that even if one were to grant that the self pervades objects, there could be no direct perception of external things by the cognition of the self; now he says "it reaches the object" (*sāpnotyartham*) to show that even this [pervasion] does not exist. "Otherwise" means:
if it were not self-luminous, it would not be a cognition. Having raised the objection regarding its difference from color and other qualities, he refutes it.

[The author] states "not that [cognition] is the means of knowledge and the object of measurement," and so forth. Anticipating the objection that there is a deviation (vyabhicāra) because cognition, pleasure, and so on—which are self-cognizable—are nonetheless seen to have the self as their substratum, he says "tadedyāntare" (with respect to other objects cognized by that).

The meaning is that there is no deviation, because there is no difference in the fact that even those other objects such as cognition and pleasure, which are cognized by that self, lack the status of having the self as their substratum.

He speaks with bold assertion: "Even if it were a modification of the Self. The meaning is that action cannot abandon its own substratum to go elsewhere. Anticipating the objection, "How could the insentient be established even for you?", he says: "But for me...
The meaning is that the status of the insentient as an object of empirical usage is possible through its illusory association with consciousness. Nevertheless...

Anticipating the objection as to how the conventional distinction between the knower and the known can exist given the oneness of Consciousness (citi), he says: "In the case of otherness," etc.
Furthermore, since anything other than consciousness (cit) is merely imagined, its very origin and so forth are refuted due to the impossibility of a cause;
thus he says, "of the consciousness that is heard [in scripture]. (51)
[Page 314] Since consciousness (*cit*) is immutable and non-dual, this is the conclusion: "It is indeed *ṛta*.

Regarding this, the Prabhākaras and others hold that immediacy resides in the knower (*pramātṛ*), while the Bhāṭṭas hold that it resides in the object of knowledge (*prameya*). As for the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)—

"The Buddhists say it has gone," he says, [referring to] "the manifold" (vicitrā). This means that it is independent, devoid of the modifications of existence such as birth and so forth, perceived in its own nature, and free from the attributes of the objects of cognition such as dimension and the like. || 52 || || 53 ||

Having concluded the intermediate point of proof (*avāntaraprameya*), he concludes the main subject with the words "by the existence or non-existence of the result. Now, having for the sake of argument accepted the establishment of the means of knowledge (*māna*), he states the defect in the failure to establish its absence (*abhāva*) with the words beginning "even if established" (*siddhe ’pi*). Non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) is the cause for the measurement of existence; if that is not established, there is no [proof] whatsoever of absence.
The meaning is that it is established by virtue of its true nature. || 54 ||

It has been stated that the inference of the existence of a means— based on the result called the cognition of an object, using the argument "it must have a means because it is a result, like boiled rice"—

and the inference of its non-existence based on the absence of a result, are not possible because the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished. Now, the linguistic usage regarding what is known (*jñāta-vyavahāra*) presupposes the establishment of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa-siddhi-purassara*), as it is a qualified usage (*viśiṣṭa-vyavahāra*).

He refutes the claim that there is an inference of cognition from the existence of the known object, and an inference of the non-existence of cognition from the non-existence of the known object— comparable to the conventional usage of the term "staff" because it is worn as a necklace— by stating, "the inference is of the known. Since the establishment of the known object depends on the establishment of the cognition, and the inference of the cognition depends on the establishment of that known object, the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished due to mutual dependence (*parasparāśraya*).
This is the meaning. Anticipating the objection that "by process of elimination, let the mere object itself be the inferential mark (liṅga)," he says, "nor is it the mere object.

The meaning is that there is no pervasion (vyāpti) such that wherever there is an object, there must be cognition, because it is admitted that an object exists even in the absence of cognition. || 55 ||

Furthermore, it is maintained that an absence is established as valid only when its locus (*dharmin*) and counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) are themselves established by valid means of cognition (*prāmāṇika*).

Since the locus and counter-correlate of the absence of knowledge—namely, the knower (*pramātṛ*) and the means of cognition (*pramāṇa*)—are not established by any means of valid cognition, the absence of knowledge cannot be established; thus he says, "And [if] the knower and the means of cognition... A means of valid cognition does not establish itself or its own substratum.

It pervades because it is dependent, like an action (*kriyā*). And in the case of the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), even the action would have to pervade, because there is an equality in both being supported by the agent and the measure, and an equality in both being dependent on the agent and the measure; such is the meaning. He raises an objection regarding this disparity.
