The word "nanu" is used to clarify the fault. Having conceded the suspected inequality, the author of the Siddhānta states his own intended position of equality with the words "it is said. Even though there is a difference in activity—where one activity is performed by one [agent] and another activity is itself the object of the desire to speak—the agent who possesses the activity is not different from the activity itself.

The meaning is that even if [the self] were an intermediate object (*antarakarma*), the contradiction between being an agent (*kartṛ*) and being an object (*karman*) remains unavoidable. Anticipating the objection, "In that case, let it be the object of the activity of another agent," he says, "Nor... If there were one agent who is the object of the activity of another agent, then, since the status of being an agent is no different, the other [agent] must likewise be said to be the object of yet another agent. [This would lead to an infinite regress, as the activity] must be preceded by an instrument (*karaṇa*).
The meaning is that because the operation (*vyāpāra*) is necessarily [distinct], another instrument (*karaṇa*) must also be postulated, which would result in a multiplicity of assumptions.

Just as the agent (*kartṛ*) and the operation do not possess the status of being the object (*karman*) of their own or another’s operation, so too the knower (*mātṛ*) and the means of knowledge (*māna*) would not possess the status of being the object of their own or another’s act of knowing; thus he says, "of the knower and the means of knowledge as well. And as for the [distinction between] being established (*siddhatva*) and being unestablished (*asiddhatva*)—
He states "yathā" (just as) to show that even that suspected dissimilarity does not exist.

Now, having raised the objection that while an object may be established by its own nature even before it is measured—despite the absence of the property of being measured—the effect is not established by any form whatsoever, he says "rūpāntarasiddhistu" (but the establishment by another form). He again raises a doubt regarding dissimilarity.

Regarding the objection "is it not unestablished? and the phrase "otherwise": if the knower is established only by an object, then for the knower herself—who is herself an object—does her status as a knower arise through herself or through another? In the first case, the establishment of oneself depends upon one's own establishment, which is the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*).
In the latter case, even another knower would only be a knower insofar as she is known by yet another knower, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). This is the meaning.

He refutes [the objection] by accepting half of it, saying "True. It is true that there is no status as a valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇikatva*). Nevertheless, the manifestation of the cognized object and its validity must necessarily be asserted; otherwise, after the object has been established, there would arise the possibility of doubt—such as "Was this known by me, or not?"—which is the meaning. As for the fault in [denying] manifestation:
He states another [objection] with the words "otherwise" (anyathā). || 56 ||
He concludes the primary great subject of inquiry with the words "of another entity" (bhāvāntarasya). || 57 ||

Now, he refutes the view of those who fall at the feet of the Digambaras and who everywhere maintain that [the soul and the body] are both different and non-different, in the verse beginning with "bhinna-abhinnam. || 58 ||

[Page 317] An objection is raised: "Is it not the case that where a cognition of non-difference is sublated by a cognition of difference, there is *anyathākhyāti* (misapprehension), but not everywhere? Anticipating this, he says: "Power is non-different" (*śakterabhinnam*). The word "shines" (*śobhate*) is used in an ironic sense (*viruddhalakṣaṇā*). The meaning is that because both difference and non-difference are established by valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇika*), it does not shine—that is, it is not tenable. || 58 || ... || 60 ||

"Because its form is different."
...he begins the established doctrine; regarding that, it is said: "O messenger! (62)

Since it is difficult to determine whether a thing is different or non-different based on a difference in form, one must ultimately conclude that the object itself is inherently both different and non-different. In that case, the previously mentioned fault remains unavoidable; such is the meaning of the two verses.
Having raised an objection regarding error from another perspective, he refutes it [in the verses] beginning with "bhinnābhinne" (65) and ending with [verse 66].
Regarding the word "false" (*mṛṣā*):

anticipating the objection that "this fault does not apply to me because I do not maintain an absolute non-difference," he says, "But even though there is non-difference. Regarding the word "otherwise": [it means] as something entirely different and independent.
The meaning is "because of [our] experience. He states another reason for the possibility of incomplete cognition with the words "and because it has the form of difference.

He refutes [the opponent's position] starting with "that," etc., by means of the argument that difference is difficult to define. The connection is as follows: "In that case, even a mere name could be known in your view," because even if difference is difficult to define, non-difference can still be known.
Anticipating the objection as to why even an atom’s worth [of difference] should not be known, he says: "Of the two forms, distinct and non-distinct.
Anticipating the objection based on what is established by experience, he refutes it with the words beginning: "But surely it appears," and so forth. || 67 ||

Now, by examining the nature of the subverting cognition (*bādhakajñāna*) as well, he states the impossibility of subversion with the words "the cognition of mother-of-pearl" (*śuktidhīḥ*), and so forth. The meaning is that the negation must be expressed only after having made that mother-of-pearl known—not before, nor simultaneously—because the cognition of the locus (*dharmijñāna*) is the cause of the cognition of negation. If that is so, then [regarding] the mother-of-pearl...
Anticipating the objection that "the negation of silver may occur simply by not cognizing it," he says: "And not of one [alone]," etc. (Kārikā 68).

It has been stated that without the cognition of the locus (*śakti*), the negation of silver therein is not possible. To this, one might raise the objection of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) by asking: "But what if [the negation occurs] even when the rope is not grasped? In response, he says: "True; however, in the case of another object... (verse 71), meaning that even there, negation does not occur without the apprehension of the substratum (*dharmin*), and thus there is no deviation.
[Page 632] Here begins the *Iṣṭasiddhivivaraṇa*.

According to the Buddhist view that the affirmation of one thing is itself the negation of another, he states the sublation [of the opponent's position] with the verse: "If affirmation were itself negation... (74).
Anticipating the objection based on the principle of parity (*pratibandinyāya*), he refutes it with the words beginning "But surely for you as well" (*nanu te'pi*). || 75 ||
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the *Iṣṭasiddhivivaraṇa*.
[Page 633] Now begins the sixth chapter.
[Page 324] Thus far, it has been shown that the doctrines of other schools are untenable without an indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*) ignorance (*avidyā*).

Having established [the point] and thereby resolved that contradiction, he now raises an objection in order to avoid the disagreement among those of his own school, beginning with the words "the locus of ignorance" (avidyāśraya), etc. || 1 ||

fearing that if individual souls (*jīvas*) were distinct from Brahman, non-duality (*advaita*) would be lost, whereas if they were not distinct, ignorance (*avidyā*) would belong to Brahman itself, [the author] says:
"Even those [souls] are imagined through ignorance. [He adds: "There is no charge of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśrayatā*) and so forth," for indeed, that fault [does not apply].
The meaning is that [investigation] may apply to an object capable of withstanding analysis, but not to ignorance, whose nature is inherently untenable. || 2 ||

He states the establishment of his own position with the words "due to their difference" (teṣāṃ bhedāt). The meaning is that because the Self is indeed one, two—the knower and the ignorant, or the teacher and the pupil—cannot possibly exist. || 3 ||

To state that ignorance (*avidyā*), which is dependent solely on pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), is the cause of all established distinctions, [the author] refutes his own schoolmate by saying, "In this regard, it is said. Since the status of insentient matter as the locus of ignorance has been rejected by the arguments stated in the verse on insentience (*jaḍaśloka*),
and since even the imagined individual soul (*jīva*) is insentient— like a snake imagined upon a rope— the meaning is that ignorance is not defective.

One should not say that even the imagined [self] is non-inert; thus he says, "not non-inert. The meaning is that its existence and manifestation are established independently of anything else. Nor should one say that the individual soul (jīva) consists of both conscious and unconscious aspects; thus he says, "for this very reason, neither inert nor non-inert. The meaning is that these two are not postulated, because that which is non-inert cannot be so postulated. || 4 ||
He states another reason for the fact that the imagined cannot be the locus of ignorance with the words "for this reason also" (*itaśca*).
Anticipating the objection, "Let Brahman not be unknown; what fault would there be then?", he says: "then [the thought] 'I am Brahman'... [Page 325]

It is well known that what is unknown becomes known through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and that which is not yet known is an object to be known by such a means. Since these conditions do not apply to Brahman, and since anything other than it lacks reality, it has been stated that there can be no such thing as "knowledge of Brahman" (*brahmavidyā*). Anticipating the objection, "Let there be no such knowledge; what of it?", he says: "Because of its non-existence [as an object], it does not lead to liberation. For this reason as well, for you—Brahman...

He says that liberation does not arise from knowledge because of the absence of ignorance regarding Brahman. Anticipating the objection that even if liberation does not come from knowledge, it might nevertheless result from ritual action, he says, "Nor from anything else," because of the absence of a locus.
[Page 634]
6,000 [ślokas]:
Commentary on the *iṣṭasiddhi*.

[Page 325] The impossibility of ignorance (*avidyā*) has been stated. To that, an objection is raised: "Of Brahman alone... He replies: "...by you, under another name, my own position has been adopted. His own school says: "That very same thing... What?

The distinction [between Brahman and the world] is either a secondary characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*) or a qualifying attribute (*viśeṣaṇa*). Regarding the first [option], he says: "In that case, of that very [Brahman]" (*tarhi tasyaiva*). Having raised the second alternative, he refutes it with the words: "of Brahman itself, which possesses a fictitious otherness" (*brahmaṇaḥ kalpitānyatvasyaiva*), and so forth.
Having raised the previously mentioned intention of the opponent, he rejects it with the words: "this fault does not apply," and so forth. [This is the view of] one of our own school (*svayūthya*).

He says: "That [ignorance] does not appear to those who are liberated. If it is argued that ignorance is not admitted for the liberated because of the absence of such a perception, then your own hypothesis also cannot be established, since there is likewise an absence of such a perception; this is what he means by saying "tat" (that).
Furthermore, it would contradict the logical principle regarding infinite regress (*anavasthā*). He restates what was said by the opponent: "And as for what was stated—"

[Page 326] Now, it may be objected: "Ignorance (*avidyā*) is a perverted cognition; therefore, its absence is being established. And the reason for that is 'freedom from grasping' (*niragrahatva*). Anticipating this doubt, he says: "If freedom from grasping... Here, in the argument that "Brahman is not the locus of ignorance because it is free from grasping, like one who is liberated," the fallacy of "unestablished for either party" (*anyatarāsiddhi*) has been stated. [The opponent replies: "No..."

According to his own view, he states that [the argument] is not a valid reason (aprayojakatva) with the words "even in the absence of apprehension" (agrahābhāve’pi). The meaning is that the position of our own school—that there is a causal relationship between error and its latent impression (saṃskāra) alone—would be lost if there were an effect of non-apprehension. Furthermore, he says "of beginningless non-apprehension" (anādyagrahasya) to show that his own position would be abandoned for this reason as well. Now, even if the individual soul (jīva) is merely imagined—

Anticipating the objection that the beginningless [world] is simply the non-apprehension of that very substratum, he says, "And not at the beginning" (*na ca sādau*). Then, regarding the possibility that even the delusion which fashions the individual soul (*jīva*) is beginningless, he says, "And all" (*sarve ca*). Anticipating the objection that although the individual manifestations of delusion are indeed beginningless, the stream of that delusion is beginningless, and therefore the soul—which is supported by that stream—is also beginningless, he says:
"And its stream as well. || 5 ||

Regarding the claim that the object of Brahman’s ignorance is the imagined [world] and its locus is the individual soul (jīva), he states another defect with the words "Furthermore" (dūtaśca). Anticipating the objection as to how ignorance could be established in that case, he says "Nor indeed" (na vai tu iti).
"Svaruk" means self-luminous. || 6 ||

[Page 327] Raising the objection, "How can the state of being unknown (ajñātatā) be possible for that which is self-luminous (svaprakāśa)?", he says: "The state of being unknown belongs to that which is self-luminous. Regarding the phrase "even by that which is self-luminous": this refers to Brahman as distinct from the imagined individual soul (kalpitajīva).
The meaning is that, although it is self-luminous, we have no experience of it as being an object of ignorance. || 7 ||
And the messenger does not speak of a distinction between the locus and the object of ignorance, saying, "The self-luminous shines.
[page 635]— [Page 330]
The Sixth Chapter. 601.
Therefore, [it is said]: "Of whom ignorance would exist. Ignorance does not depend on a distinction between its locus and its object, because it is an obscuration (āvaraṇa).
The meaning is "like darkness. || 8 ||
Anticipating the objection, "What follows if there is no distinction between the locus and the object of ignorance? he says: "In that case, of the other...
(verse 9).

If ignorance were destroyed by the destruction of ignorance, then this fault would indeed arise; however, since that is not the case, he says "it is said," and so forth. Furthermore, he states "the destruction of ignorance" in order to show that ignorance is not destroyed by knowledge. Anticipating the objection that one might be liberated while living (jīvanmukta) yet still possess scriptural knowledge, he says "nor [is there] non-liberation."
"Even though liberated" (*nmukto'pi*). He explains the portion "or as if by delusion" (*dhaurtṛthaiva vā*) differently: "or because of the absence of the fruit of delusion" (*dhauphalābhāvād vā*).

It was stated that when ignorance is destroyed at the time of birth, there would be a birth for the knower (*jña*). Anticipating the objection as to what fault there might be in that case, he says: "In knowledge, [there is] knowledge," etc. (14).
[Page 329] For this reason as well, he states that consciousness alone is unreal, beginning with the words "If the imagined... (kalpitasya cet).
[The opponent] objects: "If the effect were distinct [from the cause], there would be the fault that the cause would be dependent upon the effect.
Anticipating the objection that what is imagined through ignorance (*avidyā*) is merely ignorance itself, he says: "And this [is called] ignorance of ignorance.
The meaning is that the bondage of the Self is established by means of ignorance. Furthermore, regarding ignorance...

He says, "And not of that," [meaning] there would never be liberation if there were bondage. Having accepted bondage for the sake of argument, he has stated the impossibility of liberation because of its contradictory nature. He further states, "Nor even bondage," [meaning] that even the meaning of the word 'bondage'—namely, the perception of pleasure and pain—is not applicable [to the Self]. || 15 ||

He states that the position that the messenger is a fabrication of ignorance (*avidyā*) is untenable with the words "tatkalpitasya" (of that which is fabricated by it). He further states that one must not say that the insentient *avidyā* is removed from the insentient Brahman by means of knowledge (*vidyā*).

"And there is no other ignorance" means that knowledge (*vidyā*) cannot exist when ignorance (*ajña*) is not sublated; thus he explains the portion [of the text] with "And if ignorance is not sublated. He states the meaning of "without ignorance" by saying "the ignorant person," and so forth, beginning with "Certainly not when ignorance is not sublated. Anticipating another view in order to avoid the aforementioned fault, he raises an objection with "But surely," and so on. [The word] "imagined" (*kalpita*)...

Having raised the dilemma as to whether difference (*bheda*) is a secondary characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*) or a qualifying attribute (*viśeṣaṇa*)— as in the case of [the terms] "Brahman" or "living beings"— he refutes it with the words beginning "If [it were] non-imagined" (*akalpitasya cet*). Anticipating the objection that there is no infinite regress because [the series] is beginningless (*anāditva*), he says [on page 636]:
602 Commentary on the *iṣṭasiddhi* | [Page 330]

"...then even there. Furthermore, since difference (*bheda*) possesses a counter-correlate (*sapratyayogika*), he raises the dilemma as to from what source there could be a further conceptualization of difference for that which is itself a conceptualized difference, asking "from what? He then analyzes the first alternative in two ways.
"If it were to corrupt the other," he says; having restated the second [alternative], he refutes it with "then.

The conceptualization of difference from the nature of this individual soul (jīva) would have to be from the very nature of the Supreme (para). He states the reason for this: "because the Supreme is devoid of imagined difference. He refutes the third [alternative] with "therefore, of the individual soul..."

"It is exactly so. This means that it must belong to the Supreme Self alone, because no unreal (kalpita) distinction is admitted between the supreme and the individual soul, and because non-difference is desired.
With the words "If [there were] a distinguished difference," etc., he states a fault common to all three positions. "Otherwise" means:
if the cessation of all distinctions is intended in order to give meaning to the scriptural text, "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself."

The meaning is that, in that case, every conceptualization of difference must be accepted as ignorance (*avidyā*) belonging to pure consciousness alone. He extends the aforementioned objection to other cases as well with the words "of that which is imagined by ignorance" (*avidyā-kalpitasya*); the meaning is that there would never be a complete cessation of ignorance in its entirety. || 16 ||

[Page 331] Anticipating the objection, "If knowledge arises for me during the waking state, how can it be called dream-knowledge?", he says: "The state of ignorance is the dream. Dream is a contrary cognition (*viparīta-pratyaya*);
sleep is the non-apprehension of reality (*tattvāgrahaṇa*). [The two states] joined with these are Viśva and Taijasa—this is the meaning. These are the abodes (*āvasathāḥ*).

[The word] *avasthāḥ* [is used]. Because its usage is seen in the *Gauḍapādīya-śruti* and elsewhere, the connection is as follows: "The state of ignorance (*avidyāvasthā*) is dream; it is either equal to that [waking state], or it is indeed that very [state of ignorance]. It should be understood that the word is divided in two ways based on the support of the Sūtra: *eva cāniyoga*. || 18 ||
Regarding the objection raised by one of our own school—that the liberation of one entails the liberation of all—he replies with the verse beginning "The cause of ignorance for all," and so forth.

"Because of the non-existence of many" means because there is no plurality of individual souls (jīvas) imagined by the ignorance of a single soul. That single ignorance which is the cause for the conceptualization of all souls is destroyed for all persons.

[The opponent argues: "Liberation occurs through the knowledge of Brahman; therefore, there is no simultaneous liberation for all. To this he replies with the words "by all cognitions" (*sarvabuddhibhiḥ*). [He continues: "If not even an atom of ignorance were destroyed by the knowledge of a single person, then your knowledge would be useless and the consequence of non-liberation would follow for you. To this he says: "In the case of the liberation of one," etc. Having restated the second position, he refutes it: "In that case, let it be for each..."

[Page 332] "In the absence of a conceptualizer (*kalpaka*), there would be the fault of multiple conceptualizations, but not when a conceptualizer exists"—thus he says, "Now then" (*nanu*). The proponent of the established view (*siddhāntin*) asks: "What is that conceptualizer? [Page 637] The conceptualizer.
— Page 334] The Sixth Chapter | 603

Having restated the established doctrine (*vyavasthā*), he refutes it by means of an alternative analysis (*vikalpya*) with the words "liberated or unliberated," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "even by one":

since all established doctrines are accomplished through the *vidyā* that is dependent upon the mind (*cittādhīnā*), a differentiation of *vidyā* based on an imagined locus (*kalpitāśraya*) need not be postulated. If it were to be postulated, he says in response: "Otherwise, even for a single [individual]," etc. He then states that this is not an undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭaprasaṅga*) with the words "Now, for a single... and so forth.
[The author] states the established position with the words "by those very [means]. An adherent of his own school says "only one" based on the support of experience.

Having raised the dilemma as to whether [these appearances] manifest by way of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) or are merely imagined (*kalpita*), he refutes it with the words "not, first of all," and so forth. [Page 333] "If not"—the destruction of the subsequent does not [occur] because of the prior destruction.

In that case, it would follow that liberation had never occurred previously in the beginningless cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*); such is the meaning. Anticipating an objection regarding the avoidance of infinite regress (*anavasthā*) through another method, he refutes it with the words "of the first," and so forth. || 19 ||

[In order to state] another reason for rejecting other types of ignorance based on an imagined locus, he says "furthermore" (*kiṃca*). First of all, by the word "you" (*tva*), there is no reference to your own schoolmate standing before you, because [in our view] ignorance with a limited locus is not admitted. Rather, [it refers to...]

Through activities such as speaking and so forth, pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) alone is indicated as their cause; it is precisely through that [pure consciousness] that all worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) occurs, and not through various ignorances (*avidyā*) having imagined substrates—this is the secret. Furthermore, "where one sees nothing else, hears nothing else, and understands nothing else, that is the Infinite (*bhūman*)"—thus is the Brahman characterized as the Infinite attained.

He says, "And not another's delusion," because even by the principle of *anyathānupapatti* (the impossibility otherwise), you must accept that everything appears to you as being born solely from your own delusion. He raises the objection of possibility otherwise with the words, "of one who is deluded.
He replies, "not in a dream," stating that it is impossible to say that for one who is deluded, another's delusion and so forth appear.

Fearing that the teacher (*guru*) might also be subject to delusion (*moha*), he says: "And the teacher is not possessed of ignorance. The meaning is that it is well known that only one who possesses knowledge (*vidvas*) can be a teacher. Fearing that the knowledge belonging to him might not be sufficient to dispel all delusion, he says: "And [it is not so]. Since the state of being bodiless (*videha-sthiti*) would otherwise be untenable, it must be admitted that even the teacher has at least a trace of ignorance (*avidyā-gandha*).
Anticipating this objection, he says, "The body of the knower" (*vidvad-deha*). The opponent, who possesses verbal knowledge (*śābdajñānin*), doubts that the Guru can be deluded;

[the author] replies that it is impossible for one who possesses direct realization (*sākṣātkṛtimān*) to be deluded. He states, "Even direct realization," etc. [He continues with] "Otherwise": if direct realization were the remover of delusion, then even verbal knowledge would dispel delusion, since it is also a form of Brahman-knowledge (*brahmavidyā*).

It is like direct realization (*sākṣātkṛti*). In that case, another direct realization would be useless; this is the meaning. To address the question, "What then is this [other] proof?", he says: "If it were verbal" (*śābda*); having raised the doubt that what is called direct realization is simply the manifestation of the nature of the Self (*ātmasvarūpa*), he asks: "What is the proof for that [realization] being the remover of delusion in the case of verbal knowledge? (*śābdajñāna*)—thus he speaks.
"The nature of the self is the Veda.
The *Iṣṭasiddhivivaraṇa* [Page 334] says: "If not," etc. If verbal knowledge (*śābdavidyā*) does not become the dispeller of delusion, then it is useless.

It may be so. The meaning is that the capacity to remove delusion is established through the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the realization of the meaning of the scripture. He raises the objection that it might be possible otherwise, with the words "not useless," etc. Anticipating the question, "If the verbal [knowledge] does not remove the delusion, then what is it that removes the delusion?", he says: "And that [practice] would remove the delusion. It is indeed the practice of knowledge (*vidyā*).

The meaning is that it is the remover of that [ignorance] because it is opposed to error (*bhrama*). Now, one might object: "If it is intended that verbal knowledge (*śābdavidyā*) removes non-apprehension (*agraha*), then its removal of error is already established, since error is rooted in non-apprehension. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Error does not arise from non-apprehension. If non-apprehension is not the cause of error—because it is a non-entity (*abhāva*), like a hare's horn—then from what does it arise?

He says "but what" (*kiṃtu*) to address the notion that this is an error. Regarding the claim that there is no other direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*), he says "of those two. He states "not so" (*tan na*) to show that it cannot be said that even one who has not perceived reality (*adṛṣṭatattva*) can be a teacher.
Regarding the argument that because non-apprehension (*agraha*) is a mere absence, its status as a cause is untenable, he says "and non-apprehension" (*agrahaś ca*).

The meaning is that since non-existence has already been refuted, and because causality has been established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). Regarding what was stated—that "the impressions (*saṃskāra*) [are the cause]"—he says: "and the effect is not the cause.
Regarding what was asserted—that "the practice of knowledge (*vidyā-abhyāsa*) is the remover of ignorance (*avidyā*)"—he says: "knowledge alone [is the remover]," and nothing else.

The meaning is "the act of practice. Now, one might object: through the cultivation of defects such as impermanence, the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of permanence and so forth regarding the body and other things is removed. Therefore, how can it be said that there is no cessation of ignorance (*avidyā*) through practice? To this, he replies: "to be dispelled by knowledge" (*vidyāpanodyā*).

[Page 335] Let it be granted that ignorance (avidyā) is indeed to be dispelled by knowledge (vidyā); nevertheless, one might suspect that knowledge consists merely in repeated practice (abhyāsa). Anticipating this, he says "And that" (sā ca). Having conceded that the practice of knowledge is something to be performed, its status as true knowledge has been refuted. Now, due to the absence of any means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), even its status as something to be performed is untenable.

He says "no" and adds "nor by the practice of knowledge. Anticipating the objection that "surely when there is the practice of knowledge the fruit of knowledge is attained, and in its absence it is not attained; thus, positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) alone are the proof," he says "nor. The fruit characterized by the direct realization of the object of knowledge is caused solely by the arising of knowledge; it does not depend upon practice.

The meaning is that the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is unestablished, because the cognition of a jar and the like is seen to be fruitful even without repeated practice. Anticipating the objection that scriptural passages such as "one should meditate upon" (*nididhyāsitavya*) enjoin the practice of knowledge (*vidyā*), he says:

"The other is for the sake of knowledge. [This refers to the fact that] once knowledge has arisen and the delusion of agency and so forth has ceased, there is no longer any qualification (*adhikāra*) for knowledge—

Because there is no possibility of [the knowledge] being produced through repetition, there is no injunction for practice; rather, there is the means consisting of hearing and so forth for the purpose of accomplishing the arising of knowledge.
The Sixth Chapter | 0.00 605

The meaning is that it is enjoined as something to be practiced repeatedly. Then, raising the objection, "In that case, how is it established that [the Self] alone is the cause of all errors and so forth, which are beginningless, indeterminable, and rooted in non-apprehension (agraha)? he says, "And of everything. Raising the further objection, "Why is it that no other cause for birth and so forth is possible? he says, "Because there is nothing else apart from the Self."

Now, raising the objection that if non-apprehension (*agraha*) were the cause of the delusion of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), then because it would be removed all at once by the arising of knowledge (*vidyā*), liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*) would not be possible, he says: "And because of liberation while living. Now, he states that for one's own school (*svayūthya*), liberation while living is likewise not tenable: "And in your view," and so on. Then: "Consequently... [The wise man, due to residual impressions (*saṃskāra*), does not persist in new delusions... *moha*.

The meaning is that one should not perceive a disciple as possessing suffering and so forth. "Otherwise" means that if a new delusion were produced from the residual impression (saṃskāra), it would follow that liberation is impossible. He concludes the subject at hand with the words "therefore, not delusion. The word division is "ayuktam iti. || 21 ||

[Page 336] Having thus elaborated upon the defect that for one who is not deluded, another delusion and so forth do not appear, he now elaborates upon the point that they do appear to one who is deluded, beginning with the words "And how, even though existing... How can your delusion, even while existing, be the cause for the appearance of another delusion and so forth? Is it by producing its own essential nature (*svarūpa*)?
Or [it might be argued] by means of producing mere cognition. He refutes the first [position] with the words "if that [cognition] were imagined by another," and so forth.
Anticipating the objection that since it is imagined by another's delusion, it may also be produced by another's delusion, he says, "and because it is already established.
That which is imagined by your delusion cannot possibly be imagined by another's delusion simply because it is already established as an imagination. Otherwise, [the following would occur]:

The meaning is that there would have to be a process of conceptualization again and again. Furthermore, that other delusion which is imagined by your own delusion cannot, by its own independence, produce another conceptualization, just like the snake [imagined] on a rope. Therefore, since everything is imagined by your delusion, no other delusion or the like appears to you, the deluded one; this is the meaning. He refutes the second position with the words "And not by your delusion."

For it is well known that a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is that which establishes an object of cognition (*prameya*). The meaning is that because delusion (*moha*) lacks the status of a means of valid cognition, its capacity to make [an object] known is impossible. Furthermore, he states "and it is said to be an object of cognition" (*prameyaś coktaḥ*), because even for another delusion and so forth, the status of being an object of cognition is impossible, as that would entail the consequence of being sublated by a means of valid cognition. Even in the absence of being graspable by a means of valid cognition, there is still graspability by another delusion.

Fearing this objection, he says: "If that delusion were an object of delusion... [meaning: if it were an object of another delusion]. He states, "No, because of equality," meaning that just as one lamp cannot be the object of another lamp, so too it is impossible for one delusion to be the object of another delusion.
Furthermore, the fact that the effect of my delusion belongs to me does not arise merely from its being an effect of delusion; rather, it is because it is the delusion of *me*...

Anticipating the objection that it is "by way of being an effect," he says: "For this very reason. Even that which you consider to be the effect of another's delusion is, in fact, the effect of your own delusion.
The Commentary on the *iṣṭasiddhi*.
[Page 336] The meaning is: because it is an effect of delusion (*moha*), like that which is admitted to be an effect of delusion. For this reason as well, everything is an effect of delusion—
Thus he says: "Nor [is it] born from the delusion of another. Furthermore, for this reason as well, the inference of a cause from an effect does not hold in reality;

thus he says: "Nor [does it arise] from the manifestation of the cause. Just as the cognition of a jar or the like—which is of the nature of clay—is not possible when the clay is not manifest, so too [it is not possible] when the material cause is not manifest.

That effect does not manifest. It was stated that [the difference] cannot exist because it is non-different from itself. To this, the opponent objects: "How can there be difference?

[The author] replies with "from itself," meaning that difference is not possible because it would entail the consequence of the absence of its own nature. The proponent, employing the method of a counter-argument, asks: "What else [could it be]? If there were non-difference even from something other than the self—such as a disciple—[then the same problem would follow].

The meaning is that, in that case, there would be no "other. This is what is being said: just as you accept that even a contradictory property—namely, non-difference from what is different—is possible, so too would there be difference from itself. Therefore, the state of being both different and non-different is indistinguishable for both teacher and disciple. || 49 ||
Furthermore, he says "moreover" (*kiñca*) because it cannot be said that there is no difference between the disciple and this very Guru.
If the disciple were non-different from the Guru, yet [on the other hand] different from him, then it would follow that the Guru himself is different from the Guru.

This is explained by the second half of the verse: since there is no difference between the disciple and the teacher who is non-different from [the Absolute], there is no distinction of the teacher from the [Absolute] Teacher; thus, the meaning is that the teacher is illusory. || 42 ||
Now, raising the specific doubt that even though the disciple is non-different from the guru, he does not become the very self of the guru, [the author] says:

"The self is not of the guru. If it were the case that although non-different, the disciple does not become the self of the guru, then it would simply mean that the guru himself is not the self of the guru. And this being so, there would be difference by its own nature.
The meaning is that the sun is desired by the Guru. || 43 ||

He states another fault resulting from the application of non-difference with the words "dṛṣṭa" (seen). He clarifies the worldly statement regarding the impossibility of the established distinction—that the teacher is learned while the disciple is unlearned—even under the view of both difference and non-difference, by means of the passage beginning with "In the view of difference and non-difference," etc. || 44 || 45 ||
[Page 650] 61 6 Commentary on the *iṣṭasiddhi* (The Proof of What is Desired).

How so? Having raised the objection that if the distinction between teacher and disciple were untenable, then by the logic already stated, a lack of order would result in all matters such as liberation and the like, he says: "Therefore, due to the bondage of the person... (46).

The proponent of Pradhāna says: "Even though the position of Māyā has been refuted by the refutation of the distinction between Puruṣas, another fault is being stated. He first recalls the very same fault mentioned in the first chapter, beginning with the words "of the insentient" (*jaḍasya*). The phrase "otherwise" (*anyathā*) refers to independence characterized by the lack of dependence on [anything else] for existence and cognition.

The meaning is that if [the Pradhāna] were sentient, it would—just like the Self—possess the nature of being a seer, be devoid of the qualities such as *sattva*, and possess selfhood; thus, the consequence of its insentience (*jaḍatva*) would be lost. Furthermore, if independence were granted, he states another undesirable consequence: "the relation of cause and effect.
Now, you might object: "Is it not the case that what you call *Pradhāna*—designated by terms such as *Māyā*—is that in which the world dissolves at the time of dissolution?"

Anticipating the doubt as to how [the self] is nourished or how it is divided, he says, "What need for much? With the intention of the *Sāṅkhya* school that accepts a Lord (*seśvara-sāṅkhya*), he says, "Even in the case of independence, it is likewise. This is simply unestablished because there is a lack of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). The meaning is: even if it were true, it remains unestablished because it is based on mere experience. Even though it is not established by reasoning (*yukti*), it will nonetheless be established by scripture (*śruti*).

Anticipating this objection, he says: "Nor is it that which possesses the Veda," meaning that they speak [of it], yet they uproot it from their speech; such is the construction. Having summarized what was stated, he connects the verse with the words beginning "Therefore, that which is called Pradhāna," etc. A single Pradhāna is bound by ignorance and liberated by knowledge.

The meaning is this: since the defects stated against the doctrine of absolute monism (aikātmyavāda)—such as the consequence that "if one is liberated, the entire world is liberated"—find no room in the Sāṅkhya system, it would follow that there is no lack of systematic order in the monistic view, but rather that such disorder would exist only in the Sāṅkhya view.

Now, [the opponent might argue] that there is a systematic order in that very Pradhāna is one, while its products, such as the internal organs (antaḥkaraṇa) and so forth, are diverse; to this, he replies:

"In some way" (*kathaṃcit*) means that the defects previously mentioned regarding the positions of difference and non-difference—such as the confusion of the causes of cognition and so forth—would result in a lack of systematic order (*avyavasthā*). By the word "by this" (*etena*), he extends [the critique] to other cases as well by way of analogy. He raises an objection regarding the distinction from the Sāṅkhya position with the words "of Brahman," and having acknowledged its difference from the Sāṅkhya view, [he addresses] the defect stated in the sixth chapter.

It has been stated that because [these qualities] are adventitious, they are false—like the redness of a crystal—and thus there is no distinction [between them and the Pradhāna]. To this he says, "And how? In reality, how can Brahman, whose nature is space and so forth, possess consciousness?
Not in any way. Therefore, the meaning is that it is not distinct from the Pradhāna. This was incidental.

Having abandoned the subject at hand, [the opponent] follows the argument "if it belongs to the Pradhāna alone"; anticipating this objection regarding its meaningfulness, [the author] refutes it with the words "it is not useless. || 47 ||
The Seventh Chapter.
Now, he states that it is likewise impossible to establish that the *pradhāna* exists for the sake of the *puruṣa*.
Regarding the phrase "kiṃca": the word-division is "muktitaḥ" and "amuktitaḥ. || 48 ||
Regarding the point that "there might be a desire for it from another source," he states the fault in the verse: "Not from anything else either" (49).

The doubt arises as to whether the person (*puruṣa*) is an object (*artha*) or not. Having rejected the first alternative, he refutes the latter with the words "If it were a non-object (*anartha*), then... and so forth. || 5.11 ||

Fearing the aforementioned defects, he anticipates a specific qualification and refutes it with the words beginning "pratijñām" [Page 361]. He states the specific qualification by way of a counter-objection (prativandin) with the words beginning "kathaṃ ca. Anticipating the objection that the mind's state of being born is merely metaphorical, he refutes it with the words beginning "cittaṃ ca. [Regarding] manifestation—

If it is argued that a beginningless connection with the manifest [mind] is not tenable because [the mind] has been destroyed, then one might suspect that the connection with the unmanifest [mind] is beginningless;

anticipating this, he says, "nor with the unmanifest. The point is that for that which is unmanifest, there is no status even as the referent of the term *citta*. The beginninglessness of the connection with the unmanifest mind is stated for the sake of a bold argument (*prauḍhavāda*).
He says "even if there were no beginning" while not accepting [that position]. || 51 ||
Furthermore, he states that the postulation of the beginninglessness of the restrictive rule (*niyama*) is merely a blind tradition: "Moreover... (52).
And he says that for the Sāṃkhya, the established order of the messenger is not proven, stating "the bound and the unbound" [Page 362].
He further elaborates on the consequence of there being no distinction between the activities aimed at bondage and liberation, beginning with the words "of bondage and liberation," etc. (Verse 53).

Now he says that even the primary activity of *pradhāna* is not tenable, stating: "bondage and liberation. How could *pradhāna*, which is ignorant of the distinction between "this is bondage" and "this is liberation," exert itself for the sake of that [soul]? The meaning is: it cannot do so at all. Furthermore, he states that such activity would be purposeless: "not of the non-existent and the existent" (verse 54).

Anticipating the objection that activity is purposeful because it aims at manifestation, he says: "If [it were so] by that... Furthermore, fearing the objection that bondage and liberation would never exist because of the constant presence of non-manifestation and manifestation respectively, he says: "...nor by the latter two. (55)

When the question "How so? arises, it must be stated therein: are the manifestation and non-manifestation of liberation simply the manifestation and non-manifestation of bondage, or are they something else? Regarding the first alternative, he says: "The manifestation and its opposite are [the states of] bondage. This refers to deep sleep and so forth. [Page 652]
610 Commentary on the *iṣṭasiddhi* | [Page 362–]

There would be liberation; and because of the word "and" (ca), right knowledge would be rendered useless. The reason for this is: "due to the non-manifestation of bondage and the non-manifestation of delusion. || 56 ||

Having restated the second [position], he refutes it with the words "If [it were] by means of the manifestation of bondage or otherwise. The meaning is: that specific means which manifests liberation (*muktivyañjaka*) does not remove bondage, because there is no contradiction [between them]. || 57 ||
He states the fault in the opposing view with the words "bestowing liberation" (muktida). || 58 ||
[the author] raises an objection regarding the authority for the restriction, [saying] "otherwise...
Previously, having praised both the manifest and the unmanifest, a fault was shown; now he says, "If [the cause were] both manifest and other," meaning that even those two cannot be defined. || 60 ||

Furthermore, even upon a critical examination of the Sāṃkhya doctrine, the reality arrives at being immutable and non-dual; for in that case, no unreal distinction can possibly exist. Thus he says, beginning with "And not of the non-existent," etc.
(Verse 11).

Thus ends the seventh chapter in the *Iṣṭasiddhivivaraṇa*.
[Page 653] Now begins the eighth chapter.
[Page 364] Thus far, by resorting to a framework dependent upon ignorance (*avidyā*), those [distinctions] have been established.

Having set aside the [previous] position, he now addresses and refutes the objection regarding duality by means of the cessation of knowledge, beginning with the words "Of the proponents of Māyā" (māyāvādinaḥ). He says, "Is that very same [ignorance]? (kiṃ tadeva), meaning: if it is so, then because of the pervasion (vyāpti) that a false effect has ignorance as its material cause (upādāna), ignorance must be stated to be the material cause of destruction. || 1 ||
...he offers a rebuttal by adopting the fifth alternative mentioned in the *Siddhāntaloka*, beginning with the words "It is said" (*ucyate*).
Just as the existence of such ignorance is ultimately inexpressible in every respect, so too its non-existence is [inexpressible] in reality.

The meaning is that by saying "it cannot withstand definition," there is no contradiction with non-duality (*advaita*). He begins the critique of the very fault [of dualism] with the words "We ask you," and so forth. "It existed as itself" is an example based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*).
[Page 365] As for that which exists as distinct from the Self, is it insentient (*jaḍa*) or sentient (*ajaḍa*)? Regarding the first [option], he says:

Regarding the phrase "of the insentient" (*jaḍasya*): because it is insentient, its establishment does not occur through itself, nor from another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), since no relation [between them] can be determined. Nor is it established as an object of knowledge for the non-insentient witness (*sākṣin*), because the latter, being the establisher of what is superimposed upon itself, lacks the capacity to establish that [insentient thing] which exists independently. This is the meaning. He addresses the second [alternative] with the words "and of the non-insentient" (*ajaḍasya ca*). Furthermore:
He refutes [the opponent's view] by means of the passage beginning with "kutaśca" (and from what?), having raised the dilemma as to whether a distinct entity arises from the Self or from ignorance.

Furthermore, even upon examining the nature of that which is being born, he states in the passage beginning with "na ca sataḥ" (nor from the existent) that there is no birth of a distinct entity. By process of elimination, it follows that ignorance alone is its destruction.

He says it cannot be said that "that very thing is ignorance," nor that there is another ignorance related either to the Self or to the non-Self. Regarding the first [possibility], he says "that too": the meaning is that knowledge and ignorance are contradictory when they possess the same locus and the same object. Regarding the second, he says "nor": [ignorance] related to the non-Self.

The meaning is that this has already been refuted. Thus, when the dualists have been refuted, the partisan of a particular school (ekadeśin) states, "If [it were] of the Self," implying that by process of elimination, it is the destruction of ignorance regarding the Self. However, the two established conclusions (siddhāntau) are not in contradiction with Advaita.
Commentary on the *iṣṭasiddhi* | [Page 365]

Thinking that "just as the cessation of ignorance (*vidyānivṛtti*) is desired by the proponent of a partial view (*ekadeśin*), so too is it desired by me," he grants permission, saying, "Let it be so. It was stated that non-duality (*advaita*) would be lost due to the existence of something else;
regarding that, he asks the proponent of the partial view, "What is that non-duality? He says, "Otherwise... [referring to] the Self (*ātman*).

The meaning is that if "the state of being devoid of duality" were some kind of entity (*vastu*), then bondage could never cease, because it would always coexist with its opposite. The partisan (*ekadeśin*) states his own view regarding the meaning of the term "non-duality": "burnt by knowledge," etc. The proponent (*siddhāntin*) replies: "If even that burning is the Self itself... The aforementioned fault follows: [bondage] would exist eternally. [The opponent says: "The Self..."

The meaning is that even for the *ekadeśin* (the proponent of a partial view), the contradiction with non-duality (*advaita*) is equal if [the world] were distinct. The *ekadeśin* clarifies his own intention, stating "because of the consequence of the aforementioned defects. ... Then he raises the objection of another *ekadeśin* with the words "But [it is] like the Self," etc. He asks: by defining [ignorance] as having a beginning or being beginningless, is it not the case that the burning away of ignorance simply does not exist?

Or [the intended meaning] is that it arises from another entity. Regarding the first [alternative], he says: "Do not speak thus. Regarding the second, he says: "And all... The meaning is that it is not possible for that which is being born to be a different entity, because—like the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell—it is non-substantial (*avastu*) since it is born of ignorance (*ajñāna*). For this very reason: since only that which possesses birth is born of ignorance...

The meaning is that the burning [of ignorance] does not arise from knowledge alone, because [knowledge alone] lacks the quality of being born. Anticipating the question, "From what, then, does that burning arise?", he says, "And [it arises] from that which is born of scripture. He states, "And this has been established by me," in order to show that it should not be said that the cognition of the Self born of practice alone is the remover of ignorance. He concludes what has been stated with the words, "from scripture, ignorance..."

Regarding the word "burning": [Page 367] Having restated what was said by the opponent, he grants partial assent with the words "As for what was said," and so forth. He states that "there is no burning of ignorance arising for anyone" because there is an absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Now, even upon examining the nature of the means of valid cognition, it follows that the burning of ignorance does not arise for anyone.

He says "it exists" and so forth, beginning with "and not the remover of ignorance. It is well known that consciousness (*saṃvit*) existing [as an effect] is produced by a means of knowledge (*māna*). To the question, "How can that which exists not be produced by a means of knowledge?", he replies: "And of consciousness... He also abandons the previously granted concession regarding the parts; for how [could it be otherwise]? Only if destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) were of the nature of a further birth would it possess causality.
It might be asked: how can it be said that [the effect arises] "merely upon the disappearance of the prior form"? The meaning is that this is indeed without logical justification (*niryuktika*).

The proponent of the previous view offers a reason, stating: "Because there is no causal function (*hetukṛtya*) in the case of non-existence. He refutes this by means of a counter-question (*pratibandigraha*):
"When the activity of the potter and so forth occurs in relation to clay and other materials, the effect such as a jar is produced."
But it does not exist when [the object] is absent. And that is the function of the cause; thus he says, "Now, in another case... Then, [it would apply] only to a jar and so forth.
[Page 655]—[Page 369]
Chapter Eight.
In the case of the operation of the pestle and so forth, there would also be destruction (upamarda). Therefore, causality exists for both existence and non-existence.

The meaning is that [the point] remains [unanswered]. Anticipating the objection that the application [of the argument] is untenable, he refutes it with the words "that non-existence" (*so 'bhāvaḥ*) and so forth.

Again, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvavādī*) raises another argument with the words "of existence" (*bhāvasya*). He suggests that since there is no contact between an existence belonging to a prior time and a non-existence belonging to a subsequent time, a contradiction is impossible; thus, even when non-existence has arisen...

[Otherwise] there would be the consequence [of the non-existence] of the entity. Therefore, the meaning is that because the conventional usage of the destruction of an entity cannot otherwise be established, destruction is simply the birth of another, opposing entity. First, he refutes the claim that there is no opposition between an entity and its absence with the words, "even though it was previously non-existent. That which was stated regarding the opposition of another entity...

He now refutes what was stated regarding the opposition between one state of being and another, beginning with the words "If by a state of being" (*bhāvena cet*) and so forth. Regarding the phrase "of that too" (*tasyāpi*): if the arising of destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*) is admitted, then, because it is something that is arising, another destruction of it must be asserted; and since that too is something that is arising—

The meaning is that there is no rest anywhere else [than in Brahman]. Anticipating the objection—“Even in the absence of birth, how can there be causality and occasional occurrence?”—he says: “even without birth. Now, one might argue: since the destruction of a jar and so forth cannot possess birth in the manner described above, let it be that the destruction of ignorance (*ajñāna*) is also not a thing possessing birth; nevertheless, something else...

There would be coexistence with destruction because of its nature as a cessation (*dhvaṃsa*). Whatever is a cessation is such, just as the cessation of a jar or similar object coexists with the shards and so forth; and birth and cessation are not different [from this]. He concludes what was stated previously with the words "therefore, of these" (*tasmād eṣām*). Thus, if the burning away of ignorance is established through inference as a real entity—

If its status as being born at another time is refuted, then state its certain nature and its proof; otherwise, the subject would have a doubtful predicate and the reason would be fallacious, namely, "unestablished in its locus" (*āśrayāsiddha*). Having set forth the opponent's intended position, he refutes it with the words "If that [subject] were the Self," and so forth. [Page 369]

He provides the answer according to the opponent's own intention, saying "It is said. He states that if the status of being a locus (*āśrayatva*) is possible through mere conventional acceptance, then the search for a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is fruitless, saying "And not... He further says "Nor... because the establishment by a means of valid cognition is not even conceivable.
If the cessation of ignorance were established by a means of valid cognition, then another cessation of ignorance would have to be stated in relation to that [cessation]. Of that...

Even if [the cognition] were valid, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), and thus the cessation of ignorance (*ajñānanivṛtti*) would not be established in practice; this is because it is impossible [for that cessation to occur] as long as the cessation of ignorance regarding the object of that cessation is not itself manifested—this is the meaning. Now, is the known object different from the unknown, or non-different? In the first case, even when knowledge arises, the object remains in the state of being unknown.
Lest it be suspected that [the object] would have been known even prior to the cognition at the final moment, he says: "And it is not known," etc.
Commentary on the *iṣṭasiddhi* | [Page 369]
That very object which was unknown due to its connection with ignorance is said to be "known" when it is characterized by knowledge.

Having thus stated the refutation according to the opponent's own intention, [the author] now says, beginning with "And neither being known nor being unknown," in order to clarify his own secret doctrine— that the cessation of ignorance is indefinable— and to demonstrate that the investigation of whether "being known" is the very nature of the object or something distinct from it cannot be sustained. This is the demonstration of the indefinability of "being known."

This should be regarded as incidental. Having stated that it is impossible for each [of the two] to be the nature of a real entity (*vastu*), he states the common refutation for both cases: "And a non-established entity... Anticipating the objection, "Since the self has the nature of cognition (*jñapti*), its state of being known is its very own nature; therefore, how can there be deviation (*vyabhicāritva*)?", he says "cognition" (*jñapti*).

"Of the essential nature as well" means that, by the logic already stated—that is, by the logic of the futility of a means of knowledge (*māna*) and so forth—the state of being known (*jñātatva*) is not the essential nature of the object. It has been stated that an object can only be a "measurable" (*meyam*) through its aspects of being known or unknown.
When the question arises, "What is the fault in that case? he states the fault in its being a measurable object in its unknown aspect with the words "And not... (*na ca*).
Since that which is unknown is a qualifier of the object of knowledge (*meyaviśe�ṣaṇa*), ignorance itself has been rendered an object of knowledge (*meyatva*).

And that is not possible. The reason for this is stated as "due to the absence of another ignorance. He states the fault in accepting another ignorance with the words "because of its existence" (*tadbhāvāt*). Furthermore, he says that being an object of knowledge in the form of something unknown is not tenable.

"And [this applies] even in the case of the non-removal of ignorance. Having thus elaborated that knowability (*meyatva*) is not possible in the form of being unknown, he now states "and not" (*na ca*) to show that knowability is also not possible in the form of being already known. The meaning is that when an object has been cognized, there is no further excellence (*atiśaya*) produced by another means of knowledge (*māna*). He states the fault in assuming a further state of being cognized (*mitatva*):

"Otherwise," he says; "of that," he states another defect. ... [Pages 370–371] Having thus stated that "knownness" and "unknownness" are indefinable—both as being the very nature of the object and as being distinct from it—he explains the category of "knownness" and so forth according to his own system with the words beginning "there, unknown... [Page 372]. Now, an objection:

Since the "knownness" (jñātatā) arising from a means of knowledge is non-eternal, it would follow that the cessation of ignorance is also non-eternal; consequently, there might be a recurrence of ignorance. Anticipating this objection, he says: "And ignorance is beginningless. Precisely because no further emergence of ignorance is observed, it is established that knownness belongs to the present time. In that regard, [the cognition] colored by the means of knowledge...

Even though [the world] is eternal in its form (*rūpa*), since the state of being known (*jñātatā*) is eternal in its own nature (*svarūpa*), it should be understood that the consequence of the cessation of ignorance (*avidyānivṛtti*) being non-eternal does not follow; furthermore, because the cessation is illusory (*mithyātva*), the fact that its eternity and so forth cannot be defined is indeed an ornament. It has been stated previously that [ignorance] does not arise again due to the absence of a cause; now, it will be shown that it is also impossible for ignorance to possess the property of being born (*janidharman*).

He explains the absence of an illustrative example with the words "all delusion. Your position is that every cognition of a non-self is a delusion arising from the delusion regarding the self; therefore, through right knowledge, ignorance— [Page 377] ...is destroyed. Thus, since there is no other cognition than this, there is no example for it. Furthermore, even if one were to accept an external object, the illustration would not hold, because the cognition of a non-self is established as being produced by the delusion regarding the self. Moreover, the cognition of a non-self does not have the nature of a delusion, because it is not sublated by another cognition. For instance, the cognition of a snake in what is actually a rope is a delusion because it is subsequently sublated by the cognition of the rope; however, the cognition of a non-self is never sublated by the cognition of a self. Therefore, it is not a delusion. Consequently, the statement that "the cognition of a non-self is a delusion" is not established. Furthermore, the claim that "the cognition of a non-self is a delusion because it arises from the delusion regarding the self" is also untenable, because the relationship between cause and effect is unestablished. This is because the cognition of a non-self is not invariably preceded by the delusion regarding the self. For example, the cognition of a pot is not invariably preceded by the delusion regarding a cloth. Nor can it be argued that the cognition of a non-self is invariably preceded by the delusion regarding the self because they are co-present, like the cognition of a pot and the cognition of its color. At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the venerable Śāriputra: “Śāriputra, suppose there were a man who had been blind from birth and had never seen the sun, the moon, the stars, or the various colors and forms. Then, a skilled physician, wishing to restore his sight, would apply medicinal ointments and perform treatments, thereby enabling him to see the sun, the moon, the stars, and all manner of colors and forms. What do you think, Śāriputra? Would that man, having gained sight, think: ‘I was previously blind and could not see anything; now, through this physician’s skillful treatment, I have obtained my sight’? Śāriputra replied: “World-Honored One, it is as you say. The Buddha said: “Śāriputra, the Tathāgata is likewise. He is the Great Physician King who, out of great compassion, observes sentient beings wandering in the long night of ignorance, their minds clouded by the darkness of afflictions, unable to perceive the Four Noble Truths. Therefore, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, manifests in the world and, with great compassion, teaches the Dharma to sentient beings, enabling them to see the Four Noble Truths. Śāriputra, when sentient beings hear the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma, they give rise to the thought: ‘We were formerly ignorant and did not understand the Four Noble Truths; now, through the Tathāgata’s skillful means, we have come to know them. The Buddha then spoke a verse: “Just as a physician treats the eyes of one born blind, so does the Buddha, the Great Physician, teach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.
